chapters.title: Atmosphere
topics: Greenhouse Gases and the Greenhouse Effect

samples.prompt: By volume, dry air in the lower atmosphere consists mainly of:
options: About 78% nitrogen, 21% carbon dioxide and 1% oxygen
About 50% nitrogen, 30% oxygen and 20% water vapour
About 78% oxygen, 21% nitrogen and just under 1% argon, with carbon dioxide a small trace
About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and just under 1% argon, with carbon dioxide a small trace
samples.explanation: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.9% argon, with carbon dioxide around 0.04% and other trace gases. These proportions stay almost constant up to about 80 km because the air is well mixed. Water vapour is added on top of this, from almost nothing to about 4%, and it is the gas that matters most for weather.
whyWrong: Carbon dioxide is a trace gas of roughly 0.04%; oxygen is about 21%.
Water vapour is variable and is never more than about 4% by volume; it is also excluded from 'dry air'.
Swaps the two main gases: nitrogen, not oxygen, is the largest part.
samples.examTip: If an option makes water vapour or CO₂ a major constituent, reject it.

samples.prompt: Which set of values defines the ICAO Standard Atmosphere at mean sea level?
options: 0 °C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.293 kg/m³
15 °C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.000 kg/m³
15 °C, 1000.0 hPa and a density of 1.225 kg/m³
15 °C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.225 kg/m³
samples.explanation: ISA at mean sea level: temperature +15 °C (288.15 K), pressure 1013.25 hPa, density 1.225 kg/m³. The temperature then falls at 6.5 °C per km (1.98 °C per 1,000 ft) to −56.5 °C at 11 km (36,090 ft), stays constant to 20 km, and rises at 1 °C per km above that.
whyWrong: 0 °C and 1.293 kg/m³ are the old 'standard temperature and pressure' values used in chemistry, not ICAO ISA.
1.0 kg/m³ is a rounded guess; the ISA density at mean sea level is 1.225 kg/m³.
1000 hPa is a convenient round figure, but ISA MSL pressure is 1013.25 hPa.
samples.examTip: Learn the three MSL numbers as a set: 15, 1013.25, 1.225.

samples.prompt: Cumulonimbus tops over north India often stop rising and spread out once they reach the stratosphere. Which property of the stratosphere explains this?
options: It contains most of the atmosphere's water vapour, so cloud and precipitation are common
Temperature falls with height at about 2 °C per 1,000 ft, as in the troposphere
Its temperature is constant or rises with height (ozone heating), so it is very stable
It lies below the tropopause and contains about three-quarters of the mass of the atmosphere
samples.explanation: Above the tropopause the stratosphere is isothermal at first and then warms with height, because ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet radiation (the ozone layer is concentrated at about 20–30 km). This temperature structure makes the stratosphere very stable, so vertical motion and weather are rare. Cumulonimbus tops that reach it spread out to form an anvil.
whyWrong: Almost all the water vapour, and so almost all the weather, is in the troposphere.
A steady fall of about 2 °C per 1,000 ft describes the troposphere.
That describes the troposphere, which lies below the tropopause.
samples.examTip: An inversion caps convection: the tropopause/stratosphere acts as a lid on Cb tops.

samples.prompt: An aircraft climbs from Chennai (13°N) and a second aircraft climbs from a station at 70°N on the same day. Compared with the high-latitude station, the tropopause over Chennai is:
options: Lower, at roughly 8–9 km, and colder, often below −70 °C
Higher, at roughly 16–17 km, and colder, often below −70 °C
At the same height of 11 km, with the ISA value of −56.5 °C
Higher, at roughly 16–17 km, and warmer, about −45 °C
samples.explanation: Strong convection over the tropics lifts the tropopause to about 16–18 km, while over the poles it is only about 8–9 km. Because the temperature keeps falling all the way up, the high tropical tropopause is very cold, typically −70 to −80 °C, colder than the polar tropopause at about −45 to −55 °C. This is why the coldest temperatures on a long-haul flight are often met over the tropics.
whyWrong: Reverses the latitude effect: the tropopause is lowest over the poles and highest over the equator.
11 km and −56.5 °C are the ISA model values, a mid-latitude average, not the real tropical tropopause.
The tropical tropopause is higher, so the air has cooled for longer on the way up: it is colder, not warmer.
samples.examTip: Do not mix up the ISA tropopause (11 km, −56.5 °C) with the real tropical one.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about the tropopause: 1. It is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere. 2. It is usually higher in summer than in winter at the same place. 3. It is continuous from the equator to the poles at a single height. 4. Breaks in it are often found near jet streams. Which are correct?
options: 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
All four: 1, 2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4 only
samples.explanation: The tropopause separates the troposphere from the stratosphere. Warmer air columns are deeper, so it is higher in summer and higher over the tropics. It is not one continuous surface: there are steps (breaks) between the tropical and polar tropopauses, and the jet streams are found near these breaks.
whyWrong: Leaves out 1, which is the definition of the tropopause.
Leaves out 2 and 4, which are true, and keeps the false statement 3.
Includes 3: the tropopause is not one level, it slopes and breaks, especially near the polar front and the subtropical jet.
samples.examTip: Test statement 3 first: any 'single continuous height' claim about real air is false.

samples.prompt: The pressure that ATC passes for an aerodrome so that an altimeter set to it reads zero on the runway (at threshold level) is:
options: QFE
QFF
QNH
QNE
samples.explanation: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at aerodrome elevation (or runway threshold). With QFE set, the altimeter shows height above the aerodrome, so it reads zero on landing. QNH is that pressure reduced to MSL using the ISA, so the altimeter reads altitude (elevation on the ground).
whyWrong: QFF is a synoptic value reduced to MSL with the actual temperature, used on weather charts, not for altimeter setting.
With QNH set the altimeter reads the aerodrome elevation on the ground, not zero.
QNE is the reading (pressure altitude) on 1013.25 hPa, not a pressure setting.
samples.examTip: 'Reads zero on landing' always means QFE.

samples.prompt: An aerodrome has an elevation of 2,950 ft and QNH 1004 hPa. Taking 1 hPa = 30 ft, its pressure altitude is:
options: 270 ft
samples.explanation: Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 = 2,950 + (9 × 30) = 2,950 + 270 = 3,220 ft. With a QNH below 1013, the 1013 hPa datum lies below sea level, so the aerodrome is 'higher' on the pressure scale than its real elevation.
whyWrong: Gave the correction alone without adding it to the elevation.
Pressure altitude only equals elevation when QNH is 1013 hPa.
Applied the correction the wrong way: low QNH raises the pressure altitude.
samples.examTip: Low QNH: PA greater than elevation. High QNH: PA less than elevation.

samples.prompt: Near the equator the barometer at a station such as Thiruvananthapuram shows a regular twice-daily rise and fall with no weather system present. This is:
options: The semi-diurnal pressure variation, with maxima near 0400 and 1600 local time and minima near 1000 and 2200
The semi-diurnal pressure variation, with maxima near 1000 and 2200 local time and minima near 0400 and 1600
An instrument error that occurs only in high humidity
The passage of a western disturbance, which brings a pressure fall every 12 hours
samples.explanation: The atmosphere has a solar-driven 'tide' with two highs and two lows a day. In the tropics, where synoptic changes are small, it dominates the barograph: maxima about 1000 and 2200 local time, minima about 0400 and 1600, with an amplitude of about 2–3 hPa near the equator. A pressure change that breaks this regular pattern is a warning of a real disturbance, such as an approaching cyclone.
whyWrong: Reverses the times: the pressure peaks are mid-morning and late evening.
It is a real atmospheric tide, recorded by every accurate barometer in the tropics.
Western disturbances are synoptic systems lasting days and mainly affect north India in winter.
samples.examTip: In the tropics, a fall that the daily tide cannot explain is significant.

samples.prompt: An aircraft cruises at FL050 over the Deccan where the QNH is 1022 hPa. Taking 1 hPa = 30 ft and ignoring temperature, its altitude AMSL is:
samples.explanation: A flight level is read with 1013 hPa set. With QNH 1022 the 1013 hPa level is (1022 − 1013) × 30 = 270 ft above MSL. Altitude = 5,000 + 270 = 5,270 ft. In high pressure the aircraft is higher than the flight level suggests; in low pressure it is lower.
whyWrong: Applied the correction in the wrong direction: with high QNH the aircraft is above its flight level figure.
Doubled the correction of 270 ft.
A flight level is a pressure altitude, not an altitude, unless QNH is 1013.
samples.examTip: Check the direction with the rhyme before choosing.

samples.prompt: On a very hot afternoon at a Rajasthan aerodrome about 1,300 ft above sea level, the aerodrome QFE is converted to both QNH and QFF. Which statement is correct?
options: QNH will equal QFE, because the aerodrome is above sea level
QFF will be lower than QNH, because the warm air column used for QFF weighs less than the ISA column
QFF and QNH will be equal, because both are reduced to mean sea level
QFF will be higher than QNH, because the warm air column used for QFF weighs more than the ISA column
samples.explanation: QNH is reduced to MSL through an imaginary ISA column, while QFF is reduced using the actual temperature. When it is warmer than ISA, the actual column below the aerodrome is lighter, so less pressure is added: QFF < QNH. In colder-than-ISA conditions QFF > QNH. At a sea-level aerodrome all three (QFE, QNH, QFF) are equal.
whyWrong: QNH equals QFE only at a sea-level aerodrome.
They differ because QFF uses the actual temperature and QNH uses ISA.
Warm air is less dense, so the imaginary column below the aerodrome adds less pressure, not more.
samples.examTip: The difference only exists for elevated aerodromes; at sea level QFE = QNH = QFF.

chapters.title: Temperature
topics: Terrestrial Radiation and the Heat Budget

samples.prompt: An isothermal layer is one in which:
options: Temperature rises with height
Humidity is constant with height
Temperature does not change with height
Temperature falls with height at the DALR
samples.explanation: An isothermal layer has a lapse rate of zero: the temperature stays the same with height. Like an inversion, it is very stable, because any rising parcel cools and soon becomes colder than its surroundings. The lower stratosphere in ISA (−56.5 °C from 11 to 20 km) is the classic example.
whyWrong: A rise of temperature with height is an inversion.
'Iso-thermal' refers to temperature, not humidity.
A fall at 3 °C per 1,000 ft is a dry adiabatic profile.
samples.examTip: Both isothermal layers and inversions are absolutely stable.

samples.prompt: The lower atmosphere is warmed mainly by:
options: Long-wave radiation from the Earth's surface, which has absorbed the sun's short-wave energy
Long-wave radiation coming directly from the sun
Heat conducted downwards from the stratosphere
Direct absorption of short-wave solar radiation as it passes through the air
samples.explanation: Solar radiation is short-wave and passes through clear air with little absorption. The ground absorbs it, warms, and radiates long-wave (infrared) energy, which water vapour, carbon dioxide and cloud absorb well. So the troposphere is heated from below, which is why temperature normally falls with height.
whyWrong: The sun is very hot, so it radiates mainly short-wave energy, not long-wave.
The stratosphere is above the troposphere and heat is not conducted down to the surface layers.
The air is largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation; only a small fraction is absorbed on the way down.
samples.examTip: Hot body short wave, cool body long wave.

samples.prompt: The environmental lapse rate (ELR) is best described as:
options: The actual fall of temperature with height on the day, as measured by a radiosonde
The fixed rate of 1.98 °C per 1,000 ft defined for the ICAO Standard Atmosphere model
The rate at which the dew point of a rising parcel falls
The fixed rate of 3 °C per 1,000 ft at which a rising unsaturated parcel cools
samples.explanation: The ELR is the real vertical temperature profile of the air at a place and time, measured by a radiosonde or aircraft reports. It varies from day to day and can even be negative (an inversion). Comparing the ELR with the adiabatic lapse rates of a rising parcel tells us whether the air is stable or unstable.
whyWrong: That is the ISA lapse rate, a model average, not the real profile on the day.
The dew point of a rising parcel falls at about 0.5 °C per 1,000 ft; that is not the ELR.
That is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, which applies to a moving parcel, not to the surrounding air.
samples.examTip: 'Measured' or 'actual' points to the ELR; 'fixed' points to the DALR or ISA.

samples.prompt: Match the process to the example. Which pairing is correct?
options: Advection: moist sea air carried over the Konkan coast by the monsoon
Radiation: the warming of air that touches a hot tarmac surface
Convection: the horizontal transfer of heat by the wind
Conduction: the rising of heated bubbles of air over a sunny concrete runway
samples.explanation: Advection is horizontal movement of air and its properties (temperature, moisture). Convection is vertical transfer by rising and sinking air. Conduction is transfer by contact, important only in the thin layer touching the ground. Radiation needs no medium. Latent heat released in cloud is also a major heat source in the tropics.
whyWrong: Heating by contact with a hot surface is conduction.
Horizontal transfer by the wind is advection; convection is vertical transfer by rising air.
Rising bubbles of warm air are convection; conduction is heat transfer by contact.
samples.examTip: The word 'horizontal' or 'carried by the wind' means advection.

samples.prompt: On a clear, calm winter night at Delhi, the temperature at 500 ft above the ground becomes higher than at the surface. This is:
options: A radiation inversion, from the ground cooling at night and chilling the air touching it
A subsidence inversion, caused by air sinking and warming adiabatically in an anticyclone
A frontal inversion, caused by warm air overriding cold air at a warm front
A turbulence inversion, caused by strong winds mixing the lowest layer
samples.explanation: On clear nights the ground loses heat by long-wave radiation to space, and with little wind only the shallow layer in contact with it is cooled. The air a few hundred feet up stays warmer: a surface (radiation) inversion. It traps smoke and moisture and, over the Indo-Gangetic plain in December and January, is the setting for dense radiation fog.
whyWrong: Subsidence inversions form aloft, typically at several thousand feet, not in the lowest few hundred feet overnight.
There is no front in this scenario; a frontal inversion is found along a sloping frontal surface.
A turbulence inversion needs a strong wind, but the night is calm.
samples.examTip: Inversion at the surface overnight = radiation; inversion aloft in a high = subsidence.

samples.prompt: In low density conditions, which of the following is TRUE regarding aircraft performance?
options: Climb outs are faster
Take-off and landing speeds are lower
Longer runways are required for take-off and landing
Engine thrust increases
samples.explanation: In low density (hot, high or humid) conditions, engine and propeller thrust is reduced, the true airspeeds for take-off and landing are higher, climb-out is slower and longer runways are needed. Options A, B and D state the opposite of these effects.

samples.prompt: An aerodrome has a pressure altitude of 2,000 ft and the OAT is 41 °C. Using ISA 15 °C − 2 °C per 1,000 ft and 120 ft per °C, the density altitude is:
samples.explanation: ISA at 2,000 ft = 15 − 4 = 11 °C, so the deviation is 41 − 11 = +30 °C. Density altitude = 2,000 + 120 × 30 = 2,000 + 3,600 = 5,600 ft. The aircraft takes off and climbs as if from a 5,600 ft aerodrome: longer ground roll, lower climb rate.
whyWrong: Took the deviation from 15 °C (41 − 15 = 26 °C) instead of from the ISA value at 2,000 ft.
Applied the temperature correction with the wrong sign.
Used 2,000 ft + 1,560 ft, a correction of 60 ft per °C.
samples.examTip: Hot Indian summer afternoons add thousands of feet of density altitude: plan for it.

samples.prompt: Two air samples are at the same pressure and temperature, but one is very humid (monsoon air) and the other dry. The humid sample is:
options: More dense, because humid air is always colder
Less dense, because water vapour molecules are lighter than N₂ and O₂ molecules
Exactly as dense, because density depends only on the pressure and the temperature
More dense, because the water vapour adds weight to the air
samples.explanation: At a fixed pressure and temperature a given volume contains the same number of molecules. Water vapour molecules (mass 18) are lighter than nitrogen (28) and oxygen (32), so replacing some of them with vapour reduces the density. Hot, humid conditions therefore give the worst performance: high density altitude.
whyWrong: The samples are stated to be at the same temperature.
For moist air the gas constant changes with the vapour content, so density does change.
Water vapour (molecular mass 18) replaces heavier N₂ (28) and O₂ (32), so a given volume weighs less.
samples.examTip: 'Humid air is heavy' is the classic wrong instinct.

samples.prompt: A hot-weather departure: the aerodrome pressure altitude is 250 ft and the OAT is 19 °C. Using ISA 15 °C − 2 °C per 1,000 ft and 120 ft per °C of ISA deviation, what is the density altitude?
options: 790 ft
380 ft
730 ft
samples.explanation: Formula: DA = PA + 120 × (OAT − ISA), with ISA = 15 − 2 × (PA ÷ 1,000) °C. ISA at 250 ft = 15 − 2 × 0.25 = 14.5 °C. Deviation = 19 °C − (14.5 °C) = +4.5 °C. Density altitude = PA + 120 × deviation = 250 + 540 = 790 ft. Warmer than ISA means thinner air, so the aircraft performs as if it were higher.
whyWrong: Applied the temperature correction with the wrong sign: gives -290 ft.
Used 30 ft per °C, the pressure figure, instead of 120 ft per °C: gives 380 ft.
Took the deviation from 15 °C instead of from the ISA temperature at the aerodrome: gives 730 ft.
samples.examTip: The deviation is from the ISA temperature at the aerodrome's pressure altitude, not from 15 °C.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about air density: 1. Density decreases with height. 2. At a constant pressure, density decreases as temperature rises. 3. At a constant temperature, density increases as pressure rises. 4. A high density altitude improves take-off performance. Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
All four: 1, 2, 3 and 4
1 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
samples.explanation: From the gas law, ρ = P ÷ (R × T): density rises with pressure and falls with absolute temperature. Pressure falls rapidly with height, so density falls with height despite the falling temperature. A high density altitude means the air is thin: engines give less power, wings and propellers less lift and thrust, so performance is worse.
whyWrong: Includes 4: a high density altitude means thin air, which lengthens the take-off run and reduces climb.
Leaves out 2 and 3, the gas-law relationships, and includes the false 4.
Leaves out 1 and 3, and includes the false 4.
samples.examTip: Use the gas law to test each statement, then think performance.

chapters.title: Humidity
topics: Vapour Pressure (VP) and Saturation Vapour Pressure (SVP)
Saturation Vapour Pressure: Water vs. Ice

samples.prompt: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled:
options: Until it reaches 0 °C, at which point ice forms
At constant relative humidity to produce precipitation
By adiabatic expansion to reach its condensation level, whatever its moisture
At constant pressure and constant moisture content to become saturated
samples.explanation: The dew point is the temperature at which air, cooled at constant pressure without gaining or losing water vapour, becomes saturated. The smaller the gap between temperature and dew point (the spread), the closer the air is to saturation. A spread of 1–2 °C at dusk with a clear sky and light wind is a strong signal for fog by dawn.
whyWrong: Saturation can happen at any temperature; the frost point, not 0 °C, governs deposition of ice.
Relative humidity changes as air cools, so it cannot be held constant; precipitation also needs more than saturation.
Cooling by lifting changes the pressure; the dew point is defined at constant pressure.
samples.examTip: A small spread (T − Td) means high relative humidity.

samples.prompt: At a sea-level aerodrome the surface temperature is 12°C and the dew point is 8°C. What is the approximate base of cumulus cloud (above the surface)?
options: 800 ft
490 ft
samples.explanation: A rising parcel cools at about 3°C per 1 000 ft and its dew point at about 0.5°C per 1 000 ft, so the spread closes at 2.5°C per 1 000 ft (400 ft per °C). Spread = 12 − 8 = 4°C, so the base is 4 × 400 = 1,600 ft above the surface.
whyWrong: Used 3°C per 1 000 ft for the spread, ignoring the dew-point lapse
Used 200 ft per °C instead of 400
Gave metres labelled as feet
samples.examTip: Common trap: used 3°C per 1 000 ft for the spread, ignoring the dew-point lapse.

samples.prompt: At a sea-level aerodrome the surface temperature is 13°C and the dew point is 1°C. What is the approximate base of cumulus cloud (above the surface)?
samples.explanation: A rising parcel cools at about 3°C per 1 000 ft and its dew point at about 0.5°C per 1 000 ft, so the spread closes at 2.5°C per 1 000 ft (400 ft per °C). Spread = 13 − 1 = 12°C, so the base is 12 × 400 = 4,800 ft above the surface.
whyWrong: Used 200 ft per °C instead of 400
Used 3°C per 1 000 ft for the spread, ignoring the dew-point lapse
Gave metres labelled as feet
samples.examTip: Common trap: used 200 ft per °C instead of 400.

samples.prompt: During a clear night the air temperature falls from 24 °C towards the dew point of 18 °C while no moisture is added. What happens to the relative humidity and the dew point?
options: Both the relative humidity and the dew point rise
Relative humidity rises; the dew point stays about the same
Relative humidity stays the same; the dew point falls with the temperature
Relative humidity falls; the dew point stays about the same
samples.explanation: Relative humidity is the ratio of the actual vapour content to the maximum the air could hold at its temperature. Cooling reduces that maximum, so RH rises towards 100% as the temperature approaches the dew point. The dew point measures the actual moisture content, so with no moisture added it stays nearly constant. When the two meet, the air is saturated and dew, mist or fog can form.
whyWrong: The dew point cannot rise unless moisture is added.
The dew point depends only on the moisture content, which has not changed.
Cooling lowers the saturation vapour pressure, so the same vapour content is a larger fraction of saturation: RH rises.
samples.examTip: Dew point = moisture content; RH = how close to saturation.

samples.prompt: Why can warm air hold more water vapour than cold air before it becomes saturated?
options: Warm air is denser, so there is more room between the molecules
Cold air always contains ice crystals that remove the vapour
Warm air is at a higher pressure, which forces more vapour into it
The saturation vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature
samples.explanation: The maximum vapour pressure that can exist over a flat water surface (the saturation vapour pressure) increases roughly exponentially with temperature: it about doubles for every 10 °C rise. So tropical air can carry much more water than polar air, which is why monsoon clouds can produce such heavy rain.
whyWrong: Warm air is less dense at the same pressure; 'room between molecules' is not the mechanism.
Cold air does not need to contain ice; the limit is set by the saturation vapour pressure.
The comparison holds at the same pressure; temperature, not pressure, controls saturation.
samples.examTip: Warm air → more moisture capacity → heavier potential rainfall.

samples.prompt: Above the friction layer in the Northern Hemisphere, with straight parallel isobars, the wind blows:
options: Across the isobars directly from high to low pressure
Parallel to the isobars with low pressure on its right
Parallel to the isobars, with low pressure on its left
Across the isobars at about 30°, turned towards the high pressure
samples.explanation: Above the friction layer (roughly 2,000–3,000 ft over land) the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force, giving the geostrophic wind. It blows parallel to straight isobars; in the Northern Hemisphere Coriolis acts to the right of the motion, so low pressure lies on the left. Closer isobars mean a stronger wind.
whyWrong: Air would move straight from high to low only without the Earth's rotation; Coriolis turns it until it is parallel.
Low on the right is the Southern Hemisphere rule.
Friction turns the surface wind towards LOW pressure, not high, and only below the friction layer.
samples.examTip: Southern Hemisphere: everything mirror-imaged, low on the right.

samples.prompt: Which statement about katabatic and anabatic winds is correct?
options: Both are produced by the pressure gradient between two synoptic systems
Katabatic winds blow up slopes by day; anabatic winds blow down slopes at night
Katabatic winds blow downslope at night; anabatic winds blow upslope by day
Anabatic winds are usually stronger than katabatic winds because daytime heating is intense
samples.explanation: At night the slopes cool by radiation and chill the air touching them; the denser air drains downhill as a katabatic wind, collecting in valleys where it can give frost or fog. By day sunlit slopes warm the air in contact, which rises up the slope as an anabatic wind. In Himalayan valleys such as those around Leh or Kullu these winds can be strong enough to affect take-off and landing.
whyWrong: Both are local thermal winds driven by slope heating or cooling, not by synoptic gradients.
Reverses the two: katabatic = down (Greek kata), anabatic = up (ana).
Katabatic flows are usually the stronger, because cold dense air accelerates downhill under gravity, while anabatic flow is opposed by gravity.
samples.examTip: Mountain-valley aerodromes: expect wind reversals around dawn and late afternoon.

samples.prompt: Why is the geostrophic wind relationship not used for forecasting winds close to the equator, for example over the Maldives at 4°N?
options: The pressure gradient is always zero at the equator
Friction is greater over the sea near the equator than anywhere else
Coriolis (proportional to sin latitude) is too weak to balance the pressure gradient
The Coriolis force is greatest at the equator and so overwhelms the pressure gradient
samples.explanation: The Coriolis force is 2Ωv sin φ, so it falls to zero at the equator. Within roughly 5–15° of the equator it is too weak to balance even a small pressure gradient, so the geostrophic balance breaks down and winds are better analysed with streamlines than with isobars. This is also why tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator.
whyWrong: Pressure gradients exist near the equator (for example around tropical lows); it is the Coriolis term that fails.
Friction over the sea is relatively low; it is not the reason.
Reverses the latitude effect: Coriolis is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles.
samples.examTip: Links two topics: no geostrophic balance and no cyclone formation near the equator.

samples.prompt: A pilot flying a heading of 360° above the friction layer over central India finds the aircraft drifting steadily to the right, so the wind is from the west. Applying Buys Ballot's law, where is the low pressure?
options: To the east
To the south
To the north
To the west
samples.explanation: A drift to the right on a northerly heading means the wind blows from the left, the west. Stand with your back to the wind, facing east: in the Northern Hemisphere low pressure is on your left, which is north. An aircraft flying towards lower pressure on a constant altimeter setting is descending in true altitude.
whyWrong: East is downwind; Buys Ballot puts the low to the side of the flow, not along it.
Low on the right is the Southern Hemisphere version of the law.
West is where the wind is coming from, not where the low lies.
samples.examTip: Work it out with a quick sketch: wind direction first, then face downwind.

samples.prompt: For the same isobar spacing and latitude, how does the gradient wind around a depression compare with the geostrophic wind?
options: It is sub-geostrophic, because part of the pressure gradient force provides the centripetal force
It is zero, because air cannot circulate around a low
It is greater than geostrophic, because the centrifugal effect adds to the pressure gradient force
It is exactly geostrophic, because curvature does not affect wind speed
samples.explanation: In curved flow there must be a net force towards the centre of curvature. Around a low, the pressure gradient force points inward, so it must exceed Coriolis; Coriolis is proportional to speed, so the wind is slower than geostrophic. Around a high, Coriolis points inward and must exceed the pressure gradient force, so the wind is faster than geostrophic for the same spacing.
whyWrong: Air does circulate round a low: anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.
That applies to the wind round a HIGH, which is super-geostrophic.
Curved flow needs a net inward force, so the balance and the speed change.
samples.examTip: Same isobar spacing: winds round a high are stronger than round a low.

chapters.title: Visibility And Fog
topics: Why Fog is a Winter Hazard in India

samples.prompt: In a METAR, a reduction of visibility to 3000 m caused by water droplets, with high relative humidity, is reported as:
options: BR (mist)
HZ (haze)
DU (widespread dust)
FG (fog)
samples.explanation: Obscuration by water droplets is reported as FG (fog) when the visibility is below 1000 m and as BR (mist) from 1000 m up to 5000 m. Obscuration by dry particles is reported as HZ (haze), FU (smoke), DU (dust) or SA (sand), and is reported only when the visibility is 5000 m or less.
whyWrong: Haze is caused by dry particles, such as dust or smoke, not by water droplets.
Widespread dust is a dry lithometeor, typical of north-west India in summer.
FG is used only when the visibility is less than 1000 m.
samples.examTip: The 1000 m line separates fog from mist; humidity separates mist from haze.

samples.prompt: Which statement about advection fog is correct?
options: It forms as warm moist air crosses a colder surface, and can persist by day and in wind
It forms only on clear, calm nights over land and always clears within an hour of sunrise
It forms when rain from a warm front falls into colder air below
It forms when very cold air moves over much warmer water
samples.explanation: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air is carried over a surface cold enough to cool it below its dew point, typically over the sea or a cold coastal strip. Because the cooling comes from the surface beneath the moving air rather than from night-time radiation, it can form and persist day or night, and with wind speeds that would disperse radiation fog.
whyWrong: That is radiation fog.
That is frontal fog.
That is steam fog (sea smoke).
samples.examTip: If the fog persists all day with a moderate wind off the sea, think advection.

samples.prompt: Which set of conditions most favours the dense winter fog that closes Delhi (VIDP) for hours in late December?
options: Moist air after a western disturbance, clear skies, a wind of 2–5 kt and a long night
A strong north-westerly wind, clear skies and very dry air
Overcast low cloud, a wind of 20 kt and a short night
Warm moist air flowing in from the Arabian Sea over a much colder land surface at night
samples.explanation: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools under a clear sky and chills moist air in contact with it below its dew point. It needs high humidity (often supplied by rain from a passing western disturbance), clear skies, a light wind of about 2–5 kt to spread the cooling through a few hundred feet, and a long night. Over the Indo-Gangetic plain in December and January all these coincide, and an inversion can keep the fog for most of the day.
whyWrong: A strong wind mixes the cooled layer upward and very dry air will not reach saturation.
Cloud cover stops the radiative cooling that radiation fog needs, and a 20 kt wind prevents a shallow cold layer.
That describes advection fog; Delhi is far from the sea, and its winter fogs are radiation fogs.
samples.examTip: Calm air gives dew or a very shallow fog; 2–5 kt spreads it; strong wind gives low stratus instead.

samples.prompt: Match the fog to its cause. Which pairing is NOT correct?
options: Radiation fog: surface cooling on a clear night with a light wind
Steam fog: warm moist air moving over a cold sea
Frontal fog: rain falling through cold air ahead of a warm front
Upslope fog: moist air cooled adiabatically as it is forced up rising ground
samples.explanation: Steam fog is the opposite of advection fog: very cold air flows over much warmer water, which evaporates into it and immediately condenses, like steam over a bath. Warm moist air over a cold sea gives advection (sea) fog. Frontal fog forms ahead of warm fronts, and upslope fog where air is forced up rising ground.
whyWrong: This pairing is correct: it is the classic night-time land fog.
This pairing is correct: rain evaporating into the cold air below raises its dew point to saturation.
This pairing is correct: the lift cools the air at the dry rate until it saturates.
samples.examTip: NOT question: the steam/advection swap is the favourite trap.

samples.prompt: A radiation fog lies over an inland aerodrome at dawn. Which change is most likely to clear it fastest?
options: The wind increasing to 10–15 kt and mixing the fog upwards into stratus
The wind becoming completely calm
Moist air being advected in from a nearby river
A clear sky persisting all morning with no change at all in the light wind
samples.explanation: Radiation fog is dispersed by warming from below (sunshine heating the ground) and by mixing with drier air above. A freshening wind mixes the cold layer upwards, so the fog lifts into stratus and breaks. In midwinter, with a strong inversion and weak sun, the fog can last well into the afternoon if the wind stays light.
whyWrong: Calm air allows the fog to stay in place; it does not mix it out.
Adding moisture makes the fog thicker, not thinner.
Sunshine does help, but in midwinter a thick fog under an inversion can persist all day without a wind increase.
samples.examTip: A forecast wind increase is often the key to the fog-clearance time in a TAF.

chapters.title: Vertical Motion And Clouds
topics: Vertical Motion — Local vs Large Scale

samples.prompt: A pilot sees a thin, whitish veil covering the sky, through which the sun shows a large ring of light about 22° from it. The cloud is:
options: Cirrostratus
Nimbostratus
Stratocumulus
Altostratus
samples.explanation: Halos are produced by refraction of light through ice crystals. Cirrostratus is a thin, high ice-crystal veil, and its halo is the classic warning of an approaching warm front: cirrus and cirrostratus are followed by thickening altostratus and then nimbostratus with continuous rain.
whyWrong: Nimbostratus is dark grey and thick enough to hide the sun completely.
Stratocumulus is a low cloud of rolls or patches and does not produce halos.
Altostratus is thicker and greyer; the sun appears as through ground glass with no halo.
samples.examTip: Sun 'as through ground glass' = altostratus; halo = cirrostratus.

samples.prompt: Which group contains only cloud genera of the high étage (high cloud family)?
options: Cirrus, altocumulus and altostratus
Cirrus, cirrocumulus and cirrostratus
Cirrostratus, nimbostratus and cumulonimbus
Altocumulus, altostratus and nimbostratus
samples.explanation: WMO classifies ten genera in three étages. High: cirrus, cirrocumulus and cirrostratus (all ice crystals). Middle: altocumulus and altostratus, with nimbostratus usually counted here though it extends through several levels. Low: stratocumulus and stratus, with cumulus and cumulonimbus having low bases but great vertical development. In the tropics the high étage spans roughly 6–18 km.
whyWrong: Altocumulus and altostratus are middle-level clouds.
Nimbostratus and cumulonimbus are clouds of great vertical extent with low bases.
These are middle-level clouds (nimbostratus is usually placed with them, extending above and below).
samples.examTip: 'Cirro-' = high, 'alto-' = middle, 'strato-'/'cumulo-' alone = low.

samples.prompt: Which cloud is most typically associated with continuous moderate or heavy rain, a low base and poor visibility beneath it?
options: Nimbostratus
Cirrocumulus
Cumulonimbus
Altocumulus
samples.explanation: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark grey, layered cloud covering the whole sky, from which continuous rain or snow falls. It forms by widespread, slow ascent, typically ahead of a warm front, in a mature depression or in the monsoon, and its base is often lowered by ragged stratus fractus in the rain.
whyWrong: Cirrocumulus is a thin high ice cloud with no precipitation reaching the ground.
Cumulonimbus gives showers (heavy but intermittent) and thunderstorms rather than continuous rain.
Altocumulus is a medium cloud of patches or rolls that rarely gives more than light precipitation.
samples.examTip: 'Continuous' is the keyword for nimbostratus.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a process by which air is lifted to form cloud?
options: Convergence of air into a low or a trough
Convection from surface heating
Divergence of air at the surface beneath an anticyclone
Turbulent mixing in the lowest layers below an inversion
samples.explanation: Cloud forms when air is lifted and cools adiabatically. The lifting processes are convection, orographic ascent, frontal ascent, convergence (including the ITCZ and troughs) and turbulent mixing. Divergence at the surface is the opposite: it goes with sinking air (subsidence), which warms and dries the air and dissolves cloud, as under a high.
whyWrong: Surface convergence forces air to rise; this is a lifting process.
Convection lifts air as warm bubbles; this is the commonest lifting process.
Turbulence lifts moist air to its condensation level under the inversion, giving a layer of St or Sc.
samples.examTip: Surface divergence means sinking air above: fine weather.

samples.prompt: An early-morning report over the Western Ghats mentions altocumulus castellanus. What is its significance to a pilot?
options: It shows that a mountain wave is present downwind of the ridge
It shows a very stable atmosphere with no prospect of any convection today
Medium-level instability, often followed by thunderstorms later that day
It is a sign of approaching fog
samples.explanation: Castellanus clouds have turret-like tops rising from a common base, showing that the layer at that level is unstable. When surface heating later releases the instability in the lower layers, convection can join the two and build cumulonimbus. Seen in the morning, Ac castellanus is a well-known warning of afternoon thunderstorms.
whyWrong: A mountain wave gives smooth, lens-shaped lenticular altocumulus, not turrets.
Turreted (castellated) tops grow only when the medium-level air is unstable.
Fog is a surface phenomenon with stable conditions; turrets show instability aloft.
samples.examTip: Lenticular = wave; castellanus = instability.

chapters.title: Stability and Instability of the Atmosphere
topics: Normand Theorem and Lifting Condensation Level (LCL)

samples.prompt: Which statement about a stable atmosphere is correct?
options: A parcel displaced upward becomes warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising
The ELR is greater than the DALR
A parcel displaced upward becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back
Cumuliform cloud with good visibility is typical
samples.explanation: In stable air a lifted parcel cools faster than the surrounding air, so it becomes colder and denser and sinks back. Vertical motion is suppressed, so cloud forms in layers (stratus, stratocumulus, altostratus), haze and pollutants are trapped near the ground, visibility is poor, and flying is smooth. Unstable air gives cumuliform cloud, showers, good visibility outside them and bumpy flying.
whyWrong: That describes instability.
An ELR greater than the DALR is absolute instability.
Cumuliform cloud and good visibility are the marks of unstable air; stable air gives layer cloud and poor visibility.
samples.examTip: Look at the cloud shape: layers = stable, heaps = unstable.

samples.prompt: A surface parcel at 23°C with a dew point of 13°C is forced to rise. Taking DALR 3°C/1 000 ft, SALR 1.5°C/1 000 ft and dew point lapse 0.5°C/1 000 ft, what is its temperature at 8,000 ft?
samples.explanation: Cloud base = (23 − 13) × 400 = 4,000 ft. Below it the parcel cools at the DALR (3°C/1 000 ft): 23 − 3 × 4 = 11.0°C. Above it, at the SALR (1.5°C/1 000 ft) for 4,000 ft: 5.0°C.
whyWrong: Used the DALR all the way up, ignoring the cloud base
Used the ISA lapse rate of 2°C per 1 000 ft
Used the SALR all the way up, from the surface
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the DALR all the way up, ignoring the cloud base.

samples.prompt: A surface parcel at 21°C with a dew point of 6°C is forced to rise. Taking DALR 3°C/1 000 ft, SALR 1.5°C/1 000 ft and dew point lapse 0.5°C/1 000 ft, what is its temperature at 9,500 ft?
samples.explanation: Cloud base = (21 − 6) × 400 = 6,000 ft. Below it the parcel cools at the DALR (3°C/1 000 ft): 21 − 3 × 6 = 3.0°C. Above it, at the SALR (1.5°C/1 000 ft) for 3,500 ft: −2.3°C.
whyWrong: Used the DALR all the way up, ignoring the cloud base
Used the SALR all the way up, from the surface
Used the ISA lapse rate of 2°C per 1 000 ft
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the DALR all the way up, ignoring the cloud base.

samples.prompt: A radiosonde ascent shows an environmental lapse rate of 2.2 °C per 1,000 ft through a deep layer. Taking the DALR as 3 °C and the SALR as 1.5 °C per 1,000 ft, the layer is:
options: Absolutely stable
Absolutely unstable
Neutral for both
Conditionally unstable
samples.explanation: Compare the ELR with the adiabatic rates. ELR < SALR: absolutely stable. ELR > DALR: absolutely unstable. SALR < ELR < DALR: conditionally unstable, which is the commonest case: an unsaturated parcel cools faster than its surroundings and sinks back, but once saturated it cools more slowly than its surroundings and keeps rising. Most deep convection over India develops in conditionally unstable air.
whyWrong: Absolute stability needs an ELR less than the SALR (here 2.2 is greater than 1.5).
Absolute instability needs an ELR greater than the DALR (here 2.2 is less than 3).
Neutral stability would need the ELR to equal the parcel's lapse rate.
samples.examTip: Draw the three numbers on a line and see where the ELR falls.

samples.prompt: On a pre-monsoon morning over Kolkata, the lower layers are moist and the upper layers dry and cold. As the sun heats the ground during the day, what is the most likely development?
options: A subsidence inversion forms at the surface and fog thickens through the day
Only thin cirrus forms, because moisture near the surface prevents convection
The atmosphere becomes absolutely stable because the upper layers are so dry
Cumulus builds into cumulonimbus and a nor'wester squall may develop by evening
samples.explanation: Heating at the surface steepens the lapse rate in the lowest layers. With plenty of moisture below and cold air aloft, rising parcels saturate, release latent heat and stay warmer than their surroundings through a deep layer, so towering cumulus and cumulonimbus develop. Over West Bengal, Odisha and Assam in March to May this gives the violent nor'westers (kalbaisakhi), typically in the late afternoon or evening.
whyWrong: Surface heating removes inversions; it does not build one at the ground.
Low-level moisture is the fuel for convection; it does not prevent it.
Cold, dry air aloft over moist warm air makes the profile more unstable, not stable.
samples.examTip: Convective instability is greatest when moisture is concentrated at low levels.

samples.prompt: The small halo has a radius of:
samples.explanation: The small halo (most frequent halo phenomenon) has a radius of 22° with the sun or moon at its centre. The large halo has a radius of 46°. Primary rainbow is 42° and secondary rainbow is 52°.

samples.prompt: The radius of Bishop's Ring is approximately:
samples.explanation: Bishop's ring, caused by diffraction from fine (often volcanic) dust in the high atmosphere, has a radius of about 22°, similar to the small halo. It is whitish with a bluish tinge inside and reddish-brown outside, whereas the halo has its red on the inside. 5° is typical of a corona, and 42° and 52° are the primary and secondary rainbows.

samples.prompt: During a night flight close to an active thunderstorm, a bluish glow flickers around the windscreen frame and wing tips. This is:
options: A lightning strike on the airframe
A corona caused by diffraction of light in water droplets
An inferior mirage
St Elmo's fire, an electrical discharge
samples.explanation: St Elmo's fire is a luminous electrical discharge from pointed parts of the airframe when the aircraft is in a strong electric field, typically near or in cumulonimbus. It is harmless in itself, but it shows the field is strong and a lightning strike is possible. It can also cause radio static.
whyWrong: A strike is a sudden flash and bang; St Elmo's fire is a steady or flickering glow.
The optical corona is a coloured ring round the sun or moon, not a glow on the aircraft.
A mirage is a refraction effect near hot surfaces, not a glow on the airframe.
samples.examTip: Do not confuse the electrical 'corona discharge' with the optical 'corona' ring.

samples.prompt: Which phenomenon is caused by DIFFRACTION of light by small water droplets?
options: A rainbow seen opposite the sun in a shower
A corona: coloured rings close round the sun or moon seen through thin altocumulus
A halo: a large ring of about 22° radius round the sun, seen in a thin cirrostratus
A mirage: a shimmering 'pool of water' on a hot runway
samples.explanation: A corona is a series of small coloured rings, blue inside and red outside, very close round the sun or moon. It is caused by diffraction of light by small water droplets in thin cloud such as altocumulus or altostratus; the smaller the droplets, the bigger the rings. A halo is larger (22°) and comes from refraction in ice crystals.
whyWrong: A rainbow is produced by refraction and internal reflection inside large raindrops.
A halo is produced by refraction in ice crystals, not diffraction in droplets.
A mirage is caused by refraction through layers of air of different temperature.
samples.examTip: 'Ice' points to halo; 'droplets' with small rings points to corona.

samples.prompt: Approaching a runway on a hot afternoon at Ahmedabad, the pilot sees what looks like a sheet of water on the runway that disappears as the aircraft gets closer. The cause is:
options: Rain falling from a passing cumulus
An inferior mirage, from light refracted by the very hot air near the surface
A rainbow formed in spray from the runway
A superior mirage caused by an inversion over a cold sea surface somewhere nearby
samples.explanation: Over a very hot surface the air just above it is much warmer and less dense than the air higher up. Light from the sky passing down through these layers is refracted (bent) upwards, so the eye sees an image of the sky on the ground, which looks like water. It is an inferior mirage, common over Indian runways in the hot season.
whyWrong: Real water would not vanish as you approach it.
A rainbow needs sunlight behind the observer shining into raindrops.
A superior mirage shows images above the true position and needs cold air below warm air, the opposite of a hot runway.
samples.examTip: Hot ground below = inferior (image lower).

chapters.title: Precipitation
topics: Types of Lightning and Electrical Phenomena
Clouds and Precipitation — The Complete Table

samples.prompt: Aurora Australis occur in the:
options: Northern hemisphere
Southern hemisphere
Equatorial region
Both hemispheres equally
samples.explanation: Aurora Australis occur in the Southern hemisphere and are called Southern Lights. Aurora Borealis occur in the Northern hemisphere. Option A is incorrect as it describes Aurora Borealis. Option C is incorrect as auroras are not observed at the equator. Option D is incorrect as each type is specific to one hemisphere.

samples.prompt: Match the precipitation to its usual source. Which pairing is correct?
options: Drizzle: stratus, falling as small drops less than 0.5 mm in diameter
Showers: altostratus, starting and stopping gradually
Hail: nimbostratus, falling as continuous ice pellets
Continuous rain: cumulus, falling from isolated clouds with blue sky between
samples.explanation: Drizzle consists of fine drops (diameter below 0.5 mm) falling from stratus or low stratocumulus, often with poor visibility. Rain drops are 0.5 mm or more. Showers come from cumulus and cumulonimbus and begin and end suddenly. Hail forms in cumulonimbus where strong updraughts carry drops repeatedly above the freezing level.
whyWrong: Showers come from cumuliform cloud and start and stop abruptly.
Hail comes from cumulonimbus with strong updraughts, not from layer cloud.
Continuous rain comes from layer cloud such as nimbostratus and thick altostratus.
samples.examTip: Shape of the cloud tells you the type of precipitation.

samples.prompt: How does 'warm rain' form in tropical clouds over the Bay of Bengal that do not extend above the freezing level?
options: By melting of hail that has formed in the cloud
By collision and coalescence of droplets of different sizes
By deposition of water vapour directly onto ice nuclei
By the Bergeron process of ice crystals growing at the droplets' expense
samples.explanation: In clouds warmer than 0 °C throughout, droplets grow by collision and coalescence. Larger drops fall faster than small ones, collide with them and merge. Tropical maritime air with plenty of large salt nuclei and deep moist cloud makes this process very efficient, which is why heavy rain can fall from clouds whose tops are below the freezing level.
whyWrong: Hail needs strong updraughts carrying drops well above the freezing level.
Deposition onto ice needs sub-zero temperatures.
The Bergeron process needs ice crystals, which cannot exist in a cloud warmer than 0 °C throughout.
samples.examTip: Cloud entirely above 0 °C rules out any ice process.

samples.prompt: Freezing rain at the surface requires:
options: A warm layer above 0 °C aloft over a sub-zero layer next to the ground
A completely sub-zero atmosphere from the cloud to the ground
A surface temperature above 0 °C and snow falling from the cloud above
Strong updraughts in a cumulonimbus carrying drops above the freezing level
samples.explanation: Freezing rain needs a temperature inversion: snow or rain falls into a warm layer (above 0 °C) and melts, then falls through a sub-zero layer near the ground and becomes supercooled. The drops freeze on contact with anything below 0 °C, including an aircraft. It is typical ahead of warm fronts in winter in mid-latitudes and can occasionally occur in Himalayan regions.
whyWrong: With sub-zero air all the way down, snow would reach the ground, not rain.
If the surface air is above 0 °C the drops will not freeze on impact.
Strong updraughts produce hail, not freezing rain.
samples.examTip: Freezing rain is reported as FZRA and is a SIGMET phenomenon (severe icing).

samples.prompt: In a deep cloud containing both ice crystals and supercooled water droplets at about −15 °C, why do the ice crystals grow at the expense of the droplets?
options: The droplets freeze instantly onto the crystals because supercooled water cannot exist
Ice crystals are heavier and collect droplets only by falling through them
The saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over water
The saturation vapour pressure over ice is higher than over water
samples.explanation: This is the Bergeron–Findeisen (ice crystal) process. Air that is just saturated with respect to water is supersaturated with respect to ice, because the saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower. Water vapour deposits on the crystals, the droplets evaporate to replace it, and the crystals grow large enough to fall, as snow that may melt into rain lower down. It is most effective between about −10 and −20 °C.
whyWrong: Supercooled droplets can exist down to about −40 °C; it is the vapour transfer that matters here.
Collision with droplets (riming) also happens, but the process asked about is the vapour transfer.
Reverses the key fact: saturation vapour pressure is LOWER over ice.
samples.examTip: Tropical 'warm' rain from clouds wholly above 0 °C comes from collision and coalescence instead.

chapters.title: Ice Accretion
topics: Types of Icing: Airframe Icing and Engine Icing
Airframe Icing in Relation to Cloud Forms
Height of Freezing Level in India

samples.prompt: In which temperature range is the risk of significant airframe icing in cloud generally greatest?
options: −20 °C to about −40 °C
+10 °C to 0 °C
0 °C to about −20 °C
Below −40 °C
samples.explanation: Supercooled liquid water is most plentiful between 0 °C and about −20 °C, with the largest drops nearest 0 °C. Below about −20 °C more and more of the cloud is glaciated (ice crystals), and below about −40 °C liquid droplets freeze spontaneously, so icing becomes rare. In strong convection, however, supercooled water can be carried to much colder levels.
whyWrong: Icing is possible there, but droplets are fewer and smaller and much of the cloud is ice crystals.
Supercooled water does not exist above 0 °C, so airframe icing in cloud cannot form there (apart from kinetic and engine effects).
Below about −40 °C droplets freeze spontaneously, so cloud consists of ice crystals that do not stick.
samples.examTip: The freezing level marks the top of the 'no icing' layer, not the start of severe icing everywhere.

samples.prompt: Why is rime ice white and opaque?
options: It is mixed with dust and salt from the cloud
It forms only when the airframe is above 0 °C
It forms from dry snow crystals sticking to the cold airframe surface
Small droplets freeze instantly on impact and trap air between them
samples.explanation: Rime forms when small supercooled droplets, usually in layer cloud at about −10 to −20 °C, freeze immediately on contact. Each droplet freezes before it can spread, so air is trapped between them, giving a white, opaque, rough and brittle deposit. It builds forward into the airflow from the leading edge and is lighter and easier to remove than clear ice, though it still spoils the aerofoil.
whyWrong: Its colour comes from trapped air, not from impurities.
Ice cannot form on an airframe that is above 0 °C.
Dry snow crystals generally bounce off a cold airframe; rime is frozen droplets.
samples.examTip: Rime = Rapid freezing; clear = slow freezing with run-back.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies through cumulus at −5 °C containing large supercooled droplets. The ice that forms on the leading edges is most likely to be:
options: No ice at all, because the temperature is too close to 0 °C
Rime ice: white, opaque and brittle, building forward from the leading edge
Clear (glaze) ice, hard and heavy, spreading back before it freezes
Hoar frost: a white crystalline deposit formed without any cloud
samples.explanation: A large supercooled drop at a temperature just below 0 °C cannot freeze all at once: the latent heat released by the part that freezes warms the rest. The unfrozen water runs back over the surface and freezes gradually, forming a clear, dense, glassy layer with few air bubbles. It is heavy, adheres strongly, distorts the aerofoil shape, and is the most dangerous form of airframe ice.
whyWrong: Supercooled droplets freeze on impact at any sub-zero airframe temperature; the range just below 0 °C is one of the worst for clear ice.
Rime forms from small droplets that freeze instantly, typically at colder temperatures in layer cloud.
Hoar frost forms by deposition of vapour, not from cloud droplets.
samples.examTip: Large drops + slight sub-zero temperature → clear ice.

samples.prompt: After a night parked in the open at Srinagar under a clear sky, an aircraft has a thin white crystalline layer on its wings, although there has been no cloud, fog or precipitation. This is:
options: Rime ice, formed by supercooled fog droplets freezing on contact
Clear ice, formed by freezing rain overnight
Glaze, formed by dew that froze after it had been deposited
Hoar frost, deposited directly from water vapour as ice
samples.explanation: Hoar frost forms when water vapour is deposited directly as ice crystals on a surface whose temperature is below 0 °C and below the frost point of the air. It forms on aircraft parked under clear skies at night, and in flight when a cold-soaked aircraft descends quickly into warm, moist air. It is light, but on the wings it roughens the surface and increases the stall speed, so it must be removed before take-off.
whyWrong: Rime needs supercooled droplets, and the scenario says there was no fog or cloud.
There was no precipitation, so freezing rain is ruled out.
Frozen dew gives a clear glaze rather than a white crystalline deposit.
samples.examTip: Any frost on lifting surfaces must be removed before flight, however thin.

samples.prompt: In a cloud of supercooled droplets at −10 °C, roughly what fraction of each droplet freezes immediately on striking the airframe?
options: About 0.5 (half) of the drop
About 0.125 (one-eighth) of the drop
All of the drop, at once
None of it until the airframe is below −20 °C
samples.explanation: Freezing water releases latent heat of about 80 calories per gram, while warming water by 1 °C takes about 1 calorie per gram. A drop supercooled by 10 °C can therefore absorb only enough heat to freeze about 10/80 = 1/8 of its mass before reaching 0 °C. The remainder stays liquid, runs back and freezes more slowly: this is why clear ice and run-back are worst near 0 °C to −10 °C.
whyWrong: There is no 50% rule; the fraction depends on the degree of supercooling.
Only very small drops at very low temperatures freeze completely at once; the released latent heat stops the rest.
Supercooled droplets freeze on impact at any temperature below 0 °C.
samples.examTip: Near 0 °C most of the water runs back: clear ice and ice behind the protected areas.

chapters.title: Thunderstorms
topics: Life Cycle of a Thunderstorm Cell

samples.prompt: Which three conditions must all be present for a thunderstorm to develop?
options: Deep instability, plenty of low-level moisture, and a lifting trigger
A stable atmosphere, high humidity and a strong and gusty surface wind
Clear skies, low humidity and a cold front
A subsidence inversion, dry air and strong surface heating
samples.explanation: A thunderstorm needs (1) deep instability, so that a saturated parcel stays warmer than its surroundings to great heights; (2) abundant moisture, which provides the latent heat; and (3) a trigger such as surface heating, orographic lift, a front, convergence along a trough, or the ITCZ. Pre-monsoon India has all three over the north-east and the south-west peninsula from March to May.
whyWrong: Stable air suppresses the deep ascent that thunderstorms need.
Low humidity removes the fuel (latent heat) that powers a thunderstorm.
A subsidence inversion caps convection and dry air gives no cloud.
samples.examTip: Missing any one of the three = no thunderstorm.

samples.prompt: What marks the start of the mature stage of a thunderstorm cell?
options: The first appearance of cirrus ahead of the cell
The first appearance of cumulus cloud
Precipitation reaching the ground, with downdraughts developing alongside the updraughts
The cloud top spreading into an anvil while all of the motion in the cell becomes downward
samples.explanation: In the cumulus stage, updraughts occupy the whole cell. When the precipitation becomes too heavy to be supported, it falls and drags air down, so downdraughts develop beside the updraughts and rain reaches the ground: the mature stage. This stage has the most intense turbulence, hail, lightning and gusts. In the dissipating stage downdraughts dominate, the rain becomes lighter and the anvil spreads. A single cell typically lasts about an hour.
whyWrong: Cirrus ahead is not a stage marker for an individual cell.
The first cumulus is the start of the cumulus (developing) stage, with updraughts only.
A cell with downdraughts only is in the dissipating stage.
samples.examTip: 'Rain starts falling at the surface' = mature stage begins.

samples.prompt: Why does the top of a mature cumulonimbus over north India spread out into a flat anvil?
options: The cloud runs out of moisture at mid levels
The downdraughts push the top of the cloud outwards
The updraught meets the stable tropopause and spreads sideways
The cloud freezes and becomes heavier than the clear air around it
samples.explanation: The updraught decelerates when it reaches the very stable tropopause, so the cloud spreads sideways into an anvil of ice crystals. Strong upper winds, such as the subtropical jet in spring, stretch the anvil downwind. Hail can fall from beneath the anvil well away from the main cell, even in apparently clear air.
whyWrong: Cbs often carry moisture to the tropopause; drying is not what flattens the top.
Downdraughts are in the lower and middle parts of the cell; they do not shape the top.
Ice crystals in the anvil are light and are carried by the upper winds.
samples.examTip: Never fly under an anvil: hail can fall from it.

samples.prompt: Which type of thunderstorm is MOST common over the open sea such as the Bay of Bengal at night and in the early morning?
options: Night-time maritime convection, as cloud tops cool by radiation
Orographic storms over the Western Ghats
Air-mass storms from strong daytime surface heating
Cold-front storms from a western disturbance
samples.explanation: Over the sea the surface temperature changes little between day and night. At night the tops of cloud layers radiate heat to space and cool, which steepens the lapse rate between the warm sea and the cold cloud tops. Convection therefore peaks at night and early morning over warm tropical seas, while over land it peaks in the afternoon and evening.
whyWrong: There are no mountains over the open sea.
Over land, heating peaks in the afternoon; the sea surface hardly warms through the day.
Western disturbances affect north India, mainly in winter; they do not drive night-time storms over the Bay.
samples.examTip: Diurnal timing differs over land and sea: watch for it in route planning.

samples.prompt: An aircraft on final approach flies under a microburst. In what order will the crew typically meet the effects?
options: Increasing tailwind first, then a downdraught, then a headwind gain
Increasing headwind, then a strong downdraught, then a tailwind
Strong updraught, then headwind, then calm
A downdraught only, with no change of airspeed
samples.explanation: A microburst is a concentrated downdraught that spreads out horizontally on reaching the ground. Flying into it, the aircraft first meets the outflow as a headwind: performance increases and the aircraft balloons above the glide path. In the core it meets a strong downdraught, and then the outflow on the far side as a tailwind: the airspeed falls rapidly just when the aircraft is low and slow. The usual defence is to avoid it, and if caught, to apply the windshear escape manoeuvre at once.
whyWrong: Reverses the order: the outflow ahead of the core is met first as a headwind.
A microburst is a downdraught; the updraught belongs to a different part of the storm.
The horizontal outflow changes the airspeed sharply; that is what makes a microburst so dangerous.
samples.examTip: Do not reduce power in the initial headwind gain; it is the warning of what follows.

chapters.title: Air Masses, Fronts and Western Disturbances
topics: Air Masses Over the Indian Subcontinent

samples.prompt: An air mass coded 'mT' has which characteristics in its source region?
options: Maritime tropical: warm and moist
Maritime polar: cold and moist
Continental tropical: hot and dry
Monsoon trough: warm and unstable
samples.explanation: Air masses are named by their source region: the first letter gives the surface type (c = continental, dry; m = maritime, moist) and the capital the latitude band (A = arctic, P = polar, T = tropical, E = equatorial). mT air is warm and moist, from subtropical oceans; cT air is hot and dry, from deserts such as the Thar and Arabia.
whyWrong: Maritime polar is coded mP.
Continental tropical is coded cT.
'T' in air-mass codes stands for tropical, and 'm' for maritime; there is no 'monsoon trough' air mass code.
samples.examTip: Decode the two letters separately.

samples.prompt: In the life cycle of a mid-latitude frontal depression, the occlusion stage usually indicates that:
options: The warm sector is widening and the depression is deepening fast
The depression is just beginning to form as a wave on the polar front
The depression has become a tropical cyclone
The depression is mature and will soon begin to fill
samples.explanation: A frontal depression starts as a wave on the polar front. The warm sector is gradually squeezed as the faster cold front catches the warm front. Once occlusion begins, the warm air that powers the system is cut off from the surface, so the depression has usually reached its deepest point and will slowly fill, often slowing and turning to the left of its track.
whyWrong: In occlusion the warm sector narrows and is lifted off the surface.
The wave stage is the beginning of the cycle; occlusion comes near the end.
A tropical cyclone has no fronts and forms over warm tropical seas.
samples.examTip: Track the warm sector: as it narrows, the depression ages.

samples.prompt: Cold, dry continental air flows from a high-pressure region over a much warmer sea. What change happens to it, and what weather results downwind?
options: It becomes unstable, giving cumulus, showers and good visibility
It is cooled from below, becomes stable, and gives fog and drizzle
It sinks and warms, giving clear skies and haze
It is unchanged, because air masses keep their properties for weeks
samples.explanation: An air mass moving over a warmer surface is heated from below, which steepens its lapse rate (instability), and it picks up moisture by evaporation from the sea. The result is convective cloud (cumulus, cumulonimbus) with showers, gusty winds and good visibility between the showers. Air moving over a colder surface becomes stable: layer cloud, fog, drizzle, poor visibility.
whyWrong: Cooling from below happens when warm air crosses a colder surface; here the surface is warmer.
Heating from below makes it unstable and causes it to rise, not sink.
Air masses are modified as soon as they leave their source region; the change can be rapid over a warm sea.
samples.examTip: Ask whether the surface is warmer or colder than the air.

samples.prompt: The south-west monsoon air reaching the Kerala coast in June has its origin mainly in:
options: The north-east trade winds of the northern Indian Ocean
The south-east trades of the southern Indian Ocean, after crossing the equator
Polar air from the Southern Ocean that has not been modified
The dry continental air of central Asia, which is drawn south across the Himalaya
samples.explanation: In the northern summer the south-east trades of the southern Indian Ocean are drawn across the equator towards the heat low over north-west India and Pakistan. Once north of the equator, the Coriolis effect turns them to the right, so they arrive as a moist south-westerly. A long passage over warm water makes them very moist and conditionally unstable: the south-west monsoon.
whyWrong: The north-east trades (the winter monsoon) blow away from India, not towards it in June.
Air from such high latitudes is completely modified by the time it reaches the tropics, and it is not the source of the monsoon.
The Himalaya block air from central Asia, and that air is dry, not moist.
samples.examTip: Coriolis changes sign across the equator; that is why the wind turns.

samples.prompt: An aerodrome reports these changes over a few hours: pressure falling steadily, then steady; wind backing ahead of the front and then veering; temperature and dew point both rising; continuous rain turning to drizzle with low stratus. Which front has passed?
options: A cold front
A quasi-stationary front with no change of air mass
A warm front
A cold occlusion
samples.explanation: Ahead of a warm front the pressure falls and the wind backs. As the surface front passes, the wind veers, the pressure stops falling, and the temperature and dew point rise as the warm-sector air arrives. The warm sector is often moist and stable, with low stratus, drizzle and poor visibility.
whyWrong: A cold front brings a temperature and dew-point fall and a pressure rise after it passes.
The rising temperature and dew point show that a warmer air mass has arrived.
A cold occlusion behaves like a cold front at the surface, with colder air arriving.
samples.examTip: Temperature up after the passage = warm front; temperature down = cold front.

samples.prompt: According to the WMO definition, a jet stream is a strong, narrow current, usually near the tropopause, with a speed of at least:
options: 30 kt
150 kt
60 kt
100 kt
samples.explanation: WMO defines a jet stream as a strong, narrow current concentrated along a quasi-horizontal axis in the upper troposphere or lower stratosphere, with strong vertical and lateral wind shear, and a lower limit of speed of 30 m/s, about 60 kt. On high-level significant weather charts, jets are drawn where the speed is 80 kt or more.
whyWrong: 30 is the speed in metres per second (about 60 kt), not knots.
150 kt is reached in strong winter jets, but it is not the defining threshold.
Many jets exceed 100 kt, but the defining lower limit is lower.
samples.examTip: Do not confuse m/s and kt: 30 m/s ≈ 60 kt.

samples.prompt: An aircraft tracking 240°(T) crosses a jet stream of 250°/120 kt. What is the along-track wind component?
options: tailwind 118 kt
headwind 21 kt
headwind 118 kt
tailwind 21 kt
samples.explanation: The angle between the wind (250°) and the track (240°) is 10°. Component = 120 × cos of that angle = headwind 118 kt.
whyWrong: Mixed up headwind and tailwind
Used sin of the angle instead of cos
Used sin of the angle and reversed head and tail
samples.examTip: Common trap: mixed up headwind and tailwind.

samples.prompt: In winter the subtropical jet stream lies over northern India. Which description fits it best?
options: A westerly jet near FL390 at about 25–30°N, moving north of the Himalaya in summer
An easterly jet near FL450 over southern India during July and August
A low-level south-westerly jet near 5,000 ft over the Arabian Sea
A polar front jet at FL300 over Sri Lanka
samples.explanation: The subtropical jet (STJ) blows from the west at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell, near the 200 hPa level. In winter it lies along about 25–30°N over north India, south of the Himalaya, and is strong because of the large temperature contrast. Around the onset of the monsoon it jumps north of the Tibetan plateau. Flights between Europe and India meet strong headwinds westbound in this jet in winter.
whyWrong: That describes the tropical easterly jet of the summer monsoon.
That describes the low-level (Somali) jet of the south-west monsoon.
The polar front jet lies far to the north; Sri Lanka is in the tropics.
samples.examTip: Summer over India: easterly jet aloft (TEJ) and south-westerly jet low down (Somali jet).

samples.prompt: During the south-west monsoon, a westbound flight from Kolkata to Mumbai at FL450 is likely to meet:
options: A south-westerly headwind from the Somali jet at that level
A tailwind from the tropical easterly jet, near 100–150 hPa
Calm upper winds, because there are no jets in the tropics
A strong headwind from the subtropical westerly jet over the Bay of Bengal
samples.explanation: In June to September, the heated Tibetan plateau creates an upper high, and a strong easterly current, the tropical easterly jet (TEJ), forms on its southern side, roughly along 10–15°N at about 100–150 hPa. A westbound flight at high level over south and central India therefore benefits from a tailwind. The TEJ is one of the signatures of an established monsoon.
whyWrong: The Somali jet is a low-level jet, near 1–1.5 km, not at FL450.
The tropical easterly jet is a strong jet in the tropics.
In the monsoon season the subtropical westerly jet lies north of the Himalaya, not over central India.
samples.examTip: Easterly jet in summer, westerly jet in winter over India.

samples.prompt: Standing with a Northern Hemisphere polar-front jet stream at your back, where is the cold air and where is cirrus most often seen?
options: Cold air on the right; cirrus on the left
Cold air on the left; cirrus streaks on the warm side
Cold air above the jet core; cirrus below it
Cold air on the left; cumulonimbus along the jet core
samples.explanation: The jet follows the thermal wind, which blows with the cold air on its left in the Northern Hemisphere. Ascent on the warm, equatorward side produces long bands of cirrus parallel to the jet axis, and these can be seen from the ground or in satellite images. Clear air turbulence is most likely on the cold, polar side of the core.
whyWrong: Reverses the sides: the jet blows with cold, low pressure on its left in the Northern Hemisphere.
The temperature contrast is horizontal across the jet, not above and below.
Jets themselves do not produce cumulonimbus; their visible sign is high cirrus.
samples.examTip: Same rule as Buys Ballot: back to the wind, low on the left.

chapters.title: Clear Air Turbulence and Mountain Waves
topics: Seasonal and Diurnal Variation of Mountain Waves

samples.prompt: Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) is defined as bumpiness experienced by aircraft at high altitudes in:
options: Cloud-free conditions excluding Ci clouds
Cloud-free conditions including all cloud types
Conditions with only cumulonimbus clouds present
Conditions with only stratiform clouds present
samples.explanation: CAT is specifically defined as bumpiness in cloud-free conditions, excluding Ci clouds. Option B is wrong because Ci clouds are excluded. Options C and D are wrong because CAT occurs in cloud-free conditions, not in the presence of those cloud types.

samples.prompt: Clear air turbulence at high level is most closely associated with:
options: Strong surface heating on a sunny afternoon
Fog and low stratus under an inversion
Strong wind shear, especially near jet streams
Light winds at all levels under a large anticyclone
samples.explanation: CAT is turbulence in clear air, usually above about 15,000 ft, caused by wind shear breaking down into waves and eddies (Kelvin–Helmholtz instability). It is most frequent near jet streams, particularly on the cold side of the core and where the jet is curved or changing speed, near sharply curved upper troughs and ridges, and above mountains when waves extend to high levels.
whyWrong: Surface heating produces convective turbulence at low and medium levels, usually with cumulus.
Fog and stratus go with smooth, stable air near the ground.
Light winds at all levels mean little shear and little CAT.
samples.examTip: No cloud and no weather-radar echo: CAT cannot be seen, so use forecasts and reports.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a reliable sign of clear air turbulence?
options: A forecast CAT area on the high-level significant weather chart
Pilot reports of turbulence by other aircraft at similar levels
A strong wind shear between levels on the forecast upper wind chart
A bright return on the weather radar display
samples.explanation: Weather radar detects precipitation-sized drops; clear air gives no echo, so CAT does not appear on airborne weather radar. Crews must rely on forecast CAT areas (SIGWX), the wind shear seen on upper wind charts, pilot reports and the company's turbulence information.
whyWrong: SIGWX charts show forecast CAT areas with their vertical limits; they are a main source of warning.
Pilot reports are among the best real-time indications of CAT.
Strong vertical shear is the cause of CAT, so it is a good indicator.
samples.examTip: If the question mentions radar, it is the wrong tool for CAT.

samples.prompt: Which set of conditions is most favourable for strong mountain waves downwind of a ridge?
options: A strong wind across the ridge, increasing with height, with a stable layer near the crest
A wind parallel to the ridge, decreasing with height
A strong wind perpendicular to the ridge in a completely unstable air mass with thunderstorms
Light and variable winds with a very unstable atmosphere
samples.explanation: Mountain (lee) waves form when a fairly strong wind blows across a ridge and the air near crest level is stable. The stable layer acts like a spring, so the air oscillates downwind in a series of crests and troughs. Waves are strongest when the wind is within about 30° of perpendicular to the ridge, increases with height without much change in direction, and the stable layer is near the crest with less stable air above. The Himalaya in winter and spring, with the subtropical jet overhead, give powerful waves.
whyWrong: A wind along the ridge does not have to cross it, so it does not set up a wave.
Instability breaks up the wave pattern into convection; waves need a stable layer.
Light winds give no wave; instability gives convection instead of waves.
samples.examTip: Waves need stability; convection needs instability.

samples.prompt: A crew in cruise at FL370 enters moderate clear air turbulence near a jet stream. Which action is generally most appropriate?
options: Disconnect the autopilot and make large control inputs to hold altitude exactly
Increase speed to the maximum operating speed to get through quickly
Turn to fly along the jet axis at the same level, where the turbulence is weakest
Fly the turbulence penetration speed, secure the cabin and request a level change
samples.explanation: Turbulence penetration speed gives a margin against both the stall and the structural limits. CAT usually occurs in shallow layers, so a change of level of a few thousand feet often gets out of it, and a report helps other crews. A special air report is required for severe turbulence. Expect it near the jet core, especially on the cold (polar) side.
