whyWrong: Large inputs to hold altitude raise the structural loads; follow the operator's turbulence procedure instead.
Higher speed increases the loads from each gust and reduces the margin to the structural limits.
The strongest shear, and often the worst turbulence, is close to the jet core; staying at that level is not an escape.
samples.examTip: Severe turbulence must be reported by a special air report.

samples.prompt: The ITCZ is best described as:
options: The boundary between polar and tropical air in mid-latitudes
A belt of sinking air at about 30° latitude with clear skies
A line of thunderstorms that forms only over the Atlantic
The zone where the two trade-wind systems converge, with Cb and showers
samples.explanation: The inter-tropical convergence zone is where the north-east and south-east trades meet near the equatorial low-pressure belt. The convergence forces air to rise, so the ITCZ is marked by bands and clusters of Cu and Cb, heavy showers and thunderstorms, and squalls, with light winds (the doldrums) in between. Its width and activity vary a lot from day to day.
whyWrong: That is the polar front.
That is the subtropical high-pressure belt.
The ITCZ circles the globe over oceans and continents.
samples.examTip: Convergence = lifting = cloud.

samples.prompt: Which conditions are needed for a tropical cyclone to form over the Bay of Bengal?
options: A strong subsidence inversion and dry air at mid levels
A sea of 26.5 °C or more, latitude above about 5°, weak shear and an initial disturbance
Cold sea water, a position on the equator and strong vertical wind shear
A frontal wave between polar and tropical air
samples.explanation: A tropical cyclone needs a deep layer of warm ocean (about 26.5 °C or more), enough Coriolis effect to spin up the circulation (so at least about 5° from the equator), weak vertical wind shear so the warm core can stay upright, moist mid levels and a pre-existing disturbance such as a low or a monsoon trough. The energy comes from latent heat released in the convection.
whyWrong: A subsidence inversion and dry mid-level air both suppress the deep convection needed.
Cold water gives no energy, there is no Coriolis effect on the equator to start the rotation, and strong shear tears developing storms apart.
Tropical cyclones are non-frontal systems that draw their energy from latent heat.
samples.examTip: Strong vertical shear is the reason the north Indian Ocean has few cyclones at the height of the monsoon.

samples.prompt: IMD classifies a low-pressure system in the north Indian Ocean as a Cyclonic Storm, and assigns it a name, when its maximum sustained surface wind reaches:
samples.explanation: IMD (RSMC New Delhi) classifies systems by the maximum sustained surface wind: Depression 17–27 kt, Deep Depression 28–33 kt, Cyclonic Storm 34–47 kt, Severe Cyclonic Storm 48–63 kt, Very Severe 64–89 kt, Extremely Severe 90–119 kt and Super Cyclonic Storm 120 kt or more. A system is named when it becomes a Cyclonic Storm, using the list drawn up by the WMO/ESCAP Panel member countries.
whyWrong: 17–27 kt is a Depression.
64–89 kt is a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm.
28–33 kt is a Deep Depression.
samples.examTip: 34 kt (gale force) is where naming starts.

samples.prompt: A tropical cyclone in the Bay of Bengal is moving north towards the Odisha coast. Which side of the storm has the strongest winds and the greatest storm surge at landfall?
options: The eye, where the winds are strongest
The left-hand (western) side, where the wind blows offshore
The right-hand (eastern) side of the track
Both sides equally, because a cyclone is symmetrical
samples.explanation: Cyclones turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. On the right of the track the circulation and the forward motion of the storm add together, so the winds are strongest; this is the 'dangerous semicircle'. A storm moving north into the Odisha coast drives onshore winds to the right of its landfall point, piling up the sea as the storm surge. The eye itself is an area of light winds and sinking air, surrounded by the eye wall with the worst winds and rain.
whyWrong: The eye is relatively calm; the strongest winds are in the eye wall around it.
On the left side in the Northern Hemisphere the forward motion subtracts from the circulation.
Forward motion makes a moving cyclone asymmetric.
samples.examTip: 'Right is rough' in the Northern Hemisphere.

samples.prompt: Why are tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea most frequent in the pre-monsoon months (April–May) and especially the post-monsoon months (October–December), and least frequent in July and August?
options: The ITCZ is on the equator in July and August
Strong vertical wind shear in the core monsoon months stops cyclones organising
The sea is too cold in July and August
Western disturbances destroy all cyclones in July and August
samples.explanation: During the monsoon the low-level flow is a strong south-westerly and the upper flow is the tropical easterly jet, so the vertical wind shear is large. That shear tilts and tears the warm core of any developing system, so the season gives monsoon depressions rather than intense cyclones. In the transition seasons the shear is weak and the sea is warm, so cyclones form, with the Bay of Bengal producing considerably more than the Arabian Sea.
whyWrong: In July and August the ITCZ (monsoon trough) is far north, over north India.
The north Indian Ocean remains warm enough throughout the monsoon.
Western disturbances are mainly a winter phenomenon and stay over the north.
samples.examTip: Low shear + warm sea = cyclone season.

samples.prompt: Under IMD's long-period normal, the south-west monsoon sets in over Kerala on about:
options: 1 June
1 September
15 July
1 May
samples.explanation: The normal onset date over Kerala is 1 June, with a standard deviation of about a week. The monsoon then advances north along both the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches and normally covers the whole country by early to mid July. Withdrawal starts from north-west India in September and is complete by mid October.
whyWrong: September is the start of the monsoon's withdrawal from north-west India.
By mid-July the monsoon has normally already covered almost the whole country.
Pre-monsoon showers occur in May, but the monsoon onset over Kerala normally comes about a month later.
samples.examTip: The Kerala onset is the date examiners like most.

samples.prompt: IMD divides the Indian year into four seasons. Which is the correct set?
options: Spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), winter (December–February)
Winter (Jan–Feb), pre-monsoon (Mar–May), SW monsoon (Jun–Sep), post-monsoon (Oct–Dec)
Dry season (October–May) and wet season (June–September) only
Winter (November–March), summer (April–May), rainy season (June–October) only
samples.explanation: IMD's meteorological seasons are winter (January and February), pre-monsoon or hot weather (March to May), the south-west monsoon (June to September) and the post-monsoon or retreating monsoon (October to December). Each has typical aviation hazards: fog and western disturbances in winter, thunderstorms, dust storms and heat in pre-monsoon, heavy rain and low cloud in the monsoon, and cyclones in the post-monsoon.
whyWrong: The four temperate seasons do not fit Indian weather and are not used by IMD.
A two-season split loses the important pre- and post-monsoon periods.
The traditional three-season division is not the meteorological one used by IMD.
samples.examTip: Link each season to its main flying hazard.

samples.prompt: Which part of India receives the larger share of its annual rainfall from the north-east monsoon in October to December?
options: The Kerala coast, from the June onset onwards
Punjab
Rajasthan
Tamil Nadu and the adjoining south-east coast
samples.explanation: Much of Tamil Nadu lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats for the south-west monsoon. When the winds reverse to north-easterly in October, the air crosses the Bay of Bengal, picks up moisture and brings rain to the south-east coast. Post-monsoon cyclones and depressions add to it. Chennai's wettest months are therefore October and November.
whyWrong: June rain in Kerala is the south-west monsoon, not the north-east monsoon.
Punjab's rain comes from the south-west monsoon and from western disturbances.
Rajasthan is very dry, and most of its little rain falls in July and August.
samples.examTip: Chennai's rain peaks in October–November, not July.

samples.prompt: During a 'break' in the south-west monsoon, what happens?
options: A western disturbance brings snow to central India
The monsoon trough moves to the Himalayan foothills and central India turns dry
The monsoon trough moves south to Sri Lanka and rain falls everywhere across India
The monsoon withdraws completely for the season
samples.explanation: In a break, the monsoon trough moves north to the foothills of the Himalaya. Central and north-west India have a dry spell, while the foothills, the north-east and parts of south-east India get heavy rain, with floods in the Himalayan rivers. In an active phase, the trough lies south of its normal position and rain is heavy over central India and the west coast.
whyWrong: Snow in central India in the monsoon season does not happen.
A trough south of its normal position is an active (vigorous) phase; in a break it moves north.
A break is a temporary pause of days to a couple of weeks, not withdrawal.
samples.examTip: Follow the trough: rain is concentrated along and south of it.

samples.prompt: Why does Pune, about 100 km inland from Mumbai, receive much less monsoon rain than Mumbai?
options: Pune is in the rain shadow on the lee side of the Western Ghats
Pune is on the windward side of the Western Ghats
Pune is higher, so the air holds more moisture there
The monsoon wind does not reach Pune
samples.explanation: The moist south-west monsoon is forced up the steep western face of the Western Ghats, giving very heavy orographic rain on the Konkan coast and the Ghats. The air then descends on the eastern side, warms adiabatically and dries, so the Deccan plateau behind the Ghats is in a rain shadow.
whyWrong: Mumbai is on the windward side; Pune is east of the Ghats, on the lee side.
Height does not increase moisture capacity; colder air holds less.
The monsoon wind does reach Pune, but after crossing the Ghats and losing much of its moisture.
samples.examTip: Rain-shadow questions are föhn questions in disguise.

chapters.title: General Circulation
topics: Surface Pressure Belts and Wind Systems

samples.prompt: The summer season period in India is:
options: January to February
March to May
June to September
October to December
samples.explanation: In the IMD seasons, the summer (hot weather or pre-monsoon) season is March to May. January-February is winter, June-September is the SW monsoon and October-December is the post-monsoon.

samples.prompt: During summer season, which statement is correct regarding Western Disturbances (WDs)?
options: WDs cause TS/DS over Punjab and Rajasthan
No WD affects northern parts of the country
Track of WD is southernmost
WDs cause snowfall over Himalayas only
samples.explanation: In the hot season, Western Disturbances still cross north India, on a more northerly track than in winter, and give thunderstorms and dust storms over Punjab and Rajasthan. So it is wrong that no WD affects the north, the track is not at its southernmost, and their effect is not limited to Himalayan snowfall.

samples.prompt: In the three-cell model of the general circulation, the Hadley cell consists of:
options: Air rising at the equator, sinking near 30°, and returning as the trade winds
Sinking air at the equator and rising air at 30° latitude
An indirect cell between 30° and 60° driven by the other two cells
Rising air at 60° latitude and sinking at the poles
samples.explanation: Strong heating near the equator makes air rise (the equatorial low and the ITCZ). It flows poleward aloft, is turned by Coriolis, and sinks at about 30° in the subtropical highs. At the surface the air returns towards the equator as the trade winds, deflected to north-easterly in the Northern Hemisphere and south-easterly in the Southern. The Ferrel cell (30–60°) and the polar cell (60–90°) complete the model.
whyWrong: Reverses the Hadley cell: air rises at the equator, where heating is greatest.
That describes the Ferrel cell.
That is the polar cell, with rising at about 60° and sinking at the pole.
samples.examTip: Rising air = low pressure belt; sinking air = high pressure belt.

samples.prompt: Many of the world's hot deserts, including the Thar and the Arabian desert, lie near 25–30° latitude because:
options: The polar front lies at those latitudes
Air sinks and warms in the subtropical high-pressure belt
The trade winds bring moist air from the sea at those latitudes
The ITCZ lies at those latitudes all year
samples.explanation: The descending branch of the Hadley cell forms the subtropical high-pressure belt. Sinking air is compressed and warms, so its relative humidity falls and cloud cannot form. Combined with continental interiors, this gives the subtropical deserts. The sailors' name for these calm, high-pressure latitudes is the 'horse latitudes'.
whyWrong: The polar front is a mid-latitude feature, roughly 40–60°.
The trades blow out of these regions, and air over land there is dry.
The ITCZ, with its rising air, brings rain; it is near the equator for most of the year.
samples.examTip: Sinking air is a dry-weather answer every time.

samples.prompt: Which sequence of surface pressure belts and winds, from the equator to the North Pole, is correct?
options: Equatorial high – SE trades – subtropical low – easterlies – polar low
Equatorial low – westerlies – subtropical high – NE trades – polar high
Equatorial low – NE trades – sub-polar low – westerlies – subtropical high – polar easterlies – polar high
Equatorial low – NE trades – subtropical high – westerlies – sub-polar low – polar easterlies – polar high
samples.explanation: Rising air gives low pressure at the equator and about 60°; sinking air gives high pressure at about 30° and at the pole. Winds blow from the highs towards the lows, deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere: north-east trades between 0° and 30°, westerlies between 30° and 60°, and polar easterlies north of 60°. The whole pattern moves north and south with the seasons.
whyWrong: The equatorial belt is low pressure, and in the Northern Hemisphere the trades are north-easterly.
The westerlies and the trades are in each other's places.
The subtropical high and the sub-polar low are in each other's places.
samples.examTip: Draw it once; most questions are then simple to read off.

samples.prompt: TAF are generally valid for a minimum of:
options: 18 hr
12 hr
9 hr
6 hr
samples.explanation: Indian ground-school notes, following IMD practice, give TAF validity as at least 9 hr and at most 30 hr (short 9-hr TAFs for domestic use and longer 12-30 hr TAFs). Note that ICAO Annex 3 itself allows TAF validity of 6 to 30 hr; for the DGCA exam the expected answer is 9 hr.

samples.prompt: For Volcanic Ash and Tropical Cyclones, SIGMET is issued up to how many hours before the period of validity?
options: 4 hr
6 hr
12 hr
24 hr
samples.explanation: For Volcanic Ash and Tropical Cyclones, SIGMET is issued up to 12 hr before the period of validity and updated every 6 hr. Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

samples.prompt: Under ICAO Annex 3, which office maintains a continuous watch over the weather in a flight information region and issues SIGMET for it?
options: The meteorological watch office (MWO) responsible for that FIR
A world area forecast centre
The aeronautical meteorological station at each aerodrome
The aerodrome meteorological office at the FIR's busiest aerodrome
samples.explanation: Annex 3 assigns roles: aeronautical meteorological stations observe; aerodrome meteorological offices forecast for aerodromes and brief crews; meteorological watch offices keep a watch over an FIR, issue SIGMET (and AIRMET where required) and pass information to the area control centre and FIC. World area forecast centres, volcanic ash advisory centres and tropical cyclone advisory centres provide global and regional products. In India these services are provided by IMD.
whyWrong: WAFCs (London and Washington) produce global upper-air and significant-weather forecasts, not FIR SIGMETs.
A met station makes observations (METAR, SPECI); it does not issue SIGMET.
An aerodrome met office prepares aerodrome forecasts and briefings; the FIR watch is the MWO's job.
samples.examTip: SIGMET always traces back to an MWO.

samples.prompt: Which phenomenon would justify the issue of a SIGMET?
options: Mist reducing the visibility to 3000 m at Kolkata airport
A surface wind of 15 kt across the runway
Moderate rain at an aerodrome
Severe turbulence over the Western Ghats at FL200
samples.explanation: SIGMET warns of specified en-route weather that can affect the safety of aircraft: thunderstorms (obscured, embedded, frequent or squall line, with or without hail), tropical cyclones, severe turbulence, severe icing (including freezing rain), severe mountain waves, heavy dust or sand storms, volcanic ash and radioactive cloud. Moderate phenomena at lower levels are the subject of AIRMET where it is issued.
whyWrong: Mist is an aerodrome observation for the METAR, not an en-route hazard for SIGMET.
Crosswind is an aerodrome matter for the METAR, ATIS and ATC.
Rain at an aerodrome is reported in the METAR and TAF; it is not a SIGMET phenomenon.
samples.examTip: 'Severe' or 'tropical cyclone' or 'volcanic ash' = SIGMET; 'moderate' at low levels = AIRMET.

samples.prompt: What is the maximum period of validity of a SIGMET, and the exception?
options: 6 hours; up to 12 hours for volcanic ash
Up to 24 hours, the same as a long TAF
4 hours (6 hours for ash and cyclones)
2 hours, with no exceptions
samples.explanation: Annex 3 limits a SIGMET to a validity of not more than 4 hours. For volcanic ash cloud and tropical cyclones, which can be tracked and forecast further ahead, the validity may extend to 6 hours, and the message includes an outlook of the expected position. A SIGMET is cancelled (CNL) when the phenomenon is no longer expected.
whyWrong: Shifts both limits: 4 hours is the normal maximum and 6 hours the exception.
SIGMET deals with rapidly changing hazards; its validity is far shorter than a TAF's.
Two hours is the validity of a TREND forecast, not a SIGMET.
samples.examTip: 4 for normal, 6 for ash and cyclones.

chapters.title: Station Model
topics: The Central Circle — Total Cloud Cover (N)
Cloud Amount (Nh) and Cloud Base Height (h)

samples.prompt: For non-scheduled National Flights, an advance notice (before ETD) required to be given to AMOs is:
options: 3 hr
6 hr
12 hr
samples.explanation: For non-scheduled national flights, 18-24 hr advance notice before ETD must be given to an AMO so that it can prepare documentation. The 3 hr figure applies to notice given to an AMS.

samples.prompt: Global SIGWX Charts are valid for:
options: 18 hr
24 hr
9 hr
12 hr
samples.explanation: Global SIGWX charts from the WAFCs are fixed-time forecast charts with a 24 hr forecast period (T+24). 18, 9 and 12 hr are not the standard validity.

samples.prompt: AIRMET is SIGMET issued by a MWO for the safety of:
options: Low-level aircraft
High-level aircraft
Both low and high level
All aircraft types
samples.explanation: AIRMET is SIGMET issued by a MWO for the safety of low-level aircraft. Option B (high-level) is incorrect as high-level aircraft receive SIGMET, not AIRMET.

samples.prompt: GAMET is an area forecast in abbreviated plain language for:
options: Low level flights
High level flights
All level flights
International flights only
samples.explanation: GAMET is an area forecast in abbreviated plain language for low level flights. Options B and C are incorrect as GAMET is specifically for low-level operations.

samples.prompt: Airfield warning is issued for expected wind speed:
options: 30 kt
24 kt
15 kt
20 kt
samples.explanation: Airfield warning is issued for expected wind speed of 30 kt. Options B (24 kt) and C (15 kt) are below the threshold for issuing airfield warnings.

chapters.title: Aerodrome Met Reports METAR SPECI And Trend

samples.prompt: In METAR code, what does VRB02KT represent?
options: Wind variable, speed 2 kt
Wind variable between 0 and 2 kt
Wind variable, speed less than 3 kt
Wind variable, speed 2 kt or more
samples.explanation: VRB02KT means variable wind with speed 2 kt. Variable wind is reported if wind is less than 3 kt. Option B is incorrect as VRB02KT specifies exact speed. Option C is partially correct but not precise. Option D is incorrect as variable wind is reported when less than 3 kt.

samples.prompt: How is calm wind reported in METAR?
options: CALM
VRB00KT
0KT
samples.explanation: Calm wind (less than 1 kt) is reported as 00000KT. Option A is not standard code. Option C is incorrect as VRB is for variable wind. Option D is not a valid METAR format.

samples.prompt: For how long is a TREND forecast appended to a METAR valid?
options: 2 hours from the observation time
Until the next TAF for the aerodrome is issued
1 hour from the time of issue
9 hours, like a short TAF
samples.explanation: A TREND is a landing forecast attached to a METAR or SPECI. It describes expected significant changes in wind, visibility, weather and cloud over the 2 hours following the time of the observation, using BECMG or TEMPO with FM, TL or AT for timing. NOSIG means no significant change is expected in those 2 hours.
whyWrong: TREND is tied to the report it is attached to, not to the TAF.
TREND covers 2 hours; 1 hour is the limit on individual TEMPO fluctuations.
9 hours is the validity limit of a short TAF, not of a TREND.
samples.examTip: NOSIG at the end of a METAR is itself a TREND: no significant change for 2 hours.

samples.prompt: Which statement about NOSIG is correct?
options: No significant change is expected in the next 2 hours
The TREND forecast is not available for this report
No significant weather is present at the aerodrome
No SIGMET is currently in force for the FIR
samples.explanation: NOSIG ('no significant change') is a TREND forecast stating that none of the elements are expected to change past the thresholds that would need a TREND change group during the next 2 hours. A METAR showing fog and NOSIG means the fog is expected to persist for at least 2 hours.
whyWrong: A missing TREND is simply not reported; NOSIG is a positive forecast.
Absence of significant weather is shown by the lack of a weather group or by NSW in a forecast change; NOSIG is about change.
SIGMET status is separate and is not shown in a METAR.
samples.examTip: Fog + NOSIG = plan for no improvement before your ETA if within 2 hours.

samples.prompt: A TREND reads 'TEMPO 0800 FG'. What does it forecast?
options: Fog from 0800 UTC
A 40% probability of fog with 800 m visibility in the period
Temporary spells of 800 m in fog, each lasting less than an hour
A lasting change to 800 m in fog within the next 2 hours
samples.explanation: TEMPO describes temporary fluctuations expected to last less than 1 hour each and, in total, less than half the forecast period. 'TEMPO 0800 FG' therefore means the visibility will drop to about 800 m in fog from time to time, with the main conditions applying the rest of the time. A crew must still plan for the worse value during the TEMPO period, according to the operator's rules.
whyWrong: The four figures after TEMPO are a visibility (metres), not a time; times use FM, TL or AT.
Probability groups (PROB30/40) are used in TAFs, not in TRENDs.
A lasting change is BECMG; TEMPO is temporary.
samples.examTip: Four figures straight after TEMPO = visibility, not a time.

chapters.title: TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast)
topics: TAF vs METAR — The Fundamental Distinction

samples.prompt: A TAF is valid for a minimum of how many hours and a maximum of how many hours?
options: Minimum 6 hours, Maximum 24 hours
Minimum 9 hours, Maximum 30 hours
Minimum 12 hours, Maximum 36 hours
Minimum 3 hours, Maximum 18 hours
samples.explanation: Indian ground-school notes (IMD practice) give TAF validity as a minimum of 9 hr and a maximum of 30 hr. 24 hr and 18 hr are not the maximum, and 36 hr exceeds it. (ICAO Annex 3 itself permits 6-30 hr; the DGCA answer is 9-30 hr.)

samples.prompt: How frequently are TAFs with 9-hour validity issued?
options: Every 6 hours
Every 3 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
samples.explanation: 9-hr TAFs (domestic) are issued every 3 hr, while the longer 12-30 hr TAFs are issued every 6 hr. 12- and 24-hourly issue are not the standard.

samples.prompt: What do the groups 'TX27/2209Z TN12/2301Z' in a TAF mean?
options: Temperatures at FL270 and FL120
Maximum temperature 27 °C until 22nd 09Z; then 12 °C
Max 27 °C at 0900Z on the 22nd; min 12 °C at 0100Z on the 23rd
Temperature 27 °C and dew point 12 °C observed at the time of issue
samples.explanation: TX gives the forecast maximum temperature and TN the forecast minimum, each followed by the day and hour at which it is expected (DDHHZ). These are useful for performance planning (maximum temperature) and for judging fog or frost risk (minimum temperature).
whyWrong: TAF temperature groups are surface temperatures.
Each group gives an extreme and the time it is expected, not a period.
The T/Td group belongs to the METAR; in a TAF, TX and TN are forecast extremes with their times.
samples.examTip: A minimum close to the dew point overnight suggests fog.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT included in a TAF?
options: Prevailing visibility
Cloud amount and base
Runway visual range
Surface wind
samples.explanation: A TAF forecasts the surface wind, prevailing visibility, weather, cloud (or vertical visibility) and, where agreed, maximum and minimum temperatures, with change groups. RVR is an observed value assessed along the runway and appears in METAR and SPECI, not in a TAF.
whyWrong: Visibility is always forecast in a TAF.
Cloud amount and base (or NSC, or VV) are forecast in a TAF.
Surface wind is the first forecast element of a TAF.
samples.examTip: RVR = observed only.

samples.prompt: Which statement about change groups in a TAF is correct?
options: 'FM241430': from 1430Z on the 24th, the following conditions replace all earlier ones
'TEMPO' describes changes expected to last for more than half of the TAF period
'PROB50' is used when an alternative value has a 50% probability
'BECMG' is used for changes that occur suddenly and last less than an hour
samples.explanation: FM (from) introduces a self-contained part of the forecast: everything after FMDDHHmm replaces the earlier conditions. BECMG gives a lasting change over a period, normally of up to 2 hours. TEMPO gives temporary fluctuations. PROB30 or PROB40, alone or with TEMPO, give the probability of an alternative value; probabilities below 30% are not worth showing and 50% or more are not 'alternatives'.
whyWrong: TEMPO spells last less than 1 hour each and less than half the period in total.
Only PROB30 and PROB40 are used; at 50% or more the change is forecast directly with BECMG, TEMPO or FM.
BECMG is a lasting change over a period, normally not more than 2 hours (at most 4 hours).
samples.examTip: PROB50 or PROB20 in an option is always wrong.

samples.prompt: A route forecast gives the wind at FL180 as 260°/40 kt and at FL240 as 260°/60 kt. What is the best estimate of the wind at FL210?
samples.explanation: FL210 lies halfway between FL180 and FL240, so interpolate linearly: speed = 40 + (60 − 40) × (3 ÷ 6) = 50 kt, direction unchanged at 260°. Linear interpolation between forecast levels is standard for planning; strong shear near a jet stream can make the real profile less regular.
whyWrong: Takes the lower-level value without interpolating.
Takes the upper-level value without interpolating.
Turns the direction round: winds are given as the direction they blow from, and both levels give 260°.
samples.examTip: Check the fraction: (210 − 180) ÷ (240 − 180) = ½.

samples.prompt: A route forecast issued for a flight from Chennai to Kolkata typically contains which information?
options: En-route winds, temperatures, weather, cloud, icing and turbulence
Only the TAF for the alternate aerodrome
Only the METARs of the departure and destination aerodromes
Surface winds and runway state at every aerodrome along the coast
samples.explanation: A route forecast describes the conditions expected along a route for a stated period: winds and temperatures at specified levels, significant weather, cloud amounts and heights, icing and turbulence, the freezing level and the tropopause height. For low-level flights, area forecasts (for example GAMET where issued) give similar information for an area. Together with the TAFs and SIGMETs they form the flight documentation.
whyWrong: A TAF is an aerodrome forecast; the route forecast describes the en-route conditions.
METARs are observations at aerodromes; a route forecast covers the route between them.
Runway state is an aerodrome item, not part of a route forecast.
samples.examTip: Aerodrome products (METAR, TAF) and en-route products (route forecast, SIGWX, SIGMET) answer different questions.

samples.prompt: A route forecast gives the temperature at FL280 as ISA −3 °C. Taking ISA as 15 °C at MSL, 2 °C per 1,000 ft and −56.5 °C above 36,090 ft, what outside air temperature should the crew expect?
samples.explanation: Formula: ISA at FL = 15 − 2 × (FL ÷ 10) °C up to 36,090 ft, −56.5 °C above; OAT = ISA + deviation; deviation = OAT − ISA. ISA at FL280 = 15 − 2 × 28 = −41 °C. OAT = ISA + deviation = −41 °C − 3 = −44 °C.
whyWrong: Applied the deviation twice: gives −47 °C.
Added the deviation to the sea-level 15 °C instead of to the ISA temperature at the level: gives 12 °C.
Applied the deviation with the wrong sign: gives −38 °C.
samples.examTip: Work out ISA at the level first, then apply the deviation.

samples.prompt: A route forecast gives FL240 090108M30. Taking the ISA lapse rate as 2°C per 1 000 ft, what is the ISA deviation at that level?
options: ISA +3°C
ISA −3°C
ISA −9°C
ISA −45°C
samples.explanation: The forecast for FL240 is 090°/108 kt, −30°C. ISA at FL240 is −33.0°C, so the deviation is ISA +3.0°C.
whyWrong: Reversed the sign (ISA minus forecast)
Used 1.5°C per 1 000 ft for the ISA lapse rate
Measured the deviation from the sea-level 15°C
samples.examTip: Common trap: reversed the sign (ISA minus forecast).

samples.prompt: A route forecast for a flight across the Bay of Bengal in May mentions 'FRQ CB TOP FL450' and a freezing level of FL160. Which planning conclusion is sound?
options: Expect frequent Cb above cruise level and icing above FL160; plan deviations and extra fuel
FRQ means the CB are isolated and easy to avoid
Airframe icing is only possible below the freezing level at FL160
The cumulonimbus will be below a cruise level of FL350, so no deviation is needed
samples.explanation: 'FRQ CB' means frequent cumulonimbus with little or no separation between them, a widespread hazard of turbulence, hail, icing and lightning. With tops at FL450, most jet cruise levels are inside or close to the cloud. The freezing level at FL160 marks the bottom of the icing layer in cloud. In the pre-monsoon Bay of Bengal such forecasts call for weather-radar avoidance and extra fuel for deviations.
whyWrong: FRQ (frequent) means little or no separation between cells; ISOL means isolated.
Supercooled water, and hence icing, exists ABOVE the freezing level, not below it.
Tops near FL450 are above FL350, so the aircraft would be inside or near the cloud.
samples.examTip: Compare forecast tops with your cruise level first.

chapters.title: Meteorological Documentation and Briefing
topics: Flight Documentation — Met T-3 and Met T-4
The Briefing Process: A Critical Safety Net

samples.prompt: In the jet-stream section of a ROFOR (after 11111), the position group 27105 indicates:
options: Jet stream at 27°N/105°E
Wind at 27000 ft is 105 kt
Maximum wind at 27000 ft is 105 kt
Temperature at 27000 ft is -105°C
samples.explanation: In the jet-stream section the position group gives latitude then longitude, so 27105 locates the jet core at 27°N 105°E. Height and speed come in the following group, so B and C misread a position group as a wind group.

samples.prompt: The WAFS high-level significant weather chart (SWH) covers which band of flight levels?
options: FL100 to FL450
FL250 to FL630
FL450 to FL630
Surface to FL100
samples.explanation: The world area forecast centres (London and Washington) issue high-level SIGWX for FL250 to FL630, valid at fixed times (00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC). Medium-level charts cover FL100 to FL450 for specified regions. Low-level forecasts below FL100 are produced nationally or regionally.
whyWrong: FL100–FL450 is the medium-level SIGWX (SWM), issued for limited areas.
This band is too narrow: most jet cruise levels are below FL450.
Surface to FL100 is covered by low-level charts and area forecasts.
samples.examTip: SIGWX charts are valid at a fixed time, not for a period.

samples.prompt: Under Annex 3, which of the following normally forms part of the meteorological flight documentation for a scheduled flight from Mumbai to Delhi?
options: Only the METAR for the departure aerodrome
A forecast for the next 7 days at the destination
SIGWX, winds/temperatures, METAR, TAF and SIGMET
Climatological averages of wind and weather for the route
samples.explanation: Flight documentation includes forecasts of upper winds and temperatures, significant weather charts, METAR and SPECI (with TREND), TAFs for the departure, destination and alternate aerodromes, SIGMET and appropriate special air reports, and volcanic ash and tropical cyclone advisories when relevant. In India it is provided by IMD's aerodrome meteorological offices, increasingly through online self-briefing.
whyWrong: One METAR is not enough; documentation covers the whole flight and the alternates.
Seven-day forecasts are not aviation flight documentation.
Climatological data help long-term planning but are not flight documentation for a particular flight.
samples.examTip: Remember the alternates: their TAFs and METARs are always included.

samples.prompt: Which statement about jet streams on a WAFS high-level SIGWX chart is correct?
options: Only easterly jets are drawn on charts for the Indian region
Jets of 80 kt or more, with the core level and speed shown
Jets are drawn wherever the wind exceeds 30 kt
Jets are shown only on the medium-level chart
samples.explanation: On the high-level SIGWX chart, jet streams with speeds of 80 kt or more are drawn as heavy lines with arrowheads. The core speed is given by barbs (10 kt), half-barbs and pennants (50 kt) and the core level as FLxxx. Bars across the axis mark changes of speed of 20 kt or more. Over India expect the westerly subtropical jet in winter and the tropical easterly jet in the monsoon.
whyWrong: Both westerly and easterly jets are drawn: the subtropical jet in winter, the tropical easterly jet in summer.
The SIGWX threshold is 80 kt; 30 kt is far too low (and 60 kt is the WMO definition of a jet).
Jet streams are a key feature of the high-level chart.
samples.examTip: Pennant = 50 kt; full barb = 10 kt.

samples.prompt: During a briefing for a 0300Z departure from Lucknow in January, the crew receives a TAF with 'TEMPO 0200/0500 0300 FG' and a METAR showing 1200 m in mist with NOSIG. Which is the best course?
options: Plan for the TEMPO fog and arrange a take-off alternate
Plan only for the 1200 m visibility in the METAR
Delay the briefing until the fog is reported
Ignore the TEMPO group because the METAR shows NOSIG
samples.explanation: A METAR describes conditions now; the TAF describes the expected conditions for the departure period. A TEMPO 300 m fog during the departure window must be considered against the take-off minima and against the need to return or divert after take-off. Operators' rules decide exactly how TEMPO is applied, but a sound briefing never ignores it.
whyWrong: The METAR is an observation; the departure and the period after it must be planned against the forecast.
Delaying preparation removes the chance to plan alternates and fuel properly.
The NOSIG TREND is valid for 2 hours from the observation and does not cancel the TAF's TEMPO.
samples.examTip: Check every group that covers your departure and arrival times.

samples.prompt: A photo electric cell produces electricity when:
options: two metals are heated
exposed to a light source
a light source is removed
exposed to the heat of the sun
samples.explanation: A photoelectric cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy: light striking the photosensitive surface releases electrons and produces an EMF. Light is one of the six basic means of producing an EMF.

samples.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches the unit with its measurement?
options: current - is the volt
resistance - is the ohm
electric power - is the capacitor
EMF - is the amp
samples.explanation: Resistance is correctly measured in ohms. Current is measured in amperes (not volts). Power is measured in watts (not capacitor). EMF is measured in volts (not amps).

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the six basic means to provide EMF?
options: Friction
Chemical Action
Magnetism
Nuclear fission
samples.explanation: The six basic means are: Friction, Chemical Action, Magnetism, Heat, Light, and Pressure. Nuclear fission is not listed as a basic means of producing EMF.

samples.prompt: Two identical 14 Ω lamps are connected in parallel across a 28 V bus. One lamp filament breaks. What happens?
options: The supply current halves from 4 A to 2 A and the remaining lamp stays at the same brightness
The supply current falls to zero, because breaking one filament opens the circuit for both of the lamps
The supply current stays at 4 A and the remaining lamp becomes twice as bright
The supply current doubles to 8 A and the remaining lamp becomes dimmer
samples.explanation: Each lamp has the full 28 V across it and draws I = 28 ÷ 14 = 2 A, so the bus supplies 4 A in total. When one filament breaks, its branch carries nothing, but the other lamp still has 28 V across it and draws 2 A. The supply current halves and the good lamp is unaffected. This is why aircraft loads are wired in parallel.
whyWrong: That would happen in a series circuit; a break in one parallel branch leaves the other complete.
Each parallel branch has the full 28 V across it independently, so the good lamp's current and brightness do not change.
Removing a branch raises the total resistance, so the current falls, not rises.
samples.examTip: Ask 'has the voltage across this load changed?' If not, neither has its current or power.

samples.prompt: Which statement about a simple series DC circuit is INCORRECT?
options: The same current flows through every component
The individual voltage drops add up to the supply voltage
The voltage across each resistor is the same and equal to the supply voltage
The total resistance is found by adding together all of the individual resistances in the circuit
samples.explanation: In a series circuit there is one path, so the current is common to every component, total resistance is R1 + R2 + ..., and the voltage drops (I × R for each) add up to the supply voltage. The voltage across each resistor is therefore NOT the supply voltage: it is a share in proportion to its resistance. Equal voltage across each branch is the property of a parallel circuit.
whyWrong: True: a series circuit has only one path, so the current is the same everywhere.
True: this is Kirchhoff's voltage law; the drops share out the supply voltage.
True: series resistances simply add.
samples.examTip: Swap 'series' for 'parallel' in your head: the incorrect statement is usually the other circuit's rule.

samples.prompt: Why is a high-current load such as a hydraulic pump motor usually switched through a relay or contactor rather than directly by the cockpit switch?
options: So that the load cannot be switched off once it has been selected in flight
So that a low-current cockpit circuit can switch the heavy load current near the load
Because a relay converts the DC supply into the AC needed by the pump motor
Because the relay coil limits the motor current to a safe value and so replaces the circuit breaker
samples.explanation: A relay (or, for very heavy currents, a contactor) uses a small coil current to close contacts that carry the large load current. The cockpit switch then handles only the coil current through light wiring, while the heavy cable runs directly from the bus to the load near where it is installed. This saves weight, reduces volt drop and keeps arcing contacts out of the flight deck.
whyWrong: A relay is an ordinary remotely controlled switch; it switches off when its coil is de-energised.
A relay only makes and breaks contacts; it does not change DC into AC.
The coil only operates the contacts; the load current is set by the load, and protection is the job of the circuit breaker.
samples.examTip: Relay questions nearly always come back to 'remote switching of heavy current with light control wiring'.

samples.prompt: Which statement about time switches (time-delay relays) in aircraft circuits is correct?
options: They can be triggered only mechanically, by a cam or lever on the equipment they control
They are used only in fire-detection circuits, where they confirm a warning before it is shown
They make or break a circuit a set time after being triggered, and the trigger may be electrical or mechanical
They operate instantly when triggered and then reset after a set time, like a circuit breaker
samples.explanation: A time switch delays the operation of its contacts by a set period after it is triggered. The trigger can be electrical (a signal such as 'APU shut down') or mechanical (a lever or cam movement). A typical use is closing the APU air intake door about 30 seconds after the APU stops, so that it can run down and cool.
whyWrong: Many time switches are started by an electrical signal; mechanical triggering is only one option.
Time switches are used widely, for example to close an APU air intake door a set time after shutdown.
That reverses the idea: the delay comes before the switching action, and a circuit breaker responds to current, not time.
samples.examTip: Avoid options that say 'only': time switches can be started either way.

samples.prompt: What normally distinguishes a solenoid (contactor) from a relay in aircraft electrical systems?
options: The solenoid works only on AC, whereas a relay works only on DC
The solenoid has a moving core (plunger) and is used for heavy currents such as the starter
The solenoid has a fixed core and a hinged armature, and is used only for very light signal currents
The solenoid has no coil and is operated by a bimetallic strip
samples.explanation: In a solenoid the coil pulls a moving soft-iron plunger into its centre; the plunger carries heavy contacts, giving a strong pull for high-current circuits such as the battery, external power and starter contactors. A relay usually has a fixed core that attracts a hinged armature and is used for lighter currents.
whyWrong: Both types can be built for AC or DC coils; the supply type is not the distinction.
This describes the usual relay construction; solenoids are the heavy-current device.
A bimetallic strip operates a thermal switch or circuit breaker, not a solenoid.
samples.examTip: If an option mentions the starter or battery contactor, think solenoid.

samples.prompt: The main landing gear down-lock sensing on many modern aircraft uses proximity sensors rather than microswitches. What is the main advantage?
options: They sense a metal target without contact, so there is nothing to wear, stick or get contaminated
They act as a mechanical lock for the gear as well as giving the electrical down-and-locked signal to the cockpit
They can only fail in the 'gear down and locked' state, which is the safe state
They need no electrical supply because the target generates the signal
samples.explanation: A proximity sensor (usually inductive) detects when a metal target comes close, because the target changes the inductance of the sensor coil. There is no actuating arm and no contact to bounce, wear or ice up, which makes it more reliable than a microswitch in the dirty, wet and vibrating environment of a wheel well.
whyWrong: The sensor only signals position; the mechanical lock is a separate part of the gear.
Like any sensor it can fail in different ways; monitoring electronics detect sensor faults.
A proximity sensor is powered; the target changes the sensor's magnetic field (inductance) and the electronics detect it.
samples.examTip: 'No moving parts, no contact' is the key phrase for proximity sensors.

samples.prompt: A diode is fitted across the coil of a DC relay that is switched by a transistor. What is its purpose?
options: To stop the relay operating if the supply is connected with reversed polarity
To hold the relay closed for a short time after the switch is opened, so that the load does not drop out on brief interruptions
To rectify the DC supply so that the relay coil receives AC
To absorb the coil's back-EMF spike at switch-off, protecting the transistor and contacts
samples.explanation: When current through an inductive coil is interrupted, the collapsing magnetic field induces a large reverse voltage (back EMF) that can destroy a transistor or burn contacts. A diode connected across the coil, reverse-biased to the supply, conducts only when that spike appears, letting the coil current die away harmlessly. It is called a suppression or freewheel diode.
whyWrong: With reversed polarity the diode would conduct and short the supply; polarity protection uses a series diode, not one across the coil.
Any small delay is a side effect; the purpose is to suppress the voltage spike.
The supply is already DC; the diode is reverse-biased in normal operation and carries no current.
samples.examTip: Coil + diode in parallel = spike suppression; diode in series = polarity or reverse-current protection.

chapters.title: DC Electrics - Circuit Protection and Capacitors
topics: Circuit Protection Devices — The Two Families

samples.prompt: In an electrical circuit, a fuse normally opens the circuit:
options: After full fault current is reached
Before full fault current is reached
At the same time as full fault current is reached
Only when the circuit breaker fails
samples.explanation: A fuse normally melts and opens the circuit before the full (prospective) fault current is reached, whereas a circuit breaker opens only after the full fault current has been reached. This difference in timing is the basic distinction between the two devices.

samples.prompt: What does it mean when an aircraft circuit breaker is described as 'trip-free'?
options: Its contacts open on a fault even if the button is being held in, so it cannot be forced to stay closed
It never trips in flight, so it can be used as a switch
It resets itself automatically once the fault has cleared and the bimetal has cooled, so no crew action is needed
It can be reset any number of times without risk
samples.explanation: A trip-free breaker's mechanism is arranged so that the contacts open on overload regardless of the position of the operating button. A pilot pushing the button in, or holding it there, cannot keep a faulty circuit energised. This prevents overheating of wiring when someone tries to restore an essential service.
whyWrong: Every breaker trips on overload; 'trip-free' describes how it trips, not that it never does.
Automatic resetting describes a different (cycling) type, not a trip-free breaker.
Repeated resets onto a fault overheat wiring and are a fire risk.
samples.examTip: 'Free to trip even when held in' is the phrase to match.

samples.prompt: The rating of a fuse or circuit breaker in an aircraft circuit is chosen mainly to protect:
options: The equipment it supplies, against the voltage spikes and surges that occur when heavy loads are switched
The wiring of that circuit, so that a fault cannot overheat the cable and start a fire
The generator from overspeed when the load is high
The pilot from electric shock when operating the switch
samples.explanation: Fuses and circuit breakers respond to excess current. The rating is matched to the current-carrying capacity of the cable so that the device opens before the cable can overheat. Equipment has its own internal protection; the circuit protection device is there to stop a short circuit turning into a wiring fire.
whyWrong: A fuse is far too slow to stop a voltage spike; suppression devices do that.
Generator overspeed is a drive problem; a fuse responds only to current in its own circuit.
Shock protection is not the purpose; aircraft voltages and switch design take care of that.
samples.examTip: If in doubt between 'equipment' and 'wiring', choose wiring.

samples.prompt: What is a current limiter, and where would you expect to find one?
options: A slow-acting heavy-duty fuse that rides through short overloads, used on main feeders such as bus ties
A fast-acting fuse that opens on the slightest overload, used in avionics circuits
A thermal circuit breaker that can be reset from the flight deck, used mainly in the cabin and cockpit lighting circuits
A variable resistor that reduces current as the battery voltage rises, used in the charging circuit
samples.explanation: A current limiter is a heavy-duty fuse with a high-melting-point (typically copper) element. It has a long time lag, so it carries large overloads for short periods without blowing, but it will open on a sustained heavy fault. That makes it suitable for protecting main feeders and bus ties, where a fast fuse would blow on normal transients.
whyWrong: A current limiter is deliberately slow: heavy feeders must ride through short overloads and motor starting currents.
A current limiter is a fuse element; it cannot be reset.
Battery charging current is controlled by the voltage regulator or charger, not by a current limiter fuse.
samples.examTip: Think 'big cables, slow fuse' for current limiters.

samples.prompt: A 2 µF and a 6 µF capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V DC supply and allowed to charge fully. What is the voltage across the 2 µF capacitor?
options: 9 V
6 V
3 V
samples.explanation: Capacitors in series carry the same charge. Total C = (2 × 6) ÷ (2 + 6) = 1.5 µF, so Q = CV = 1.5 µF × 12 V = 18 µC. Across the 2 µF capacitor V = Q ÷ C = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 V, and across the 6 µF it is 18 ÷ 6 = 3 V. The two add to 12 V.
whyWrong: Splits the voltage equally, which only happens when the capacitors are equal.
Shares the voltage in proportion to capacitance; in series the SMALLER capacitor takes the larger voltage.
Puts the full supply across one capacitor; in series the voltage is shared.
samples.examTip: Check your answer by adding the two capacitor voltages: they must equal the supply.

samples.prompt: A 24 V aircraft battery is to be built from lead-acid cells, and another from nickel-cadmium cells. How many cells does each need?
options: 12 lead-acid cells; 19 or 20 nickel-cadmium cells
24 cells of either type
12 nickel-cadmium cells; 20 lead-acid cells
6 lead-acid cells; 12 nickel-cadmium cells
samples.explanation: A lead-acid cell has a nominal voltage of about 2 V, so 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cells. A nickel-cadmium cell is about 1.2 V, so 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20 cells (19-cell batteries are also used). Cells are connected in series to add their voltages.
whyWrong: Assumes 1 V per cell; lead-acid is about 2 V and Ni-Cd about 1.2 V per cell.
Swaps the cell voltages of the two chemistries.
Six lead-acid cells make a 12 V battery, and 12 Ni-Cd cells only about 14 V.
samples.examTip: Divide the battery voltage by the cell voltage; series cells add volts.

samples.prompt: A battery of 72 Ah supplies an emergency load of 8 A. Ideally, how long will it last?
options: 7 min
270 min
900 min
540 min
samples.explanation: Endurance = capacity ÷ load = 72 ÷ 8 = 9.00 h = 540 min (in practice less: capacity falls at high discharge rates).
whyWrong: Divided the load by the capacity
Ignored the parallel strings
Read the decimal hours as minutes ×100
samples.examTip: Common trap: divided the load by the capacity.

samples.prompt: An aircraft's 24 V battery is rated 36 Ah and only 80% of its rated capacity can be relied on. After both generators fail, the essential loads draw 12 A. For about how long can the battery supply them?
options: 3 h 45 min
2 h 24 min
2 h 40 min
3 h 00 min
samples.explanation: Usable capacity = 36 Ah × 0.8 = 28.8 Ah. Time = capacity ÷ current = 28.8 ÷ 12 = 2.4 h. Convert the decimal: 0.4 h × 60 = 24 min, so 2 h 24 min. In practice the time is shorter at high discharge rates and in the cold.
whyWrong: Divides by 0.8 instead of multiplying, as if the battery had more capacity than its rating.
Reads 2.4 h as 2 h 40 min; 0.4 h is 0.4 × 60 = 24 minutes.
Uses the full 36 Ah and ignores the 80% usable capacity.
samples.examTip: Decimal hours trap: 0.4 h is 24 minutes, not 40.

samples.prompt: Why can a hydrometer NOT be used to judge the state of charge of a nickel-cadmium battery?
options: Its potassium hydroxide electrolyte is not consumed, so the specific gravity hardly changes with charge
The cells are sealed with a pressure relief valve that must never be opened
The specific gravity rises to 1.280 at full charge, which is beyond the range of a standard servicing hydrometer
The electrolyte is a solid paste that cannot be sampled
samples.explanation: In a Ni-Cd cell the potassium hydroxide electrolyte only carries ions between the plates and is not consumed, so its specific gravity stays almost constant whatever the state of charge. Charge is judged instead by voltage under load or a capacity check. In a lead-acid cell the sulphuric acid IS used up during discharge, so its SG falls and a hydrometer works.
whyWrong: Vented Ni-Cd cells have removable vent caps for servicing; sealing is not the reason.
1.280 is about the fully charged value of a LEAD-ACID cell, not a Ni-Cd figure.
The electrolyte is a liquid (potassium hydroxide solution) that can be checked for level.
samples.examTip: Hydrometer = lead-acid only.

samples.prompt: Thermal runaway in a nickel-cadmium battery is best described as:
options: A slow loss of capacity caused by repeated shallow discharges
A fall in electrolyte temperature that freezes the cells and stops the battery delivering current
Heat lowers the cells' internal resistance, so the charger drives more current, making still more heat
A reverse current flowing from the battery back into the generator after the generator fails, heating its windings
samples.explanation: When a Ni-Cd battery gets hot, its internal resistance falls. On a constant-voltage charging bus that lets the charging current increase, which heats the cells further and lowers the resistance again: a self-feeding cycle that can boil the electrolyte and destroy the battery. Signs are a battery overheat warning and a high or rising charge current; the action is to disconnect the battery from the charging source.
whyWrong: Loss of capacity from shallow cycling is a separate effect, not a heating chain reaction.
Cold reduces capacity, but runaway is an overheating process.
Reverse current is prevented by the reverse current relay or the rectifier; it is not thermal runaway.
samples.examTip: Battery overheat or high charging current after start = think thermal runaway; isolate the battery.

chapters.title: DC Electrics - Magnetism
topics: The Magnetic Effect of a Current
The Magnetic Field of a Solenoid

samples.prompt: When a magnet is freely suspended and comes to rest, the end nearest to the earth's magnetic north pole is called:
options: South seeking pole
North seeking pole
Neutral pole
Equatorial pole
samples.explanation: A freely suspended magnet aligns with the earth's field. The end that points towards the earth's magnetic north is the north-seeking, or N, pole of the magnet.

samples.prompt: The core of an electromagnet used in a relay is made of soft iron rather than hardened steel because soft iron:
options: Keeps most of its magnetism after the current stops, so the relay stays latched without needing coil power
Magnetises strongly with little current and loses almost all of its magnetism when the current stops
Cannot be magnetised at all, so the field comes from the coil alone
Is a poor conductor of magnetic flux, which limits the coil current
samples.explanation: Soft iron has high permeability, so it concentrates the coil's flux and gives a strong pull for a modest current. It also has low retentivity (little residual magnetism), so the armature releases when the coil is de-energised. Hard steel keeps its magnetism and is used for permanent magnets. The strength of an electromagnet depends on the ampere-turns and the core material.
whyWrong: High retentivity is the property of hard steel, used for permanent magnets.
Soft iron is strongly magnetic; that is why it concentrates the coil's field.
Soft iron has a HIGH permeability; it conducts flux very well.
samples.examTip: Temporary magnet = soft iron; permanent magnet = hard steel or special alloys.

samples.prompt: Which rule gives the direction of motion of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, as in an electric motor?
options: Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion
The right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, fingers showing the motion
Lenz's law: the motion always opposes the field
Fleming's right-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion
samples.explanation: For a motor, current flows in a conductor lying in a field and a force results. Fleming's left-hand rule, with the thumb, first and second fingers at right angles, gives the direction: First finger = Field (N to S), seCond finger = Current (conventional), thuMb = Motion. Generators use the right-hand rule.
whyWrong: The grip rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a conductor, not the force on it.
Lenz's law gives the direction of an induced current, not the motor force.
The right-hand rule is for generators, where the motion is given and the induced current is found.
samples.examTip: Ask whether current is supplied (motor, left hand) or produced (generator, right hand).

samples.prompt: A straight conductor 0.2 m long carries 10 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What force acts on it?
options: 4 N
1 N
samples.explanation: The force on a conductor at right angles to a field is F = B × I × L = 0.5 T × 10 A × 0.2 m = 1 N. If the conductor were at an angle θ to the field, F = BIL sin θ, and it would be zero along the field lines.
whyWrong: Divides the current by the field instead of multiplying (10 ÷ 0.5 × 0.2).
Divides by the current instead of multiplying (0.5 × 0.2 ÷ 10).
Divides the field by the length and multiplies by the current instead of using B × I × L.
samples.examTip: Check the units: tesla × ampere × metre gives newtons.

samples.prompt: A conductor is moved through a magnetic field and a current is induced in a closed circuit. According to Lenz's law, the direction of that current is such that:
options: Its magnetic field aids the motion, so the conductor accelerates
Its own magnetic field opposes the change (the motion) that produces it
It flows from the north pole to the south pole of the field magnet
It always flows in the same direction whatever the direction of motion of the conductor
samples.explanation: Faraday's law says an EMF is induced whenever the magnetic flux linking a circuit changes, in proportion to the rate of change. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced current sets up a field that opposes the change causing it. That is why a loaded generator is harder to turn: the work done against this opposition becomes electrical energy.
whyWrong: If the induced current aided the motion, energy would be created from nothing; it opposes it.
Field lines run N to S outside a magnet; the current direction depends on the motion, not on the poles alone.
Reversing the motion reverses the induced current, which is why a rotating coil produces AC.
samples.examTip: 'Opposes the change' is the Lenz answer; Faraday gives the size (rate of change of flux).

chapters.title: DC Electrics - Generators and Alternators
topics: Characteristics of the Series Wound DC Generator
Characteristics of the Shunt Wound DC Generator

samples.prompt: In a DC generator, what is the function of the commutator?
options: To supply the field winding with alternating current
To reverse the coil connections each half-turn, so the AC induced in the armature leaves as DC
To disconnect the generator from the bus when its voltage falls
To regulate the output voltage by varying the field current as the engine speed and the load change
samples.explanation: Any coil rotating in a magnetic field has an alternating EMF induced in it. The commutator, a split copper ring on the armature shaft with brushes bearing on it, swaps the coil connections to the external circuit each time the EMF reverses. The output current therefore always flows the same way: a mechanical rectifier.
whyWrong: The field of a DC generator is fed with DC from the generator itself.
Disconnection is done by the reverse current relay (cut-out).
Voltage regulation is the job of the voltage regulator acting on the field current.
samples.examTip: Brushes and commutator: DC generator. Rectifier diodes: alternator.

samples.prompt: The voltage regulator of an aircraft DC generator keeps the output voltage constant by:
options: Varying the current in the field winding as engine speed and electrical load change
Switching loads off the bus when the voltage rises
Varying the resistance of the armature winding through a carbon pile in series with it
Varying the engine speed to keep the generator rpm constant
samples.explanation: Generated EMF is proportional to the field flux and the speed of rotation. Speed varies with engine rpm and load varies with demand, so the regulator adjusts the field current: more field current when the voltage drops, less when it rises. Older systems used a carbon pile or vibrating-contact regulator; modern ones are transistorised.
whyWrong: Load shedding is a separate function and does not regulate voltage.
The armature resistance is fixed by its construction; the field is what is controlled.
Generator speed follows the engine; the regulator cannot control it.
samples.examTip: Any question about controlling generator VOLTAGE: the answer involves the field.

samples.prompt: A DC generator runs in parallel with the battery on the main bus. During engine shutdown its voltage falls below the battery voltage. What does the reverse current relay (cut-out) do?
options: Closes to connect a second generator in its place
Stays closed so that the battery keeps the generator turning
Increases the field current to restore the generator voltage, so that it can continue to share the bus load
Opens and disconnects the generator, so the battery cannot discharge through it and drive it as a motor
samples.explanation: The reverse current relay closes when the generator voltage exceeds the bus/battery voltage and the generator can supply current. If the generator voltage falls below the bus voltage, current flows back from the bus into it. The relay senses this reverse current and opens at its set value, isolating the generator.
whyWrong: The cut-out does not switch in other machines; bus-tie logic does that.
A battery motoring a generator would discharge quickly; preventing that is the cut-out's purpose.
Field control is the regulator's job, and at low rpm it cannot restore the voltage.
samples.examTip: A light-aircraft alternator needs no cut-out: its rectifier diodes block reverse current.

samples.prompt: Why will the alternator on a typical light aircraft not come on line if the battery is completely flat?
options: Its reverse current relay stays open until the battery is above 24 V
Its field is excited from the battery through the master switch, and with no battery voltage there is no field
Its output is AC, and a charged battery is needed to convert that AC into DC before it can reach the aircraft bus
Its rectifier diodes conduct only when the battery is fully charged
samples.explanation: A light-aircraft alternator has a rotating field (rotor) supplied through brushes and slip rings from the aircraft bus via the master switch and regulator. Unlike a self-excited DC generator, it has little or no residual magnetism to build up from, so with a completely flat battery the field gets no current and the alternator produces nothing.
whyWrong: Light-aircraft alternators do not use a reverse current relay; the diodes block reverse current.
Conversion to DC is done by the rectifier inside the alternator, not by the battery.
The diodes conduct whenever the alternator voltage exceeds bus voltage; they do not depend on battery charge.
samples.examTip: Self-excited DC generator: builds up on residual magnetism. Light alternator: needs the battery.

samples.prompt: Two DC generators share the load on a common bus. One is supplying much more current than the other. The load-sharing (equalising) circuit corrects this by:
options: Increasing the speed of the generator carrying less load
Opening the reverse current relay of the generator carrying more load, until the other generator catches up
Connecting the battery in series with the lightly loaded generator
Reducing the field current of the generator carrying more load and increasing that of the other
samples.explanation: Paralleled DC generators share load according to their output voltages. The equalising circuit compares the currents (often across the generators' interpole or series windings) and feeds a signal to each voltage regulator: the heavily loaded generator's field is weakened and the lightly loaded one's is strengthened until the load is shared.
whyWrong: Generator speed is set by the engine; it is not used to balance DC load.
Disconnecting a healthy generator would lose a power source, not share the load.
Batteries are never put in series with a generator to balance load.
samples.examTip: DC load sharing: adjust excitation. AC real-load sharing: adjust speed (CSD).

samples.prompt: Fleming's Left Hand Rule is used to determine:
options: The direction of induced EMF
The direction of rotation of a motor
The magnitude of back EMF
The strength of the magnetic field
samples.explanation: Fleming's Left Hand Rule determines the direction of motion (rotation) of a motor. The first finger represents Field, second finger represents Current, and thumb represents Motion. Option A relates to Fleming's Right Hand Rule for generators.

samples.prompt: Why is a series-wound DC motor used as an engine starter?
options: It runs at an almost constant speed whatever the load
It draws very little current when starting
It produces very high torque at low speed, when the current through both field and armature is greatest
It can be run safely with no load connected, because its speed is limited automatically by the back EMF at high rpm
samples.explanation: In a series motor the field and armature carry the same current. At low speed there is little back EMF, so the current is large, and torque (proportional to field flux × armature current) is very high: ideal for turning a heavy engine from rest. As speed rises the back EMF increases and the current and torque fall. With no load the speed keeps rising, so starters engage the engine before being energised.
whyWrong: Near-constant speed is the property of the shunt motor.
At standstill there is no back EMF, so a series motor draws its highest current, which is what gives its torque.
Unloaded, a series motor's speed rises dangerously (runaway); it must always drive a load.
samples.examTip: Constant speed = shunt; high starting torque = series.

samples.prompt: An electric motor drawing a large current at the moment of starting draws much less once it reaches running speed. The main reason is that:
options: The armature winding resistance rises sharply as it heats up
The brushes lift off the commutator at high speed
The rotating armature generates a back EMF that opposes the supply and grows with speed
The field winding is switched out of circuit once the motor is running, leaving only the armature
samples.explanation: A motor's armature turning in its own field also acts as a generator. The EMF it generates (back EMF) opposes the supply voltage and is proportional to speed. Armature current = (V − back EMF) ÷ armature resistance, so at standstill, with no back EMF, the current is very large, and it falls as the motor speeds up.
whyWrong: Resistance does rise a little with temperature, but far too little to explain the large reduction.
The brushes must stay in contact or the motor would stop working.
In normal DC motors the field stays in circuit; removing it would cause overspeed.
samples.examTip: Starting current surges are why motors need slow-blow protection.

samples.prompt: Which statement about a starter-generator, as fitted to many turboprops and small jets, is correct?
options: It is engaged to the engine through a clutch that disconnects it once the engine is running, like a piston-engine starter
It is a battery charger that also starts the APU
One machine acts as a motor to start the engine and is then switched to run as a generator, saving weight
It produces AC when starting and DC when generating
samples.explanation: A starter-generator is a DC machine permanently driven from the engine accessory gearbox. For starting it is fed from the battery or ground power and runs as a motor (using its series field for high torque). Once the engine is self-sustaining the starter circuit is switched off and the machine operates as a shunt generator. One unit instead of two saves weight and space.
whyWrong: It stays permanently geared to the engine; in generator mode it is driven by the engine.
It is a rotating electrical machine on the engine gearbox, not a charger.
It is a DC machine in both modes.
samples.examTip: No clutch, no separate starter: that is the point of a starter-generator.

samples.prompt: A DC actuator motor must be able to drive in both directions. How can the direction of rotation of a DC motor be reversed?
options: Reverse the current through either the field or the armature, but not both
Reverse the polarity of the supply to the whole motor at its two input terminals
Increase the field current beyond its normal value
Reverse the current through both the field and the armature
samples.explanation: The direction of the force on the armature conductors depends on both the field direction and the armature current (Fleming's left-hand rule). Reversing one of them reverses the rotation; reversing both cancels out. Reversible actuators often use a split-field series motor, with two opposite field windings selected by the control switch.
whyWrong: For a wound-field motor, reversing the whole supply reverses both field and armature, so the direction does not change.
Field strength changes speed and torque, not direction.
Reversing both leaves the direction of the force unchanged.
samples.examTip: Watch for 'reverse the supply': with a wound field that changes nothing.

chapters.title: DC Electrics - Aircraft Electrical Power Systems
topics: Single Pole (Unipole or Earth Return) System
Generator Cut-out or Reverse Current Relay

samples.prompt: In a dipole or two wire system, the current requires a complete circuit to flow. This system is required when:
options: The aircraft is made of conductive material
The aircraft is made of non-conductive material
The aircraft has a metal airframe
The aircraft uses earth return
samples.explanation: A dipole or two wire system is required where an aircraft is made of a non-conductive material because the current needs a negative wire to complete the circuit. Option A is incorrect because conductive material allows earth return. Option C is incorrect because metal airframes use single pole system. Option D is incorrect because earth return is a different system.

samples.prompt: What is a 'hot battery bus'?
options: A bus wired directly to the battery, live even with the battery switch off
A busbar that is powered only when the battery temperature is high
A busbar that is energised only during engine start
The busbar through which the generator charges the battery, which becomes hot during heavy charging
samples.explanation: A hot battery bus is wired directly to the battery terminals, bypassing the battery contactor and master switch. It powers a few services that must always be available, such as fire extinguisher squibs, some emergency lighting, a clock or the memory of avionics. Because it is always live it is kept to a minimum to avoid draining the battery on the ground.
whyWrong: The name refers to it being permanently live, not to battery temperature.
Start circuits are fed through the starter contactors, not a dedicated start bus.
The charging path is through the battery bus and battery contactor, not the hot bus.
samples.examTip: 'Even with the battery switch off' points to the hot battery bus.

samples.prompt: Most aircraft DC systems are single-pole (earth-return) systems. What does this mean, and what is the main advantage?
options: Each load has its own separate positive and negative cables, which prevents any possibility of short circuits
The airframe is the negative return for every load, which saves the weight of return cables
The battery has only one terminal connected, so it cannot discharge
Only one pole of each switch is used, which halves the number of switches
samples.explanation: In a single-pole system the positive feeds go to each load through cables and protection devices, while the negative side of the battery, generators and loads is connected to the metal airframe, which is the return path. It saves a great deal of cable weight. It also depends on good bonding, because a high-resistance joint in the structure would cause volt drop and heating.
whyWrong: That is a two-wire (double-pole) system, used on composite aircraft or where interference must be avoided.
A battery needs both terminals connected to supply current.
'Single-pole' refers to the distribution, not to the switches.
samples.examTip: Earth return requires good bonding; on composite airframes return wires or a conductive network are needed.

samples.prompt: In cruise the generator fails and the battery ammeter (centre-zero) swings to show a discharge. Why does the checklist call for load shedding?
options: To prevent the battery from overcharging
To reduce the load on the battery so that the essential services can be kept running for longer
To raise the bus frequency to its normal value
To allow the failed generator to be reset more easily, because a reset is refused while the bus is heavily loaded
samples.explanation: With the generator off line the battery is the only source and it has a limited capacity. Time available = usable capacity ÷ load current, so switching off non-essential loads (galley, cabin services, some lights and radios) increases the time the essential bus can be powered. Many aircraft shed some loads automatically on generator failure.
whyWrong: With the generator off line the battery is discharging, not charging.
A DC bus has no frequency.
Shedding loads does not help reset a generator; that is done with the generator control switch.
samples.examTip: A centre-zero ammeter showing discharge after a generator failure confirms the battery is carrying the load.

samples.prompt: Ground power is connected with reversed polarity. On a typical aircraft with an external power protection circuit, what happens?
options: The external power contactor does not close, so the ground supply is not connected to the aircraft bus
The aircraft circuit breakers trip one after another to protect the equipment
The bus works normally, because aircraft DC equipment is protected internally and is not sensitive to polarity
The contactor closes and the aircraft battery is charged in reverse
samples.explanation: The external power contactor's control circuit is fed through a polarity-sensitive element (often a diode) and, on larger aircraft, also through overvoltage protection. If the polarity is wrong or the voltage is outside limits, the contactor is not energised and the ground supply never reaches the aircraft bus.
whyWrong: The protection acts at the contactor, before the supply reaches the bus and its circuits.
Many DC loads are polarity-sensitive: motors would run backwards and electronics could be damaged.
Protection exists to stop exactly that: reversed connection could damage the battery and equipment.
samples.examTip: Protection systems disconnect at the source contactor, not by tripping individual breakers.

chapters.title: DC Electrics - Bonding and Screening
topics: The Static Discharge System or Static Wicks

samples.prompt: What is the primary purpose of bonding on an aircraft?
options: To increase the electrical resistance between components
To ensure all metal parts are at the same electrical potential
To provide insulation against lightning strikes
To reduce the weight of the aircraft structure
samples.explanation: Bonding ensures all metal parts of the aircraft are maintained at the same electrical potential, preventing differences in potential that could cause sparking and fire. Option A is wrong because bonding reduces resistance, not increases it. Option C is incorrect as bonding is not primarily for lightning protection. Option D is wrong as bonding adds weight through bonding strips.

samples.prompt: Which of these is NOT a purpose of bonding the metal parts of an airframe together?
options: To carry lightning current safely through the structure
To keep all metal parts at the same electrical potential so that sparks cannot jump between them
To provide a low-resistance return path for an earth-return electrical system
To increase the resistance between components so that static cannot build up
samples.explanation: Bonding connects metal parts with low-resistance straps or joints. It keeps the airframe at one potential (no sparks between parts), gives the return path for single-pole circuits, conducts lightning current safely, reduces radio interference and protects people from shocks. Bonding LOWERS resistance; a high resistance would do the opposite of what is wanted.
whyWrong: True purpose: a lightning strike must pass through the structure without damaging hinges, bearings or control runs.
True purpose: equal potential prevents arcing, which could ignite fuel vapour.
True purpose: single-pole systems rely on the bonded structure as the return conductor.
samples.examTip: Bonding is always about LOW resistance; any option saying 'increase resistance' is wrong.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of the static dischargers (static wicks) on the trailing edges of the wings and tail?
options: To bleed off static charge into the air gradually, reducing the radio interference caused by corona discharge
To earth the aircraft through the surrounding air when it is parked on the apron, so that no earthing lead is needed
To prevent the aircraft from being struck by lightning
To measure the electrical charge on the aircraft for the weather radar
