options: Layer tinting
Hachuring
Spot heighting
Hill shading
samples.explanation: Layer tinting shades the bands between chosen contours (for example green for low ground through browns for high ground) so that the pilot sees the general relief at a glance. The legend of the chart gives the elevation for each tint.
whyWrong: Hachures are short lines drawn down the direction of slope.
Spot heights are single points with their elevation printed.
Hill shading uses shadow as if lit from the north-west, not bands of colour.
samples.examTip: Know the four relief methods: contours, layer tints, hill shading, spot heights (plus hachures).

samples.prompt: A spot height on an aeronautical chart shows:
options: The elevation of a specific point, usually a summit, above mean sea level
The highest point within a quadrangle of latitude and longitude
The height above the aerodrome reference point
The height of an obstacle above the ground
samples.explanation: A spot height is a dot with a number giving the elevation of that point above mean sea level. Charts often mark the highest spot height on the sheet specially. Obstacles show elevation (AMSL) and often height above ground in brackets.
whyWrong: That is the maximum elevation figure (or area minimum altitude), not a spot height.
Chart elevations refer to mean sea level, not to an aerodrome.
Obstacle heights above ground are given separately (often in brackets) beside the obstacle's elevation.
samples.examTip: Elevation is AMSL; height is above ground.

samples.prompt: On a 1:250,000 topographical map, two spot heights of 300 ft and 2,900 ft are 3 cm apart. What is the average slope between them?
samples.explanation: Formula: Gradient = height difference ÷ horizontal distance (same units); 1 nm = 6,076 ft. Horizontal distance = 3 cm × 250,000 = 4.05 nm = 24,606 ft. Height difference = 2,600 ft. Slope = atan(2,600 ÷ 24,606) = 6.0°.
whyWrong: Metres: gives 1.8°.
Used km-feet mix: gives 36.6°.
1 in 60 with distance: gives 6.4°.
samples.examTip: Convert nm to ft before dividing.

samples.prompt: On a 1:500,000 topographical map, two spot heights of 900 ft and 2,800 ft are 4.5 cm apart. What is the average slope between them?
samples.explanation: Formula: Gradient = height difference ÷ horizontal distance (same units); 1 nm = 6,076 ft. Horizontal distance = 4.5 cm × 500,000 = 12.15 nm = 73,819 ft. Height difference = 1,900 ft. Slope = atan(1,900 ÷ 73,819) = 1.5°.
whyWrong: Metres: gives 0.4°.
Used km-feet mix: gives 9.0°.
samples.examTip: Convert nm to ft before dividing.

chapters.title: Convergency and Conversion Angle
topics: Convergency and the Great Circle Track
Conversion Angle — The Bridge Between Great Circle and Rhumb Line
The D-I-I-D Rule for Track Changes
Practical Problem Solving — The Diagram Method

samples.prompt: Convergency of the meridians on the Earth is:
options: Zero at the equator and equal to the change of longitude at the poles
Equal to the change of longitude at the equator and zero at the poles
Constant at all latitudes
Greatest at latitude 45°
samples.explanation: Convergency is the angle at which two meridians are inclined to each other at a given latitude: d.long × sin lat. At the equator sin 0° = 0, so meridians are parallel; at the poles sin 90° = 1, so the angle equals the d.long.
whyWrong: Reversed: meridians are parallel at the equator and meet at the poles.
It varies with sin latitude.
sin lat keeps increasing up to 90°.
samples.examTip: Do not confuse with departure, which uses cos lat.

samples.prompt: What is the earth convergency between A (51°00'S 071°00'W) and B (17°00'S 067°00'W)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Earth convergency = d.long × sin(mean latitude). Convergency = ch.long × sin(mean lat). Mean latitude = 34°00'S, ch.long = 4°, so convergency = 4 × sin 34° = 2.2°.
whyWrong: Cos instead of sin: gives 3.3°.
Doubled: gives 4.5°.
Gave the conversion angle: gives 1.1°.
samples.examTip: Use the mean latitude for a route.

samples.prompt: What is the earth convergency between A (29°00'N 052°00'E) and B (59°00'N 080°00'E)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Earth convergency = d.long × sin(mean latitude). Convergency = ch.long × sin(mean lat). Mean latitude = 44°00'N, ch.long = 28°, so convergency = 28 × sin 44° = 19.5°.
whyWrong: Cos instead of sin: gives 20.1°.
Doubled: gives 38.9°.
Gave the conversion angle: gives 9.7°.
samples.examTip: Use the mean latitude for a route.

samples.prompt: The rhumb line track from A (53°S 057°00'E) to B (57°S 041°00'E) is 246°(T). What is the great-circle track at A (the initial great-circle track)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Conversion angle = ½ × convergency = ½ × d.long × sin mean lat; GC track = RL track ∓ CA (the GC is on the poleward side). Convergency = ch.long × sin mean lat = 16 × sin 55° = 13.1°, so the conversion angle = 6.6°. The great circle lies on the polar side of the rhumb line. Westbound in the southern hemisphere, the great-circle track at A (the initial great-circle track) is 246° − 6.6° = 239.4°(T).
whyWrong: Applied CA on the wrong side: gives 252.6°(T).
Convergency on the wrong side: gives 259.1°(T).
Applied convergency, not CA: gives 232.9°(T).
samples.examTip: Draw it: the great circle always lies poleward of the rhumb line.

samples.prompt: The rhumb line track from A (49°S 013°00'W) to B (49°S 003°00'W) is 090°(T). What is the great-circle track at A (the initial great-circle track)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Conversion angle = ½ × convergency = ½ × d.long × sin mean lat; GC track = RL track ∓ CA (the GC is on the poleward side). Convergency = ch.long × sin mean lat = 10 × sin 49° = 7.5°, so the conversion angle = 3.8°. The great circle lies on the polar side of the rhumb line. Eastbound in the southern hemisphere, the great-circle track at A (the initial great-circle track) is 090° + 3.8° = 093.8°(T).
whyWrong: Convergency on the wrong side: gives 082.5°(T).
Applied convergency, not CA: gives 097.5°(T).
Applied CA on the wrong side: gives 086.2°(T).
samples.examTip: Draw it: the great circle always lies poleward of the rhumb line.

chapters.title: Departure
topics: Variations on the Basic Departure Formula
Given Departure at One Latitude, Find It at Another

samples.prompt: The formula for calculating departure is:
options: Departure (NM) = ch.long (degrees) × cos lat
Departure (NM) = ch.long (minutes) × cos lat
Departure (NM) = ch.long (minutes) × sin lat
Departure (NM) = ch.long (degrees) × sin lat
samples.explanation: The correct formula is Departure (NM) = ch.long (in minutes) × cos lat. Option A is incorrect because change of longitude must be in minutes, not degrees. Options C and D are incorrect because the formula uses cosine, not sine.

samples.prompt: Find the departure (rhumb line distance along the parallel) between 56°15'S 052°00'E and 56°15'S 066°00'E.
samples.explanation: Formula: Departure (nm) = d.long (minutes) × cos latitude. Departure = d.long (minutes) × cos lat. The d.long is 14°00' = 840 minutes, so departure = 840 × cos 56°15' = 466.7 nm.
whyWrong: Sin instead of cos: gives 698.4 nm.
Divided by cos: gives 1,512.0 nm.
No cos: gives 840.0 nm.
samples.examTip: Departure uses cos lat; convergency uses sin lat.

samples.prompt: Find the departure (rhumb line distance along the parallel) between 69°00'N 092°00'E and 69°00'N 123°00'E.
samples.explanation: Formula: Departure (nm) = d.long (minutes) × cos latitude. Departure = d.long (minutes) × cos lat. The d.long is 31°00' = 1860 minutes, so departure = 1860 × cos 69°00' = 666.6 nm.
whyWrong: No cos: gives 1,860.0 nm.
Sin instead of cos: gives 1,736.5 nm.
Divided by cos: gives 5,190.2 nm.
samples.examTip: Departure uses cos lat; convergency uses sin lat.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies due east along the parallel of 58°00'S for 811 nm. What change of longitude has it made?
samples.explanation: Formula: d.long (minutes) = departure (nm) ÷ cos latitude. d.long (minutes) = departure ÷ cos lat = 811 ÷ cos 58°00' = 1530.4', which is 25°30'.
whyWrong: Multiplied by cos: gives 7°10'.
Divided by sin: gives 15°56'.
No correction: gives 13°31'.
samples.examTip: d.long is always larger than the departure (except on the equator).

samples.prompt: Find the departure (rhumb line distance along the parallel) between 50°30'N 050°00'E and 50°30'N 089°20'E.
samples.explanation: Departure = d.long (minutes) × cos lat. The d.long is 39°20' = 2360 minutes, so departure = 2360 × cos 50°30' = 1501.1 nm.
whyWrong: Took the d.long in minutes as the distance, leaving out the cos lat factor
Used sin lat instead of cos lat
Divided by cos lat (that turns departure into d.long, not the reverse)
samples.examTip: Common trap: took the d.long in minutes as the distance, leaving out the cos lat factor.

chapters.title: Scale
topics: Converting from a Statement in Words to a Representative Fraction

samples.prompt: Which of the following is the largest-scale chart?
samples.explanation: Scale is a fraction: 1/250,000 is larger than 1/2,000,000. A larger-scale chart shows a smaller area in more detail.
whyWrong: Quarter the scale.
The smallest of the four.
Half the scale of 1:250,000.
samples.examTip: Think of the fraction's value, not the size of the number.

samples.prompt: On a chart of scale 1:2,000,000, a track measures 19 cm. What distance does it represent?
samples.explanation: Formula: Earth distance = chart distance × scale denominator (convert cm to nm: 1 nm = 185,200 cm). Ground distance = 19 cm × 2,000,000 = 38,000,000 cm. One nautical mile is 185 200 cm, so the distance = 205.2 nm.
whyWrong: Used statute miles: gives 236.1 nm.
Dropped a factor of 10: gives 20.5 nm.
Gave kilometres: gives 380.0 nm.

samples.prompt: On a chart of scale 1:1,000,000, a track measures 29.5 cm. What distance does it represent?
samples.explanation: Formula: Earth distance = chart distance × scale denominator (convert cm to nm: 1 nm = 185,200 cm). Ground distance = 29.5 cm × 1,000,000 = 29,500,000 cm. One nautical mile is 185 200 cm, so the distance = 159.3 nm.
whyWrong: Used statute miles: gives 183.3 nm.
Dropped a factor of 10: gives 15.9 nm.
Gave kilometres: gives 295.0 nm.

samples.prompt: A distance of 162 nm measures 7.5 cm on a chart. What is the chart's scale (to the nearest 10 000)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Scale denominator = Earth distance ÷ chart distance (same units). 162 nm = 162 × 185 200 = 30,002,400 cm. Scale = chart length ÷ ground length = 7.5 ÷ 30,002,400 = 1:4,000,000 (to the nearest 10 000).
whyWrong: Factor of 10: gives 1:40,000,000.
Km the other way: gives 1:2,160,000.
Used km: gives 1:7,410,000.
samples.examTip: 'Large scale' means 1:50,000, not 1:1,000,000.

samples.prompt: On a chart of scale 1:3,000,000, a track measures 13 cm. What distance does it represent?
samples.explanation: Ground distance = 13 cm × 3,000,000 = 39,000,000 cm. One nautical mile is 185 200 cm, so the distance = 210.6 nm.
whyWrong: Converted centimetres to kilometres instead of nautical miles
Converted to statute miles instead of nautical miles
Used 1 852 000 cm per nm (one zero too many)
samples.examTip: Common trap: converted centimetres to kilometres instead of nautical miles.

samples.prompt: On a conformal chart, the meridians and parallels:
options: Are equally spaced
Are always straight lines
Intersect at the angle of convergence
Intersect at right angles
samples.explanation: Because angles are preserved, the right angle between meridians and parallels on the Earth is preserved on any conformal chart.
whyWrong: On Mercator the parallels' spacing increases with latitude.
On Lambert and polar stereographic charts the parallels are arcs, not straight lines.
Convergence is between meridians, not between meridians and parallels.
samples.examTip: Right-angle graticule is a necessary condition for conformality.

samples.prompt: A conformal (orthomorphic) chart is one on which:
options: Great circles are straight lines
Scale is constant over the whole chart
Angles are correctly represented and the scale at any point is the same in all directions
Areas are correctly represented
samples.explanation: Orthomorphism (conformality) means that at any point the scale is equal in all directions over short distances, so shapes of small areas and angles are true. Meridians and parallels therefore cross at right angles. Mercator, Lambert conformal and polar stereographic charts are conformal.
whyWrong: That is the gnomonic property, which is not conformal.
No flat chart of a large area has a constant scale.
That is an equal-area (equivalent) projection; no chart can be both conformal and equal-area.
samples.examTip: Name the big three conformal charts: Mercator, Lambert, polar stereographic.

samples.prompt: Which property can NOT be achieved on any single flat chart of a large part of the Earth?
options: Rhumb lines as straight lines
Constant scale over the whole chart
Conformality
Great circles as straight lines
samples.explanation: A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, so scale must vary over a chart of any large area. Individual properties (conformality, straight rhumb lines, straight great circles, equal area) can be obtained, but not all at once and never a constant scale.
whyWrong: Mercator makes all rhumb lines straight.
Conformality is achieved by Mercator, Lambert and polar stereographic projections.
The gnomonic projection makes all great circles straight.
samples.examTip: 'Ideal chart' questions: constant scale is the unattainable property.

samples.prompt: The Mercator chart is constructed as a:
options: Normal cylindrical projection, mathematically adjusted to be conformal
Perspective projection from the Earth's centre onto a tangent plane
Conical projection with two standard parallels
Azimuthal projection tangent at the pole
samples.explanation: Mercator wraps a cylinder around the equator (normal aspect). A pure perspective cylinder would not be conformal, so the spacing of the parallels is adjusted mathematically (stretching north-south by sec lat to match the east-west stretch). This keeps angles true and makes rhumb lines straight.
whyWrong: That is the gnomonic projection.
That is the Lambert conformal conic.
That is the polar stereographic.
samples.examTip: Cylinder → Mercator; cone → Lambert; plane at pole → polar stereographic.

samples.prompt: The polar stereographic projection is a perspective projection onto a plane tangent at the pole, with the point of projection at:
options: Infinity
The equator
The centre of the Earth
The opposite pole
samples.explanation: Stereographic projections project from the point diametrically opposite the tangent point. For a polar chart, that is the other pole. This projection is conformal, and on it great circles near the pole are nearly straight.
whyWrong: Projecting from infinity gives the orthographic projection.
The equator is not used as a point of projection for polar charts.
Projecting from the centre gives the gnomonic projection.
samples.examTip: Remember the three perspective sources: centre, antipode, infinity.

samples.prompt: On a direct Mercator chart, with the exception of the meridians and the Equator, great circles are represented as:
options: Curves concave to the nearer Pole
Curves convex to the Equator
Curves concave to the Equator
Straight lines
samples.explanation: All great circles except the Equator and meridians project as curves that are concave to the Equator (convex to the nearer Pole) on a Mercator chart.

samples.prompt: On a Mercator chart, a great circle (other than a meridian or the equator) appears as a:
options: Curve concave to the nearer pole
Curve concave to the equator
Series of straight segments
Straight line
samples.explanation: On Mercator rhumb lines are straight. The great circle lies on the poleward side of the rhumb line, so it appears as a curve bulging towards the nearer pole, which means it is concave to the equator.
whyWrong: Reversed: the curve bulges towards the pole, so it is concave towards the equator.
The great circle is a smooth curve; flight plans approximate it by straight rhumb-line segments.
On Mercator the rhumb line is straight, not the great circle.
samples.examTip: Mercator straight line = rhumb line = constant track.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the Mercator chart is correct?
options: It is the best chart for polar navigation
Scale is correct along two standard parallels
Scale expands with the secant of latitude, so areas at high latitude look much too large
Meridians converge towards the pole
samples.explanation: Mercator stretches east-west distances by sec lat (to keep meridians parallel) and north-south distances by the same amount (to stay conformal), so scale = equator scale × sec lat. Greenland looks as big as Africa, and the poles cannot be shown.
whyWrong: Scale becomes infinite at the poles, so Mercator is useless there; polar stereographic is used instead.
That describes Lambert's conformal conic.
On Mercator the meridians are parallel straight lines.
samples.examTip: Mercator: chart convergency is zero everywhere.

samples.prompt: On a Mercator chart the chart convergency between two meridians is:
options: Equal to d.long × sin(parallel of origin)
Zero at all latitudes
Equal to the Earth convergency
Equal to the d.long
samples.explanation: Meridians are drawn as parallel straight lines on Mercator, so the angle between them on the chart is zero everywhere. Earth convergency (d.long × sin lat) is only zero at the equator, which is why great circles appear curved on Mercator.
whyWrong: That is the Lambert chart convergency.
Mercator's meridians are parallel, so it cannot match Earth convergency except at the equator.
That is the polar stereographic chart convergency.
samples.examTip: Compare chart and Earth convergency to decide where a chart's straight line is a great circle.

samples.prompt: A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:2,000,000 at 20°N. What is the scale at 67°N (to the nearest 1 000)?
samples.explanation: Mercator scale varies as sec lat, so the scale denominator varies as cos lat. N at 67° = 2,000,000 × cos 67° ÷ cos 20° = 1:832,000 (to the nearest 1 000). The scale is larger away from the equator.
whyWrong: Assumed a Mercator chart has the same scale at every latitude
Applied the cos ratio upside down: the scale gets LARGER (denominator smaller) away from the equator
Used the sine of the latitudes instead of the cosine
samples.examTip: Common trap: assumed a Mercator chart has the same scale at every latitude.

samples.prompt: What is the alternative way to express the 8° band of constant scale in nautical miles?
samples.explanation: 8° of latitude is 8 × 60 = 480 NM, so the band in which Mercator scale is within 1% of correct is often quoted as about 480–500 NM either side of the Equator.

samples.prompt: A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:5,000,000 at 10°N. What is the scale at 65°N (to the nearest 1 000)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Scale at lat = scale at equator × sec lat; scale at lat2 = scale at lat1 × cos lat1 ÷ cos lat2. Mercator scale varies as sec lat, so the scale denominator varies as cos lat. N at 65° = 5,000,000 × cos 65° ÷ cos 10° = 1:2,146,000 (to the nearest 1 000). The scale is larger away from the equator.
whyWrong: Scale gets smaller towards the pole is wrong: gives 1:11,651,000.
No change: gives 1:5,000,000.
samples.examTip: Higher latitude = larger scale = smaller denominator.

samples.prompt: A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:2,000,000 at 40°N. What is the scale at 65°N (to the nearest 1 000)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Scale at lat = scale at equator × sec lat; scale at lat2 = scale at lat1 × cos lat1 ÷ cos lat2. Mercator scale varies as sec lat, so the scale denominator varies as cos lat. N at 65° = 2,000,000 × cos 65° ÷ cos 40° = 1:1,103,000 (to the nearest 1 000). The scale is larger away from the equator.
whyWrong: No change: gives 1:2,000,000.
Scale gets smaller towards the pole is wrong: gives 1:3,625,000.
samples.examTip: Higher latitude = larger scale = smaller denominator.

samples.prompt: A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:5,000,000 at 20°N. What is the scale at 52°N (to the nearest 1 000)?
samples.explanation: Mercator scale varies as sec lat, so the scale denominator varies as cos lat. N at 52° = 5,000,000 × cos 52° ÷ cos 20° = 1:3,276,000 (to the nearest 1 000). The scale is larger away from the equator.
whyWrong: Applied the cos ratio upside down: the scale gets LARGER (denominator smaller) away from the equator
Assumed a Mercator chart has the same scale at every latitude
Used the sine of the latitudes instead of the cosine
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied the cos ratio upside down: the scale gets LARGER (denominator smaller) away from the equator.

samples.prompt: A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:5,000,000 at 30°N. What is the scale at 62°N (to the nearest 1 000)?
samples.explanation: Mercator scale varies as sec lat, so the scale denominator varies as cos lat. N at 62° = 5,000,000 × cos 62° ÷ cos 30° = 1:2,710,000 (to the nearest 1 000). The scale is larger away from the equator.
whyWrong: Used the sine of the latitudes instead of the cosine
Assumed a Mercator chart has the same scale at every latitude
Applied the cos ratio upside down: the scale gets LARGER (denominator smaller) away from the equator
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the sine of the latitudes instead of the cosine.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert conformal chart, a straight line drawn between two points approximates:
options: A great circle
A parallel of latitude
A rhumb line
A small circle
samples.explanation: Lambert's chart convergency nearly equals the Earth convergency between the standard parallels, so a straight line on the chart is very close to a great circle. Strictly, the great circle is a slight curve concave to the parallel of origin, but for navigation a straight line is taken as the great circle.
whyWrong: Parallels are arcs of concentric circles on Lambert.
Rhumb lines are straight on Mercator, not on Lambert.
Small circles appear as arcs.
samples.examTip: Mercator → rhumb straight; Lambert → great circle (nearly) straight.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, the meridians are:
options: Parallel straight lines
Curves concave to the pole
Arcs of concentric circles
Straight lines converging towards the nearer pole
samples.explanation: Unrolling the cone gives meridians as straight lines radiating from the apex of the cone (beyond the pole) and parallels as arcs of circles centred on that apex.
whyWrong: Parallel meridians are a Mercator property.
Lambert meridians are straight radial lines.
The parallels, not the meridians, are concentric arcs.
samples.examTip: Lambert's apex lies beyond the pole, so the pole cannot be shown at the apex.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert conformal conic chart with two standard parallels, the scale is:
options: Constant over the whole chart
Too large between the standard parallels and too small outside them
Correct on the standard parallels, too small between them and too large outside them
Correct only at the parallel of origin
samples.explanation: The cone is secant to the Earth along the two standard parallels, where scale is correct. Between them the chart is slightly contracted (smallest scale near the parallel of origin); outside them it is expanded. Placing the standard parallels about one-sixth of the chart's latitude range in from its edges (the 'one-sixth rule') keeps the scale error small, around 1%.
whyWrong: No chart has constant scale over a large area.
Reversed: the cone cuts the Earth along the standard parallels, so the Earth is compressed between them.
The parallel of origin is where the scale is SMALLEST, not correct.
samples.examTip: Smallest scale at the parallel of origin.

samples.prompt: A Lambert conformal chart has standard parallels 12°N and 24°N. What chart convergence is there between meridians 34° apart? (Take the parallel of origin as midway between the standard parallels.)
samples.explanation: On a Lambert conformal chart the chart convergence = ch.long × sin(parallel of origin). With standard parallels 12°N and 24°N, the parallel of origin is about 18°N, so n = sin 18° = 0.309. Chart convergence = 34 × 0.309 = 10.5°.
whyWrong: Used the lower standard parallel instead of the parallel of origin
Used cos of the parallel of origin instead of sin
Used a convergence factor of 1 (polar stereographic) instead of sin of the parallel of origin
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the lower standard parallel instead of the parallel of origin.

samples.prompt: A Lambert conformal chart has standard parallels 16°N and 28°N. What chart convergence is there between meridians 33° apart? (Take the parallel of origin as midway between the standard parallels.)
samples.explanation: On a Lambert conformal chart the chart convergence = ch.long × sin(parallel of origin). With standard parallels 16°N and 28°N, the parallel of origin is about 22°N, so n = sin 22° = 0.375. Chart convergence = 33 × 0.375 = 12.4°.
whyWrong: Used cos of the parallel of origin instead of sin
Used the lower standard parallel instead of the parallel of origin
Used a convergence factor of 1 (polar stereographic) instead of sin of the parallel of origin
samples.examTip: Common trap: used cos of the parallel of origin instead of sin.

samples.prompt: The scale on a Lambert's conformal chart:
options: Is constant everywhere on the chart
Expands outside the standard parallels and contracts inside them
Expands inside the standard parallels and contracts outside them
Is constant only along the equator
samples.explanation: Scale expands outside the standard parallels and contracts inside them. Option A is incorrect because the scale is not constant everywhere. Option C reverses the correct relationship. Option D is incorrect as Lambert charts are not based on the equator.

samples.prompt: A Lambert conformal chart has standard parallels 45°N and 49°N. What chart convergence is there between meridians 12° apart? (Take the parallel of origin as midway between the standard parallels.)
samples.explanation: Formula: Chart convergency = d.long × n, where n (constant of the cone) = sin(parallel of origin). On a Lambert conformal chart the chart convergence = ch.long × sin(parallel of origin). With standard parallels 45°N and 49°N, the parallel of origin is about 47°N, so n = sin 47° = 0.731. Chart convergence = 12 × 0.731 = 8.8°.
whyWrong: Cos: gives 8.2°.
Polar stereographic factor: gives 12.0°.
Used a standard parallel: gives 8.5°.
samples.examTip: Use the chart's parallel of origin, not the mean latitude of the route.

samples.prompt: A Lambert conformal chart has standard parallels 12°N and 18°N. What chart convergence is there between meridians 9° apart? (Take the parallel of origin as midway between the standard parallels.)
samples.explanation: Formula: Chart convergency = d.long × n, where n (constant of the cone) = sin(parallel of origin). On a Lambert conformal chart the chart convergence = ch.long × sin(parallel of origin). With standard parallels 12°N and 18°N, the parallel of origin is about 15°N, so n = sin 15° = 0.259. Chart convergence = 9 × 0.259 = 2.3°.
whyWrong: Polar stereographic factor: gives 9.0°.
Cos: gives 8.7°.
Used a standard parallel: gives 1.9°.
samples.examTip: Use the chart's parallel of origin, not the mean latitude of the route.

samples.prompt: A straight line drawn on a Lambert conformal chart has a track of 053°(T) at 010°E and 069.0°(T) at 033°E. What is the parallel of origin?
samples.explanation: Formula: n = sin(parallel of origin) = chart convergency ÷ d.long. A straight line on a Lambert chart changes direction by the chart convergence: 69.0° − 53° = 16.0° over 23° of longitude. n = sin(PO) = 16.0 ÷ 23 = 0.6957, so the parallel of origin is 44.1°.
whyWrong: Acos: gives 45.9°N.
Halved: gives 22.0°N.
Took convergence as the latitude: gives 16.0°N.
samples.examTip: Parallel of origin ≈ mid-way between the standard parallels.

samples.prompt: A Lambert conformal chart has standard parallels 23°N and 33°N. What chart convergence is there between meridians 11° apart? (Take the parallel of origin as midway between the standard parallels.)
samples.explanation: On a Lambert conformal chart the chart convergence = ch.long × sin(parallel of origin). With standard parallels 23°N and 33°N, the parallel of origin is about 28°N, so n = sin 28° = 0.469. Chart convergence = 11 × 0.469 = 5.2°.
whyWrong: Used cos of the parallel of origin instead of sin
Used a convergence factor of 1 (polar stereographic) instead of sin of the parallel of origin
Used the lower standard parallel instead of the parallel of origin
samples.examTip: Common trap: used cos of the parallel of origin instead of sin.

samples.prompt: Between latitudes 90° and 78°, the scale on a polar stereographic chart is within what percentage of the scale at the Pole?
samples.explanation: At 78° the co-latitude is 12° and sec²6° ≈ 1.01, so between 90° and 78° the scale is within about 1% of the Pole scale (1:989,000 against 1:1,000,000).

samples.prompt: On a polar stereographic chart, the chart convergency between two meridians is:
options: Equal to half the change of longitude
Equal to the change of longitude
Equal to d.long × sin(mean latitude)
Zero
samples.explanation: The constant of the cone for the polar stereographic projection is n = sin 90° = 1. Meridians are straight lines radiating from the pole at angles equal to their longitude difference, so chart convergency = d.long. It matches Earth convergency at the pole, so near the pole a straight line is very nearly a great circle.
whyWrong: Half the convergency is the conversion angle.
That is Earth convergency, which matches the polar chart only at the pole.
Zero is Mercator.
samples.examTip: n = 0 Mercator, sin PO Lambert, 1 polar stereo.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the polar stereographic chart is correct?
options: Scale decreases away from the pole
Rhumb lines are straight lines
Scale increases away from the pole, and the chart is conformal
Its meridians are parallel straight lines
samples.explanation: The plane touches the Earth at the pole, so scale is correct there and expands with distance from the pole. The expansion is small near the pole (about 3% at 70°), so it is the standard chart for polar regions. It is conformal, great circles near the pole are close to straight, and rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.
whyWrong: Reversed: the scale is correct at the pole and expands away from it (by sec² of half the co-latitude).
Rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.
Meridians radiate from the pole.
samples.examTip: Use polar stereographic above about 70° latitude.

samples.prompt: On a polar stereographic chart (convergence factor 1) in the northern hemisphere, the grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. An aircraft at 065°W has a true track of 068°(T). What is its grid track?
samples.explanation: The grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. In the northern hemisphere, Grid = True + W long, − E long (× n). Convergence = 1 × 65° = 65.0°, so the grid track = 068° + 65.0° = 133.0°(G).
whyWrong: Applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle
Gave the true track with no grid convergence applied
Applied the convergence with the wrong sign (east/west rule reversed)
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle.

samples.prompt: On a polar stereographic chart of the north polar region, an aircraft flies a straight line from 80°N 000° to 80°N 090°E. Compared with the great circle, the straight line is:
options: Far south of the great circle, which passes over the pole
Identical to the rhumb line along 80°N
Very close to the rhumb line, which is also straight
Very close to it, the great circle being slightly concave towards the pole
samples.explanation: Near the pole, polar stereographic chart convergency equals Earth convergency closely, so a straight line is nearly a great circle. Strictly, the great circle curves very slightly towards the pole. The rhumb line along the parallel is a circular arc centred on the pole, well equatorward of the straight line.
whyWrong: The great circle between these points does not pass over the pole; only meridian pairs do.
The rhumb line along 80°N is an arc around the pole, not a straight line on this chart.
Rhumb lines are curved (concave to the pole) on this chart.
samples.examTip: Draw it: the parallel is an arc, the chord is the (near) great circle.

samples.prompt: The seasons on Earth are caused mainly by:
options: The tilt of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°) to the plane of its orbit
The precession of the equinoxes
The varying distance between the Earth and the Sun
The Earth's rotation on its axis
samples.explanation: The Earth's axis is inclined at about 23.5° to the perpendicular of its orbital plane. As it orbits, each hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun for half the year (longer days, higher Sun: summer) and away from it for the other half. The Sun's declination ranges between 23.5°N and 23.5°S.
whyWrong: Precession takes about 26,000 years and does not cause annual seasons.
The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January (northern winter), so distance is not the main cause.
Rotation causes day and night, not seasons.
samples.examTip: Perihelion is in early January: a classic trap.

samples.prompt: The difference between apparent solar time and mean solar time is called:
options: The zone correction
The equation of time
The sidereal correction
Precession
samples.explanation: The equation of time is the difference between the apparent (real) Sun and the mean Sun. It varies through the year and reaches about ±16 minutes. It is why a sundial and a clock differ.
whyWrong: Zone corrections relate zone time to UTC.
Sidereal time is star time, not this difference.
Precession is a slow change in the Earth's axis direction.
samples.examTip: If a question mentions a sundial, think equation of time.

samples.prompt: Convert 141°07' of arc into time.
options: 9 h 24 min 28 s
14 h 06 min 42 s
4 h 42 min 14 s
10 h 24 min 28 s
samples.explanation: Formula: 360° = 24 h; 15° = 1 h; 1° = 4 min; 15' = 1 min; 1' = 4 s. 15° of arc = 1 hour, so 1° = 4 min and 1' = 4 s. 141°07' = 8467 minutes of arc × 4 s = 33868 s = 9 h 24 min 28 s.
whyWrong: Used 6 min per degree: gives 14 h 06 min 42 s.
Used 30° per hour: gives 4 h 42 min 14 s.
An hour out: gives 10 h 24 min 28 s.
samples.examTip: Convert degrees to minutes of time first (× 4), then add arc minutes ÷ 15.

samples.prompt: Convert a time interval of 5 h 37 min 40 s into arc.
whyWrong: Halved: gives 42°12.5'.
15° out: gives 99°25'.
10° per hour: gives 56°16.7'.
samples.examTip: Multiply minutes of time by 15 to get minutes of arc.

samples.prompt: Convert 105°29' of arc into time.
options: 8 h 01 min 56 s
3 h 30 min 58 s
7 h 01 min 56 s
10 h 32 min 54 s
samples.explanation: 15° of arc = 1 hour, so 1° = 4 min and 1' = 4 s. 105°29' = 6329 minutes of arc × 4 s = 25316 s = 7 h 01 min 56 s.
whyWrong: Added an extra hour when counting the 15° blocks
Used 30° per hour instead of 15°
Used 6 minutes of time per degree instead of 4
samples.examTip: Common trap: added an extra hour when counting the 15° blocks.

samples.prompt: One degree of arc is equivalent to how many minutes of time?
options: 15 minutes
4 minutes
1 minute
60 minutes
samples.explanation: Since 360° = 24 hours, dividing both sides by 360 gives 1° = 24/360 hours = 0.0667 hours = 4 minutes. 15 minutes would be 3.75°, 1 minute would be 0.25°, and 60 minutes would be 15°.

samples.prompt: At a place at longitude 126°00'E, the UTC is 2333 on 20 Mar. What is the LMT?
options: 1509 on 20 Mar LMT
1957 on 21 Mar LMT
0857 on 21 Mar LMT
0757 on 21 Mar LMT
samples.explanation: Formula: UTC = LMT − longitude east (in time) or + longitude west. Longitude 126°00'E in time = 504 min (8 h 24 min). Longitude east, LMT best; longitude west, LMT least. So UTC = LMT − the arc in time, and LMT = UTC + the arc in time. UTC 2333 on 20 Mar gives LMT 0757 on 21 Mar.
whyWrong: Longitude correction the wrong way: gives 1509 on 20 Mar LMT.
12 hours out: gives 1957 on 21 Mar LMT.
An hour out: gives 0857 on 21 Mar LMT.
samples.examTip: Places east of Greenwich are ahead of UTC.

samples.prompt: At a place at longitude 068°30'E, the LMT is 1514 on 8 Mar. What is the UTC?
options: 1948 on 8 Mar UTC
1040 on 8 Mar UTC
1140 on 8 Mar UTC
2240 on 8 Mar UTC
samples.explanation: Formula: UTC = LMT − longitude east (in time) or + longitude west. Longitude 068°30'E in time = 274 min (4 h 34 min). Longitude east, LMT best; longitude west, LMT least. So UTC = LMT − the arc in time. LMT 1514 on 8 Mar gives UTC 1040 on 8 Mar.
whyWrong: Longitude correction the wrong way: gives 1948 on 8 Mar UTC.
An hour out: gives 1140 on 8 Mar UTC.
12 hours out: gives 2240 on 8 Mar UTC.
samples.examTip: Places east of Greenwich are ahead of UTC.

samples.prompt: At a place at longitude 145°15'E, the UTC is 1518 on 13 Mar. What is the LMT?
options: 1518 on 13 Mar LMT
0537 on 13 Mar LMT
0118 on 14 Mar LMT
0059 on 14 Mar LMT
samples.explanation: Longitude 145°15'E in time = 581 min (9 h 41 min). Longitude east, LMT best; longitude west, LMT least. So UTC = LMT − the arc in time, and LMT = UTC + the arc in time. UTC 1518 on 13 Mar gives LMT 0059 on 14 Mar.
whyWrong: Gave the time unchanged (no longitude correction)
Applied the longitude correction the wrong way (longitude east, LMT best)
Rounded the longitude correction to whole hours, like a time zone
samples.examTip: Common trap: gave the time unchanged (no longitude correction).

samples.prompt: At a place at longitude 144°00'W, the LMT is 0653 on 7 Mar. What is the UTC?
options: 2117 on 6 Mar UTC
1629 on 7 Mar UTC
0653 on 7 Mar UTC
1653 on 7 Mar UTC
samples.explanation: Longitude 144°00'W in time = 576 min (9 h 36 min). Longitude east, LMT best; longitude west, LMT least. So UTC = LMT + the arc in time. LMT 0653 on 7 Mar gives UTC 1629 on 7 Mar.
whyWrong: Applied the longitude correction the wrong way (longitude east, LMT best)
Gave the time unchanged (no longitude correction)
Rounded the longitude correction to whole hours, like a time zone
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied the longitude correction the wrong way (longitude east, LMT best).

samples.prompt: Civil twilight ends in the evening when the centre of the Sun is:
options: 6° below the horizon
12° below the horizon
On the horizon
18° below the horizon
samples.explanation: Civil twilight runs from sunset until the Sun's centre is 6° below the horizon (and before sunrise from 6° below). Nautical twilight uses 12°, astronomical twilight 18°. ICAO Annex 2 defines night by reference to the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight.
whyWrong: 12° defines nautical twilight.
The Sun on the horizon is sunset (upper limb), not the end of twilight.
18° defines astronomical twilight.
samples.examTip: ICAO Annex 2 defines night using civil twilight.

samples.prompt: An aircraft crosses the International Date Line flying westbound, from 170°W to 170°E. Its date:
options: Advances by one day
Advances by one day only if it crosses at midnight
Goes back by one day
Does not change
samples.explanation: Places just west of the date line (170°E) are 24 hours ahead of places just east of it (170°W). Flying westbound across it, add one day; flying eastbound, subtract one day. The time of day (zone time) changes only by the zone difference.
whyWrong: The change happens whenever the line is crossed, not only at midnight.
Going back a day happens when crossing eastbound.
The date always changes by one day across the date line.
samples.examTip: Do the UTC arithmetic first, then the date line correction.

samples.prompt: How does the duration of twilight change with latitude?
options: It is the same at all latitudes
It is longest at the equator and decreases with latitude
It depends only on longitude
It is shortest at the equator and increases with latitude
samples.explanation: At the equator the Sun rises and sets almost vertically, so it passes the 6° band quickly (about 20–25 minutes). At higher latitudes it crosses the horizon at a shallow angle, so twilight lasts longer; near the poles in summer it can last all night.
whyWrong: The Sun's path relative to the horizon depends on latitude.
Reversed: the Sun sets steeply at the equator, so twilight is short there.
Longitude affects the clock time, not the duration of twilight.
samples.examTip: Equatorial twilight is short; polar twilight is long.

samples.prompt: An aircraft departs Kolkata (UTC+0530) at 0415 local time on 20 Apr. The flight time to Dubai (UTC+0400) is 11 h 40 min. What is the local time of arrival at Dubai?
options: 1725 on 20 Apr local
1555 on 20 Apr local
1425 on 20 Apr local
1025 on 20 Apr local
samples.explanation: Formula: Standard time = UTC + zone offset (India: IST = UTC + 5 h 30 min). Convert the departure to UTC: 0415 Kolkata time (UTC+0530) = 2245 UTC on 19 Apr. Add the flight time 11 h 40 min to get 1025 UTC. Dubai is UTC+0400, so the arrival is 1425 on 20 Apr local time.
whyWrong: Zone difference the wrong way: gives 1725 on 20 Apr local.
Ignored the time zones: gives 1555 on 20 Apr local.
Gave UTC: gives 1025 on 20 Apr local.
samples.examTip: IST is UTC+0530, based on 82°30'E.

samples.prompt: An aircraft departs Singapore (UTC+0800) at 0330 local time on 3 Apr. The flight time to Karachi (UTC+0500) is 2 h 00 min. What is the local time of arrival at Karachi?
options: 0230 on 3 Apr local
0830 on 3 Apr local
2130 on 2 Apr local
0530 on 3 Apr local
samples.explanation: Formula: Standard time = UTC + zone offset (India: IST = UTC + 5 h 30 min). Convert the departure to UTC: 0330 Singapore time (UTC+0800) = 1930 UTC on 2 Apr. Add the flight time 2 h 00 min to get 2130 UTC. Karachi is UTC+0500, so the arrival is 0230 on 3 Apr local time.
whyWrong: Zone difference the wrong way: gives 0830 on 3 Apr local.
Gave UTC: gives 2130 on 2 Apr local.
Ignored the time zones: gives 0530 on 3 Apr local.
samples.examTip: IST is UTC+0530, based on 82°30'E.

chapters.title: Gridded Charts
topics: East or West Convergence? — The Hemisphere Rule
Steering by Gyro — No Transport Wander Correction

samples.prompt: Grivation is the angle between:
options: Magnetic north and compass north
True north and magnetic north
Grid north and magnetic north
Grid north and true north
samples.explanation: Grivation is the angular difference between grid north and magnetic north at a point, combining variation and the convergence of the meridian from the grid datum. Lines of equal grivation are isogrivs.
whyWrong: That is deviation.
That is variation.
Grid north to true north is the convergence from the datum meridian.
samples.examTip: Isogriv = line of equal grivation.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert chart with convergence factor 0.77 in the northern hemisphere, the grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. An aircraft at 104°E has a true track of 156°(T). What is its grid track?
samples.explanation: Formula: Grid direction = true direction + (or −) convergence from the datum meridian; grivation = grid north to magnetic north (grivation = variation + convergence). The grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. In the northern hemisphere, Grid = True + W long, − E long (× n). Convergence = 0.77 × 104° = 80.1°, so the grid track = 156° − 80.1° = 075.9°(G).
whyWrong: Half convergence: gives 116.0°(G).
No convergence: gives 156.0°(G).
Wrong sign: gives 236.1°(G).
samples.examTip: Draw the three norths at the point; signs become obvious.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert chart with convergence factor 0.63 in the northern hemisphere, the grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. An aircraft at 146°W has a true track of 003°(T). What is its grid track?
samples.explanation: Formula: Grid direction = true direction + (or −) convergence from the datum meridian; grivation = grid north to magnetic north (grivation = variation + convergence). The grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. In the northern hemisphere, Grid = True + W long, − E long (× n). Convergence = 0.63 × 146° = 92.0°, so the grid track = 003° + 92.0° = 095.0°(G).
whyWrong: Half convergence: gives 049.0°(G).
Wrong sign: gives 271.0°(G).
No convergence: gives 003.0°(G).
samples.examTip: Draw the three norths at the point; signs become obvious.

samples.prompt: On a polar stereographic chart (convergence factor 1) in the southern hemisphere, the grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. An aircraft at 129°W has a true track of 299°(T). What is its grid track?
samples.explanation: The grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. In the southern hemisphere, Grid = True − W long, + E long (× n). Convergence = 1 × 129° = 129.0°, so the grid track = 299° − 129.0° = 170.0°(G).
whyWrong: Applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle
Gave the true track with no grid convergence applied
Applied the convergence with the wrong sign (east/west rule reversed)
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle.

samples.prompt: On a Lambert chart with convergence factor 0.65 in the northern hemisphere, the grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. An aircraft at 160°W has a true track of 021°(T). What is its grid track?
samples.explanation: The grid is aligned with the Greenwich meridian. In the northern hemisphere, Grid = True + W long, − E long (× n). Convergence = 0.65 × 160° = 104.0°, so the grid track = 021° + 104.0° = 125.0°(G).
whyWrong: Applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle
Applied the convergence with the wrong sign (east/west rule reversed)
Gave the true track with no grid convergence applied
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied only half the convergence, as if it were a conversion angle.

chapters.title: Plotting
topics: Bearings Measured by a Ground Station
Bearings Measured by Aircraft — ADF or Airborne Weather Radar (AWR)
Converting a Relative Bearing into a True Bearing

samples.prompt: What does the abbreviation QTE represent in radio navigation?
options: The magnetic bearing of the aircraft from a DF station
The true bearing of the aircraft from a DF station
The magnetic track from the aircraft to the DF station
The relative bearing of the aircraft from a DF station
samples.explanation: QTE is defined as the true bearing of an aircraft from a ground station. QDM is the magnetic track from aircraft to station, QDR is the magnetic bearing of aircraft from station, and relative bearing is measured from the aircraft's heading, not from a ground station.

samples.prompt: A DR (dead reckoning) position is a position calculated from:
options: Heading and TAS only, ignoring the wind
Two or more simultaneous position lines
A known position, using track and groundspeed based on a known or forecast wind
A single radio bearing
samples.explanation: DR uses the best known wind to turn heading/TAS into track/GS, then runs the track and distance from the last known position. An air position ignores the wind. A fix comes from position lines.
whyWrong: Heading and TAS only gives the air position.
Two or more position lines give a fix.
A single bearing gives only a position line.
samples.examTip: Know the three positions in order of accuracy: fix > DR > air position.

samples.prompt: A position line is obtained from a single VOR radial. Which statement is correct?
options: The aircraft is somewhere on that line; a second position line is needed to fix the position
A position line is only valid if the aircraft is flying towards the station
The aircraft's position is fixed at the VOR station
The aircraft's position is fixed if the heading is known
samples.explanation: A position line is a line on which the aircraft is known to be at a given time. A single radial, bearing or DME arc gives one position line. A second, crossing it at a good angle (ideally 90°), gives a fix. With a DME at the same station, the radial and arc fix the position.
whyWrong: A radial is valid whether the aircraft is flying to or from the station.
The station is just one end of the line.
Heading does not identify a point along the line.
samples.examTip: Best fix angle between position lines: 90°; poor below 30°.

samples.prompt: In plotting, what does the navigator's term 'cocked hat' describe?
options: The symbol for an air position
The small triangle formed when three position lines do not meet at a single point
The area of uncertainty around a GPS position
A DR position marked with a triangle
samples.explanation: Three position lines rarely meet perfectly because of errors in each bearing. They form a small triangle, the cocked hat, and the most probable position is normally taken at its centre (unless one line is known to be less accurate).
whyWrong: An air position is shown by a cross or plus symbol in the convention used.
GPS uncertainty is not called a cocked hat.
DR positions are shown by a triangle symbol, but that is not the cocked hat.
samples.examTip: A small cocked hat means good bearings.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is 040° (QDR from a VOR with 2°W variation at the station) at a DME range of 25 nm. To plot this on a chart based on true north, the line drawn from the VOR is:
samples.explanation: A QDR (radial) is the magnetic bearing FROM the station. Convert using the variation at the station: true = magnetic − west variation = 040° − 2° = 038°(T). Draw the line from the VOR on 038°(T) and mark 25 nm.
whyWrong: Applied the variation the wrong way.
Plotted the reciprocal (QDM) from the station.
Reciprocal with the wrong variation sign.
samples.examTip: Plot radials from the station outwards.

chapters.title: The Direct Indicating Compass
topics: The Vertical Card Compass (B-type or E-type)

samples.prompt: The magnetic compass uses which component of the Earth's magnetic field as its directional datum?
options: Total field
Vertical component
Horizontal component
Inclination component
samples.explanation: The magnetic compass uses the horizontal component of the Earth's field as its directional datum. Option A is wrong because the total field includes the vertical component which would cause the magnet to tilt. Option B is wrong because the vertical component is used for dip, not direction. Option D is wrong because inclination is the angle of dip, not a directional datum.

samples.prompt: In a vertical card compass, the heading is read by reference to:
options: A grid ring that must be aligned with north
A vertical lubber line on the glass window of the bowl
A horizontal lubber line on the compass card
An external gyroscopic reference
samples.explanation: A vertical lubber line on the glass window of the bowl enables the heading to be read off the compass card. Option A is wrong because that describes the grid ring compass procedure. Option C is wrong because the lubber line is vertical, not horizontal. Option D is wrong because the compass is direct reading, not gyroscopic.

samples.prompt: Flying over central India on 090°(M), a pilot increases power and the aircraft accelerates. What does the direct-reading compass show while the speed is increasing?
options: An apparent turn towards north
No error
An apparent turn towards west, through south
An apparent turn towards south
samples.explanation: On east or west headings, the pendulous magnet's centre of gravity lags during acceleration. The vertical component of the field then turns the magnet system so that the compass shows an apparent turn towards north (Northern Hemisphere). Deceleration gives an apparent turn towards south. There is no error on north or south headings.
whyWrong: Acceleration errors are greatest on east and west headings.
The error is a small swing towards north, not a big turn through south.
Southward apparent turns happen when decelerating on east/west headings in the NH.
samples.examTip: Acceleration errors: E/W headings. Turning errors: N/S headings.

samples.prompt: Compass turning and acceleration errors are zero:
options: At the magnetic poles
At latitude 45°
At the magnetic equator
Along the agonic line
samples.explanation: These errors exist because the vertical component of the Earth's field (Z) acts on the tilted or displaced magnet system. At the magnetic equator, dip is zero, so Z = 0 and there is no turning or acceleration error.
whyWrong: At the magnetic poles the compass is unusable, because H is zero.
Mid-latitudes have significant vertical component.
The agonic line concerns variation, not the field's vertical component.
samples.examTip: Turning and acceleration errors increase with magnetic latitude.

samples.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, an aircraft with a direct-reading magnetic compass turns left from a heading of 030°(C) to a heading of 330°(C). To roll out correctly, the pilot should:
options: Roll out after the compass passes 330°, because the compass leads
Roll out before the compass reads 330°, because the compass lags when turning through north
Roll out exactly as the compass reads 330°
Ignore the compass; turning errors are zero on northerly headings
samples.explanation: Turning through north in the Northern Hemisphere, the magnet system is tilted by the vertical component of the field and lags behind the turn. The pilot must undershoot (roll out early). Turning through south, the compass leads, so overshoot (roll out late). The errors reverse in the Southern Hemisphere.
whyWrong: In the NH the compass lags (under-indicates the turn) through north, so you roll out early, not late.
Turning errors are at their greatest on northerly and southerly headings.
Turning errors are largest near north and south, not zero.
samples.examTip: Roll out using the DI and a timed rate one turn instead.

samples.prompt: A newly installed avionics unit changes the standby compass error on some headings. This error, deviation, comes from:
options: Changes in the Earth's field over time
The difference between true and magnetic north
Magnetic fields within the aircraft itself
The vertical component of the Earth's field acting during turns
samples.explanation: Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north caused by the aircraft's own magnetism: hard iron (permanent, from the steel structure and manufacture) and soft iron (induced by the Earth's field), plus electrical circuits. It changes with heading and is recorded on the compass deviation card.
whyWrong: That is secular change.
That is variation.
That causes turning errors, not deviation.
samples.examTip: Deviation card: compass heading to fly for each magnetic heading, or the correction.

samples.prompt: A compass swing should be carried out in each of the following circumstances EXCEPT:
options: After the compass or a major magnetic component has been replaced
After every flight that crossed the magnetic equator
When the aircraft is to carry a large magnetic cargo
After the aircraft has been struck by lightning
samples.explanation: A compass swing is required after installation or replacement, when components that may affect the compass are fitted or removed, after lightning strikes or heavy landings, after long storage or a large change of magnetic latitude for a prolonged period, when carrying magnetic cargo, and periodically. Simply crossing the magnetic equator on a flight does not require one.
whyWrong: Replacing the compass or changing magnetic components always requires a swing.
A significant magnetic load can alter the deviation; a swing (or check) is required.
Lightning can change the aircraft's permanent magnetism, so a swing is needed.
samples.examTip: The NOT option is the routine event that does not change the aircraft's magnetism.

samples.prompt: The true heading is 061°T, with variation 7°E and deviation 4°W. What is the compass heading?
samples.explanation: Going from compass to magnetic to true, add easterly and subtract westerly corrections; reverse them going the other way. True 061° − variation 7° = 054°M; 054°M + deviation 4° = 058°C.
whyWrong: Reversed the sign of the deviation only
Applied variation and deviation the wrong way (east/west rule reversed)
Reversed the sign of the variation only
samples.examTip: Common trap: reversed the sign of the deviation only.

samples.prompt: The compass heading is 209°C, with variation 11°W and deviation 6°W. What is the magnetic heading?
samples.explanation: Going from compass to magnetic to true, add easterly and subtract westerly corrections; reverse them going the other way. Only deviation lies between compass and magnetic. Compass 209° − 6° = 203°M.
whyWrong: Applied both variation and deviation, but only one lies between these two headings
Applied both corrections, and the wrong way
Applied the correction the wrong way (east/west rule reversed)
samples.examTip: Common trap: applied both variation and deviation, but only one lies between these two headings.

samples.prompt: During a compass swing the engineer adjusts corrector magnets to cancel the effect of hard iron. What is hard-iron magnetism?
options: The magnetism of the compass magnets themselves
Permanent magnetism that is acquired during manufacture and stays largely the same whatever the heading
Magnetism caused only by electrical currents in the wiring
Induced magnetism that changes with the aircraft's heading and magnetic latitude
samples.explanation: Hard iron retains magnetism (acquired during building, from hammering, or in a fixed direction for a long time). Its field is fixed to the aircraft, so the deviation it causes varies with heading in a sine/cosine pattern. Soft iron is magnetised by the Earth's field and changes as heading and latitude change.
whyWrong: The compass magnets are the sensor, not the source of deviation.
Electrical fields add to deviation but are not called hard iron.
That describes soft-iron magnetism.
samples.examTip: Hard iron effects are compensated with the corrector magnets during a swing.

samples.prompt: In a three-pointer altimeter, the long pointer covers how many feet in one revolution?
options: 100 feet
1000 feet
10,000 feet
samples.explanation: In a three-pointer altimeter, the long pointer covers 1000 feet in one revolution, with each division representing 100 feet. The middle pointer covers 10,000 feet per revolution, and the smallest pointer covers 100,000 feet per revolution.

samples.prompt: What is the standard sea level temperature in Kelvin?
samples.explanation: The standard sea level temperature in Kelvin is +288K (also written as 288°A). Option A is Celsius, option C is Fahrenheit, and option D is the freezing point of water in Kelvin, not standard sea level temperature.

samples.prompt: An altimeter's pointer moves 2 mm for every 10 ft change of altitude at low level, but only 1 mm per 10 ft at high altitude. Which property of the instrument is changing?
options: Its sensitivity: the size of the output change for a given input change
Its accuracy: how close the reading is to the true value
Its lag: the delay between a change and its indication
Its hysteresis: the difference between readings taken with the input rising and falling
samples.explanation: Sensitivity is the ratio of output movement to input change (here, millimetres of pointer travel per 10 ft). A capsule altimeter loses sensitivity with height because the pressure change per foot gets smaller as the air thins, so the capsule moves less for each foot climbed.
whyWrong: Accuracy concerns the error of the reading, not how far the pointer moves per unit of input; an instrument can be very sensitive and still inaccurate.
Lag is a time delay; the question describes the scale of the response, not its timing.
Hysteresis compares the same input approached from two directions; this question compares the response at two different heights.
samples.examTip: Sensitivity is about 'how much it moves'; accuracy is about 'how right it is'.

samples.prompt: Many glass cockpits show airspeed and altitude as moving tapes with a trend vector, rather than as plain digital numbers. What is the main reason?
options: Tapes need no air data computer, so they keep working if it fails
A moving scale shows trend and rate of change at a glance
Moving tapes are more accurate than digital readouts of the same data
Digital numbers cannot show values below 100
samples.explanation: Digital readouts are precise but hard to scan: the pilot must read and compare successive numbers to see a trend. An analogue pointer or tape shows movement directly, so the rate and direction of change are seen instantly. Modern displays combine both, with a digital window on a moving tape and a trend vector.
whyWrong: A tape is just a display of ADC data and fails with it.
The tape and the digits come from the same air data, so neither is more accurate; the difference is in how easy the trend is to read.
There is no such limit: digital readouts show any value.
samples.examTip: Questions on 'presentation' usually reward the analogue = trend, digital = precision distinction.

samples.prompt: After a long climb to 30,000 ft and a descent back to 5,000 ft, an altimeter reads 40 ft higher than it did when passing 5,000 ft on the way up, although the pressure is the same. What is this error called, and what causes it?
options: Lag, caused by the time air takes to pass through the static line
Barometric error, caused by a change in the regional pressure
Hysteresis, from the imperfect elasticity of the capsule material
Position error, caused by the airflow around the static vent changing with speed
samples.explanation: Hysteresis is a difference in reading for the same input, depending on whether the input was approached from above or below. In a capsule it comes from the imperfect elasticity of the metal: after being stretched for a long time at low pressure it does not return exactly to its earlier shape. Good capsule materials and design keep it small.
whyWrong: Lag disappears once the aircraft is level for a few seconds; this error is a property of the capsule's recent history, not of time.
The question states the pressure is the same at both readings, so a pressure change cannot explain the difference.
Position error depends on speed and configuration, not on whether the instrument has just been to a higher altitude.
samples.examTip: If the clue is 'same pressure, different reading after a large change', the answer is hysteresis.

chapters.title: Pitot and Static Sources
topics: Pitot Covers and Static Vent Plugs

samples.prompt: Which instrument does NOT need pitot pressure?
options: Machmeter
Altimeter
Airspeed indicator
Air data computer
samples.explanation: The altimeter (and the VSI) use static pressure only. The ASI, the Machmeter and the air data computer all need pitot (total) pressure as well, because airspeed and Mach number depend on dynamic pressure.
whyWrong: The Machmeter uses (pitot − static) ÷ static, so it needs both.
The ASI measures pitot minus static pressure, so it needs both.
The ADC takes pitot, static and temperature inputs to compute speeds.
samples.examTip: Pitot blockage affects only the speed instruments.

samples.prompt: The static vent becomes completely blocked by ice at 20,000 ft, and the alternate static is not selected. While climbing to 21,800 ft at a constant CAS, how does the ASI read?
options: It reads correctly
It under-reads
It over-reads
It reads zero
samples.explanation: The trapped static pressure is that of 20,000 ft. Climbing, the true static pressure becomes lower than the trapped value, so the ASI's pitot − static difference is too small: it under-reads.
whyWrong: Assumed the ASI is unaffected because the pitot input is still correct
Reversed the effect: climbing, the trapped static is higher than the true static, so the ASI under-reads
Confused a static blockage with a total pitot blockage and drain
samples.examTip: Common trap: assumed the ASI is unaffected because the pitot input is still correct.

samples.prompt: Why are the static vents normally fitted on both sides of the fuselage and connected together?
options: To average out the pressure errors that appear on each side in a sideslip
So that one vent can serve as a drain for the other
To supply a separate static source to each pilot's instruments
To double the airflow into the static line and so reduce lag
samples.explanation: In a sideslip the vent on the side facing the airflow senses a higher pressure and the vent on the other side a lower one. Connecting the two sides averages the pressures, so the static error from sideslip largely cancels.
whyWrong: Drains are separate fittings at the low points of the lines.
Separate captain and first officer systems use separate pairs of vents; the cross-connection of the two sides is for sideslip, not duplication.
Static vents sense pressure; there is no flow through them in steady flight, so doubling them does not change lag much.
samples.examTip: 'Sideslip' in an option about static vents is usually the right one.

samples.prompt: Position error in a pitot-static system changes when the flaps are lowered. Why?
options: The flaps change the airflow and angle of attack around the pressure sources
Flap extension changes the density of the air entering the pitot tube
Lowering the flaps reduces the static pressure everywhere on the aircraft
The pitot heater current changes when the flap motor runs
samples.explanation: Position (pressure) error is the difference between the pressure sensed at the vent and the true free-stream static pressure. It depends on the pattern of flow around the aircraft, which changes with IAS, angle of attack and configuration (flaps, gear). That is why position-error tables in the flight manual are given for each flap setting.
whyWrong: Density is a property of the free air; the flaps cannot change it.
Static pressure in the free stream does not change with configuration; only the local pressure at the vent does, and it can rise or fall.
The pitot heater and the flap motor are unrelated, and heater current does not affect pressure.
samples.examTip: Position error is the 'P' in the IAS → CAS correction.

samples.prompt: An unpressurised aircraft's static vent ices up and the pilot selects the alternate static source inside the cabin. How do the instruments typically respond?
options: The altimeter and ASI read slightly high, and the VSI briefly shows a climb
The altimeter and ASI read slightly low, and the VSI briefly shows a descent
All three read exactly as before, because cabin and outside pressure are equal
The ASI reads zero and the altimeter freezes at the selection height
samples.explanation: In flight the airflow over the cabin usually lowers the cabin pressure slightly below ambient (a venturi effect, plus heater and vent flows). A lower static pressure makes the altimeter read higher, makes the ASI's pitot − static difference larger so it reads high, and the sudden pressure drop shows briefly on the VSI as a climb. The flight manual gives the corrections.
whyWrong: This is the response to a source pressure higher than ambient; the cabin of an unpressurised aircraft is usually slightly below ambient.
Cabin pressure differs slightly from ambient because of the airflow over the fuselage, so small errors do appear.
This describes a blocked source; selecting the alternate source restores a live static pressure.
samples.examTip: Lower static pressure always means a higher altimeter reading.

chapters.title: Air Temperature Measurement
topics: Remote Reading Thermometers and the TAT Probe
The Aspirator — Measuring Temperature on the Ground
Correction Methods — Getting Back to SAT
Calibration and the International Standard Atmosphere

samples.prompt: A direct reading aircraft thermometer usually consists of a bimetallic helix protruding into the airstream. Movement of the pointer over the temperature scale will depend upon:
options: Difference in electrical resistance of the two metals
Increase in pressure as airspeed increases
Increase in adiabatic cooling as airspeed increases
Different coefficients of expansion of the two metals
samples.explanation: Bimetallic strips work on differential expansion. Brass expands more than invar when heated, causing the strip to curl. Electrical resistance is used in remote reading thermometers, not direct reading.

samples.prompt: Why must the static air temperature, not the TAT, be used to find the local speed of sound and the TAS?
options: The speed of sound depends on the temperature of the undisturbed air, and TAT includes the ram rise
TAT is always lower than SAT in flight, because the probe is cooled by the airflow, so it underestimates the TAS
TAT is measured in kelvin while the formulae use Celsius
SAT already includes compressibility, which the TAS formula needs
samples.explanation: The speed of sound, LSS = 38.97 √T, is a property of the free air the aircraft flies through, at its static temperature. The probe brings the air nearly to rest and heats it by compression (the ram rise), so TAT is warmer than the air outside. Using TAT would overestimate the LSS and the TAS.
whyWrong: TAT is higher than SAT whenever the aircraft is moving, never lower.
Both temperatures can be expressed in either unit; the issue is which air they describe.
Compressibility is a correction to airspeed, not something contained in a temperature.
samples.examTip: Any question that gives both SAT and TAT is checking that you pick SAT for LSS and TAS.

samples.prompt: An aircraft accelerates from M0.40 to M0.80 at a constant static air temperature. How does the ram rise change?
options: It stays the same, because the SAT is constant
It becomes about four times as large
It becomes about eight times as large
It doubles
samples.explanation: Ram rise = 0.2 K M² × SAT(K). At a fixed SAT, doubling M (0.40 to 0.80) multiplies M² by 4, so the ram rise becomes four times as large. The same follows from ram rise = K V² ÷ 2cp with the TAS doubled.
whyWrong: Ram rise depends on speed; a constant SAT does not make it constant.
Eight times would follow from a cube law, which does not apply.
The ram rise is proportional to M² (or TAS²), not to M.
samples.examTip: Speed squared appears again and again: dynamic pressure, ram rise and kinetic heating all go with V².

samples.prompt: An aircraft cruises at M0.80 with a static air temperature of −45 °C. Its temperature probe has a recovery factor of 0.9. What does the TAT gauge show, to the nearest degree?
whyWrong: Subtracts the ram rise; the probe always reads warmer than the static air.
Ignores the recovery factor: −16 °C is the full adiabatic ram rise (K = 1), but the probe only recovers 90% of it.
Uses M instead of M² in the ram-rise term (0.2 × 0.9 × 0.80 instead of × 0.64).
samples.examTip: Always convert to kelvin before multiplying; a Celsius answer from a Celsius multiplication is wrong.

samples.prompt: A temperature probe has a recovery factor of 0.85. What does this mean?
options: It reads 85% of the static air temperature in kelvin
It is accurate to within 15% of the true outside temperature
It senses 85% of the ram rise, so it reads between SAT and the full TAT
Its reading reaches 85% of a sudden change in temperature within one second
samples.explanation: Bringing moving air to rest raises its temperature by the adiabatic ram rise, 0.2 M² × SAT(K). A real probe does not quite stop all the air or keep all the heat, so it senses only a fraction K of that rise. A good total-air-temperature probe has K close to 1; simpler probes are lower. The indicated value is therefore SAT + K × ram rise.
whyWrong: The recovery factor applies to the ram rise only, not to the whole temperature.
The recovery factor is a known property used in the calculation, not an accuracy limit.
That describes a time response (lag), not the recovery factor.
samples.examTip: With K below 1 the probe reads less than the true total temperature but still more than SAT.

chapters.title: The Airspeed Indicator (ASI)
topics: Airspeed Indicator Errors — Application of Corrections

samples.prompt: What pressure does the airspeed indicator actually measure?
options: Total pressure from the pitot tube alone
The ratio of pitot pressure to static pressure
Static pressure, corrected for the aircraft's speed
Dynamic pressure: pitot (total) pressure minus static pressure
samples.explanation: The ASI capsule is fed with pitot (total) pressure inside and static pressure outside, so it responds to the difference: dynamic pressure, ½ρV². The dial is calibrated with ISA sea-level density, so it shows TAS only at sea level in ISA conditions; elsewhere it shows IAS.
whyWrong: Total pressure alone would change with altitude even at zero speed; the static part must be removed.
A pressure ratio is what a Machmeter uses, not an ASI.
Static pressure is what the altimeter measures; on its own it contains no speed information.
samples.examTip: ASI: difference. Machmeter: ratio.

samples.prompt: An aircraft climbs from 2,000 ft to 12,000 ft at a constant CAS of 150 kt in ISA conditions. What happens to its TAS?
options: It increases, by roughly 2% per 1,000 ft
It increases, by roughly 10% per 1,000 ft
It decreases, because the air is colder
It stays at 150 kt
samples.explanation: For the same dynamic pressure (CAS), TAS = EAS ÷ √σ. Density falls with height, so the TAS needed to make the same dynamic pressure rises. A useful rule of thumb is about 2% of CAS per 1,000 ft: over 10,000 ft that is about 20%, so the TAS is roughly 180 kt at 12,000 ft.
whyWrong: Ten times too large: the rule of thumb is about 2% per 1,000 ft.
Colder air raises density slightly, but the fall in pressure dominates: density falls and TAS rises for the same CAS.
TAS equals CAS only at sea level in ISA.
samples.examTip: Climbing at a constant CAS, TAS and Mach number both increase.

samples.prompt: On a light aircraft's ASI, the lower end of the white arc and the lower end of the green arc mark which speeds?
options: VSO and VS1, both measured at the aircraft's lowest operating mass
VFE, the maximum flap speed, and VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed
VS1 (stall, clean configuration) and VSO (stall, landing configuration), at maximum mass
VSO (stall, landing configuration) and VS1 (stall, specified or clean configuration)
samples.explanation: The white arc runs from VSO (stall speed in the landing configuration, flaps down, at maximum mass) to VFE. The green arc runs from VS1 (stall speed in a specified configuration, normally clean, at maximum mass) to VNO. Because flaps lower the stall speed, the white arc starts below the green arc.
whyWrong: The marked stall speeds are at maximum mass, which gives the highest (most conservative) values.
VFE and VNO mark the tops of the white and green arcs, not the bottoms.
Swaps the two: the flaps-down stall speed is lower, so it marks the bottom of the white arc.
samples.examTip: The bottom of the white arc is the lowest number on the dial's markings.

samples.prompt: Put the airspeed corrections in order, starting from the reading on the ASI:
options: IAS → density → CAS → compressibility → EAS → instrument and position error → TAS
IAS → instrument and position error → CAS → compressibility → EAS → density → TAS
IAS → compressibility → CAS → instrument and position error → EAS → density → TAS
IAS → instrument and position error → EAS → density → CAS → compressibility → TAS
samples.explanation: IAS corrected for instrument and position (pressure) error gives CAS. CAS corrected for compressibility gives EAS. EAS corrected for density (TAS = EAS ÷ √σ) gives TAS.
whyWrong: Density is the last correction, from EAS to TAS.
Swaps the first two corrections: instrument and position error turn IAS into CAS; compressibility turns CAS into EAS.
EAS comes after CAS, not before it, and density is applied last.
samples.examTip: If an option has density anywhere except the last step, it is wrong.

samples.prompt: An aircraft cruises at FL350 at 290 kt CAS. Compared with its CAS, its EAS is:
options: Higher, because compressibility makes the ASI under-read
Lower, because the air density at FL350 is less than at sea level
Lower, because at high speed and altitude the ASI over-reads from compressibility
The same, because compressibility only affects TAS
samples.explanation: At high speed the air is compressed as it is brought to rest in the pitot tube, so the pressure sensed is more than ½ρV². The ASI is calibrated with the sea-level compressibility only, so at altitude it over-reads. The compressibility correction is therefore subtracted: EAS < CAS, by several knots at high speed and altitude.
whyWrong: Reverses the effect: air compressed in the pitot tube raises the pressure sensed, so the ASI reads high and EAS is less than CAS.
Lower is right, but density is the EAS-to-TAS correction, not the reason EAS is below CAS.
Compressibility is exactly the CAS-to-EAS correction; it does not act on TAS separately.
samples.examTip: The compressibility correction is always subtracted.

samples.prompt: What does the pressure altimeter actually measure, and how is it turned into an altitude?
options: The time taken for a radio signal to return from the ground
Pitot pressure minus static pressure, scaled into feet
The density of the air, sensed by a sealed capsule and converted to height using the actual outside air temperature
Static pressure, sensed by an evacuated capsule and converted to height using ISA
samples.explanation: An aneroid (evacuated) capsule stack expands as the static pressure falls. Its movement drives the pointers through a mechanism calibrated to the ISA pressure–height relationship, so the altimeter shows the height in the ISA that matches the pressure, measured from the datum set on the subscale.
whyWrong: That is the radio altimeter, a completely different instrument.
Pitot − static is dynamic pressure, used by the ASI.
The capsule responds to pressure, not density, and the scale assumes ISA temperatures, not the actual ones.
samples.examTip: Because it is calibrated to ISA, temperature away from ISA causes an error.

samples.prompt: A pilot winds the altimeter subscale from 1013 hPa down to 1003 hPa without changing altitude. How does the reading change? (Take 1 hPa = 30 ft.)
options: It decreases by about 30 ft
It decreases by about 300 ft
It does not change, because the aircraft has not moved
It increases by about 300 ft
samples.explanation: The altimeter shows height above the pressure level set on the subscale. Lowering the setting by 10 hPa moves the datum level up by about 10 × 30 = 300 ft, so the reading falls by about 300 ft. Subscale and reading move in the same direction.
whyWrong: Forgets to multiply by the 10 hPa change.
The reading is height above the datum set on the subscale, so changing the datum changes the reading.
Reverses the sense: a lower datum pressure moves the datum up towards the aircraft, so the height above it shrinks.
samples.examTip: If the subscale goes up by n hPa, the reading goes up by about 30n ft.

samples.prompt: With a completely blocked static source, an aircraft descends. What is the main danger from the ASI indication?
options: The ASI under-reads, so the pilot may exceed VNE
The ASI behaves like an altimeter, so it reads high during the descent
The ASI shows zero, so the pilot has no speed information
The ASI over-reads, so the pilot may slow down too much and approach the stall
samples.explanation: In the descent the real static pressure rises above the trapped (lower) value. The ASI senses pitot − trapped static, which is too large, so it over-reads. A pilot flying the indicated speed is really slower than shown and may get close to the stall.
whyWrong: Under-reading happens in a climb with a blocked static, not in a descent.
Altimeter-like behaviour comes from a fully blocked pitot system, and it reads LOW in a descent.
A zero reading comes from a pitot inlet blockage with the drain open, not a static blockage.
