samples.examTip: Static blocked: climb → reads low; descent → reads high.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies at a constant indicated altitude with the departure QNH set, from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure, in air colder than ISA. Compared with the indicated altitude, its true altitude is:
options: Lower because of the pressure, but higher because of the temperature, so it is unchanged
Higher, because flying into low pressure raises the aircraft
Higher, because the pressure error and the temperature error cancel
Lower, and both the pressure change and the cold air add to the error
samples.explanation: Flying towards lower pressure without resetting, the aircraft follows a falling pressure level, so it is lower than indicated ('high to low, look out below'). In air colder than ISA the pressure levels are closer together, so again the aircraft is lower than indicated. Both errors make the altimeter over-read, which is the dangerous case over high ground.
whyWrong: Cold air also makes the altimeter over-read; the two errors add rather than cancel.
Flying towards low pressure with the old setting makes the aircraft descend to keep the same reading.
Both effects act in the same direction here, so they do not cancel.
samples.examTip: Cold and low pressure are both 'look out below'.

samples.prompt: In an emergency, a pilot with a blocked static system and no alternate static breaks the glass of the VSI to admit cabin air to the static line. Which statement is correct afterwards?
options: All three instruments work normally, including the VSI
The altimeter works, but the ASI and VSI both read zero
Only the VSI works, because its case is now open to the cabin
The altimeter and ASI work again on cabin pressure, but the VSI reads in reverse
samples.explanation: Breaking the glass lets cabin air straight into the VSI case. From there it reaches the static line, and so the altimeter, the ASI and the VSI's own capsule, only through the metered leak. The altimeter and ASI work again (with some lag and small cabin-pressure errors), but the VSI's roles are swapped: the case now responds at once while the capsule lags, so its indications are reversed. The pilot should ignore it.
whyWrong: The VSI capsule remains on the blocked line while its case is open to the cabin, so it does not work normally.
The ASI has live pitot pressure and now a live static pressure, so it works (with a small cabin-pressure error).
The static line now receives cabin air through the broken case, so the altimeter and ASI work again.
samples.examTip: This last-resort method is a classic scenario question: remember 'VSI reverses'.

samples.prompt: In level flight, the pressures on each side of the choke in the VSI are:
options: Different, with higher pressure inside the capsule
Different, with higher pressure outside the capsule
The same
Different, depending on altitude
samples.explanation: During level flight, static pressure is constant, so pressures on both sides of the choke equalize. Options A, B, and D are incorrect as no pressure differential exists in level flight.

samples.prompt: How does a conventional VSI sense a rate of climb?
options: The capsule senses pitot pressure and the case senses static pressure
It differentiates the altimeter reading electronically
An accelerometer measures vertical acceleration and integrates it into vertical speed
Static goes to the capsule directly but to the case only through a metered leak
samples.explanation: The capsule is fed with static pressure directly and the case through a metered leak (a calibrated restriction). In a climb the static pressure falls; the capsule follows at once, but the case pressure lags behind, so the case is at a higher pressure and the capsule contracts. The difference, and so the reading, is proportional to the rate of change of pressure, that is the vertical speed.
whyWrong: Pitot pressure is not used by a VSI at all.
A mechanical VSI has no electronic processing; it works on the pressure difference across the metered leak.
That describes the extra element of an IVSI, not the basic VSI principle.
samples.examTip: In a climb the case pressure is higher than the capsule pressure.

samples.prompt: What is the main advantage of an instantaneous VSI (IVSI) over a conventional VSI?
options: It needs no static pressure at all
It measures the true vertical speed relative to the terrain
Accelerometer-driven dashpots give an immediate reading when a climb or descent starts
It is not affected by a static blockage
samples.explanation: A conventional VSI lags by several seconds because the leak takes time to build the pressure difference. An IVSI adds small spring-loaded pistons (dashpots) that move with vertical acceleration and immediately pump air into or out of the capsule, so the needle responds as soon as the vertical speed changes. The metered leak then takes over as the rate settles.
whyWrong: The dashpots only speed up the response; the instrument still works on static pressure.
It measures rate of change of pressure height, not height above terrain.
An IVSI still uses static pressure, so it fails with a static blockage.
samples.examTip: IVSI cures lag; it does not cure static-system faults.

samples.prompt: On an ILS with a 3° glidepath, the groundspeed is 120 kt. Roughly what rate of descent should the VSI show?
options: About 365 ft/min
About 1,270 ft/min
About 555 ft/min
About 640 ft/min
samples.explanation: Horizontal speed = 120 kt × 6,076 ft ÷ 60 = 12,152 ft/min. ROD = 12,152 × tan 3° = 12,152 × 0.0524 = 637 ft/min. The rule of thumb 'GS × 5' gives 600 ft/min, close enough for flying.
whyWrong: Uses a 3% gradient; 3° is about 5.2%.
Doubles the rate, as for a 6° path.
Uses 5,280 ft (a statute mile) instead of 6,076 ft for each nautical mile.
samples.examTip: Quick check: 300 ft per nm × nm per minute (GS ÷ 60).

samples.prompt: Why does the metered leak of a VSI combine a capillary tube and a sharp-edged orifice?
options: To filter dust and moisture out of the static line before it reaches the capsule and the case
To provide a back-up path if the capsule ruptures
To keep the calibration steady as viscosity and density change with height and temperature
To stop the needle from moving in turbulence
samples.explanation: Flow through a capillary depends mainly on viscosity, and flow through an orifice mainly on density. Both change with altitude and temperature, in opposite senses as far as the leak rate is concerned. Combining the two keeps the leak rate, and so the calibration, nearly constant over the operating range.
whyWrong: Filters are separate; the leak's design is about flow characteristics.
There is no back-up path; a ruptured capsule makes the instrument unserviceable.
The leak sets the response; damping turbulence is not its purpose.
samples.examTip: 'Compensation for temperature and altitude' is the reason for the leak design.

chapters.title: The Machmeter
topics: Climb at Constant CAS in Standard Atmosphere
Descent at Constant Mach Number in Standard Conditions
Climb and Descent through an Isothermal Layer
Climb and Descent through an Inversion

samples.prompt: The Machmeter uses how many capsules to indicate Mach number?
options: One capsule
Two capsules
Three capsules
Four capsules
samples.explanation: The Machmeter uses two capsules: an airspeed capsule (pitot inside, static outside) that responds to dynamic pressure, and a sealed altimeter capsule that responds to static pressure. Their linkages combine to show TAS as a proportion of the LSS.

samples.prompt: What does a Machmeter measure to give Mach number?
options: Static pressure and outside air temperature
The difference between pitot and static pressure only
TAS divided by a speed of sound that the instrument computes from the TAT probe's reading
The ratio (pitot − static) ÷ static, using an airspeed capsule and an altitude capsule
samples.explanation: Mach number depends on the ratio of dynamic to static pressure, (P − S) ÷ S. A Machmeter uses an airspeed capsule (fed with pitot inside, static outside) and an aneroid altitude capsule, linked through a ratio arm. Temperature cancels out of the ratio, so the Machmeter needs no temperature input.
whyWrong: It also needs pitot pressure; static pressure and temperature alone give no speed information.
That is what the ASI measures; it needs the static pressure as well to form a ratio.
A mechanical Machmeter has no temperature input; it uses a pressure ratio.
samples.examTip: The Machmeter has no temperature error: temperature cancels in the ratio.

samples.prompt: An aircraft climbs through the troposphere at a constant CAS. What happens to its Mach number and TAS?
options: Mach number increases and TAS stays constant
Mach number decreases and TAS increases
Mach number increases and TAS increases
Mach number stays constant and TAS increases
samples.explanation: At a constant CAS, TAS increases with height because the density falls. Meanwhile the temperature, and so the local speed of sound, falls. A rising TAS divided by a falling LSS gives a rising Mach number. That is why jets climb at a constant CAS and then change to a constant Mach.
whyWrong: TAS rises at constant CAS because the density falls.
Mach number rises: TAS increases while the speed of sound falls in the colder air.
Constant Mach needs a falling CAS in a climb.
samples.examTip: Draw three arrows (CAS, TAS, Mach) for every climb or descent question.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about a climb at constant Mach number above the tropopause (ISA): 1. The TAS stays constant. 2. The CAS decreases. 3. The local speed of sound decreases. 4. The Machmeter has a temperature error that grows with height. Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
samples.explanation: In the ISA lower stratosphere the temperature is constant at −56.5 °C, so the speed of sound is constant (about 573 kt). A constant Mach number therefore means a constant TAS. The density keeps falling, so the CAS for that TAS decreases. The Machmeter uses a pressure ratio, so temperature does not enter it.
whyWrong: Statement 3 is false: above the tropopause ISA temperature is constant (−56.5 °C), so the LSS is constant.
Statements 3 and 4 are both false: the LSS is constant in the isothermal layer, and the Machmeter has no temperature error.
Statement 1 is true: constant Mach at a constant LSS gives a constant TAS.
samples.examTip: Isothermal layer: LSS constant, so Mach and TAS change together.

samples.prompt: The static source of an aircraft becomes blocked during the cruise. The aircraft then descends. How does the Machmeter read?
options: It over-reads
It reads correctly, because Mach number needs no static pressure
It under-reads
It reads zero
samples.explanation: Both the dynamic-pressure term (P − S) and the divisor S use the trapped static pressure. In the descent the real static pressure rises above the trapped value, so (P − S_trapped) is too big and S_trapped is too small: the ratio is too large and the Machmeter over-reads, exactly like the ASI.
whyWrong: Static pressure is one of the two inputs to the Machmeter's ratio.
Under-reading happens in a climb with the static blocked.
Zero needs the pitot pressure to equal static, as with a pitot inlet blocked and drain open.
samples.examTip: Machmeter and ASI fail the same way for any pitot or static blockage.

chapters.title: Air Data Computer
topics: Air Data Computer Types — Analogue vs Digital
Advantages of an Air Data System

samples.prompt: In an Air Data System (ADS), which of the following is NOT a primary input sensor?
options: Pitot pressure
Static pressure
Air temperature
Fuel flow
samples.explanation: The basic inputs to an Air Data System are pitot pressure, static pressure and air temperature (plus angle of attack on many systems). Fuel flow is measured by the fuel system, not the ADS.

samples.prompt: Which set lists the usual inputs to an air data computer?
options: Pitot pressure, inertial vertical speed and fuel flow
Static pressure, GNSS altitude and radio altitude
IAS, TAS and Mach number, taken from the pilots' flight instruments
Pitot pressure, static pressure and TAT (plus angle of attack on some types)
samples.explanation: The ADC receives pitot pressure, static pressure and TAT (some installations also take angle of attack to correct static source error). From these it computes pressure altitude, baro-corrected altitude, vertical speed, IAS/CAS, Mach number, TAS and SAT, and sends them to the displays, the FMS, the autopilot and the transponder.
whyWrong: Inertial vertical speed and fuel flow come from other systems.
GNSS and radio altitudes are not air data; the ADC computes pressure altitude from static pressure.
IAS, TAS and Mach are the ADC's outputs, not its inputs.
samples.examTip: If an option lists speeds as 'inputs', it is the wrong way round.

samples.prompt: Which correction does the air data computer apply to remove the known error of the static source at different speeds and configurations?
options: Barometric correction from the subscale
Compressibility correction only
Hysteresis correction
Static source error correction (SSEC)
samples.explanation: The ADC stores the static source position-error characteristics (as a function of Mach number, and sometimes configuration or angle of attack) and corrects the measured static pressure before computing altitude and speeds. This is SSEC, and it is one reason ADC-driven altimeters are more accurate than stand-alone instruments.
whyWrong: The baro setting shifts the altitude datum; it does not correct the static pressure itself.
Compressibility is applied too, but it corrects CAS to EAS; it does not remove the static source's position error.
Hysteresis is a capsule property of mechanical instruments, not something the ADC corrects.
samples.examTip: SSEC = position error, done in software.

samples.prompt: Which system takes pressure altitude from the air data computer and reports it to ATC?
options: The weather radar
The radio altimeter's height output
The SSR transponder (Mode C or S)
The GNSS receiver's altitude output
samples.explanation: The transponder replies to Mode C or Mode S interrogations with the pressure altitude (referenced to 1013.25 hPa) supplied by the ADC or an encoding altimeter. Because it is always referenced to 1013.25 hPa, ATC ground equipment converts it to altitude using the local QNH where needed.
whyWrong: The weather radar has no altitude-reporting function.
The radio altimeter measures height above the ground by radio and does not report it to ATC.
GNSS altitude is geometric, not pressure altitude, and is not the Mode C/S report.
samples.examTip: Mode C/S altitude does not change when the pilot changes the subscale.

samples.prompt: An ADC's total air temperature input fails, while pitot and static pressures are still good. Which output is NOT affected?
options: True airspeed
Static air temperature
Mach number
Wind velocity shown on the navigation display
samples.explanation: Mach number comes from the pressure ratio (P − S) ÷ S, so it needs no temperature. TAS needs the speed of sound, which needs SAT, which the ADC derives from TAT and Mach. Losing TAT therefore loses SAT, TAS and anything built on TAS, such as the wind display.
whyWrong: TAS = M × LSS, and the LSS needs the temperature.
SAT is computed from TAT and Mach number, so it is lost.
Wind is computed from TAS and the ground vector, so it is lost with TAS.
samples.examTip: Ask: does this output need the speed of sound? If yes, it needs temperature.

samples.prompt: A magnetised needle that is free to swing in the vertical plane hangs 65° below the horizontal at one aerodrome and lies level at another. What does this angle measure, and where is the second aerodrome?
options: The angle of dip; the second aerodrome is at a magnetic pole
The deviation; the second aerodrome has no local magnetic anomaly
The magnetic variation; the second aerodrome is on the agonic line
The angle of dip; the second aerodrome is on the magnetic equator
samples.explanation: The earth's field lines are horizontal only at the magnetic equator and point steeply downwards towards the magnetic poles. The angle they make with the horizontal is the dip (inclination): 0° at the magnetic equator, 90° at the magnetic poles.
whyWrong: At a magnetic pole the field is vertical, so the needle would hang straight down (90° dip), not lie level.
Deviation is caused by the aircraft's own magnetism and is measured in the horizontal plane.
Variation is a horizontal angle between true and magnetic north; a needle swinging in the vertical plane measures dip.
samples.examTip: Lines of equal dip are isoclinals; the line of zero dip is the aclinic line (magnetic equator).

samples.prompt: The earth's total magnetic field strength at a place is 39 µT and the angle of dip is 62°. What is the horizontal (H) component?
samples.explanation: H = T cos dip and Z = T sin dip. Horizontal = 39 × cos 62° = 18.3 µT.
whyWrong: Swapped sin and cos (H = T cos dip, Z = T sin dip)
Gave the total field strength
Used tan of the dip angle
samples.examTip: Common trap: swapped sin and cos (H = T cos dip, Z = T sin dip).

samples.prompt: At a place, the earth's total magnetic field is 50 µT and the angle of dip is 60°. What is the horizontal component (H), the part that aligns a compass?
samples.explanation: H = T cos dip = 50 × cos 60° = 25.0 µT. The vertical component Z = T sin dip = 43.3 µT. As dip increases towards the magnetic pole, H shrinks and the compass loses its directive force.
whyWrong: Uses sin dip, which gives the vertical component Z.
Divides by cos dip instead of multiplying.
This is the total field; only its horizontal part acts on a compass.
samples.examTip: H is largest at the magnetic equator; Z is largest at the magnetic poles.

samples.prompt: Why does a direct-reading magnetic compass become unreliable close to the magnetic poles?
options: Magnetic variation becomes zero there
The vertical component disappears, so the compass card cannot stay level
The magnetic field reverses direction every few hours
The horizontal component of the field becomes too weak to align the magnets
samples.explanation: Only the horizontal component H aligns a compass needle with the magnetic meridian. Near the magnetic poles the field points nearly straight down, so H is very small and the needle's directive force is too weak against friction, aircraft magnetism and turning and acceleration errors. Also the vertical component Z, which is large there, causes those errors.
whyWrong: Variation near the poles changes rapidly and can be very large, not zero.
The vertical component is at its strongest near the poles, not weakest; it is the horizontal one that fades.
The field does not reverse on such timescales.
samples.examTip: Pair 'weak H' with 'unreliable compass'.

samples.prompt: The red end of a compass needle points to the earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic. What is the magnetic polarity of that pole?
options: It behaves as a blue (south-seeking type) magnetic pole
Its polarity changes with the season
It behaves as a red (north-seeking type) magnetic pole
It has no polarity; it is only a geographic reference
samples.explanation: Unlike poles attract. The red (north-seeking) end of the needle is drawn towards the earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic, so that pole must have blue (south-type) magnetism, even though it is called the 'north magnetic pole'. In the Antarctic the earth's pole is red-type and attracts the blue end.
whyWrong: The polarity is fixed on human timescales; only the pole's position wanders slowly.
Like poles repel; a red pole would push the red end of the needle away.
The magnetic pole is the point where the field is vertical, so it certainly has a polarity.
samples.examTip: Answer by the attraction rule, not by the name of the pole.

samples.prompt: In the northern hemisphere, the residual tilt of the north-seeking end of the compass magnet in mid-latitudes is approximately:
options: 5° down
2° down
2° up
10° down
samples.explanation: In the northern hemisphere, the north-seeking end of the magnet tilts down by about 2° in mid-latitudes due to the vertical component Z. Option A and D are incorrect values. Option C is wrong because the north-seeking end tilts down, not up, in the northern hemisphere.

samples.prompt: The friction at the pivot of a compass magnet system is reduced by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Using an iridium-tipped pivot in a jewelled cup
Lubricating the pivot with the compass liquid
Reducing the effective weight of the magnet assembly through liquid buoyancy
Increasing the magnetic moment of the magnet
samples.explanation: Increasing magnetic moment increases sensitivity but does not reduce friction. Options A, B, and C are all methods specifically used to reduce friction. Iridium-tipped pivot in jewelled cup (A), liquid lubrication (B), and buoyancy reducing effective weight (C) all reduce friction.

samples.prompt: During a compass swing, normal flying conditions should be simulated with:
options: Engines off and electrical services off
Engines running and electrical/radio services switched on
Only the compass system powered
Aircraft in a nose-up attitude
samples.explanation: During a compass swing, normal flying conditions should be simulated as far as possible, with engines running, electrical/radio services switched on, and the aircraft in a level flight attitude. Option A would not represent normal conditions. Option C is incomplete. Option D is incorrect because level attitude is required.

samples.prompt: Why is a direct-reading magnetic compass filled with liquid?
options: To increase the strength of the magnets
To keep the magnets at a constant temperature so that their strength does not vary
To magnify the card so it is easier to read
To damp the card's oscillations and, by buoyancy, reduce the load on the pivot
samples.explanation: The liquid damps the swinging of the magnet system so it settles quickly (aperiodicity) and, by supporting part of the weight, reduces friction at the pivot (better sensitivity). The liquid must stay clear, not freeze at low temperatures and have little change in viscosity; an expansion chamber allows for its volume change.
whyWrong: A liquid cannot strengthen the magnets.
Temperature control is not the purpose, and the liquid's expansion actually needs an expansion chamber.
The window may magnify, but that is not why the bowl is filled.
samples.examTip: Requirements of a compass: horizontality, sensitivity, aperiodicity.

samples.prompt: In the northern hemisphere an aircraft is heading 270°M. The pilot accelerates. What does the direct-reading compass show while the speed increases?
options: No error, because the aircraft is on an easterly or westerly heading
The card spins freely until the acceleration stops
An apparent turn towards south
An apparent turn towards north
samples.explanation: The magnet system is pivoted above its centre of gravity, which in the northern hemisphere is displaced towards the equator to balance the dip. When the aircraft accelerates on an east or west heading, the CG lags behind the pivot, the vertical field component then turns the magnets, and the card shows an apparent turn towards north. Deceleration shows a turn towards south.
whyWrong: East and west are the headings on which the acceleration error is greatest, not zero; it is zero on north and south.
The card is disturbed, not set spinning.
An apparent turn towards south happens when decelerating, in the northern hemisphere.
samples.examTip: Acceleration error: maximum on east/west headings, zero on north/south.

chapters.title: Gyroscopes.
topics: The Relationship Between Precession and Rigidity
Types of Gyro — Suction or Electric Power

samples.prompt: Which change would increase a gyroscope's rigidity in space?
options: Increasing the friction in the gimbal bearings
Reducing the rotor's mass
Moving the rotor's mass closer to the spin axis
Increasing the rotor speed
samples.explanation: Rigidity is the gyro's resistance to a change in the direction of its spin axis. It is proportional to its angular momentum, H = Iω: the moment of inertia (mass, and how far it lies from the axis) times the spin rate. Rotors are therefore heavy, with the mass concentrated at the rim, and spun fast.
whyWrong: Friction applies torques that cause wander; it does not add rigidity.
Less mass means less angular momentum, so less rigidity.
Moving mass towards the axis reduces the moment of inertia, and with it the rigidity.
samples.examTip: Mass at the rim and high rpm: both increase rigidity.

samples.prompt: Which gyro type is used in a turn indicator?
options: A free (space) gyro with two gimbals and no restraint
A rate gyro: one gimbal, restrained by a spring
An earth gyro, kept vertical by an erection system
A tied gyro, kept in the yawing plane by a levelling system
samples.explanation: A rate gyro has only one gimbal, and a spring opposes its precession. When the aircraft turns, the gyro precesses against the spring by an amount proportional to the rate of turn. Free/tied gyros (DGI) and earth gyros (attitude indicator) measure angles, not rates.
whyWrong: A free gyro holds its direction in space; it does not measure a rate.
The earth (vertical) gyro is used in the attitude indicator.
The tied gyro is used in the directional gyro (DGI).
samples.examTip: One gimbal and a spring always means a rate gyro.

samples.prompt: A force is applied to the rim of a spinning gyro rotor. In which direction does the rotor respond?
options: Opposite to the direction of the force
Directly in the direction of the force
As if the force were moved 90° round the rotor against the direction of spin
As if the force were moved 90° round the rotor in the direction of spin
samples.explanation: Precession: the rotor behaves as if the force acted at a point 90° further round in the direction of spin. The rate of precession equals the applied torque divided by the angular momentum, so a faster, heavier rotor precesses more slowly for the same torque.
whyWrong: It neither yields nor resists head-on; it precesses at right angles.
A gyro does not move in the direction of the applied force; that is the essence of precession.
The 90° displacement is in the direction of rotation, not against it.
samples.examTip: Draw the rotor, mark the force, then rotate it 90° with the spin.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is parked at 30°N. Its directional gyro has no latitude correction and is set to 090°. Ignoring real wander, what will it read 2 hours later?
samples.explanation: Earth-rate wander = 15 × sin lat = 15 × sin 30° = 7.5°/h. Over 2 h, 15°. In the northern hemisphere the indicated heading falls, so the DGI reads 090 − 15 = 075°.
whyWrong: Applies earth-rate wander in the wrong sense: in the northern hemisphere the reading decreases.
Uses the full 15°/h without the sin latitude factor.
Uses cos 30° (13.0°/h) instead of sin 30°.
samples.examTip: At 30° the factor is exactly ½: an easy number to remember.

samples.prompt: The suction (vacuum) supply to an air-driven turn indicator falls, so its rotor runs slowly. How does the instrument read in a turn?
options: It over-reads the rate of turn
It shows a turn in the opposite direction
It reads correctly, because a rate gyro does not depend on rotor speed
It under-reads the rate of turn
samples.explanation: In a rate gyro the turn produces a precessional torque proportional to the rotor's angular momentum times the rate of turn, balanced by a spring. A slower rotor produces less torque for the same turn, the spring stretches less, and the instrument under-reads. An overspeeding rotor would over-read.
whyWrong: The deflection is proportional to rotor speed; a slow rotor gives a smaller deflection, not a larger one.
A slower rotor changes the size of the indication, not its direction.
The precessional torque of a rate gyro is proportional to its angular momentum, so rotor speed matters.
samples.examTip: Low suction: turn indicator under-reads, so the pilot may turn faster than rate 1.

chapters.title: Directional Gyro Indicator (DGI)
topics: The Principle and Construction of the DGI
Apparent Wander (Due to Rotation of the Earth)
Effect of Change of Aircraft Latitude on Compensated DGI

samples.prompt: Why must a directional gyro indicator be reset to the magnetic compass at regular intervals?
options: It reads true heading, which must be converted to magnetic
Its rotor slows down and stops after about 15 minutes unless it is re-spun
It has no north-seeking property, so its reading drifts with wander
Its card is magnetised by the aircraft's electrical systems
samples.explanation: A DGI is a tied gyro with a horizontal spin axis. It gives a steady, easily read heading that is free from the compass's turning and acceleration errors, but it has no directional reference of its own. Earth rate, transport wander and real wander make its reading drift, so it is set to the compass heading in steady flight, typically every 10–15 minutes.
whyWrong: The DGI reads whatever it was set to; it has no reference of its own.
The rotor keeps running as long as suction or power is available; the problem is drift, not stopping.
The DGI is not a magnetic instrument; aircraft magnetism does not act on it.
samples.examTip: Reset only in straight, level, unaccelerated flight, when the compass is reliable.

samples.prompt: A DGI's latitude nut is set for 23°N. The aircraft operates at 49°N. Ignoring transport wander, how does the indicated heading change in 0.5 h?
options: decreases by 2.0°
decreases by 2.7°
increases by 2.7°
decreases by 3.3°
samples.explanation: The latitude nut corrects for 15 sin 23° = 5.86°/h. Earth rate at 49°N is 15 sin 49° = 11.32°/h. The residual is +5.46°/h of uncorrected wander, so over 0.5 h the reading decreases by 2.7°.
whyWrong: Used cos lat instead of sin lat
Got the direction of the residual drift the wrong way round
Took the residual as proportional to the latitude difference instead of the difference of the sines
samples.examTip: Common trap: used cos lat instead of sin lat.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of the latitude nut (latitude correction) on a directional gyro?
options: To keep the spin axis horizontal during turns
To correct the reading for the magnetic variation at the latitude where the aircraft is flying
To make the gyro precess against earth-rate wander at a chosen latitude
To correct for transport wander when flying east or west
samples.explanation: The latitude nut is an adjustable weight on the inner gimbal. Its offset produces a small torque, and the gyro precesses in azimuth at a steady rate. Set correctly, this rate equals 15 sin lat °/h in the opposite sense to earth-rate wander, so the drift cancels at that latitude. Away from the set latitude a residual remains.
whyWrong: The spin axis is kept horizontal by the erection system (air jets or a torque motor), not by the latitude nut.
The DGI is not a magnetic instrument; variation is a separate correction.
Transport wander depends on speed and track, which a fixed nut cannot know.
samples.examTip: The nut only corrects earth rate, and only at the latitude it is set for.

samples.prompt: During a steep turn, a DGI shows a heading error that disappears when the wings are levelled. What is the error called?
options: Gimbal error
Real wander
Earth-rate wander
Transport wander
samples.explanation: When the aircraft is banked or pitched, the gimbal rings are no longer at right angles, so the geometry between the card and the spin axis introduces an error in the reading. It is a geometric error only, and vanishes when the aircraft returns to level flight. That is why the DGI is read and reset with the wings level.
whyWrong: Real wander is a permanent movement of the spin axis; it does not disappear on rolling level.
Earth-rate wander builds up steadily with time and does not vanish when the wings are levelled.
Transport wander depends on movement over the earth and also persists.
samples.examTip: 'Disappears when wings level' = gimbal error.

samples.prompt: A DGI's latitude nut is correctly set for operation at 50°N. The aircraft is moved to 50°S and the nut is not changed. Ignoring real and transport wander, what is the drift of the indicated heading there?
options: Zero, because the latitude is numerically the same
About 11.5°/h, with the reading increasing
About 23°/h, with the reading increasing
About 11.5°/h, with the reading decreasing
samples.explanation: At 50°N the nut produces 15 sin 50° = 11.5°/h of precession making the reading increase, cancelling earth rate (which makes it decrease). At 50°S earth rate makes the reading increase by 11.5°/h, and the nut still adds its 11.5°/h in the same sense. Total ≈ 23°/h, reading increasing.
whyWrong: Earth-rate wander changes sense between hemispheres, so a nut set for the north adds to the error in the south.
Remembers the southern-hemisphere earth rate but forgets that the uncorrected nut now adds its own 11.5°/h in the same sense.
Applies northern-hemisphere thinking: earth rate alone, in the sense it has in the north. In the south it makes the reading increase, and the nut adds to it.
samples.examTip: Earth rate changes sign at the equator; the nut does not.

chapters.title: The Artificial Horizon
topics: Acceleration Error in the Air Driven Artificial Horizon
Turning Errors in the Air Driven Artificial Horizon

samples.prompt: What is the maximum pitch limit in older design artificial horizons?
samples.explanation: With older designs, typical limits are ± 60° in pitch and 110° each way in roll. Modern instruments have complete freedom in roll and up to ± 85° in pitch.

samples.prompt: What is the typical suction pressure used in an air driven artificial horizon?
options: 2 inches of mercury
4 inches of mercury
6 inches of mercury
8 inches of mercury
samples.explanation: In the air driven artificial horizon, an engine-driven suction pump creates a suction of about 4 inches of mercury in the instrument case. This draws replacement air through a filter to spin the rotor.

samples.prompt: What is the maximum rotor speed of an air driven artificial horizon?
samples.explanation: The air driven artificial horizon spins the rotor at up to 15,000 rpm. Electric horizons achieve higher speeds of 22,500 rpm, giving greater rigidity.

samples.prompt: Which gyro type, and with what spin-axis orientation, is used in the attitude indicator?
options: A free gyro with its spin axis along the aircraft's longitudinal axis
A tied gyro with its spin axis horizontal, kept in the aircraft's yawing plane
An earth gyro with its spin axis vertical, held there by an erection system
A rate gyro with its spin axis horizontal and athwartships
samples.explanation: The attitude indicator uses an earth gyro: a two-gimbal gyro whose spin axis is held vertical by an erection system (pendulous vanes in air-driven instruments, torque motors and levelling switches in electric ones). The aircraft moves around the stable vertical gyro, and the horizon bar is linked to it.
whyWrong: A longitudinal axis would not give a stable horizon in both pitch and roll.
That is the directional gyro.
That is the turn indicator's rate gyro.
samples.examTip: Vertical axis = AI; horizontal fore–aft-free axis = DGI; one gimbal = turn indicator.

samples.prompt: Why is the roll (lateral) erection of an electric attitude indicator cut out when the aircraft is turning?
options: Levelling switches would sense centripetal acceleration and erect to a false vertical
To stop the gyro from precessing in the opposite direction to the turn
Because the gyro cannot topple during a balanced turn, so erection would serve no purpose
To save electrical power during manoeuvres
samples.explanation: In a balanced turn the apparent vertical (the resultant of gravity and centripetal acceleration) is tilted towards the outside of the turn, at the bank angle. If erection stayed active, the gyro would slowly align with that false vertical and show an error after rolling out. Cutting out roll erection during turns avoids this; normal erection resumes when the wings are level.
whyWrong: The cut-out prevents erection to a wrong vertical; it does not deal with any reverse precession.
The gyro can still wander in a turn; erection is cut out only because it would erect to the wrong reference.
Power consumption is tiny and not the reason.
samples.examTip: Acceleration in any direction gives the erection system a false vertical.

chapters.title: The Turn and Slip Indicator.
topics: Operating Principles of the Slip Indicator

samples.prompt: How long does a rate 1 turn through 180° take?
options: 3 minutes
2 minutes
1 minute
30 seconds
samples.explanation: Rate 1 is 3°/s, so 360° takes 120 s (2 min) and 180° takes 180 ÷ 3 = 60 s, one minute.
whyWrong: Three minutes is wrong for any standard rate: rate 1 covers 180° in one minute.
Two minutes is the time for a full 360° at rate 1.
Thirty seconds is a rate 2 turn through 180°.
samples.examTip: Timed turns in the hold and on a procedure all use 3°/s.

samples.prompt: What bank angle is needed for a rate ½ (1.5°/s) turn at a TAS of 190 kt (nearest degree)?
whyWrong: Used the rule of thumb TAS/10 + 7, which is only approximate
Used half the rate of turn
Used double the rate of turn
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the rule of thumb TAS/10 + 7, which is only approximate.

samples.prompt: How is the rate gyro in a turn-and-slip indicator mounted?
options: Spin axis fore-and-aft, with its gimbal on the lateral axis
Spin axis horizontal and fore-and-aft, with no gimbal at all
Spin axis vertical, with gimbals on the pitch and roll axes
Spin axis horizontal and athwartships, with its single gimbal on the fore-and-aft axis
samples.explanation: The rotor spins about a horizontal athwartships (lateral) axis and is mounted in one gimbal pivoted fore and aft. When the aircraft yaws, the gyro precesses about the fore-and-aft gimbal axis, against a spring, by an amount proportional to the rate of turn. The pointer shows that rate.
whyWrong: With the spin axis fore-and-aft, a yaw would not produce the required precession about the longitudinal gimbal.
Without a gimbal the rotor could not precess against the spring, so no rate would be shown.
A vertical axis with two gimbals is the attitude indicator.
samples.examTip: One gimbal → one degree of freedom → rate gyro.

samples.prompt: In a turn to the right, the slip ball of the turn-and-slip indicator lies to the right of centre. What is happening and what corrects it?
options: The aircraft is skidding out of the turn; apply left rudder
The aircraft is slipping into the turn; apply more right rudder or reduce bank
The turn is balanced; no correction is needed
The aircraft is slipping; apply left rudder and increase bank
samples.explanation: The ball moves to where the resultant of gravity and centrifugal force points. In a right turn with too much bank for the rate of turn (or too little right rudder), the aircraft slips inwards and the ball falls to the inside, the right. 'Step on the ball': right rudder, or less bank, centres it.
whyWrong: A skid puts the ball to the outside of the turn (left, in a right turn).
A balanced turn keeps the ball centred.
Left rudder and more bank would make the slip worse.
samples.examTip: The ball's side tells you which rudder pedal to press.

samples.prompt: What bank angle gives a rate ½ (1.5°/s) coordinated turn at a TAS of 350 kt (to the nearest degree)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Balanced turn: tan φ = Vω ÷ g (V in m/s, ω in rad/s); ω = g tan φ ÷ V. Rate 1 = 3°/s. In a balanced turn tan φ = Vω ÷ g. V = 350 kt × 0.5144 = 180.1 m/s; ω = 1.5°/s = 0.0262 rad/s. tan φ = 180.1 × 0.0262 ÷ 9.81 = 0.481, so φ = 25.7°.
whyWrong: Used sin instead of tan: tan φ = Vω ÷ g, because the vertical lift component balances the weight: gives 29°.
Used twice the required rate of turn: rate 1 is 3°/s, rate 2 is 6°/s and rate ½ is 1.5°/s: gives 44°.
Left the TAS in knots instead of converting it to m/s: gives 43°.
samples.examTip: Convert knots to m/s (× 0.5144) and degrees per second to radians per second (× π ÷ 180) before using the formula.

chapters.title: The Turn Co-ordinator
topics: Rate of Turn and Time Calculations

samples.prompt: The primary difference between a Turn Co-ordinator and a Turn and Bank indicator is in the:
options: Rotor speed of the gyroscope
Setting of the precession axis of the rate gyroscope and method of display
Type of power source used to drive the gyroscope
Number of gimbal rings employed
samples.explanation: The turn co-ordinator differs from the turn and bank (turn and slip) indicator in how its rate gyro's precession axis is set (tilted about 30°) and in its display, a small aircraft symbol instead of a needle.

samples.prompt: What is the radius of a rate 1 turn at a TAS of 430 kt?
options: 2.3 nm
4.3 nm
4.6 nm
7.2 nm
samples.explanation: A rate 1 turn takes 2 min for 360°, covering 430/30 nm. Radius = circumference ÷ 2π = 14.33 ÷ 2π = 2.28 nm (≈ TAS ÷ 200).
whyWrong: Used TAS ÷ 100 instead of about TAS ÷ 200
Gave the diameter instead of the radius
Gave the distance flown per minute, not the radius
samples.examTip: Common trap: used TAS ÷ 100 instead of about TAS ÷ 200.

samples.prompt: What is the radius of a rate 1 turn at a TAS of 270 kt?
options: 1.4 nm
2.7 nm
2.9 nm
4.5 nm
samples.explanation: A rate 1 turn takes 2 min for 360°, covering 270/30 nm. Radius = circumference ÷ 2π = 9.00 ÷ 2π = 1.43 nm (≈ TAS ÷ 200).
whyWrong: Used TAS ÷ 100 instead of about TAS ÷ 200
Gave the diameter instead of the radius
Gave the distance flown per minute, not the radius
samples.examTip: Common trap: used TAS ÷ 100 instead of about TAS ÷ 200.

samples.prompt: Why is the gimbal axis of a turn coordinator's gyro tilted up at the front by about 30°?
options: To stop the gyro from toppling in steep turns
To make it read pitch attitude in a climbing turn
To sense rate of roll as well as rate of yaw, for an earlier indication
So that the instrument can show the aircraft's bank angle directly on its dial
samples.explanation: Tilting the gimbal axis makes the gyro sensitive to rotation about both the yaw and the roll axes. The pilot therefore sees an indication as soon as the aircraft starts to roll into a turn, before the turn rate builds up. Once the turn is established it shows the rate of turn.
whyWrong: Toppling is limited by stops; the tilt is about sensing roll.
It gives no pitch information.
It still shows a rate, not an angle; a turn coordinator cannot be used as an attitude indicator.
samples.examTip: The miniature aircraft looks like a bank indicator but it shows rate, not bank angle.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the turn coordinator is INCORRECT?
options: It responds to the rate of roll as well as the rate of yaw
It uses a rate gyro restrained by a spring
Its miniature aircraft shows the bank angle directly
Its ball shows whether the turn is balanced
samples.explanation: The turn coordinator's miniature aircraft looks like an attitude display, but it shows the rate of turn (with an early indication from roll rate), not the bank angle. Many instruments carry the words 'no pitch information'. The ball is a simple inclinometer showing slip or skid.
whyWrong: This is true: the tilted gimbal makes it sense roll rate too.
This is true: like the turn indicator, it uses a spring-restrained rate gyro.
This is true: the ball is an inclinometer showing slip or skid.
samples.examTip: 'Shows bank angle' is false for both the turn indicator and the turn coordinator.

samples.prompt: Deviation is defined as the angular difference between:
options: True north and magnetic north
Compass north and magnetic north
Compass north and true north
Magnetic north and grid north
samples.explanation: Deviation is specifically the angular difference between the direction taken up by a compass needle and the magnetic meridian. Option A describes variation, not deviation. Option C combines true and compass which includes both variation and deviation. Option D involves grid north which is unrelated to aircraft compass deviation.

samples.prompt: What is the difference between hard-iron and soft-iron magnetism in an aircraft?
options: Hard iron is permanently magnetised; soft iron's magnetism is induced and varies with heading
Soft iron keeps permanent magnetism; hard iron changes with heading
Hard iron is magnetised by electric currents; soft iron by the earth's field only while on the ground
Hard iron affects only the vertical field; soft iron affects only the horizontal field
samples.explanation: Hard iron (for example steel parts) acquires magnetism during manufacture and keeps it, so it behaves like a fixed magnet in the aircraft. Soft iron is magnetised only while it sits in the earth's field; its induced magnetism changes with heading and magnetic latitude. Together they cause deviation, which is measured in a compass swing and reduced by correctors.
whyWrong: Reverses the two.
Electrical currents are a separate source; soft-iron magnetism is induced in flight too, on every heading.
Both kinds can have horizontal and vertical components.
samples.examTip: Soft iron's induced field explains why deviation changes after moving to a very different magnetic latitude.

samples.prompt: An aircraft's technical log lists four recent events. Which one does NOT normally call for a compass swing before further flight?
options: A lightning strike on the aircraft
Installation of new electrical equipment near the compass
A routine refuelling
Replacement of the compass
samples.explanation: A swing is needed whenever the aircraft's magnetic condition or the compass may have changed: a new or refitted compass, major structural work or new equipment near it, a lightning strike, long storage on one heading, a move to a very different magnetic latitude, and at the periods in the maintenance schedule. Refuelling does not change the aircraft's magnetism.
whyWrong: A lightning strike can magnetise parts of the structure and change the deviation.
New electrical equipment or wiring near the compass can change its deviation.
A new compass must be swung and its deviation card renewed.
samples.examTip: Look for the event with no magnetic effect.

samples.prompt: The required true heading is 095°(T). The variation is 4°W and the compass deviation on this heading is 2°E. What compass heading should be flown?
samples.explanation: True to magnetic: variation west is added ('west is best'): 095 + 4 = 099°M. Magnetic to compass: deviation east is subtracted ('east is least'): 099 − 2 = 097°(C).
whyWrong: Applies both corrections with the wrong sign.
Adds the easterly deviation instead of subtracting it on the way from magnetic to compass.
Subtracts the westerly variation instead of adding it on the way from true to magnetic.
samples.examTip: Write the magnetic heading as a separate line before applying deviation.

samples.prompt: A compass swing finds a deviation of +4° (east) on 090°M and −2° (west) on 270°M. What is coefficient B?
options: +1° (easterly)
+6° (easterly)
+3° (easterly)
−3° (westerly)
samples.explanation: Coefficient B = (deviation on 090 − deviation on 270) ÷ 2 = (+4 − (−2)) ÷ 2 = +3°. Coefficient B is caused by fore-and-aft magnetic fields and gives a deviation of B sin(heading), greatest on east and west. Coefficient C = (deviation on 000 − deviation on 180) ÷ 2, greatest on north and south.
whyWrong: Averages the two values (4 − 2) ÷ 2; coefficient B uses the difference of the readings on 090 and 270.
Forgets to divide by 2.
Takes 270 minus 090 and so reverses the sign.
samples.examTip: B goes with sin heading (E/W), C with cos heading (N/S).

chapters.title: Remote Indicating Magnetic Compass
topics: Limitations of the Direct Reading Compass
Limitations of the Directional Gyro Indicator
Operation with Steady Heading — Correction for Gyro Drift
Operation in a Turn — Gyro Drift Small Over Period of Turn

samples.prompt: Where is the flux valve (detector unit) of a remote-indicating compass usually fitted, and why?
options: On the flight-deck panel, so the crew can check it
Next to the main battery, so it has a short power lead
In the engine nacelle, where the temperature is stable
In a wingtip or the fin, as far as possible from the aircraft's magnetic fields
samples.explanation: The flux valve senses the earth's weak horizontal field, so it is mounted where the aircraft's own magnetism is smallest, usually a wingtip or the fin. Its signal is sent electrically to the gyro unit and indicators, which can then be placed wherever is convenient.
whyWrong: The flight deck is full of electrical and magnetic sources, the reason a remote sensor is used at all.
Batteries and heavy current cables produce strong magnetic fields.
Nacelles contain engine steel and electrical machines that would cause large deviations.
samples.examTip: 'Remote' in the name refers to the sensor's location.

samples.prompt: What is the main benefit of slaving a directional gyro to a flux valve in a remote-indicating compass?
options: It makes the compass read true heading, so no variation needs to be applied at all
It joins the gyro's short-term stability to a long-term magnetic reference
It removes deviation, so no compass swing is ever needed
It removes the need for the gyro, so the system has no moving parts
samples.explanation: The gyro gives a steady heading free from turning and acceleration errors but drifts with time. The flux valve gives a magnetic reference that does not drift but is disturbed by manoeuvres. Slaving precesses the gyro slowly towards the flux valve's heading, so short-term disturbances are averaged out while long-term drift is removed.
whyWrong: The flux valve senses magnetic north; true heading still needs variation applied.
Remote compasses still have deviation and are swung; correctors compensate it.
The gyro is still essential: it smooths out the flux valve's turning and acceleration errors.
samples.examTip: Slaving is deliberately slow, so brief flux-valve errors in turns are filtered out.

samples.prompt: A flux valve's primary coil is excited with 400 Hz AC. At what frequency is the signal in its pick-off (secondary) coils that carries the heading information?
options: 400 Hz
800 Hz
200 Hz
Direct current
samples.explanation: The 400 Hz excitation saturates the soft-iron spokes twice per cycle. Without an external field the pick-off voltages cancel; the earth's horizontal field upsets the symmetry and produces an output at twice the excitation frequency, 800 Hz. The amplitudes in the three spokes (120° apart) define the direction of the field.
whyWrong: The 400 Hz components cancel; the earth's field shows up as the second harmonic.
No sub-harmonic is produced.
The output is an AC signal, which the system resolves into heading.
samples.examTip: Second harmonic: double the excitation frequency.

samples.prompt: The annunciator (synchronising indicator) of a slaved compass is seen oscillating slightly either side of its centre position during straight and level flight. What does this show?
options: The system is slaving normally, making small corrections to the gyro
The compass needs an immediate swing
The flux valve has failed and the system is in free gyro mode
The gyro has toppled and must be re-erected
samples.explanation: The annunciator shows the error signal between the gyro's heading and the flux valve's heading. In normal slaved operation that signal keeps changing sign as the small corrections are made, so the annunciator oscillates slightly. A steady deflection to one side means the system is not synchronised and needs fast slaving or investigation.
whyWrong: Small oscillations are normal behaviour, not a sign of changed deviation.
In free (DG) mode there is no slaving, so the annunciator would not oscillate in this way.
A toppled gyro would give a large, wandering heading error, not small oscillations.
samples.examTip: A steady offset of the annunciator, not a small oscillation, is the warning sign.

samples.prompt: Why is the slaving of a remote-indicating compass normally cut out during turns?
options: Slaving would make the gyro topple in the turn
The flux valve cannot work when the aircraft is banked more than 5°
The aircraft's heading changes too quickly in a turn for the indicator's servo to follow
The tilted flux valve senses part of the vertical field and gives a false heading
samples.explanation: The flux valve is pendulously mounted to stay horizontal, but in a turn it hangs along the apparent vertical, tilted from the true vertical. It then picks up part of the vertical component Z, giving a false magnetic heading. Cutting out slaving during turns stops the gyro from being corrected towards this wrong value.
whyWrong: Slaving acts in azimuth; it does not topple the gyro.
The flux valve continues to produce a signal when banked; the problem is that the signal is wrong.
The indicator follows the gyro, which handles turn rates easily.
samples.examTip: Any pendulous sensor (AI erection, flux valve) is cut out in turns for the same reason: false vertical.

samples.prompt: The two accelerometers in an INS are mounted on the platform to measure acceleration in which directions?
options: North-south and vertical
East-west and vertical
North-south and east-west
Pitch and roll axes
samples.explanation: The platform carries one accelerometer aligned north-south and one aligned east-west, which give the horizontal accelerations needed for navigation. A third, vertical accelerometer may be added.

samples.prompt: An INS measures velocity components of 68 kt south and 338 kt west. What are the track and groundspeed?
samples.explanation: GS = √(68² + 338²) = 345 kt. The track is the direction of the combined vector: 68 kt south and 338 kt west gives 259°(T).
whyWrong: Added the components instead of using Pythagoras
Gave the reciprocal track
Swapped the north and east components
samples.examTip: Common trap: added the components instead of using Pythagoras.

samples.prompt: How does an inertial navigation system find distance travelled?
options: By measuring the Doppler shift of signals reflected from the ground
By integrating measured acceleration once to get velocity and again to get distance
By timing radio signals from satellites
By counting the earth's rotation with a gyro
samples.explanation: Accelerometers on a platform kept level and aligned to north and east measure the aircraft's accelerations. The computer integrates acceleration with respect to time to get velocity, and integrates velocity to get distance, from which it updates latitude and longitude. No external signals are needed.
whyWrong: That is a Doppler navigation system.
That is GNSS; the INS is self-contained.
The gyros keep the reference directions; the distance comes from the accelerometers.
samples.examTip: Two integrations: that is why accelerometer errors grow quickly.

samples.prompt: During ground alignment of a gimballed INS, what happen in the levelling and gyrocompassing phases?
options: Gyros detect tilt to level the platform, then accelerometers sense the earth's rotation to find magnetic north
The system loads a position from GNSS, then the aircraft is taxied to calibrate the accelerometers
The platform is levelled by gravity, then aligned to north using the magnetic compass
Accelerometers detect tilt to level the platform, then gyros sense the earth's rotation to find true north
samples.explanation: With the aircraft stationary, any output from the horizontal accelerometers means the platform is tilted, so the platform is driven level (levelling). Then, in gyrocompassing, the system detects the component of the earth's rotation sensed by the east gyro and turns the platform until that component is zero, which points it to true north. Present position must be entered.
whyWrong: Reverses the sensors' roles, and an INS finds true north, not magnetic.
The aircraft must stay stationary during alignment; taxiing would spoil it.
An INS does not use the magnetic compass for alignment.
samples.examTip: INS gives true heading; magnetic needs variation from a stored table.

samples.prompt: Why does INS alignment take longer at high latitudes, and become impossible near the poles?
options: The horizontal component of earth rate, 15 cos lat, becomes too small to find north
The magnetic variation is too large to compute
Gravity is too weak near the poles to level the platform
The vertical component of earth rate becomes zero at the poles
samples.explanation: Gyrocompassing finds north from the horizontal component of the earth's rotation, which is 15 cos lat °/h: 15°/h at the equator but very small near the poles. The smaller the signal, the longer the system needs to find north accurately; very close to the poles it cannot do so.
whyWrong: The INS finds true north; it does not need the magnetic variation to align.
Gravity is actually slightly stronger at the poles.
The vertical component (15 sin lat) is largest at the poles; it is the horizontal component that fades.
samples.examTip: Horizontal earth rate (cos lat) finds north; vertical earth rate (sin lat) causes DGI drift.

chapters.title: Inertial Reference System
topics: Principles of Laser Gyros and IRS

samples.prompt: What distinguishes a strapdown inertial reference system from a gimballed INS?
options: It needs GNSS signals to measure acceleration
It uses magnetic sensors instead of gyros
Its platform is kept level and aligned with north by gimbals and torque motors
The sensors are fixed to the airframe and the computer resolves their outputs
samples.explanation: In a strapdown system the sensors are rigidly mounted to the aircraft structure. Instead of a physically stabilised platform, the computer uses the gyro outputs to keep track of the aircraft's attitude and to resolve the accelerometer readings into north, east and vertical components. With no gimbals or moving parts, it is lighter and more reliable.
whyWrong: An IRS is self-contained; GNSS may be blended in later, but it is not needed to measure acceleration.
An IRS still uses gyros (usually ring laser gyros), not magnetic sensors.
That describes the gimballed (stable platform) INS.
samples.examTip: No gimbals → no gimbal lock and fewer moving parts.

samples.prompt: How does a ring laser gyro measure rotation?
options: A single laser beam is bent by rotation, and the bend is measured
Counter-rotating laser beams in a closed path; rotation makes their frequencies differ
A laser measures the distance to the airframe as it rotates
A spinning rotor precesses against a spring by an amount proportional to the rotation rate
samples.explanation: A ring laser gyro has two beams circulating in opposite directions round a triangular cavity. When the unit rotates about its axis, one beam's path becomes effectively longer and the other's shorter (the Sagnac effect), so their frequencies differ. The beat frequency between them is proportional to the rotation rate.
whyWrong: Two counter-rotating beams are needed; the effect is a path-length (frequency) difference, not a bend.
It measures the effect of rotation on light inside a closed path, not distances to the structure.
That is a mechanical rate gyro; a ring laser gyro has no spinning mass.
samples.examTip: No rotor, no spin-up time: ring laser gyros are ready almost at once.

samples.prompt: How does an IRS provide magnetic heading?
options: It applies magnetic variation from a stored table to the true heading it computes
It contains a flux valve that senses the earth's field
It measures the earth's magnetic dip with its accelerometers
It cannot: magnetic heading always comes from the standby compass
samples.explanation: The IRS determines true heading during alignment and keeps it by gyro measurement. For magnetic heading it applies the variation for the present position from a stored magnetic variation table. Near the magnetic poles, where variation changes rapidly, crews often switch the displays to true heading.
whyWrong: The IRS has no magnetic sensor; any flux valve belongs to a separate compass system.
Accelerometers sense specific force, not magnetism.
IRSs routinely output magnetic heading for the displays and FMS.
samples.examTip: Old variation tables (or polar regions) make IRS magnetic heading less reliable.

samples.prompt: What is lock-in in a ring laser gyro, and how is it usually prevented?
options: The mirrors freeze at altitude; a heater prevents it
At high rotation rates the lasers stop lasing; a rate limiter in the computer prevents it
At very low rotation rates the beams' frequencies lock together; dither prevents it
The beams lock to the frequency of the aircraft's AC supply; a filter prevents it
samples.explanation: Small imperfections in the mirrors scatter a little light from each beam into the other. At very low rotation rates this coupling pulls the two frequencies together, so the gyro shows no rotation. Dithering the gyro with a small, rapid mechanical vibration keeps it moving through the lock-in band, and the dither motion is removed from the output.
whyWrong: Lock-in is an optical coupling effect, not icing.
The problem appears at low rotation rates, not high ones.
Lock-in is caused by back-scatter coupling between the beams, not by the power supply.
samples.examTip: Lock-in + low rotation + dither always go together.

samples.prompt: During alignment an IRS can work out its own latitude. Why must the crew still enter present position?
options: Without the entry, the ring laser gyros will not start
The entry sets the magnetic variation, which the IRS needs to find north
The IRS cannot determine longitude, and the entered latitude is used to check its own computation
The IRS cannot determine latitude without the entry
samples.explanation: During alignment the IRS measures the direction and size of the earth's rotation: the ratio of its vertical and horizontal components gives latitude. Nothing about the earth's rotation reveals longitude, so it must be entered. Most systems compare the entered latitude with their own and alert the crew to a mismatch.
whyWrong: The gyros start regardless; the position is needed for navigation.
The IRS finds true north from earth rate; magnetic variation comes from a stored table later.
The IRS does compute latitude from the earth rate it senses; the entry is compared with it.
samples.examTip: A latitude-mismatch message during alignment means the entered position is wrong.

samples.prompt: One function of the Radio Altimeter in the latter stage of an approach is to:
options: Increase autopilot sensitivity
Desensitize the autopilot and flight director response to the ILS glidepath
Disconnect the autopilot
Activate the go-around mode
samples.explanation: Late in an ILS approach, the radio altimeter desensitises (gain-schedules) the autopilot and flight director response to the glidepath, because the beam converges and becomes more sensitive near the threshold.

samples.prompt: Which frequency band and technique does a typical civil radio altimeter use?
options: About 9.3 GHz, pulsed radar scanning ahead of the aircraft
About 108–118 MHz, amplitude modulation
About 1030–1090 MHz, pulse interrogation and reply
About 4.2–4.4 GHz, frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW)
samples.explanation: Civil radio altimeters operate in the 4.2–4.4 GHz band. Most use FMCW: the transmitter frequency is swept continuously, and the difference between the frequency being transmitted and the one being received from the ground is proportional to the time delay, and therefore to height.
whyWrong: About 9.3 GHz is a typical weather radar frequency; the radio altimeter looks down, not ahead.
108–118 MHz is the VOR/ILS localiser band.
1030/1090 MHz is used by SSR, ACAS and DME-style interrogation, not radio altimeters.
samples.examTip: Radio altimeter = SHF, looking down; weather radar = X band, looking ahead.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies level on the barometric altimeter over the edge of a coastal cliff, out over the sea. What does the radio altimeter show?
options: No change, because the barometric altitude is constant
A sudden increase in height, because it measures height above whatever lies directly below
A sudden decrease in height
A gradual change, as it averages the terrain over the previous minute
samples.explanation: The radio altimeter measures the actual height above the surface (terrain, water, buildings) beneath the aircraft. When the surface drops away at the cliff edge, the indicated height jumps up by the cliff height, even though the aircraft's pressure altitude is unchanged.
whyWrong: The radio altimeter is independent of pressure; it measures to the surface below.
Flying off a cliff the surface drops away, so the height above it rises.
It responds quickly; it does not average over a minute.
samples.examTip: Rising ground under a level aircraft shows a falling radio height, the basis of GPWS mode 2.

samples.prompt: Over what height range is a typical civil radio altimeter display used?
options: Only between 500 ft and 5,000 ft
Only above 1,000 ft
From the ground up to about 2,500 ft
From the ground up to about 25,000 ft
samples.explanation: The radio altimeter is designed for the approach and landing. Its readings are displayed from 2,500 ft down to touchdown and are used for decision height alerts, autoland flare and retard, GPWS modes and ACAS RA inhibitions near the ground. Above about 2,500 ft the display is normally blanked.
whyWrong: It is most important below 500 ft, for decision height, flare and GPWS.
It is designed for low heights, so it is used near the ground, not only above 1,000 ft.
Reflected signal strength and usefulness limit it to low heights, so it is not shown at cruise heights.
samples.examTip: 2,500 ft is also where many displays first show the radio height on approach.

samples.prompt: A radio altimeter's signal returns 2.0 µs after it was sent. What height does this represent?
options: About 300 ft
About 1,970 ft
About 980 ft
About 490 ft
samples.explanation: Height = c × t ÷ 2 = 3 × 10⁸ m/s × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s ÷ 2 = 300 m ≈ 984 ft. The division by 2 is because the signal makes a round trip.
whyWrong: This is the height in metres (300 m), wrongly labelled as feet.
Forgets that the signal travels down and back up, so the time must be halved.
Halves the result twice.
samples.examTip: Every radar timing question needs the ÷ 2 for the round trip.

chapters.title: Flight Management System
topics: Operational Procedures - Control and Display Unit (Key Groups)

samples.prompt: In a B747-400, how many CDUs are typically fitted?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
samples.explanation: The B747-400 has three CDUs: one each side of the centre console for the pilots, and a third on the centre console mainly for engineering use.

samples.prompt: Which pair of functions best describes what a flight management system provides?
options: Air data computation and attitude reference
Navigation (position, flight plan, guidance) and performance (speeds, levels, fuel)
Radar weather detection and terrain warning
Engine control (fuel scheduling and thrust limits) and automatic cabin pressurisation control
samples.explanation: The FMS combines a navigation function (best position from IRS, GNSS and radio aids, the flight plan, and lateral/vertical guidance to the autopilot) with a performance function (optimum and economy speeds, cruise altitudes, top of descent, fuel predictions). It takes inputs from the ADC, IRS, radios and fuel system.
whyWrong: Air data and attitude come from the ADC and IRS, which feed the FMS.
Weather and terrain detection are separate systems (weather radar, TAWS).
Engine fuel scheduling is done by FADEC; pressurisation has its own controller.
samples.examTip: The FMS uses ADC and IRS data; it does not produce them.

samples.prompt: How often is the FMS navigation database normally updated, and why are there two databases loaded?
options: Every 28 days (AIRAC); the second lets the crew change cycle on the effective date
Every 56 days; the second database holds the pilot's own waypoints
Once a year; the second database holds the previous year's data for comparison
Every 7 days; the second database is a backup in case the first one becomes corrupted
samples.explanation: Aeronautical data changes on the 28-day AIRAC cycle, so a new navigation database is loaded every 28 days. The FMS holds the current and the next cycle; the crew selects the active one so the new data takes over on its effective date without a gap. Using an expired database can be a no-go item.
whyWrong: 56 days is the notice period for major changes; the database still changes every 28 days, and pilot waypoints are stored separately.
A yearly update would leave the data badly out of date.
Updates follow the 28-day AIRAC cycle, not a weekly one.
samples.examTip: Check the database validity dates on the identification page before flight.

samples.prompt: Which source normally gives the FMS its most accurate position update when all are available?
options: DME/DME
GNSS
VOR/DME
IRS alone
samples.explanation: Most FMSs blend IRS position with radio updates, choosing the most accurate source available: typically GNSS first, then DME/DME, then VOR/DME, and IRS alone as the last resort. The IRS gives smoothness and continuity; radio and GNSS updates remove its drift.
whyWrong: DME/DME is a good update, but less accurate than GNSS; it is used when GNSS is not available.
VOR/DME is a less accurate update; VOR bearing error grows with distance.
IRS position drifts with time since alignment, so it is the least accurate after a long flight.
samples.examTip: DME/DME beats VOR/DME because two ranges fix position better than a range and a bearing.

samples.prompt: An operator sets a cost index of zero in the FMS. What will the FMS optimise for?
options: Minimum fuel burn, flying close to the maximum range speed
The lowest cruise altitude available
Minimum flight time, flying at the maximum permitted speed
Maximum passenger comfort, avoiding all turbulence
samples.explanation: Cost index = time-related cost ÷ fuel cost. With a cost index of 0, time costs nothing, so the FMS chooses speeds that minimise fuel burn (around the maximum range speed). A high cost index favours speed and minimum time at the expense of extra fuel.
whyWrong: The cost index affects speeds, not a choice of the lowest altitude.
That is the maximum cost index, where time is expensive relative to fuel.
The cost index is a ratio of costs; it has nothing to do with turbulence.
samples.examTip: Low CI, slow and frugal; high CI, fast and thirsty.

chapters.title: Ground Proximity Warning System
topics: A Table of the GPWS Operating Modes
MODE 3 — Altitude Loss After Take-off or Go-around
MODE 4A — Unsafe Terrain Clearance with Landing Gear Not Down
MODE 4B — Unsafe Terrain Clearance with Flaps Not in Landing Configuration
MODE 5 — Below Glide Slope Deviation Alert

samples.prompt: According to the chapter, GPWS enhances flight safety and can prevent accidents resulting from all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Crew errors or distraction
Malfunction or misinterpretation of navigational equipment
Structural failure of the aircraft
Inappropriate ATC instructions
samples.explanation: GPWS guards against controlled flight into terrain, whatever its cause: crew error or distraction, misused or faulty navigation equipment, or inappropriate ATC instructions. It cannot help with a structural failure.

samples.prompt: In Mode 4A, what alert is generated when there is proximity to terrain with gear not locked down?
options: "Too Low Flaps"
"Too Low Gear"
"Too Low Terrain"
"Don't Sink"
samples.explanation: The table shows that Mode 4A provides the alert "Too Low gear" when there is proximity to terrain with gear not locked down. Option A is for Mode 4B. Option C is the warning for both 4A and 4B. Option D is for Mode 3.

samples.prompt: A pilot is flying an approach and receives a "GLIDE SLOPE" alert. Which GPWS mode has been activated?
options: Mode 3 - Altitude Loss after Take-off or Go-around
Mode 4B - Unsafe Terrain Clearance with Flaps Not in Landing Configuration
Mode 5 - Below Glide Slope Deviation Alert
Mode 6A - Below Selected Minimum Radio Altitude
samples.explanation: The "GLIDE SLOPE" alert is specifically associated with Mode 5 (Below Glide Slope Deviation Alert). Mode 3 provides "Don't Sink." Mode 4B provides "Too Low Flaps." Mode 6A provides "Minimums."

samples.prompt: Shortly after take-off the aircraft starts losing height, and the GPWS calls 'DON'T SINK'. Which mode has been triggered?
options: Mode 4: unsafe terrain clearance with gear or flaps up
Mode 1: excessive rate of descent
Mode 2: excessive terrain closure rate
Mode 3: altitude loss after take-off or go-around
samples.explanation: Mode 3 protects the climb after take-off or a go-around: if the aircraft loses a significant amount of the height it has gained before reaching a safe height, it calls 'DON'T SINK'. The response is to stop the descent and climb.
whyWrong: Mode 4 gives 'TOO LOW GEAR', 'TOO LOW FLAPS' or 'TOO LOW TERRAIN'.
Mode 1 gives 'SINK RATE' and 'PULL UP', based on the rate of descent against height.
Mode 2 gives 'TERRAIN TERRAIN' and 'PULL UP' when the ground rises towards the aircraft.
samples.examTip: Match the call to the mode: SINK RATE (1), TERRAIN (2), DON'T SINK (3), TOO LOW (4), GLIDESLOPE (5).

samples.prompt: In night IMC, the GPWS gives 'TERRAIN TERRAIN, PULL UP'. What should the crew do?
options: Level off and ask ATC for the minimum safe altitude
Turn away from the nearest high ground shown on the chart, keeping the same altitude
Immediately apply maximum thrust and climb at the maximum safe pitch, wings level
Check the position on the map display before reacting, in case the warning is false
samples.explanation: A 'PULL UP' warning means terrain is close and closing. The escape manoeuvre is immediate: disconnect the autopilot, apply maximum thrust, roll wings level and pitch up to the maximum safe attitude (up to the stall warning or pitch limit indicator), retract speedbrakes, and climb until the warning stops and safe altitude is reached. Only then is the cause investigated.
whyWrong: Levelling off does not give any terrain clearance; the manoeuvre requires a maximum-performance climb.
Turning without climbing may not clear the terrain; the escape is a straight climb at maximum performance.
Delaying to verify uses up the few seconds the warning gives; react first.
samples.examTip: In IMC or at night, react to a GPWS warning first and analyse it afterwards.

samples.prompt: The aural messages provided by TCAS II include:
options: Threat, Climb; Threat, Descend
Climb left; Climb right; Descend left; Descend right
Climb; Descend; Increase Climb; Increase Descent
Turn Left, Turn Right, Increase Turn, Decrease Turn
samples.explanation: TCAS II RA aural messages are vertical: 'CLIMB', 'DESCEND', 'INCREASE CLIMB', 'INCREASE DESCENT', 'MONITOR VERTICAL SPEED', 'ADJUST VERTICAL SPEED' and so on. It never commands turns.

samples.prompt: An intruder is 3 nm away with a closure rate of 240 kt. What is the ACAS range tau (time to closest approach)?
samples.explanation: Tau = range ÷ closure rate = 3 nm ÷ 240 kt = 0.0125 h = 45 s. This is inside the TA threshold (about 40–48 s).
whyWrong: Converted the range to km but kept the closure rate in knots
Used twice the closure rate
Used half the closure rate (one aircraft's speed only)
samples.examTip: Common trap: converted the range to km but kept the closure rate in knots.

samples.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the advisories of ACAS II (TCAS II)?
options: Resolution advisories only, without any traffic advisories
Traffic advisories only, with no manoeuvre guidance
Resolution advisories in both the vertical and horizontal planes
Traffic advisories and resolution advisories in the vertical plane only
samples.explanation: ACAS II issues traffic advisories (TAs) to alert the crew to nearby traffic and, if a collision risk develops, resolution advisories (RAs) that tell them to climb, descend, or adjust vertical speed. It gives no horizontal manoeuvre guidance, because its bearing information is not accurate enough.
whyWrong: A TA normally comes before an RA, warning the crew to look out and prepare.
TA-only is the capability of ACAS I (TCAS I).
ACAS II gives vertical RAs only; it never commands turns.
samples.examTip: Any option offering turn instructions from ACAS is wrong.

samples.prompt: During a climb, ACAS issues 'DESCEND, DESCEND' while ATC has just instructed the crew to continue climbing. What should the crew do?
options: Follow the ATC instruction, because ATC has the full traffic picture
Level off as a compromise between the RA and the ATC instruction
Look for the traffic first and follow the RA only if it is seen
Follow the RA promptly and inform ATC 'TCAS RA' as soon as workload permits
samples.explanation: ICAO procedures require the crew to respond to an RA promptly and smoothly, following it even when it conflicts with an ATC instruction, and never manoeuvring in the opposite sense. The crew reports 'TCAS RA' to ATC; ATC then stops issuing instructions to that aircraft until the crew reports 'clear of conflict, returning to' the clearance.
whyWrong: The RA takes priority over a conflicting ATC instruction; ATC may not know about the threat or may be wrong.
A compromise can put the aircraft right into the conflict, especially when the other aircraft is following a coordinated RA.
RAs must be followed even if the traffic is not seen; visual acquisition can be wrong.
samples.examTip: Never manoeuvre opposite to an RA, and never 'split the difference'.

samples.prompt: An intruder's transponder replies in Mode A only (no altitude reporting). What can ACAS II do about it?
options: Give horizontal resolution advisories instead of vertical ones
Nothing: the intruder is invisible to ACAS
Give full resolution advisories as for any other aircraft
Show it and give traffic advisories, but not resolution advisories
samples.explanation: ACAS measures range from the reply timing and gets the intruder's altitude from its Mode C or S reply. With Mode A only, there is no altitude, so ACAS can show the target and give a TA based on range, but it cannot compute a vertical miss distance or issue an RA. An aircraft with no working transponder is not seen at all.
whyWrong: ACAS II never gives horizontal RAs.
ACAS can still detect and range on a Mode A reply, so the target is displayed.
RAs need the intruder's altitude to choose a vertical sense; Mode A gives none.
samples.examTip: ACAS relies entirely on the other aircraft's transponder.

chapters.title: Mass and Balance and Fuel Requirements
topics: Maximum Structural Take-off Mass (MSTOM) and Landing Mass (MSLM)

samples.prompt: An aeroplane's dry operating mass is loaded with passengers, baggage and cargo, but no usable fuel. Which mass has been reached?
options: Zero fuel mass
Operating mass
Ramp mass
Basic empty mass
samples.explanation: Dry operating mass (DOM) is the aeroplane ready for the flight without usable fuel or traffic load. Adding the traffic load (passengers, baggage, cargo) gives the zero fuel mass (ZFM). Adding the take-off fuel then gives the take-off mass, and adding the taxi fuel on top of that gives the ramp mass.
whyWrong: Operating mass is the dry operating mass plus the take-off fuel, with no traffic load.
Ramp mass is the full mass at the start of taxi, including the taxi and take-off fuel.
Basic empty mass is the aeroplane with unusable fuel and full operating fluids, before crew, pantry or any load.
samples.examTip: If a question says 'no usable fuel' the answer is ZFM; 'no traffic load' points to DOM or operating mass.
