samples.prompt: Which item is NOT part of the traffic load?
options: Non-revenue company cargo
Passengers' checked baggage
The flight crew's baggage
Mail carried in the forward hold
samples.explanation: Traffic load is the total mass of passengers, their baggage and cargo, including any non-revenue load. Crew, crew baggage, catering and removable passenger service equipment are already included in the dry operating mass, so they are not traffic load.
whyWrong: Traffic load includes non-revenue load: company material still has to be carried and counted.
Checked baggage belongs to the passengers, so it is part of the traffic load.
Mail is cargo, and cargo is part of the traffic load whether or not it earns revenue.
samples.examTip: Anything belonging to the crew or the operation of the aircraft is DOM; anything being carried for someone is traffic load.

samples.prompt: Basic empty mass 39,900 kg; crew, crew baggage, pantry and service equipment 2,450 kg; passengers, baggage and cargo 13,800 kg; block fuel 11,200 kg including 250 kg of taxi fuel; trip fuel 7,400 kg. What are the take-off mass and the planned landing mass?
options: TOM 67,100 kg; LM 59,700 kg
TOM 67,350 kg; LM 59,950 kg
TOM 64,650 kg; LM 57,250 kg
TOM 67,100 kg; LM 56,150 kg
samples.explanation: DOM = 39,900 + 2,450 = 42,350 kg. ZFM = DOM + traffic load = 42,350 + 13,800 = 56,150 kg. Take-off fuel = block − taxi = 11,200 − 250 = 10,950 kg. TOM = ZFM + take-off fuel = 56,150 + 10,950 = 67,100 kg. LM = TOM − trip fuel = 67,100 − 7,400 = 59,700 kg.
whyWrong: Kept the taxi fuel in the take-off mass; 67,350 kg is the ramp mass.
Built up from the basic empty mass and left out the crew and pantry, which belong to the dry operating mass.
Took off all the fuel for the landing mass (that is the ZFM); only the trip fuel is burnt, so the reserves land with the aircraft.
samples.examTip: Ramp mass − taxi fuel = TOM: if one option is exactly the taxi fuel heavier, it is the ramp mass trap.

samples.prompt: Why is a maximum zero fuel mass imposed on many transport aeroplanes, and why does extra fuel not count against it?
options: Fuel in the wing tanks relieves wing-root bending, so any mass above MZFM must be carried as fuel in the wings
Fuel is lighter than cargo for the same volume, so it causes less structural stress per kilogram in any tank
MZFM protects the fuselage floor, which carries the traffic load but none of the fuel or its tanks
The landing gear is designed for the zero fuel mass, and fuel is assumed to be burnt before any landing
samples.explanation: In flight the wings carry the lift, and the fuselage load hangs from the wing roots, producing a bending moment there. Fuel carried in the wings acts down along the wing and relieves that bending. Above a certain mass with empty wing tanks the wing root would be overstressed, so any mass above the MZFM must be fuel in the wings.
whyWrong: Stress depends on mass and where it acts, not on volume: a kilogram of fuel weighs the same as a kilogram of cargo.
Floor strength is protected by floor and compartment load limits, not by the MZFM.
Landing gear is protected by the maximum landing mass, and the aircraft always lands with reserve fuel on board.
samples.examTip: MZFM controls the traffic load directly: max traffic load from MZFM = MZFM − DOM, with no fuel term.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about aeroplane masses: 1. Ramp mass = take-off mass + taxi fuel. 2. Operating mass = dry operating mass + take-off fuel. 3. The zero fuel mass contains no fuel of any kind. 4. Landing mass = take-off mass − trip fuel. Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
samples.explanation: Ramp mass is the take-off mass plus the taxi fuel. Operating mass is the DOM plus take-off fuel, with no traffic load. Landing mass is the take-off mass less the trip fuel. The zero fuel mass excludes usable fuel only: unusable fuel is included in the basic empty mass and therefore in the DOM and ZFM.
whyWrong: Leaves out statement 1: the taxi fuel is on board at the ramp and burnt before take-off.
Statement 3 is false: unusable fuel is part of the basic empty mass, so it is inside every mass built on it, including the ZFM.
Accepts the false statement 3 and leaves out the true statements 2 and 4.
samples.examTip: Words like 'no fuel of any kind' are the trap in mass definitions: think usable versus unusable.

topics: Effects of Overloading — The Hidden Damage
Effects of Out of Limit CG Position — The Stability Trade-off
Movement of CG in Flight — The Dynamic Reality
Definitions — The Vocabulary of Mass and Balance
Weighing of Aircraft — How We Know the Numbers
Calculation of Fuel Mass — Volume to Mass Conversion
Calculation of Basic Empty Mass and CG Position
Calculation of Loaded Mass and CG Position for Light Aircraft
CG Position as a Percentage of Mean Aerodynamic Chord (MAC)

samples.prompt: During loading, 500 kg of baggage is moved from the forward hold to the aft hold of a 60,000 kg aeroplane. Which statement is correct?
options: The CG moves forward and the total mass is unchanged
The CG moves aft and the zero fuel mass increases by 500 kg
The CG does not move, because the total mass is unchanged
The CG moves aft and the total mass is unchanged
samples.explanation: Moving a load changes only its arm. The total moment changes by mass × distance moved, while the total mass stays the same, so the CG moves in the direction of the load by m × d ÷ M.
whyWrong: The CG always moves in the same direction as the mass that is moved.
Moving baggage within the aeroplane does not change any mass total, including the ZFM.
The total mass is the same, but its distribution changes, so the moment and the CG change.
samples.examTip: Moving = same total mass; adding or removing = new total mass. Decide which before choosing a formula.

samples.prompt: A light aeroplane: basic empty mass 820 kg at 2.31 m; front seats 165 kg at 2.05 m; rear seat 70 kg at 2.95 m; baggage 25 kg at 3.60 m; fuel 120 litres of AVGAS (SG 0.72) at 2.42 m. All arms are aft of the datum. Where is the take-off CG?
options: 2.67 m aft of the datum
2.35 m aft of the datum
3.34 m aft of the datum
2.31 m aft of the datum
whyWrong: Averaged the five arms without weighting them by mass.
Divided the total moment (2,738 kg m) by the basic empty mass instead of by the total mass of 1,166 kg; the CG cannot lie behind almost every station.
Left the rear-seat passenger out of both the moment and the mass totals.
samples.examTip: Convert fuel volume to mass first, and sense-check that the CG lies between the most forward and most aft stations.

samples.prompt: Compared with a CG near the forward limit, a CG near the aft limit (both within limits) gives:
options: Lower stall speed and greater longitudinal stability, with heavier stick forces
Lower stall speed and less trim drag, but reduced longitudinal stability
No change in stall speed or drag; only the elevator trim position changes
Higher stall speed and more trim drag, but greater longitudinal stability
samples.explanation: With an aft CG the tailplane needs less down-load to balance the aeroplane, so the wing produces less lift for a given weight: stall speed falls and trim drag falls, improving range. The price is that the CG moves closer to the neutral point, so longitudinal static stability and stick forces decrease; beyond the aft limit the aeroplane may become unstable.
whyWrong: An aft CG reduces the stability margin and lightens the stick forces; it does not increase stability.
The CG position changes the tail load, which changes both the stall speed and the trim drag.
Describes the forward CG: more tail down-load means more lift needed, so a higher stall speed and more trim drag.
samples.examTip: Stability and performance trade against each other along the CG range: forward helps stability, aft helps performance.

samples.prompt: The datum of a light aeroplane is at the wing leading edge, so some stations are forward of it (negative arms). Basic empty mass 1,050 kg at +0.45 m; front occupants 170 kg at −0.20 m; rear occupants 150 kg at +0.70 m; fuel 160 kg at +0.30 m. Where is the CG?
options: 0.31 m aft of the datum
0.43 m aft of the datum
0.39 m aft of the datum
0.56 m aft of the datum
whyWrong: Averaged the four arms without weighting them by mass.
Treated the front-seat arm as +0.20 m; a station forward of the datum gives a negative moment.
Divided the total moment by the basic empty mass instead of the total mass.
samples.examTip: Write the sign in front of every arm before multiplying; the sign error is the commonest slip with a mid-aircraft datum.

samples.prompt: Dry operating mass 42,500 kg at 18.12 m; passengers 11,800 kg at 16.65 m; forward hold 1,100 kg at 11.3 m; aft hold 2,200 kg at 24.6 m; take-off fuel 9,000 kg at 18.26 m (all arms aft of the datum). LEMAC is 17.24 m aft of the datum and the MAC is 3.79 m. Where is the take-off CG in %MAC?
whyWrong: Measured the CG back from the trailing edge of the MAC instead of from the leading edge: gives 80.5% MAC.
Averaged the arms without weighting them by mass, then converted to %MAC: gives 14.4% MAC.
Found the zero fuel CG by leaving out the fuel, instead of the take-off CG: gives 18.4% MAC.
samples.examTip: Keep the arms to two decimals and the moments unrounded until the final division.

chapters.title: PET, PSR and PNR
topics: The Triangle of Velocities — Foundation of All Calculations

samples.prompt: Which of the following does NOT change the position of the point of equal time between two aerodromes?
options: The fuel on board
The TAS assumed after a failure
The distance between the aerodromes
The wind component along the track
samples.explanation: The PET is where the time to continue equals the time to return: distance from A = D × H ÷ (O + H). It depends only on the distance and the groundspeeds. Fuel does not appear, which is the key difference from the point of safe return, which depends on endurance.
whyWrong: A lower TAS after an engine failure or depressurisation changes both groundspeeds, so it moves the PET.
The PET distance is a fraction of the total distance, so it changes in proportion to it.
The wind changes the groundspeeds on and home, which are the H and O in the formula.
samples.examTip: If 'fuel' or 'endurance' is in the options for a PET question, it is the odd one out.

samples.prompt: Distance A to B is 1,240 nm, TAS 440 kt, with a 45 kt headwind component outbound (towards B). How far from A is the point of equal time?
options: 653 nm
683 nm
557 nm
620 nm
samples.explanation: O (on to B) = 440 − 45 = 395 kt; H (home to A) = 440 + 45 = 485 kt. Distance to PET = D × H ÷ (O + H) = 1,240 × 485 ÷ 880 = 683 nm from A. Check: from 683 nm, on to B takes 557 ÷ 395 = 1.41 h and back to A takes 683 ÷ 485 = 1.41 h.
whyWrong: Used the TAS instead of the groundspeed home (485 kt) in the numerator.
Swapped the groundspeeds: D × O ÷ (O + H) gives the distance from B, not from A.
Took the midpoint; the PET is at half way only in still air.
samples.examTip: With a headwind outbound the PET is beyond half way; with a tailwind outbound it is short of half way.

samples.prompt: On a long oceanic sector with a strong headwind outbound, the point of equal time compared with the mid-point of the route is:
options: Short of the mid-point, closer to the departure aerodrome
Beyond the mid-point, closer to the destination
At the mid-point, because the wind affects both directions equally
Beyond the destination, so the aircraft can always continue
samples.explanation: With a headwind outbound, continuing is slow (low O) and returning is fast (high H), so the aircraft can afford to be further out before turning back takes as long as going on. D × H ÷ (O + H) is then more than D ÷ 2: the PET moves into wind, towards the destination.
whyWrong: This is the tailwind-outbound case: a tailwind outbound brings the PET back towards the departure aerodrome.
The wind does not cancel: the aircraft spends longer flying into a headwind than it gains flying with a tailwind.
The PET is always between the two aerodromes; it is where continuing and returning take equal time.
samples.examTip: Sketch it: the PET always moves towards the aerodrome the wind is blowing from.

samples.prompt: Distance A to B is 2,110 nm. TAS 450 kt, with a 25 kt tailwind component on the outbound track. How far from A is the point of equal time?
options: 996 nm
samples.explanation: Formula: PET distance from A = D × H ÷ (O + H). PET distance from A = D × H ÷ (O + H), with O and H the groundspeeds on and home at the cruise TAS. O = 450 + 25 = 475 kt, H = 425 kt. Distance = 2,110 × 425 ÷ 900 = 996.4 nm from A.
whyWrong: Took the midpoint; the PET is only at half way in still air: gives 1,055 nm.
Swapped the groundspeeds: the numerator must be the groundspeed home (H), so this is the distance from B, not from A: gives 1,114 nm.
Used the TAS instead of the groundspeed home in the formula: gives 1,026 nm.
samples.examTip: Headwind outbound: PET beyond half way. Tailwind outbound: short of half way.

samples.prompt: A twin-jet flies A to B, 900 nm, at a normal cruise TAS of 420 kt. With one engine inoperative it would cruise at 320 kt TAS. The wind component is a 30 kt tailwind outbound at either speed. How many minutes after passing A will the aircraft reach the one-engine-inoperative PET?
options: 70 min
56 min
54 min
60 min
samples.explanation: For the engine-failure case, O = 320 + 30 = 350 kt and H = 320 − 30 = 290 kt. PET distance = 900 × 290 ÷ (350 + 290) = 407.8 nm. The aircraft flies to that point on both engines at 420 + 30 = 450 kt, so time = 407.8 ÷ 450 × 60 = 54.4 min.
whyWrong: Used the one-engine groundspeed (350 kt) to reach the PET; the aircraft gets there at its normal cruise groundspeed.
Used the normal cruise TAS to find the PET distance (418 nm), although the flight after the failure is flown at 320 kt.
Placed the PET at half way (450 nm) and flew there at 450 kt.
samples.examTip: Two different speeds in one question: one locates the PET, the other times the flight to it.

samples.prompt: The absolute ceiling is defined as the altitude at which the theoretical rate of climb, with all engines operating at maximum continuous power, is reduced to:
options: 100 feet per minute
50 feet per minute
Zero feet per minute
300 feet per minute
samples.explanation: The absolute ceiling is the altitude at which the theoretical rate of climb (all engines at maximum continuous power) falls to zero; the service ceiling is the lower altitude at which a specified small rate of climb remains.

samples.prompt: A runway has a TORA of 2,500 m, a stopway of 200 m and a clearway of 400 m. What are the TODA and the ASDA?
options: TODA 2,900 m, ASDA 2,700 m
TODA 2,900 m, ASDA 3,100 m
TODA 2,700 m, ASDA 2,900 m
TODA 3,100 m, ASDA 2,700 m
samples.explanation: TODA = TORA + clearway = 2,500 + 400 = 2,900 m. ASDA = TORA + stopway = 2,500 + 200 = 2,700 m. A clearway is for the airborne part of the take-off, so it extends the distance available to climb, not to stop; a stopway is a surface to stop on, so it extends the accelerate-stop distance.
whyWrong: Added both extensions to the ASDA; only the stopway counts.
Swaps the two: clearway belongs to the TODA and stopway to the ASDA.
Added both the clearway and the stopway to the TODA; only the clearway counts.
samples.examTip: Write each declared distance next to what it adds before choosing.

samples.prompt: Which statement about a stopway and a clearway is INCORRECT?
options: A stopway is a prepared rectangular area beyond the TORA, suitable for stopping in an abandoned take-off
A stopway must be able to support the aeroplane during a normal take-off run, so it may be included in the TORA
A clearway need not be able to support the weight of an aeroplane
A clearway is an area beyond the TORA, under the control of the aerodrome, over which the initial climb may be made
samples.explanation: A stopway only needs to support the aeroplane in an abandoned take-off without structural damage; it is not built for normal take-off runs, so it is never part of the TORA. It extends the ASDA. A clearway is an obstacle-free area over which the aeroplane climbs to the screen height; it extends the TODA and need not bear weight.
whyWrong: Correct: that is what a stopway is for.
Correct: a clearway can even be water; nothing has to roll on it.
Correct: a clearway is defined for the airborne part of the take-off and must be clear of obstacles.
samples.examTip: 'Stopway included in TORA' is always wrong.

samples.prompt: Under the performance-class system used for commercial air transport, which aeroplane must always be operated in Performance Class A?
options: A twin piston aeroplane with 6 seats and an MTOM of 2,000 kg
Any single-engine piston aeroplane
A single-engine turboprop with 9 seats
Any multi-engine turbojet aeroplane
samples.explanation: Class A covers all multi-engine turbojet aeroplanes and multi-engine turboprops with more than 9 passenger seats or an MTOM above 5,700 kg; they must be able to cope with an engine failure at any point of the take-off. Class B covers propeller aeroplanes with 9 seats or fewer and an MTOM of 5,700 kg or less. Class C covers larger piston-engine aeroplanes.
whyWrong: A small propeller aeroplane with up to 9 passenger seats and an MTOM up to 5,700 kg is Class B.
Single-engine piston aeroplanes fall into Class B.
A propeller aeroplane with 9 seats or fewer and an MTOM up to 5,700 kg is Class B, and single-engine types cannot meet Class A engine-failure requirements.
samples.examTip: 'Multi-engine jet' always means Class A.

samples.prompt: ICAO Annex 14 recommends a maximum length for a clearway. That maximum is:
options: 60 m, the length of the runway strip beyond the runway end
The length of the stopway
Half the length of the take-off run available
The full length of the take-off run available
samples.explanation: Annex 14 recommends that the length of a clearway should not exceed half the TORA. When declared distances are worked out, the TODA therefore cannot exceed 1.5 × TORA. Performance rules apply further limits on how much clearway the aeroplane may use.
whyWrong: 60 m is a typical strip extension beyond the runway end, not the clearway limit.
Clearway and stopway lengths are independent; one is not limited by the other.
A clearway as long as the TORA would greatly overstate the distance the aeroplane can use for its airborne segment.
samples.examTip: If a question gives a long clearway, check this limit before adding it to the TORA.

chapters.title: General Principles - Take-off
topics: Effect of Variable Factors on Take-off Distance

samples.prompt: The screen height for Class A aeroplanes is:
options: 35 feet
50 feet
25 feet
40 feet
samples.explanation: The screen height varies from 35 ft for Class A aeroplanes to 50 ft for Class B aeroplanes. Options B is for Class B, while C and D are incorrect values.

samples.prompt: Which statement best describes V1?
options: The take-off safety speed that must be reached by 35 ft with an engine inoperative
The maximum speed at which the crew can begin to reject the take-off and still stop within the ASDA, and the minimum speed from which the take-off can be continued after an engine failure
The minimum speed at which the aeroplane can be controlled on the ground with the critical engine failed, using rudder only
The speed at which the pilot begins to rotate the aeroplane to lift the nose wheel
samples.explanation: V1 is the take-off decision speed. If a failure is recognised before V1 the crew must be able to stop within the ASDA; at or after V1 the take-off can be continued, reaching the screen height within the TODA with one engine inoperative. It is chosen by the crew from the performance data, within the limits set by VMCG, VR and VMBE.
whyWrong: That is V2.
That is VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground.
That is VR, the rotation speed.
samples.examTip: 'Begin to reject' and 'continue' are both in a good V1 definition.

samples.prompt: Which sequence of take-off speeds is always correct for a Class A aeroplane?
options: V1 ≤ VR ≤ VMCG < V2
VMCG ≤ V1 ≤ VR < V2
V1 ≤ VMCG ≤ VR < V2
VMCG ≤ VR ≤ V1 < V2
samples.explanation: V1 must be at least VMCG, so a failure at V1 can be controlled with aerodynamic controls alone if the take-off is continued. V1 must not exceed VR, because the decision must be made before rotation. V2 is reached after lift-off by the screen height and is above VR.
whyWrong: VMCG is a ground control speed far below VR.
V1 cannot be below VMCG: an engine failure just before V1 must still be controllable on the ground if continuing.
V1 cannot exceed VR: the decision must be made before rotation begins.
samples.examTip: Place VMCG first and V2 last, then check V1 ≤ VR.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a valid limit on the choice of V1?
options: V1 must not be less than V2
V1 must not be greater than VMBE
V1 must not be less than VMCG
V1 must not be greater than VR
samples.explanation: V1 is bounded below by VMCG and above by VR and VMBE (and the tyre speed limit, which is a groundspeed). V2 is reached after lift-off, so V1 is always well below V2; requiring V1 ≥ V2 would be impossible.
whyWrong: Correct limit: above VMBE the brakes could not absorb the energy of a rejected take-off.
Correct limit: below VMCG a continued take-off after engine failure could not be controlled on the ground.
Correct limit: the decision must be made before rotation.
samples.examTip: V1 lies inside the take-off run, so it cannot be tied to an airborne speed like V2.

samples.prompt: A twin-jet's V2 must not be less than a set margin above its air minimum control speed. That margin is:
options: 1.05 × VMCG
1.10 × VMCA
1.20 × VMCG
1.30 × VMCA
samples.explanation: V2 must be at least 1.10 × VMCA so that the aeroplane is safely controllable in the climb with the critical engine inoperative. It must also be at least the minimum V2 based on the reference stall speed, and VR must be at least 1.05 × VMCA. The highest of these limits applies.
whyWrong: VMCG relates to V1 and VR on the ground; V2 is an airborne speed.
There is no 1.2 × VMCG rule for V2.
1.3 is the old landing reference factor on stall speed, not the V2 control margin.
samples.examTip: Ground speeds relate to VMCG; airborne speeds relate to VMCA.

samples.prompt: During take-off, the net thrust of a jet engine at constant rpm:
options: Increases with airspeed
Remains constant throughout the take-off
Decreases with airspeed
Is independent of airspeed
samples.explanation: For a jet engine during take-off, increasing speed increases intake momentum drag which reduces net thrust. The ram effect at low take-off speeds is insufficient to counteract this loss. Option A is incorrect because ram effect only becomes significant at very high speeds. Option B is incorrect because thrust does vary. Option D is incorrect because thrust is affected by airspeed.

samples.prompt: An unfactored take-off distance is 600 m. The flight manual requires increases of 10% for a dry grass surface and 20% for an elevation of 2,000 ft. What is the corrected take-off distance?
samples.explanation: Each factor corrects the distance already corrected by the others, so they multiply: 600 × 1.10 × 1.20 = 600 × 1.32 = 792 m. Adding the percentages (600 × 1.30 = 780 m) understates the distance.
whyWrong: Added the percentages (30%) instead of multiplying the factors.
Applied only the 10% grass factor.
Applied only the 20% elevation factor.
samples.examTip: The multiplied answer is always a little larger than the added one.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane's take-off distance is 800 m at a given mass. Assuming take-off distance varies with the square of mass, what is the distance after a 10% increase in mass?
samples.explanation: s ∝ m², because the lift-off speed squared rises with mass and the acceleration falls with mass. s₂ = 800 × 1.10² = 800 × 1.21 = 968 m: a 10% mass increase gives about a 21% distance increase.
whyWrong: Doubled the distance, confusing a square law with a factor of two.
Used the square root of the mass ratio, the rule for lift-off speed rather than distance.
Increased the distance by 10% in proportion to mass, forgetting the square.
samples.examTip: Square the mass ratio first, then multiply.

samples.prompt: The reported wind gives a headwind component of 20 kt for one runway direction, and a tailwind component of 6 kt for the reciprocal. Which components should be used for the take-off performance calculation if the chart does not include wind factoring?
options: 20 kt headwind, or 6 kt tailwind
10 kt headwind, or 9 kt tailwind
30 kt headwind, or 3 kt tailwind
10 kt headwind, or 3 kt tailwind
samples.explanation: Factored wind: 50% of the headwind, 20 × 0.5 = 10 kt; 150% of the tailwind, 6 × 1.5 = 9 kt. Factoring takes little credit for a helpful wind and adds a margin for a harmful one.
whyWrong: Uses the reported components unfactored.
Reverses the factors: 150% of the headwind and 50% of the tailwind.
Halved both; the tailwind must be INCREASED by 50%.
samples.examTip: The factor is always the unfavourable direction for the pilot.

samples.prompt: A light aeroplane's take-off distance to 50 ft is 490 m at sea level, ISA, on a level, dry, paved runway. Using the factors given, what is the take-off distance with an uphill slope of 1% (5% per 1%); an aerodrome elevation of 1,000 ft (10% per 1,000 ft); a dry grass surface (+20%)?
samples.explanation: Formula: Take-off distance ∝ mass² and ∝ (lift-off groundspeed)²; correction factors multiply. Correction factors are applied one after another, so they multiply: 1.05 × 1.10 × 1.20 = 1.3860. Distance = 490 × 1.3860 = 679 m.
whyWrong: Left out the largest factor: gives 570 m.
Added the percentages together; each factor must multiply the distance already corrected by the others: gives 660 m.
Applied only the first factor and forgot the others: gives 510 m.
samples.examTip: Never add percentage factors; multiply them.

chapters.title: General Principles - Climb
topics: The Effect of Weight on Climb Angle
The Effect of Flaps on Climbing

samples.prompt: In the climb at 210 kt TAS an aircraft has an excess thrust (T − D) of 14.5% of its weight. What is its rate of climb in still air?
options: 5,710 ft/min
3,080 ft/min
1,850 ft/min
4,270 ft/min
whyWrong: Used the TAS in km/h
Divided by 100 instead of 60 when converting to feet per minute
Used the total thrust instead of the excess (T − D)
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the TAS in km/h.

samples.prompt: For a twin-engine Class A aeroplane with one engine inoperative, what is the minimum gross climb gradient required in the second segment of the take-off flight path?
samples.explanation: The second segment (gear up, take-off flap, take-off thrust, V2) is usually the most limiting. With one engine inoperative a twin must achieve at least 2.4% gross; three-engine aeroplanes 2.7% and four-engine 3.0%. The final segment requirement for a twin is 1.2%.
whyWrong: 3.0% is the four-engine aeroplane's second-segment requirement.
1.2% is the twin's final take-off segment requirement.
0.8% is the twin's gross-to-net margin, not a gradient requirement.
samples.examTip: Second segment limits often set the climb-limited take-off mass on hot, high days.

samples.prompt: A twin-jet's gross take-off climb gradient with one engine inoperative is 3.1%. What net gradient must be used to check obstacle clearance?
samples.explanation: For obstacle clearance the net flight path is used: the gross gradient reduced by 0.8% for twins, 0.9% for three-engine and 1.0% for four-engine aeroplanes. Net = 3.1% − 0.8% = 2.3%.
whyWrong: Added the margin instead of subtracting it.
Used the 1.0% margin for a four-engine aeroplane.
Used the 0.9% margin for a three-engine aeroplane.
samples.examTip: The margin is subtracted as percentage points, not as a percentage of the gradient.

samples.prompt: An obstacle lies 4.0 nm beyond the end of the take-off distance. The net climb gradient is 2.5% and the net flight path starts at 35 ft above the end of the TOD. How high is the net flight path above the TOD end when it reaches the obstacle? (1 nm = 6,076 ft)
options: 100 ft
608 ft
643 ft
samples.explanation: Height gained = gradient × distance = 0.025 × (4.0 × 6,076) = 0.025 × 24,304 = 608 ft. The net flight path starts at 35 ft, so it is 608 + 35 = 643 ft above the TOD end at the obstacle. It must clear the obstacle by at least 35 ft.
whyWrong: Took 2.5% of 4,000 ft, treating nautical miles as thousands of feet.
Gave the distance in feet, not the height gained.
Forgot to add the 35 ft screen height at which the net flight path starts.
samples.examTip: Convert nm to ft first, then apply the gradient.

samples.prompt: As an aeroplane climbs towards its absolute ceiling, what happens to its Vx and Vy (as IAS)?
options: Both stay constant in IAS, and only the rates change
Vx decreases and Vy increases until they are equal at the absolute ceiling
Vx increases and Vy decreases until they are equal at the absolute ceiling
Both increase at the same rate, so the gap between them stays the same
samples.explanation: As altitude increases the thrust and power available fall, so the excess thrust and excess power curves shrink. The speed for maximum excess thrust (Vx) creeps up and the speed for maximum excess power (Vy) comes down. At the absolute ceiling there is only one speed at which level flight is possible, and Vx = Vy.
whyWrong: As thrust and power available fall with height, the speeds for maximum excess thrust and power move together.
Reverses the trends.
They converge; the gap shrinks to zero.
samples.examTip: At the absolute ceiling the rate and the angle of climb are both zero.

chapters.title: General Principles - Descent
topics: Minimum Angle of Descent (Best Glide Angle)
Minimum Rate of Descent (Best Glide Endurance)

samples.prompt: A pilot is flying a jet aircraft at FL350 when a sudden depressurization occurs. The pilot must descend to FL100 as quickly as possible. What should be the pilot's primary action regarding aircraft configuration?
options: Maintain clean configuration and reduce speed
Deploy speed brakes, set thrust to idle, accelerate to VMO/MMO
Extend flaps partially and reduce thrust
Maintain current speed and deploy landing gear
samples.explanation: For an emergency descent the drag must be maximised and thrust minimised at high speed: speed brakes out, thrust idle, accelerating to VMO/MMO (within the limiting speeds for flap and gear).

samples.prompt: Two aeroplanes of the same type, one heavy and one light, glide from the same height at their own best-glide speeds in still air. Which statement is correct?
options: They cover the same distance in exactly the same time
The heavy one covers more distance because it has more potential energy
They cover the same distance; the heavy one flies faster and takes less time
The light one covers more distance because its best-glide speed is lower
samples.explanation: The best glide is flown at the angle of attack for (L/D)max, which does not depend on mass. Both therefore glide at the same angle and cover the same still-air distance. The heavy aeroplane needs a higher speed (∝ √mass) at that angle of attack, so its rate of descent is higher and the glide takes less time.
whyWrong: The heavy one must fly faster to hold the best-L/D angle of attack, so it arrives sooner.
The extra energy is matched by more drag at the higher speed needed; the glide ratio does not change.
Lower speed does not mean a better glide ratio; the best L/D is the same for both.
samples.examTip: Endurance (time in the air) is better when light; range is the same.

samples.prompt: During a descent at constant IAS, the pilot deploys the speed brakes. What is the effect?
options: The rate and angle of descent increase at the same IAS
The angle of descent decreases because lift increases
The stall speed decreases, allowing a slower descent
The IAS increases at the same rate of descent
samples.explanation: In a steady descent the component of weight along the flight path balances the excess drag. Speed brakes add drag, so at the same IAS the aeroplane must descend more steeply, and with the same speed that means a higher rate of descent. This lets the crew lose height quickly without gaining speed.
whyWrong: Speed brakes add drag and reduce lift slightly; they do not increase lift.
Speed brakes do not lower the stall speed; spoilers on the wing can even raise it.
Extra drag at constant IAS has to be balanced by a steeper descent, not a higher speed.
samples.examTip: Descent angle ≈ (D − T)/W: more drag, steeper.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane glides for maximum range into a strong headwind. How should the pilot adjust the speed compared with the still-air best-glide speed?
options: Fly a little slower, to reduce the rate of descent and stay airborne longer
Fly at the minimum sink speed, which always gives the greatest ground distance
Fly exactly the still-air best-glide speed, because the glide angle through the air is unchanged
Fly a little faster, to reduce the time spent exposed to the headwind
samples.explanation: In a headwind the groundspeed is lower and the ground distance per height lost is reduced. Flying a little faster than the still-air best-glide speed reduces the time spent in the descent, so the headwind has less time to act, and the ground distance improves. In a tailwind a slightly lower speed gives the wind longer to carry the aeroplane.
whyWrong: Flying slower into a headwind gives the wind longer to push the aeroplane back, reducing ground distance.
Minimum sink gives the longest time, not the longest distance, and is worse into wind.
The air-relative angle is unchanged at that speed, but ground distance is what matters.
samples.examTip: Same logic as the cruise: headwind, speed up.

samples.prompt: A jet descends at a constant Mach number from high altitude. What happens to its IAS and TAS during the constant-Mach part of the descent?
options: Both remain constant
IAS increases and TAS decreases
Both increase
IAS decreases and TAS increases
samples.explanation: Descending at constant Mach, the air becomes warmer, so the local speed of sound and the TAS (M × LSS) increase. The air also becomes denser, and at a higher TAS in denser air the dynamic pressure, and so IAS, rises quickly. When the IAS reaches the planned descent IAS (the crossover altitude), the aeroplane continues at constant IAS and the Mach number then decreases.
whyWrong: Constant Mach does not mean constant IAS or TAS when altitude and temperature change.
TAS = M × LSS, and the LSS rises as the air warms in the descent, so TAS increases too.
At constant Mach in denser air the IAS rises, not falls.
samples.examTip: Climbing is the mirror image: constant IAS, then constant Mach above the crossover.

chapters.title: General Principles - Cruise
topics: Balance of Forces in Level Flight

samples.prompt: The speed displayed on the airspeed indicator without any corrections is called:
options: Calibrated airspeed
Equivalent airspeed
True airspeed
Indicated airspeed
samples.explanation: Indicated airspeed (IAS) is the raw speed from pressure probes without correction for instrument or position errors. CAS (A) includes these corrections. EAS (B) includes compressibility correction. TAS (C) includes density correction.

samples.prompt: An aircraft cruises at 360 kt TAS with a 51 kt tailwind, burning 6,400 kg/h. What is its specific air range (nm per 1 000 kg)?
samples.explanation: Specific air range = TAS ÷ fuel flow = 360 ÷ 6,400 = 0.0563 nm/kg = 56.2 nm per 1 000 kg.
whyWrong: Gave the range in kilometres
Moved the decimal point one place
Multiplied the speed by the fuel flow
samples.examTip: Common trap: gave the range in kilometres.

samples.prompt: A jet cruises at 450 kt TAS with a total fuel flow of 2,500 kg/h into a 50 kt headwind. What are its specific air range and specific ground range?
options: SAR 0.16 nm/kg, SGR 0.18 nm/kg
SAR 0.18 nm/kg, SGR 0.16 nm/kg
SAR 5.6 nm/kg, SGR 6.3 nm/kg
SAR 0.18 nm/kg, SGR 0.20 nm/kg
samples.explanation: SAR = TAS ÷ fuel flow = 450 ÷ 2,500 = 0.18 nm/kg. Groundspeed = 450 − 50 = 400 kt, so SGR = 400 ÷ 2,500 = 0.16 nm/kg. The headwind costs about 11% of the range.
whyWrong: Swaps them: the air range uses TAS, the ground range uses groundspeed.
Inverted the ratio: fuel flow ÷ speed gives kg per nm, not nm per kg.
Added the headwind to get the groundspeed.
samples.examTip: Distance per kilogram: speed on top, fuel flow underneath.

samples.prompt: As a jet burns fuel in a long cruise, what happens to its optimum cruise altitude, and why?
options: It increases, because a lighter aeroplane reaches its best lift/drag angle of attack at lower density
It increases, because the temperature falls as the fuel tanks empty
It stays the same, because the optimum altitude depends only on the Mach number
It decreases, because the engines produce more thrust at lower levels
samples.explanation: The best specific range is achieved at a particular angle of attack and Mach number. A lighter aeroplane needs less lift, so it reaches that angle of attack at a lower density, i.e. higher altitude. The optimum altitude therefore rises as fuel is burnt, which is why crews request step climbs during long flights.
whyWrong: Fuel temperature has no bearing on the optimum altitude.
Optimum altitude depends strongly on mass.
The optimum altitude rises as mass falls, and higher altitude improves jet engine efficiency too.
samples.examTip: Heavier = lower optimum altitude.

samples.prompt: A jet is cruising for maximum ground range. A strong headwind develops. How should the cruise speed change?
options: Increase it slightly above the still-air maximum-range speed
Reduce it slightly below the still-air maximum-range speed
Keep it the same, because the wind affects the groundspeed, not the specific air range
Reduce it to the maximum endurance speed
samples.explanation: Maximum ground range comes at the best ratio of groundspeed to fuel flow. A headwind reduces the groundspeed by the same amount at every TAS, which proportionally hurts slow speeds more. The best speed therefore moves higher: fly faster into a headwind and slightly slower with a tailwind.
whyWrong: A slower speed in a headwind spends longer exposed to it, reducing ground range.
Specific GROUND range is what matters, and it depends on groundspeed.
Endurance speed minimises fuel per hour, not fuel per ground mile.
samples.examTip: Same rule as for a max-range glide.

chapters.title: General Principles - Landing
topics: Effect of Variable Factors on Landing Distance

samples.prompt: The landing stage of flight is defined as commencing from:
options: 35 feet above the landing threshold
50 feet above the landing threshold
100 feet above the landing threshold
The point of flare initiation
samples.explanation: The landing stage commences from 50 feet above the landing threshold. Option A (35 feet) is the take-off screen height for Class A aeroplanes. Option C (100 feet) is not correct. Option D is incorrect as flare occurs after the screen height.

samples.prompt: Which of the following does NOT increase the landing distance required?
options: A tailwind component
A higher aerodrome pressure altitude
A wet runway surface
An upslope on the runway
samples.explanation: An upslope adds a component of weight opposing the motion, helping the aeroplane decelerate, so it shortens the landing distance. Tailwind, high pressure altitude or temperature, a wet or contaminated runway, higher mass and a downslope all lengthen it.
whyWrong: A tailwind increases the groundspeed at touchdown, so the landing run is longer.
At a higher pressure altitude the same IAS is a higher TAS and groundspeed.
A wet surface reduces braking friction.
samples.examTip: Slope helps the opposite phase: uphill hurts take-off but helps landing.

samples.prompt: A Class A jet's landing distance from the flight manual (unfactored, dry) is 1,200 m. What landing distance is required on a wet runway?
samples.explanation: Dry: the landing must be completed within 60% of the LDA, so LDR = 1,200 ÷ 0.6 = 2,000 m. Wet: at least 115% of the dry requirement, 2,000 × 1.15 = 2,300 m.
whyWrong: Multiplied by 1.6 instead of dividing by 0.6.
Gave the dry requirement only (1,200 ÷ 0.6) and forgot the 15% wet increment.
Applied only the 15% wet increment to the unfactored distance.
samples.examTip: Turboprops use ÷ 0.7 for the dry requirement.

samples.prompt: A main-wheel tyre is inflated to 196 psi. Using the rule of thumb for dynamic aquaplaning of a rotating tyre, at what groundspeed can aquaplaning begin?
options: 126 kt
108 kt
196 kt
samples.explanation: Dynamic aquaplaning speed ≈ 9 × √(tyre pressure in psi) kt for a rotating tyre. √196 = 14, so 9 × 14 = 126 kt. A non-rotating tyre can aquaplane at a lower speed, about 7.7√p ≈ 108 kt, so touchdown on a flooded runway is especially risky.
whyWrong: Used 7.7√p, the lower figure for a tyre that is not rotating, such as touching down with spun-down wheels.
Used the tyre pressure as the speed.
Multiplied the pressure by 9 instead of its square root.
samples.examTip: Higher tyre pressure raises the aquaplaning speed.

samples.prompt: Why is credit for reverse thrust NOT taken in the dry-runway landing distance used to schedule a Class A jet?
options: The requirement is demonstrated with wheel brakes alone, so reverse thrust stays as an extra margin
Reverse thrust increases the landing distance because it lifts the nose
Reverse thrust is not effective at landing speeds
Reverse thrust may only be used on wet runways
samples.explanation: Dry-runway certified landing distances are determined with wheel brakes and without reverse thrust. Reverse thrust is therefore an additional margin in normal operations, which also protects the aeroplane if a reverser fails. Some regulations allow credit for reverse thrust in contaminated-runway data.
whyWrong: Reverse thrust does not lengthen the landing; it shortens it.
Reverse thrust is most effective at high speed, just after touchdown.
It may be used on any runway; the question is only whether it is credited.
samples.examTip: Reverse thrust is most effective at high speed; use it early in the landing roll.

chapters.title: Piston Engines - Introduction
topics: The Application of the Combined Gas Law — The Four Strokes

samples.prompt: According to the Law of Conservation of Energy:
options: Energy can be created but not destroyed
Energy can be destroyed but not created
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed; only its form may be changed
Energy is always lost as heat in any conversion process
samples.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Options A and B are incorrect, and option D is not a statement of conservation.

samples.prompt: One horsepower is equal to how many foot pounds per minute?
samples.explanation: One horsepower equals 33,000 foot pounds per minute. Option B (550) is foot pounds per second, option C (746) is watts per horsepower, and option D is incorrect.

samples.prompt: In one cylinder of a four-stroke piston engine, how many revolutions of the crankshaft are needed to complete one full cycle?
options: Two revolutions (720° of crank rotation)
Four revolutions, one for each stroke
Half a revolution (180° of crank rotation)
One revolution (360° of crank rotation)
samples.explanation: Each stroke moves the piston from one dead centre to the other, which is half a crankshaft revolution. Four strokes (induction, compression, power, exhaust) therefore take two revolutions, 720° of crank travel, and each cylinder fires once in that time.
whyWrong: Each stroke is half a revolution (top to bottom or bottom to top), not a whole one.
Half a revolution is one stroke, not the whole cycle of four strokes.
One revolution per cycle is the two-stroke engine, which fires every time the piston reaches the top.
samples.examTip: Strokes are half-turns: count strokes ÷ 2 to get crank revolutions.

samples.prompt: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 2,400 rpm. How many power strokes does the engine as a whole deliver each minute?
samples.explanation: Each cylinder fires once every two revolutions, so one cylinder gives 2,400 ÷ 2 = 1,200 power strokes per minute. Six cylinders give 6 × 1,200 = 7,200 per minute, which is why a six-cylinder engine runs more smoothly than a four: the impulses overlap.
whyWrong: Assumes each cylinder fires every revolution, which is two-stroke behaviour.
Gives the power strokes of one cylinder only (2,400 ÷ 2), forgetting to multiply by six.
Counts the power strokes of only one cylinder at one per revolution, and ignores the other five cylinders.
samples.examTip: Write the ÷ 2 first; forgetting it is the usual slip.

samples.prompt: In the ideal (air-standard) Otto cycle on which the spark-ignition piston engine is based, heat is added:
options: At constant pressure, as in the gas turbine
At constant temperature, during the power stroke
Gradually, throughout the compression stroke
At constant volume, with the piston at top dead centre
samples.explanation: The ideal Otto cycle has four processes: adiabatic compression, heat addition at constant volume (combustion so quick that the piston barely moves near TDC), adiabatic expansion, and heat rejection at constant volume. Its efficiency rises with compression ratio, which is why compression ratio matters so much in piston engines.
whyWrong: Constant-pressure heat addition is the Brayton cycle of the gas turbine (and, approximately, the diesel cycle).
Constant-temperature (isothermal) processes belong to the theoretical Carnot cycle, not the Otto cycle.
Compression in the ideal cycle is adiabatic: no heat is added until the charge is ignited.
samples.examTip: If the question contrasts piston and turbine engines, the key words are 'constant volume' versus 'constant pressure'.

chapters.title: Piston Engines - General
topics: The Operation of the Practical Otto Cycle
The Four-Stroke Cycle — A Mechanical Ballet
The Theoretical Otto Cycle — The Ideal

samples.prompt: The correct working cycle of a four-stroke engine is:
options: exhaust, power, induction, compression
compression, power, exhaust, induction
induction, power, compression, exhaust
induction, compression, power, exhaust
samples.explanation: The correct sequence is Induction (intake of mixture), Compression (compressing the mixture), Power (expansion after combustion), and Exhaust (expelling burnt gases). Option A has the order reversed. Option B starts with compression before induction. Option C places power before compression, which is impossible.

samples.prompt: A cylinder has a swept volume of 540 cm³ and a clearance (combustion chamber) volume of 90 cm³. What is its compression ratio?
samples.explanation: Compression ratio = volume above the piston at BDC ÷ volume at TDC = (swept + clearance) ÷ clearance = (540 + 90) ÷ 90 = 630 ÷ 90 = 7. The ratio is 7:1.
whyWrong: Inverted the ratio: total volume divided by swept volume.
Subtracted the clearance volume from the swept volume instead of adding it.
Divided the swept volume by the clearance volume; the ratio uses the total volume at BDC (swept + clearance).
samples.examTip: Sense check: CR is always greater than swept ÷ clearance by exactly 1.

samples.prompt: A 4-cylinder engine has a bore of 12 cm and a stroke of 8.8 cm. What is its total swept volume?
samples.explanation: Swept volume per cylinder = π × (12/2)² × 8.8 = 995 cm³. × 4 = 3,981 cm³ = 3.98 L.
whyWrong: Used the bore as the radius
Left out π/4 (used bore × stroke)
Gave the swept volume of one cylinder
samples.examTip: Common trap: used the bore as the radius.

samples.prompt: Near the end of the exhaust stroke both the inlet and the exhaust valves are open together for a short period. What is this called and what does it achieve?
options: Valve overlap: it raises the effective compression ratio and so reduces the risk of detonation
Valve overlap: exhaust gas momentum helps scavenge the cylinder and draw in the fresh charge
Valve lag: it lets the piston push the last of the exhaust gas out through the inlet port
Valve lead: it ensures the spark occurs before the inlet valve has fully closed
samples.explanation: Around TDC between exhaust and induction, the inlet valve opens early (lead) and the exhaust valve closes late (lag), so both are open together. The momentum of the exhaust gas leaving creates a low pressure that helps start the fresh charge moving in, scavenging the clearance volume and filling the cylinder more completely.
whyWrong: Overlap has nothing to do with compression ratio, and a higher compression ratio would increase detonation risk, not reduce it.
Lag means a valve closing after a dead centre; and the exhaust leaves through the exhaust port, never back through the inlet.
Lead means a valve opening before a dead centre; ignition timing is a separate matter.
samples.examTip: Lead = opens early, lag = closes late, overlap = both open around TDC at the exhaust/induction change.

samples.prompt: Why does the exhaust valve open well before the piston reaches bottom dead centre on the power stroke?
options: To raise the pressure in the cylinder so that the power stroke lasts longer and delivers more work to the crankshaft
To admit cooling air into the cylinder before the next induction stroke begins
To use the remaining gas pressure to expel the burnt gas, reducing the work of the exhaust stroke
To allow some of the fresh charge to escape and prevent an over-rich mixture
samples.explanation: Late in the power stroke the gas has done most of its useful work, but it is still at a pressure well above atmospheric. Opening the exhaust valve early (exhaust valve lead) lets that pressure blow the gas out ('blowdown'), so the piston meets little resistance on the exhaust stroke. The small loss of expansion work is more than repaid.
whyWrong: Opening the exhaust valve releases pressure; it cannot raise it.
No air is admitted through the exhaust valve; cooling is by fins, baffles and the oil.
At this point there is no fresh charge in the cylinder, only burnt gas.
samples.examTip: Every valve-timing 'early/late' question is answered by gas inertia or gas pressure, never by cooling.

chapters.title: Piston Engines - Lubrication
topics: The Wet and Dry Sump Lubricating Systems

samples.prompt: An increase in friction within a piston engine will cause:
options: An increase in Brake Horse Power
A decrease in Friction Horsepower
An increase in Friction Horsepower and a reduction in Brake Horse Power
No change in engine power output
samples.explanation: Friction horsepower is the power used up overcoming friction inside the engine, and BHP = IHP − FHP. More friction therefore raises the friction horsepower and reduces the brake horsepower delivered to the propeller.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of the lubricating oil in a piston engine?
options: Helping to seal the gap between the piston rings and the cylinder walls
Carrying heat away from the pistons and bearings
Raising the octane rating of the fuel/air charge
Carrying away carbon and metal particles to the filter
samples.explanation: Engine oil lubricates, cools, seals, cleans and protects against corrosion; in a constant-speed installation it also works the propeller pitch mechanism. Octane rating is a property of the fuel and its additives; the oil plays no part in it.
whyWrong: The oil film between rings and cylinder wall helps seal the combustion gases.
Cooling is a major oil function: the oil removes heat from parts the air cannot reach, such as the piston underside.
Cleaning is a function: the oil carries contaminants to the filter.
samples.examTip: In a NOT question, look for the option that belongs to a different system (fuel, ignition).

samples.prompt: In a dry-sump lubrication system, why does the scavenge pump have a greater capacity than the pressure pump?
options: The returning oil is hot and aerated, so it occupies a larger volume than the oil delivered
A larger scavenge pump raises the oil pressure at the bearings
The pressure pump is only used during engine starting, so the scavenge pump carries the normal load
The scavenge pump also supplies oil pressure to the constant-speed unit
samples.explanation: Oil draining from the bearings is hot and full of air bubbles, so it occupies a greater volume than the cool, solid oil the pressure pump delivers. A scavenge pump of greater capacity keeps the sump dry and returns everything to the separate oil tank, where the air is removed.
whyWrong: The scavenge pump is on the return side; bearing pressure is set by the pressure pump and the relief valve.
The pressure pump runs whenever the engine turns; it feeds the bearings throughout.
The CSU is fed from the pressure side of the system, not by the scavenge pump.
samples.examTip: 'Why is the scavenge pump bigger' always comes back to aeration and expansion of the returning oil.

samples.prompt: Shortly after levelling off, the pilot of a single-engine aircraft sees oil pressure falling slowly while oil temperature rises. What is the most likely cause and the best response?
options: A cold oil cooler; open the cowl flaps fully and continue to destination
An over-rich mixture; lean the mixture until the oil pressure recovers
A faulty oil pressure gauge; no action is needed while temperature stays in the green
Loss of oil; reduce power and land as soon as possible, expecting engine failure
samples.explanation: Less oil in circulation removes less heat (temperature rises) and the pump can no longer hold its delivery pressure (pressure falls). Two indications moving together confirm a real problem, usually loss of oil through a leak. Reducing power cuts the heat load; the engine may fail, so the pilot should plan a landing at once.
whyWrong: A cold cooler would give low temperature, not high; the readings point the other way.
Mixture does not affect oil pressure; leaning at this stage would also raise cylinder temperatures further.
A gauge fault affects one reading; two related indications changing together point to a real loss of oil.
samples.examTip: One odd gauge may be the gauge; two related gauges changing together is the engine.

samples.prompt: When the engine is started on a cold morning, the oil cooler is bypassed. Which component causes this and why?
options: The oil tank vent, so that no air is drawn into the cooler
The scavenge filter bypass, so that cold oil is not filtered at all
A thermostatic valve, so that cold, thick oil reaches the bearings quickly
The pressure relief valve, so that the pump does not over-pressurise the bearings
samples.explanation: Cold oil is very viscous and would struggle through the fine passages of the cooler, possibly damaging it with surge pressure, and would stay cold. A temperature-sensitive valve routes cold oil around the cooler; as the oil warms, the valve closes the bypass and sends the oil through the cooler.
whyWrong: The vent keeps the tank at near atmospheric pressure; it does not route oil.
A filter bypass opens only when the filter is blocked; it has no link to oil temperature.
The relief valve limits maximum pressure in the delivery line; it does not choose the cooler path.
samples.examTip: 'Cold oil' + 'bypass' = thermostatic valve; 'blocked' + 'bypass' = filter bypass.

samples.prompt: The thermal efficiency of a typical piston engine is at best:
samples.explanation: A piston engine converts at best only about 25-28% of the fuel's heat energy into useful work; roughly 40% leaves in the exhaust and about 32% heats the engine and is removed by the cooling and oil systems.

samples.prompt: What percentage of heat energy is lost through the exhaust gases in a piston engine?
options: Approximately 20%
Approximately 32%
Approximately 40%
Approximately 70%
samples.explanation: About 40% of the fuel's heat energy is lost in the exhaust gas. Roughly 32% goes into heating the engine components (removed by cooling), and only about 28% becomes useful work.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of the baffles fitted around the cylinders of an air-cooled aero engine?
options: To keep exhaust gas away from the induction system
To reduce propeller noise reaching the cabin
To prevent the cooling air touching the hottest parts of the cylinders, which would cause shock cooling
To make the cooling air pass close to the fins on its way from above the engine to below it
samples.explanation: In pressure cooling, the ram air enters the cowling and builds up a higher pressure above the cylinders. Baffles and seals force this air to pass through the fins on its way to the lower-pressure region below the engine and out past the cowl flaps, so the fins get all of it.
whyWrong: Separating exhaust from induction is done by the manifold layout; baffles direct cooling air.
Baffles are an airflow device; cabin noise is dealt with by insulation.
The hottest parts (the heads) need the most air, not the least; shock cooling comes from sudden power reductions.
samples.examTip: A damaged baffle or seal gives one hot cylinder; look for that in scenario questions.

samples.prompt: A pilot closes the throttle fully at high altitude and starts a fast, steep descent. What is the main engine risk?
options: Detonation caused by the rich mixture at low power
Vapour lock in the fuel lines as the ambient pressure rises
Shock cooling: the cylinders cool too quickly and may crack
Overspeeding of the magnetos as the propeller windmills
samples.explanation: A sudden large power reduction combined with high airspeed cools hot cylinder heads very fast. Aluminium heads and steel barrels contract at different rates, which can crack the heads or distort the cylinders. Reduce power gradually and keep some power on during the descent.
whyWrong: Detonation needs high power and high temperature; at idle in a descent the risk is negligible.
Vapour lock comes from heat and low pressure (climbing, hot days), not from a descent into higher pressure.
Magnetos are geared to the crankshaft; a fixed-pitch propeller may overspeed the engine in a dive, but that is not the main thermal risk here.
samples.examTip: Plan descents with gradual power reductions; examiners link 'steep, idle descent' with shock cooling.

samples.prompt: During a long, full-power climb in a hot climate, the cylinder head temperature approaches its upper limit. Which combination of actions will help most?
options: Lean the mixture to peak EGT and reduce airspeed to lower the drag and the power needed for the climb
Apply carburettor heat and increase the climb angle to reach cooler air sooner
Close the cowl flaps, lean the mixture, and climb at the best angle of climb speed
Open the cowl flaps, check the mixture is rich, and lower the nose to climb at a higher airspeed
samples.explanation: An air-cooled engine relies on airflow through the cowling. Open cowl flaps increase that flow, a rich mixture uses the excess fuel to absorb heat, and a higher climb speed (cruise-climb) pushes more air past the fins. Reducing power also helps if terrain permits.
whyWrong: Peak EGT at high power gives the hottest cylinders and the greatest detonation risk; less airspeed means less cooling.
Carb heat brings in hot air and enriches slightly but reduces power; a steeper climb reduces airflow over the cylinders.
Closing the cowl flaps and leaning both raise CHT, and a slow climb reduces cooling airflow.
samples.examTip: Any option that reduces airflow or leans the mixture makes the engine hotter.

samples.prompt: The spark appears at the plug electrodes when:
options: The contact breaker closes
The contact breaker opens
The contact breaker stays open
The magneto switch is made
samples.explanation: The spark occurs when the contact breaker points open, causing the primary magnetic field to collapse rapidly, inducing EHT voltage in the secondary coil. Option A is incorrect because closing the points builds the magnetic field, not produces spark. Option C is incorrect because no change in magnetic field occurs when points stay open. Option D is incorrect because the magneto switch controls the primary circuit grounding, not spark timing.

samples.prompt: Which statement about aircraft magneto ignition is correct?
options: The magneto needs the alternator to be on line to produce a spark
Turning the ignition switch to OFF connects the magneto to the battery
Dual ignition is fitted only for redundancy and has no effect on combustion
The engine keeps running if the aircraft battery and master switch fail
samples.explanation: A magneto is a self-contained generator: a rotating magnet, a coil and a contact breaker. It needs no external power, so the engine keeps running after an electrical failure. Two magnetos and two plugs per cylinder give redundancy and also faster, more even burning.
whyWrong: The magneto generates its own current from a rotating magnet.
OFF connects the magneto primary to earth; the battery is not involved at all.
Two plugs per cylinder also give two flame fronts and quicker, more complete combustion.
samples.examTip: An electrical failure never stops a magneto-ignition engine; a fuel or mechanical problem does.

samples.prompt: After shutdown, a pilot notices that the P-lead of the left magneto is broken. Why is this dangerous?
options: The magneto will overheat because its primary coil is no longer cooled
The magneto can no longer be grounded, so it stays live and may fire if the propeller is turned
The broken lead allows battery current to reach the spark plugs whenever the master switch is on
The left magneto loses its source of electrical power, so the engine cannot be restarted on it
samples.explanation: The ignition switch stops a magneto by connecting its primary circuit to earth through the P-lead. If the P-lead is broken, selecting OFF does nothing: the magneto is 'hot' and will produce a spark whenever the crankshaft is turned. Treat every propeller as live.
whyWrong: The P-lead carries no cooling function; it is only an earthing (grounding) wire.
Magnetos are independent of the aircraft battery and master switch.
A magneto generates its own electricity from its rotating magnet; it needs no outside power.
samples.examTip: Ignition switch logic is backwards: OFF = earthed (grounded), ON = earth removed.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of the impulse coupling fitted to a magneto?
options: It gives a strong, retarded spark at cranking speed by flicking the magnet round
It connects the magneto to the battery during starting to boost the spark
It disconnects the magneto from the engine if the propeller strikes an object
It advances the ignition timing at high engine speed to improve power and smoothness in the cruise
samples.explanation: At cranking speed the magnet turns too slowly to make a good spark. The impulse coupling holds the magnet back with a spring, then releases it so it flicks round quickly, producing a strong spark. This happens later than normal (retarded), near TDC, which also prevents the engine 'kicking back' against the starter.
whyWrong: Magnetos are self-contained and are not connected to the battery.
There is no such protective function; a prop strike needs an engine inspection.
Most aircraft magnetos have fixed timing in normal running; the coupling only works at very low speed.
samples.examTip: Two words go with impulse coupling: 'stronger' and 'retarded'.

samples.prompt: During the pre-take-off magneto check, the pilot selects each magneto in turn and sees no rpm drop at all on the left magneto. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The right magneto is not being grounded, so both are still firing
The left magneto is perfectly timed and is in better condition than the right
The mixture is too rich for a valid magneto check
The spark plugs are fouled on the right-hand side of the engine
samples.explanation: With one magneto selected, each cylinder has only one flame front, so combustion is slower and a small rpm drop is normal. Selecting 'L' should ground the right magneto. No drop at all means the right magneto is still firing, usually because its P-lead or switch contact is open, so it would also stay live on the ground.
whyWrong: A healthy single magneto always gives a small drop, because one plug per cylinder burns the charge more slowly.
A rich mixture does not remove the drop; the check is normally done at the mixture setting the manual gives.
Fouled plugs on the right magneto would show as rough running when the right magneto is selected alone.
samples.examTip: Big drop or rough running = plug or magneto fault; no drop = grounding (P-lead or switch) fault.

samples.prompt: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure is:
options: Less than atmospheric pressure
Equal to atmospheric pressure
Greater than atmospheric pressure
Independent of atmospheric pressure
samples.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the pressure acting on its surface; vapour bubbles can then form throughout the liquid. Because atmospheric pressure falls with altitude, fuel boils at a lower temperature at altitude (low pressure boiling).

samples.prompt: Fuel of grade 100LL is dyed which colour, and what does 'LL' indicate?
options: Green; low lead, meaning no tetraethyl lead at all
Blue; low lead, meaning less tetraethyl lead than the older grade 100/130
Red; long life, meaning extra stabilisers for storage
Straw-coloured; low lead, meaning the fuel is a kerosene type
samples.explanation: AVGAS 100LL is dyed blue. 'Low lead' means it contains less tetraethyl lead (the anti-knock additive) than 100/130, while keeping the same anti-knock performance. It is not lead-free. Colour coding helps the pilot check the right grade on the fuel strainer sample.
whyWrong: Green was the colour of the older 100/130 grade; 100LL still contains tetraethyl lead, only less of it.
Red was used for grade 80; 'LL' means low lead, not long life.
Straw or colourless is turbine fuel (kerosene), which must never be put in a piston engine.
samples.examTip: 'Low lead' is not 'no lead'; that is the usual trap.

samples.prompt: The octane rating of an aviation gasoline is a measure of:
options: Its volatility, that is how easily it vaporises in the carburettor and how prone it is to vapour lock
The proportion of eight-carbon hydrocarbons in the fuel
Its resistance to detonation, compared with iso-octane and heptane reference fuels
The energy it releases per kilogram when burnt
samples.explanation: A fuel is tested in a standard engine and compared with mixtures of iso-octane (very resistant to knocking, rated 100) and normal heptane (knocks easily, rated 0). A fuel with an octane rating of 80 knocks like a mixture of 80% iso-octane and 20% heptane. Higher ratings allow higher compression ratios and boost.
whyWrong: Volatility is measured by vapour pressure, not octane rating.
The name comes from iso-octane in the reference fuel; the rating is a test result, not a chemical count.
Calorific value is a separate property; AVGAS grades have similar energy per kilogram.
samples.examTip: Higher octane does not mean more power from the fuel itself; it means the engine can be run harder without detonating.

samples.prompt: What is the difference between detonation and pre-ignition in a piston engine?
options: They are the same process, named differently for spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines
Detonation occurs before the spark; pre-ignition is a late burn caused by a weak mixture
Detonation: end gas explodes after the spark. Pre-ignition: a hot spot fires the charge before the spark
Detonation is caused by a hot spark plug; pre-ignition is caused by a fuel of too high an octane rating
samples.explanation: In normal combustion the flame front spreads smoothly from the plug. In detonation, the spark ignites the charge normally but the remaining unburnt end gas, compressed and heated by the advancing flame, explodes spontaneously, hammering the piston. Pre-ignition is ignition before the spark, from a glowing carbon deposit, plug electrode or valve; it can itself lead to detonation.
whyWrong: They are distinct: one is spontaneous explosion of unburnt gas, the other premature ignition from a hot surface.
Reverses the two: it is pre-ignition that happens before the spark.
High octane fuel resists detonation; it does not cause pre-ignition.
samples.examTip: Ask 'before or after the spark?' and the answer follows.

samples.prompt: Which of the following would NOT increase the risk of detonation in a piston engine?
options: Using a fuel of lower octane rating than specified
Enriching the mixture at high power
A high cylinder head temperature
A high manifold pressure at low rpm
samples.explanation: Detonation is promoted by high charge temperature and pressure: high CHT, high manifold pressure (especially at low rpm), lean mixtures at high power, high compression ratios and low-octane fuel. A rich mixture cools the charge through fuel evaporation, which is why full rich is used for take-off and climb.
whyWrong: A lower octane fuel has less resistance to detonation.
A hot cylinder heats the charge towards its self-ignition point, making detonation more likely.
High manifold pressure at low rpm means high cylinder pressure and temperature with slow piston movement: a classic detonation condition.
samples.examTip: In a NOT question, the safe option is the one that cools the charge.

samples.prompt: The chemically correct air/fuel ratio by weight is:
samples.explanation: The chemically correct (stoichiometric) air/fuel ratio for complete combustion is about 15:1 by weight. About 12.5:1 is used for maximum power, about 10:1 for take-off, and about 18:1 for economical cruise.

samples.prompt: An aircraft climbs from sea level to 8,000 ft without the pilot touching the mixture control. What happens to the mixture?
options: It becomes leaner, because colder air at altitude carries less fuel vapour
It becomes leaner, because the fuel pump delivers less fuel at altitude
It becomes richer, because the air is less dense but the fuel flow hardly changes
It stays chemically correct, because the carburettor automatically meters by mass
samples.explanation: The carburettor meters fuel according to the volume (velocity) of air through the venturi. At altitude each cubic metre contains less air by mass, but the fuel flow stays about the same, so the fuel-to-air ratio by mass increases. The pilot leans the mixture to restore the correct ratio.
whyWrong: Colder air is denser, which would lean the mixture, but the fall in pressure dominates and the mixture richens.
The float carburettor meters by volume of air; fewer kilograms of air per cubic metre at altitude means relatively more fuel.
A simple float carburettor has no automatic altitude compensation; that is why there is a mixture control.
samples.examTip: Altitude → less dense air → richer mixture → lean it.

samples.prompt: Why is a piston engine normally set to full rich (or the manufacturer's take-off setting) for take-off and initial climb?
options: The extra fuel cools the cylinders and suppresses detonation at high power
Full rich gives the highest exhaust gas temperature and therefore the most power
A rich mixture gives the lowest fuel consumption at high power
A rich mixture prevents carburettor icing during take-off
samples.explanation: At take-off power the cylinder pressures and temperatures are highest. Running rich of best power uses the surplus fuel as an internal coolant: its evaporation and the extra mass carry heat away, keeping CHT down and the charge below its detonation point. At high-elevation aerodromes the manual may call for leaning to restore power.
whyWrong: Full rich gives a lower EGT than peak; the cooling effect is the reason for using it.
Rich mixtures give the highest fuel consumption, not the lowest.
Icing depends on temperature drop and humidity; mixture setting does not stop it.
samples.examTip: If the aerodrome is high and hot, expect the manual to call for leaning before take-off; at sea level, full rich.

samples.prompt: The chemically correct (stoichiometric) air/fuel ratio for aviation gasoline is about:
options: 15:1 by volume
25:1 by mass
8:1 by mass
15:1 by mass
samples.explanation: Complete burning of gasoline needs roughly 15 kg of air for each kilogram of fuel (about 14.7:1). Best power is obtained slightly rich of this, around 12–13:1, and best economy slightly lean. The usable range in a piston engine is roughly 8:1 to 20:1.
whyWrong: The ratio is defined by mass; by volume air outnumbers fuel vapour by a very different figure.
25:1 is far leaner than the weak limit of combustion in a piston engine.
8:1 is far richer than any usable mixture; the engine would choke.
samples.examTip: All mixture ratios in exams are by mass (weight); options 'by volume' are traps.

samples.prompt: While leaning in cruise, the pilot watches the exhaust gas temperature. As the mixture is leaned from full rich, how does EGT behave?
options: It rises to a peak near the chemically correct mixture, then falls as the mixture becomes leaner still
It stays constant until the engine starts to run rough, then rises sharply
It rises steadily until the engine stops, so the highest EGT is reached just at the idle cut-off position
It falls steadily, because less fuel is being burnt
samples.explanation: On the rich side, surplus fuel absorbs heat and lowers the gas temperature. Leaning removes that surplus, so EGT climbs until it peaks close to the chemically correct ratio, where all the fuel and oxygen are used. Leaner still, surplus air dilutes and cools the gas, and EGT falls. Pilots lean with reference to this peak, following the engine manual.
whyWrong: EGT responds smoothly to every change in mixture; that is why it is used for leaning.
Past the peak, the surplus air dilutes and cools the gas, so EGT falls before the engine stops.
Excess fuel cools the gas on the rich side, so removing it raises EGT at first.
samples.examTip: Peak EGT is not peak power: best power is on the rich side of peak.

chapters.title: Piston Engines - Carburettors
topics: The Basic Requirements of a Carburettor
The Principle of the Air Bleed Diffuser

samples.prompt: In a simple float chamber carburettor, the constant fuel level in the float chamber is maintained by:
options: The fuel pump pressure regulator
The float and needle valve mechanism
The venturi depression
The throttle valve position
samples.explanation: The float and needle valve mechanism regulates fuel flow from the fuel pump to maintain a constant level in the float chamber. Fuel pump pressure regulator controls system pressure, not chamber level. Venturi depression draws fuel but does not maintain level. Throttle valve controls airflow, not fuel level.

samples.prompt: In a float-type carburettor, what causes fuel to flow from the main jet into the airstream?
options: The engine-driven fuel pump, which sprays fuel through the jet under high pressure
Gravity alone, which is why the fuel tank must be above the carburettor
The rise in pressure in the venturi throat, which forces the fuel out of the float chamber and through the jet
The venturi depression, acting against the near-atmospheric pressure in the vented float chamber
samples.explanation: Air accelerates through the venturi and its static pressure falls (Bernoulli). The float chamber is vented to the air intake or atmosphere, so the pressure above the fuel is higher than at the jet outlet in the throat. That pressure difference, which increases with airflow, pushes fuel out of the discharge nozzle.
whyWrong: Fuel pumps only supply the float chamber; the float needle valve controls entry, and spraying is done by the pressure difference.
Gravity or a pump only fills the float chamber; flow out of the jet is driven by the venturi pressure drop.
Air speeds up in the venturi throat, so its pressure falls; it does not rise.
samples.examTip: If an option says the venturi pressure rises, discard it.

samples.prompt: Why is an accelerator pump fitted to many float carburettors?
options: To keep the engine running when the throttle is closed for idling
To add a brief squirt of fuel when the throttle is opened quickly, avoiding a weak cut
To pump fuel back to the tank when the float chamber overfills during a long descent at low power
To increase fuel pressure at high altitude where the air is less dense
samples.explanation: When the throttle opens suddenly, the light air accelerates almost at once but the heavier fuel lags behind. The mixture briefly goes very weak and the engine may hesitate or cut. The accelerator pump, linked to the throttle, injects a small extra charge of fuel to bridge the gap.
whyWrong: Idling is handled by the slow-running (idle) jet.
Overfilling is prevented by the float and needle valve; nothing pumps fuel back.
Altitude effects make the mixture richer, not weaker; the pilot leans it.
samples.examTip: 'Rapid throttle opening' and 'hesitation' point to the accelerator pump.

samples.prompt: An engine idles with the throttle valve almost closed. How is fuel delivered to the engine at this setting?
options: Through the accelerator pump, which delivers a continuous flow at idle
Through the float chamber vent, which feeds fuel directly into the intake
Through the idle jet, which discharges near the edge of the throttle valve where pressure is lowest
Through the main jet, because the venturi depression is greatest when the throttle is almost closed at idle
samples.explanation: With the throttle nearly closed, very little air passes the venturi, but the air squeezing past the edge of the throttle plate is fast and at very low pressure. The idle jet discharges just there, so it supplies the small amount of fuel the engine needs at idle.
whyWrong: The accelerator pump only works when the throttle is moved, not continuously.
The vent passes air to the float chamber; it never discharges fuel.
At idle the airflow through the venturi is tiny, so the depression at the main jet is too weak to draw fuel.
samples.examTip: Venturi suction is proportional to airflow: no airflow, no main-jet flow.

samples.prompt: As the airflow through a simple float carburettor increases, the mixture tends to become richer. What device counteracts this?
options: The diffuser (air bleed), which admits air to the fuel as airflow rises and so weakens the mixture
The carburettor heat valve, which admits warm air at high power
The float needle valve, which closes progressively as the airflow increases and so restricts the fuel supply
The accelerator pump, which reduces fuel flow when the throttle is fully open
samples.explanation: In a plain jet, fuel flow rises faster than air mass flow as the venturi depression increases, so the mixture richens with throttle opening. A diffuser or air bleed admits air into the fuel passage; as the depression increases, more air is drawn in, emulsifying the fuel and reducing the effective fuel flow, so the mixture stays nearer the correct value.
whyWrong: Carburettor heat is for ice and, if anything, richens the mixture.
The needle valve maintains the float chamber level; it does not respond to airflow.
The accelerator pump only adds fuel, and only during throttle movement.
samples.examTip: Distinguish the three: accelerator pump (sudden opening), idle jet (closed throttle), diffuser (high airflow).

chapters.title: Piston Engines - Icing
topics: Action to be Taken if Engine Icing is Suspected

samples.prompt: What is the approximate temperature drop in the carburettor throat area compared to incoming air temperature?
