samples.explanation: Fuel vaporisation and the low pressure in the venturi can cool the air in the carburettor throat by as much as about 22°C below the temperature of the incoming air, which is why icing can occur even on warm days.

samples.prompt: Why can carburettor icing occur at outside air temperatures well above freezing?
options: Ice forms on the intake filter from supercooled droplets only
The air entering the carburettor is cooled by contact with the cold fuel tank
The engine-driven fuel pump cools the fuel below zero before it enters the jet, freezing the water in it
Fuel evaporation and the venturi pressure drop can cool the air far below the outside temperature
samples.explanation: Two effects cool the air inside the carburettor: absorption of latent heat as the fuel evaporates (the larger effect) and expansion as the pressure falls in the venturi and past the throttle. The temperature can drop by around 20–30 °C, so moisture freezes out even on a warm, humid day. Risk is highest with high humidity and at reduced power, when the partly closed throttle adds to the cooling.
whyWrong: Impact ice on the intake is one type, but carburettor icing can form in clear, humid air with no supercooled water.
The fuel tank is not in the induction airflow.
The fuel pump does not refrigerate the fuel.
samples.examTip: High humidity matters more than low temperature; a warm, moist day is a carb-ice day.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an effect of selecting carburettor heat?
options: Engine power is reduced
The induction air may be unfiltered
The mixture becomes weaker
The density of the charge falls
samples.explanation: Carburettor heat replaces cold dense air with hot, less dense air. The fuel flow stays about the same while the air mass falls, so the mixture becomes RICHER, not weaker. Power falls, and because the hot-air source is usually unfiltered, the heat should not be used for long on the ground.
whyWrong: Power falls because the hot air is less dense and so a smaller mass of charge reaches the cylinders.
On many installations the hot air bypasses the intake filter, so dust and debris can enter: avoid prolonged use on the ground.
Hot air is less dense: that is the basic reason for the power loss and the richer mixture.
samples.examTip: Hot air richens: the same logic as climbing to altitude.

samples.prompt: Under which conditions is the risk of carburettor icing greatest?
options: Any power setting, but only when flying in visible precipitation
Full power in dry, clear air at −20 °C, when the induction air is at its coldest
Reduced power during a descent in moist, cloud-free air at around +15 °C
Cruise power in dry desert air at +35 °C
samples.explanation: Carburettor icing needs moisture and a temperature drop. Humid air from a little below freezing up to about +30 °C is the main risk band, and the risk is greatest at reduced power, when the nearly closed throttle adds extra cooling and the warm engine gives less heat to the induction system.
whyWrong: Visible moisture is not needed: carburettor ice forms readily in clear humid air.
Very cold dry air holds little moisture, so little ice can form from it.
Hot dry air has a low relative humidity; the moisture does not condense and freeze.
samples.examTip: Low power in a descent is the classic case: apply carb heat before reducing power, not after.

samples.prompt: In an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller, carburettor ice is forming in cruise. What is the first indication, and what happens when full carburettor heat is applied?
options: A gradual fall in rpm; with heat applied rpm drops further and the engine may run rough before rpm recovers
A fall in manifold pressure with constant rpm; with heat applied manifold pressure rises immediately
A rise in rpm; with heat applied rpm falls and stays low
A rise in oil temperature; with heat applied oil temperature returns to normal
samples.explanation: Ice restricts the venturi and throttle, so less charge reaches the cylinders and a fixed-pitch propeller slows down. Hot air is less dense, so applying heat costs some power at once, and the melting ice passes through the engine as water, causing rough running. Once the ice has gone, rpm recovers to a higher value than before.
whyWrong: Constant rpm with falling manifold pressure is the constant-speed propeller picture.
Ice restricts the airflow, so power and rpm fall, not rise.
Oil temperature is not a primary carb-ice indication.
samples.examTip: With a CSU, look at manifold pressure instead: rpm is held constant by the governor.

samples.prompt: The advantages of low-pressure continuous-flow fuel injection include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Low operating pressure
Good fuel distribution
Higher fuel consumption compared to carburettors
Freedom from icing problems
samples.explanation: Low-pressure continuous-flow injection offers low operating pressure, good fuel distribution between cylinders and freedom from carburettor icing. Higher fuel consumption is not an advantage; good distribution actually improves economy.

samples.prompt: In the indirect injection system, the air throttle metering valve varies:
options: The pressure of fuel according to engine speed
The airflow according to fuel pressure
The ignition timing according to throttle position
The mixture strength automatically
samples.explanation: In this indirect (port) injection system the air throttle metering valve varies the pressure of the fuel according to engine speed, so fuel delivery follows the airflow the engine is drawing. It does not alter airflow, ignition timing or mixture strength; mixture is set separately by the manual mixture control.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a fuel-injection system over a float carburettor?
options: Freedom from fuel-evaporation (carburettor) icing
Easier starting when the engine is hot after a short shutdown
More even distribution of fuel to each cylinder
Better throttle response and lower fuel consumption across the power range
samples.explanation: Fuel injection meters fuel accurately to each cylinder and has no venturi in which evaporation ice can form. Its main disadvantage is hot starting: after shutdown the fuel in the lines near the hot engine can vaporise, giving vapour lock and a difficult restart. Manufacturers give special hot-start procedures for this reason.
whyWrong: Without a venturi and evaporating fuel at a throttle, there is no fuel-evaporation ice; this is a genuine advantage.
Metered fuel goes to each cylinder's port, so distribution is more even than through a shared manifold.
Accurate metering and no fuel lag give better response and economy.
samples.examTip: Hot starts are the injected engine's weak spot; expect it in NOT questions.

samples.prompt: In a typical light-aircraft fuel-injection system, where is the fuel delivered?
options: Directly into each combustion chamber, timed to the compression stroke
Into the exhaust manifold, to drive the turbocharger
Into the venturi of a single throttle body, as in a carburettor
Continuously into each cylinder's inlet port, close to the inlet valve
samples.explanation: Most light-aircraft injection systems are continuous-flow port injection: metered fuel is sent through a distributor (flow divider) to a nozzle in each intake port, spraying continuously towards the back of the inlet valve. The fuel enters the cylinder when the valve opens.
whyWrong: Timed direct injection is used in diesel engines and some automotive engines, not in typical light-aircraft engines.
Fuel in the exhaust would simply burn there; the turbocharger is driven by exhaust gas, not fuel.
A single discharge point in a venturi is the carburettor arrangement the system replaces.
samples.examTip: 'Continuous' and 'port' are the two words to look for.

samples.prompt: An aircraft with a fuel-injected engine flies into freezing precipitation and the air filter becomes blocked with ice. What protects the engine?
options: An alternate air door, which opens to supply air from inside the cowling
The accelerator pump, which enriches the mixture to melt the ice
The flow divider, which reduces fuel flow to match the reduced airflow
Nothing is needed, because fuel-injected engines cannot suffer any induction icing
samples.explanation: Fuel injection eliminates fuel-evaporation ice, but impact ice from supercooled water can still build up on the intake and filter. An alternate air door, often opened automatically by suction when the filter blocks, admits warm unfiltered air from inside the cowling so the engine keeps breathing. A small power loss is normal on alternate air.
whyWrong: Injected engines have no accelerator pump, and enriching would not melt filter ice.
The flow divider distributes fuel between cylinders; it does not supply air.
Injection removes fuel-evaporation ice only; impact ice can still block the intake.
samples.examTip: 'Impact ice' affects every engine; 'carburettor (fuel) ice' does not affect injected engines.

chapters.title: Piston Engines - Performance and Power Augmentation
topics: Superchargers and Turbochargers — The Fundamental Distinction
Manifold Pressure Indication — Boost vs MAP

samples.prompt: An Automatic Boost Control Unit:
options: Prevents detonation and dissociation in the cylinder
Maintains an automatic preset boost pressure
Maintains the correct mixture strength for the boost pressure set
Sets the position of the wastegate to ensure the preset boost is maintained
samples.explanation: The ABC unit maintains an automatic preset boost pressure by progressively opening the throttle valve as altitude increases. Option A is incorrect because detonation prevention is not the primary function of ABC. Option C is incorrect because mixture control is separate. Option D is incorrect because ABC controls the throttle butterfly, not the wastegate.

samples.prompt: Before start, the manifold pressure gauge of a normally aspirated engine at a sea-level aerodrome reads about 30 inHg. Once the engine is running at idle, the reading will:
options: Fall to zero, because the manifold is under a perfect vacuum at idle
Rise above 30 inHg, because the pistons compress the charge in the manifold
Stay at 30 inHg, because manifold pressure equals ambient pressure in a normally aspirated engine
Fall well below ambient, because the nearly closed throttle restricts the airflow into the manifold
samples.explanation: With the engine stopped, the manifold is open to the atmosphere through the intake, so the gauge reads ambient pressure. Running, the pistons draw air past the partly closed throttle, and the pressure downstream of it falls well below ambient. A normally aspirated engine can never exceed ambient manifold pressure.
whyWrong: The pressure is low, but far from zero; an idling engine still shows a clear positive reading.
Compression happens inside the cylinder, not in the manifold; without a supercharger the manifold is always below ambient.
Only with the engine stopped, or at full throttle with low airflow, does manifold pressure approach ambient.
samples.examTip: A stationary engine's MP gauge is a check that the gauge reads ambient pressure.

samples.prompt: What is the main reason for fitting an intercooler between the turbocharger compressor and the engine?
options: To cool the engine oil that lubricates the turbocharger bearings
To cool the compressed air, making it denser and less prone to detonation
To warm the induction air, preventing ice in the throttle body
To cool the exhaust gas before it reaches the turbine, protecting the turbine blades
samples.explanation: Compressing the air also heats it. Hot air is less dense, so for a given manifold pressure fewer kilograms of charge enter the cylinders, and the hot charge is closer to detonation. An intercooler (air-to-air heat exchanger) removes some of that heat, giving a denser, cooler charge.
whyWrong: Turbo bearings are cooled by engine oil returning to the oil system, not by the intercooler.
It removes heat; anti-icing is not its purpose.
The intercooler sits on the induction side, after the compressor, not in the exhaust.
samples.examTip: Compression heats air; any 'cool the charge' answer is about density and detonation.

samples.prompt: An engine develops a torque of 500 N m at 2,400 rpm. What brake power is it producing?
samples.explanation: Power = torque × angular velocity. ω = 2π × 2,400 ÷ 60 = 251.3 rad/s. P = 500 N m × 251.3 rad/s = 125,664 W ≈ 125.7 kW (about 168.5 hp).
whyWrong: Multiplied torque by rpm without converting rpm to radians per second (× 2π ÷ 60).
Converted rpm to revolutions per second but forgot the 2π radians in each revolution.
Converted kilowatts to horsepower (÷ 0.7457) and then labelled the figure as kilowatts.
samples.examTip: Quick check: 100 kW is about 134 hp, so a light-aircraft engine answer should be in the low hundreds of kW at most.

samples.prompt: A turbocharged engine maintains its rated manifold pressure as the aircraft climbs. How is this achieved, and what limits it?
options: The gear ratio of the compressor is increased by the pilot at the critical altitude
The wastegate closes progressively to drive the turbine harder, until it is fully closed at the critical altitude
The wastegate opens progressively, sending more exhaust through the turbine, until it is fully open at the critical altitude
The throttle valve closes progressively until it reaches its idle stop at the service ceiling
samples.explanation: Exhaust that passes through the turbine drives the compressor; exhaust that passes the wastegate goes straight overboard. As the air thins, the controller closes the wastegate to drive the turbine faster. When the wastegate is fully closed, no more boost is available: this is the critical altitude, above which manifold pressure falls as in a normally aspirated engine.
whyWrong: A two-speed gear is a feature of some gear-driven superchargers, not of exhaust-driven turbochargers.
Opening the wastegate dumps exhaust overboard and reduces turbine speed; that reduces boost.
The throttle is opened, not closed, to hold manifold pressure in a climb; the ceiling is an aircraft performance limit.
samples.examTip: Wastegate closed = more boost; wastegate open = less boost.

samples.prompt: The blade angle of a propeller is defined as the angle between:
options: The chord of the blade and the relative airflow
The chord of the blade and the plane of rotation
The chord of the blade and the longitudinal axis of the aircraft
The root chord and the tip chord of the blade
samples.explanation: Blade angle (pitch angle) is the angle between the chord line of the propeller blade and the plane of rotation. Option A describes angle of attack. Option C is incorrect as blade angle is not referenced to aircraft longitudinal axis. Option D describes blade twist, not blade angle.

samples.prompt: Why is fine pitch (low blade angle, high rpm) selected for take-off with a variable-pitch propeller?
options: Fine pitch reduces the propeller noise during take-off
A fine blade angle gives an efficient angle of attack at low speed and lets the engine reach full rpm
Fine pitch prevents the engine from overspeeding at low airspeed
Fine pitch gives the greatest blade angle of attack, which is needed to lift the nose wheel at the rotation speed
samples.explanation: At low TAS the helix angle is small. A fine blade angle then gives a sensible angle of attack, low propeller drag, and allows the engine to turn at its maximum rpm, where it develops full power. In cruise, as TAS rises, a coarser angle keeps the angle of attack efficient at lower rpm.
whyWrong: Fine pitch with high rpm is noisier, not quieter.
Fine pitch allows high rpm; it is coarse pitch that resists overspeed.
At low speed a coarse blade would have too high an angle of attack and stall; fine pitch gives an efficient angle, not the greatest one.
samples.examTip: Fine pitch = low gear in a car; coarse pitch = high gear.

samples.prompt: An aircraft with a constant-speed propeller enters a shallow dive with the throttle and rpm lever unchanged. How does the constant-speed unit respond?
options: It reduces the manifold pressure to keep the power constant
It decreases the blade angle (fines pitch) to keep the rpm constant
It increases the blade angle (coarsens pitch) to keep the rpm constant
It leaves the blade angle alone and the rpm rises with the airspeed
samples.explanation: As airspeed rises, the helix angle increases and the blade's angle of attack falls, so the propeller absorbs less torque and starts to speed up. The governor senses the overspeed and, using engine oil pressure, coarsens the blade angle until the angle of attack and absorbed torque restore the selected rpm.
whyWrong: The CSU governs rpm through blade angle only; it has no control over manifold pressure.
Fining the pitch would let the propeller speed up further; the governor does the opposite.
That is what happens with a fixed-pitch propeller; the CSU exists to prevent it.
samples.examTip: Constant-speed propeller: the rpm gauge stays put, so a power change shows on the manifold pressure gauge.

samples.prompt: After an engine failure on a twin, the pilot feathers the propeller. What does this do?
options: Turns the blades to fine pitch so the propeller windmills freely and the engine can be restarted
Locks the propeller at its last blade angle so it cannot overspeed
Turns the blades to a negative angle to provide reverse thrust after landing
Turns the blades to about 90°, edge-on to the airflow, so the propeller stops and drag is least
samples.explanation: Feathering rotates the blades until the chord is nearly parallel to the airflow (blade angle near 90°). The blades then produce almost no torque from the airflow, so the propeller stops turning, which removes windmilling drag and prevents further damage to the failed engine.
whyWrong: A windmilling propeller in fine pitch produces the most drag; that is what feathering avoids.
Locking at the existing angle would leave the propeller windmilling with high drag.
Negative pitch (reverse) is a separate ground-only mode on some turboprops.
samples.examTip: Windmilling drag in fine pitch is much greater than feathered drag: on a twin, feathering transforms single-engine performance.

samples.prompt: In an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller, what is the correct order of control movements to increase power?
options: Increase manifold pressure, then increase rpm, then enrich the mixture
Mixture rich (as required), then increase rpm, then increase manifold pressure
Increase manifold pressure first, then rpm, so the engine is never overspeed
Increase rpm and manifold pressure together, then lean the mixture
samples.explanation: High manifold pressure at low rpm overstresses the engine and invites detonation. To increase power: mixture first, then rpm, then manifold pressure (from right to left on most quadrants). To decrease power, reverse it: manifold pressure first, then rpm, then mixture.
whyWrong: Raising manifold pressure first gives high cylinder pressures at low rpm, the classic detonation condition.
Overspeed is controlled by the governor; the order protects against over-boosting at low rpm, not overspeed.
Leaning while increasing power is the wrong way round; and the levers are moved in sequence, not together.
samples.examTip: Avoid any sequence that ends up with high MP and low rpm.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Introduction
topics: The History of the Gas Turbine Engine
The Principles of the Gas Turbine Engine
The Working Cycle of the Gas Turbine Engine
A Pressure Volume Diagram of the Working Cycle
The Temperature Limit of the Engine
Application of the Gas Laws in the Gas Turbine Engine
Airflow Through a Pure Straight Turbojet Engine

samples.prompt: Which type of gas turbine delivers almost all of its useful output as shaft power through a free power turbine, and is typical of helicopters?
options: Ramjet
Turboshaft
Turbojet
High-bypass turbofan
samples.explanation: In a turboshaft, a free power turbine extracts nearly all the remaining gas energy after the gas generator and drives an output shaft through a gearbox, for example a helicopter rotor transmission. Very little residual thrust is left in the exhaust. A turboprop is similar but keeps a small residual jet thrust.
whyWrong: A ramjet has no compressor or turbine at all and works only at high speed.
A turbojet produces all its thrust from the hot jet and has no output shaft.
A turbofan's fan is driven by a turbine, but its output is thrust from the fan and core streams, not shaft power.
samples.examTip: Shaft power + helicopter = turboshaft; shaft power + propeller = turboprop.

samples.prompt: How does the working cycle of a gas turbine differ from that of a four-stroke piston engine?
options: The gas turbine has no compression phase; the intake ram effect supplies all the pressure rise
The processes are continuous and simultaneous, each taking place in its own part of the engine
The four processes happen one after another in the same chamber, as in the piston engine, but much faster
Combustion takes place at constant volume, whereas the piston engine burns at constant pressure
samples.explanation: A gas turbine works on the Brayton (constant-pressure) cycle. The intake, compressor, combustion chamber, turbine and exhaust each perform one process, all at once and continuously, so the engine produces power without the intermittent strokes of a piston engine. This continuous flow is why it can handle such large air mass flows.
whyWrong: The compressor provides most of the pressure rise; ram compression only helps at speed (a ramjet is the exception).
That is the intermittent piston-engine cycle; the gas turbine has a separate component for each process.
Reversed: the gas turbine burns at roughly constant pressure (Brayton), the piston engine at constant volume (Otto).
samples.examTip: 'Continuous' and 'constant pressure' go with the gas turbine; 'intermittent' and 'constant volume' with the piston engine.

samples.prompt: A turbofan has a total intake mass flow of 630 kg/s and a bypass ratio of 6:1. What is the mass flow through the core (gas generator)?
options: 90 kg/s
126 kg/s
540 kg/s
105 kg/s
samples.explanation: Bypass ratio = bypass (cold) mass flow ÷ core (hot) mass flow. Total = core + 6 × core = 7 × core, so core = 630 ÷ 7 = 90 kg/s and the bypass flow is 6 × 90 = 540 kg/s.
whyWrong: Divided by 5, confusing the ratio with (bypass ratio − 1).
Gave the bypass (cold) flow, which is six times the core flow.
Divided the total flow by the bypass ratio; the total is core × (1 + bypass ratio), so divide by 7.
samples.examTip: Write total = core (1 + BPR) before dividing; it avoids the divide-by-BPR slip.

samples.prompt: Why is a high-bypass turbofan more efficient than a turbojet for a subsonic airliner?
options: It gives a small mass of air a large velocity increase, which is the most efficient way to make thrust
It gives a large mass of air a small velocity increase, so less kinetic energy is wasted in the jet
Its core runs at a higher turbine temperature, so all of its thrust comes from the hot jet
The bypass air is burnt in the jet pipe, adding thrust without extra compressor work
samples.explanation: Thrust depends on mass flow × velocity change, but the energy wasted in the jet depends on the velocity change squared. Accelerating a large mass slightly gives the same thrust with a jet velocity much closer to the flight speed, so propulsive efficiency is higher, fuel burn and noise are lower. At subsonic speeds this outweighs the larger fan's weight and drag.
whyWrong: Reversed: a large velocity increase leaves a fast jet carrying away a lot of wasted kinetic energy.
Most of a high-bypass engine's thrust comes from the fan (cold) stream, not the hot jet.
Bypass air is not burnt in a civil turbofan; burning in the jet pipe is reheat, used on military jets.
samples.examTip: Propulsive efficiency rises as jet velocity approaches flight speed.

samples.prompt: An engine flies at a TAS of 250 m/s with a mean jet velocity of 350 m/s. Using ηp = 2V ÷ (V + Vj), what is its propulsive efficiency?
samples.explanation: ηp = 2V ÷ (V + Vj) = (2 × 250) ÷ (250 + 350) = 500 ÷ 600 = 0.833, about 83%. A turbojet with a jet velocity of 600 m/s at the same speed would manage only 500 ÷ 850 ≈ 59%, which shows why high-bypass engines are used on airliners.
whyWrong: Left out the factor 2 in the numerator: V ÷ (V + Vj).
Gave 1 − V ÷ Vj, the fraction of jet velocity that is the velocity increase.
Used V ÷ Vj, the velocity ratio, instead of the propulsive efficiency formula.
samples.examTip: Sense check: the answer must be below 100%, and closer to 100% the nearer Vj is to V.

samples.prompt: In a high bypass engine with a pitot intake, when the aircraft is stationary and the engine is running, the pressure within the intake is:
options: Equal to ambient pressure
Greater than ambient pressure
Less than ambient pressure
Equal to compressor discharge pressure
samples.explanation: When the engine is running on a stationary aircraft, the high velocity airflow through the intake causes the pressure within the intake to be below ambient pressure. Option A is incorrect because ram pressure recovery has not yet occurred. Option B is incorrect because pressure rises only when the aircraft moves forward. Option D is incorrect as compressor discharge pressure is much higher than intake pressure.

samples.prompt: The simplest form of intake used in gas turbine engines is the:
options: S-duct intake
Convergent-divergent intake
Pitot type intake
Variable geometry intake
samples.explanation: The pitot type intake is described as the simplest form of intake with a single entrance circular cross-section. Option A is incorrect as S-duct is a shaped variant for tailcone mounted engines. Option B is incorrect as convergent-divergent intakes are used for supersonic aircraft. Option D is incorrect as variable geometry intakes are more complex.

samples.prompt: In a subsonic pitot-type intake, how do the velocity and static pressure of the air change between the intake lip and the compressor face?
options: Velocity increases and static pressure decreases, because the duct is convergent
Both stay constant, because the intake only guides the air
Both velocity and static pressure increase, because of ram compression
Velocity decreases and static pressure increases, because the duct is divergent
samples.explanation: A subsonic intake is a divergent duct (diffuser). Subsonic air slowing in a widening passage converts kinetic energy into a rise in static pressure. This delivers air to the compressor at a suitable subsonic speed and with a pressure rise (ram recovery) that helps the compressor at high flight speeds.
whyWrong: A convergent duct accelerates subsonic air, which is what the intake must avoid.
The intake is shaped as a diffuser, so it deliberately changes both.
Velocity and static pressure cannot both rise in a passive duct; energy is only exchanged between them.
samples.examTip: Subsonic flow: divergent slows it, convergent speeds it up. Supersonic flow does the opposite.

samples.prompt: During a ground run at high power with a strong tailwind, the engine starts to make loud bangs and the EGT rises. What has the intake airflow most likely caused?
options: Uneven airflow at the compressor face, causing compressor stall or surge
Overheating of the fuel by hot exhaust gas blown forwards into the fuel tank vents
Fuel starvation, because the tailwind pressurises the fuel tank vents
Intake icing, because the tailwind brings in colder air
samples.explanation: An intake is designed for air arriving from ahead. A strong tailwind or crosswind makes the air separate from the lip and arrive unevenly, so some compressor blades see large angles of attack and stall. Bangs, rising EGT and fluctuating rpm are the signs; reduce power and turn the aircraft into wind for ground runs.
whyWrong: Fuel temperature is not affected this way, and it would not cause bangs with a rising EGT.
Tank venting has nothing to do with the bangs and EGT rise of a stall.
Icing needs moisture and freezing temperatures, not a tailwind.
samples.examTip: Engine ground runs are done into wind for this reason.

samples.prompt: How does a supersonic intake slow the air to a subsonic speed before it reaches the compressor?
options: Through oblique shocks and a final weak normal shock, positioned by a variable ramp or cone
By bleeding off most of the air so that the remainder slows naturally
By one strong normal shock at the compressor face, which slows the air in a single step with little loss
By a simple divergent duct, as in a subsonic intake
samples.explanation: Supersonic air can be slowed efficiently only through shocks. A ramp or centre-body (cone) produces one or more oblique shocks that slow the flow with small losses, and a final weak normal shock brings it to subsonic speed, after which a divergent section slows it further. Variable geometry keeps the shocks positioned correctly as Mach number changes.
whyWrong: Bleeding is used to control the shock position and boundary layer, not to slow the main flow.
A strong normal shock at the face gives large pressure losses and very distorted flow into the compressor.
Supersonic air in a divergent duct would accelerate, not slow down.
samples.examTip: Weak shocks lose less pressure; the design aim is several weak shocks rather than one strong one.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Compressors
topics: The Pros and Cons of the Centrifugal Compressor
The Principles of the Centrifugal Flow Compressor
The Principles of the Axial Flow Compressor
Maintaining the Axial Velocity of the Airflow

samples.prompt: In a centrifugal compressor, approximately what percentage of the total pressure rise occurs in the impeller?
samples.explanation: In a centrifugal compressor about half of the pressure rise occurs in the impeller and the other half in the diffuser, where the high-velocity air is slowed and its kinetic energy converted to pressure.

samples.prompt: Which comparison of axial and centrifugal compressors is correct?
options: The centrifugal compressor gives a higher overall pressure ratio for a given frontal area and is used on most large airliners
The axial compressor gives a higher pressure ratio per stage and is less sensitive to damage
The centrifugal compressor needs many more stages than the axial to reach the same pressure ratio
Axial: higher overall pressure ratio and smaller frontal area. Centrifugal: more robust and simpler
samples.explanation: A centrifugal stage achieves a large pressure rise and is robust and cheap, but has a large frontal area and is hard to stage more than twice. An axial compressor rises only a little per stage, but many stages in line give high overall pressure ratios and efficiency with a small frontal area, so it is used for large engines. Small turboprops and turboshafts often combine axial stages with a final centrifugal stage.
whyWrong: Large airliners use axial compressors; the centrifugal type's diameter grows rapidly with mass flow.
Reversed: a centrifugal stage achieves a higher pressure ratio, while axial blades are more delicate.
Reversed: one or two centrifugal stages do the work of several axial stages.
samples.examTip: 'Per stage' favours the centrifugal; 'overall' and 'frontal area' favour the axial.

samples.prompt: In an axial-flow compressor, why does the annulus area decrease from the front to the rear of the compressor?
options: To keep the axial velocity of the air roughly constant as its density increases through the stages
To increase the angle of attack on the rear blades and so delay stall
To accelerate the air so it enters the combustion chamber at high speed
To reduce the weight of the rear stages, which run hottest
samples.explanation: Each stage raises the pressure and density of the air. If the passage stayed the same size, the denser air would slow down and the blade angles of attack would be wrong. Reducing the annulus area towards the rear keeps the axial velocity roughly constant so every stage works near its design angle of attack.
whyWrong: Higher angles of attack would encourage stall, not delay it.
The air must reach the combustion chamber slowly enough for the flame to be stable, not fast.
Weight is a by-product; the area is set by the airflow requirement.
samples.examTip: Mass flow = density × area × velocity: if density rises and velocity is to stay constant, area must fall.

samples.prompt: During a rapid throttle advance at high altitude, a turbofan gives a loud bang, the EGT rises sharply and N1 fluctuates. What has happened and what should the pilot do first?
options: A flameout; select continuous ignition and advance the thrust lever to full power to relight it
A compressor surge; retard the thrust lever until it clears, then re-advance slowly
Normal acceleration noise; continue the throttle advance
A turbine overspeed; shut the engine down immediately in all cases
samples.explanation: Too rapid an acceleration means more fuel than the compressor can take, raising combustion pressure; at high altitude this is more likely. The airflow through the compressor breaks down and may reverse (surge): loud bangs, EGT rising, rpm fluctuating, possibly flames from the intake or exhaust. Reducing the fuel flow restores the airflow; then the engine is accelerated slowly within limits.
whyWrong: A flameout causes a fall in EGT, not a rise; advancing the thrust lever further would worsen a surge.
Bangs with rising EGT and unstable rpm are never normal.
Shutdown may become necessary if the surge persists or limits are exceeded, but the first step is to reduce power.
samples.examTip: EGT rising points to surge; EGT falling points to flameout.

samples.prompt: Why are bleed valves opened in the compressor, or the variable stator vanes closed, at low engine speeds?
options: To keep the front-stage angle of attack low when the rear stages cannot pass all the air
To supply extra bleed air to the air-conditioning packs at idle
To cool the rear compressor stages, which run hot at low rpm because the airflow through them is small
To increase the pressure ratio at low rpm and so improve idle thrust
samples.explanation: A compressor is designed for its high-rpm condition. At low rpm the density rise is smaller, so the rear stages cannot pass all the air the front stages deliver. Axial velocity at the front falls, and the front blades' angle of attack rises towards stall. Opening bleed valves lets air out between stages, and closing the variable stators reduces the angle at which air meets the rotor blades, so the front stages stay unstalled.
whyWrong: Handling bleed valves dump air overboard or into the bypass duct; they do not feed the packs.
The rear stages are not overheating at low rpm; the problem is aerodynamic mismatch.
Dumping air or closing vanes reduces the pressure ratio; their purpose is stall protection, not idle thrust.
samples.examTip: Low rpm + front stages + high angle of attack is the chain behind every stall-protection device.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Combustion Chambers
topics: The Task of the Combustion Chamber

samples.prompt: Modern materials allow a gas temperature initially in the combustion chamber of:
options: 2000°C plus
samples.explanation: Modern materials allow gas temperatures of about 2000°C plus in the primary zone of the combustion chamber. Before the gas leaves the chamber, dilution air reduces it to about 1000-1500°C to protect the nozzle guide vanes and turbine.

samples.prompt: Which statement about annular combustion chambers is correct?
options: They use space best and give an even outlet temperature, but are harder to maintain
They need interconnecting tubes to carry the flame from one can to the next during the start
They consist of separate cans, each with its own igniter and flame tube
They are heavier and longer than can-type systems for the same airflow
samples.explanation: An annular chamber is one ring-shaped flame tube round the engine axis. It uses the space best, has the smallest pressure loss and gives an even temperature to the turbine, which is why modern engines use it. Its drawback is maintenance: the liner is a single unit and the engine must usually be split to reach it.
whyWrong: Interconnectors are needed in multiple-can and can-annular systems, not in a single annular chamber.
Separate cans describe the multiple-can type; an annular chamber is a single ring.
The annular chamber is the shortest and lightest arrangement.
samples.examTip: Interconnectors and cans go together; annular has neither.

samples.prompt: How is the air from the compressor divided inside a gas turbine combustion chamber?
options: All of it passes through the swirl vanes and burns at the chemically correct ratio
Half is burnt and half is ducted straight to the exhaust nozzle
Almost all of it is burnt with the fuel to give the highest possible temperature at the turbine entry
About a fifth burns with the fuel; the rest cools the liner and dilutes the gas for the turbine
samples.explanation: Only about a fifth of the air enters the primary zone, where it mixes with fuel at a ratio that will burn well. The rest enters through holes in the flame tube to complete combustion, form a cooling film on the liner, and dilute the hot gas to a temperature the turbine can tolerate. The overall air/fuel ratio is therefore very weak.
whyWrong: Only the primary air passes the swirl vanes; the overall air/fuel ratio is very weak.
Air for the jet pipe is not separated in the combustion chamber; all the air passes through the turbine.
If all the air were burnt at a correct ratio, the gas would be far too hot for the turbine.
samples.examTip: 'Dilution' means bringing the gas temperature down for the turbine.

samples.prompt: In a multiple-can combustion system only two cans contain igniters. How do the others light during a start?
options: Each can has its own glow plug, used only during starting
Each can lights from the heat of the compressor delivery air
Interconnecting (cross-fire) tubes carry the flame from the lit cans to the others
The fuel is sprayed hotter into the unlit cans so it self-ignites
samples.explanation: The cans are linked by short interconnecting tubes. When the igniters light the two cans, the pressure difference pushes flame through the tubes and lights the next can, and so on around the engine. The tubes also equalise pressure between cans in operation.
whyWrong: The premise is that only two cans have igniters; glow plugs are a diesel device.
Compressor delivery air is hot, but nowhere near hot enough to ignite the fuel on its own during a start.
Fuel is not preheated to self-ignition; it would be dangerous and impractical.
samples.examTip: Expect 'interconnector' in can and can-annular questions only.

samples.prompt: Why does a combustion chamber need swirl vanes and a recirculation zone in its primary zone?
options: To separate the fuel from the air until the turbine inlet
To create the pressure rise that the compressor cannot provide
To speed the air up so the fuel leaves the chamber before it can burn the liner
The air arrives far faster than the flame can burn, so a slow, recirculating zone is needed to hold the flame
samples.explanation: Air leaves the compressor at a speed far above the flame speed of kerosene. The diffuser slows it, and swirl vanes and flow reversal create a region of low axial velocity and strong recirculation in the primary zone. The flame anchors there, and hot gas recirculates to ignite the incoming mixture continuously.
whyWrong: The fuel must be mixed with air, not kept apart.
Pressure falls slightly through the combustor; it does not rise there.
Speeding the air up would blow the flame out.
samples.examTip: Combustion chamber pressure falls slightly (a few per cent); it never rises.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - The Turbine Assembly
topics: The Task of the Turbine Assembly

samples.prompt: The energy available in the gases flowing through the turbine takes the form of:
options: Heat energy and potential energy only
Kinetic energy and potential energy only
Heat energy, potential energy, and kinetic energy
Mechanical energy and heat energy only
samples.explanation: The gas reaching the turbine carries heat energy, potential (pressure) energy and kinetic (velocity) energy, and the turbine draws on all three.

samples.prompt: What is creep in a turbine blade?
options: A sudden fracture caused by a single overspeed
Slow, permanent stretching under centrifugal load at high temperature
Erosion of the blade leading edge by sand and dust
Vibration of the blade at its natural frequency, which slowly loosens it in its fir-tree root
samples.explanation: Creep is time-dependent plastic deformation of a material under steady stress at high temperature. Turbine blades carry huge centrifugal loads at temperatures close to their material limits, so they slowly lengthen. Blade life is consumed fastest at the highest temperatures, which is why every exceedance of the TGT limit matters and why reduced take-off thrust prolongs engine life.
whyWrong: A single overload fracture is not creep; creep is gradual and time-dependent.
Erosion is surface damage from particles, a different mechanism.
Resonant vibration causes fatigue, a different failure mode.
samples.examTip: Creep = heat + stress + time.

samples.prompt: What is the function of the nozzle guide vanes ahead of each turbine stage?
options: To slow the gas and raise its pressure before the rotor
To mix cooling air with the gas to reduce its temperature
To accelerate the gas and turn it onto the rotor blades at the correct angle
To straighten the gas flow so it leaves the engine axially
samples.explanation: The nozzle guide vanes form convergent passages. They convert some of the gas's pressure and heat energy into velocity and direct it onto the rotor blades at the best angle. The NGVs of the first stage see the highest gas temperature in the engine and are usually internally cooled.
whyWrong: Slowing the gas to raise pressure is what a compressor stator or diffuser does; turbine nozzles do the opposite.
The vanes may be internally cooled, but mixing in dilution air is the combustor's job.
Straightening the flow is the job of the exhaust struts behind the last turbine stage.
samples.examTip: Compressor stators slow the air (diverge); turbine nozzles speed the gas (converge).

samples.prompt: How are the first-stage turbine blades of a modern turbofan kept within their temperature limits when the gas entering the turbine is hotter than the melting point of the blade alloy?
options: Fan air is ducted onto the outer surface of the turbine casing only
Compressor air flows through internal passages and leaves through holes to form a cooling film
Oil from the turbine bearings is sprayed onto the blade roots
Fuel is passed through the hollow blades to absorb their heat before it is sent on to the burners for combustion
samples.explanation: Air bled from the HP compressor, which is cool compared with the gas, flows through passages inside the hollow blades and leaves through rows of small holes. It forms a thin insulating film over the surface (film cooling). Thermal barrier coatings and single-crystal alloys add to the protection.
whyWrong: Casing cooling helps tip clearance control but does not cool the blades themselves.
Bearing oil cools the bearings; it is kept well away from the gas path.
Fuel is never routed through turbine blades; it would decompose and the fire risk is extreme.
samples.examTip: The cooling air comes from the compressor; that is a cost to engine efficiency.

samples.prompt: In an impulse-reaction turbine blade, how does the design typically change from root to tip?
options: The root works mainly by impulse and the tip mainly by reaction, so the blade is twisted along its length
The root works by reaction and the tip by impulse, so the blade is thicker at the tip
The blade is the same section along its length because the gas velocity is uniform
The tip is cut off square to reduce reaction and increase impulse
samples.explanation: Blade speed increases from root to tip, while the gas leaving the nozzle guide vanes has a fairly uniform velocity. To give each section an equal share of the work, the root is shaped mainly as an impulse section and the tip mainly as a reaction (aerofoil) section, so the blade is twisted. Most aero-engine turbines are of this impulse-reaction type.
whyWrong: Reversed: impulse at the root, reaction at the tip.
Blade speed rises with radius, so the gas angles change and the section must change with them.
Tip shape does not decide the impulse/reaction split; it is set by the blade and nozzle angles along the span.
samples.examTip: Impulse: pressure drop in the nozzles. Reaction: pressure drop shared with the blades.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - The Exhaust System
topics: Gas Parameter Changes and Exhaust Mach Numbers
The Low Ratio Bypass Engine Exhaust System
The High Ratio Bypass Engine Exhaust System

samples.prompt: The temperature of gases entering the exhaust system in a turbojet engine without reheat is typically between:
samples.explanation: Without reheat, gases enter the exhaust system at about 550°C to 850°C. With afterburning (reheat) the temperature can rise to around 1500°C.

samples.prompt: The fuselage of an aircraft with the exhaust system running through it is protected from high temperatures by:
options: Only using heat insulation materials
Only allowing a clearance for air circulation
Both allowing a clearance for air circulation and insulating the jet pipe with fibrous material sandwiched between thin layers of stainless steel
Using a water cooling system around the jet pipe
samples.explanation: The fuselage is protected in two ways: a clearance between the jet pipe and the aircraft skin lets cooling air circulate, and the jet pipe is insulated with fibrous material sandwiched between thin layers of stainless steel.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of the exhaust cone and support struts behind the last turbine stage?
options: To remove swirl and give a smooth passage from the turbine to the jet pipe
To slow the turbine down when the thrust levers are retarded
To create the choked condition that gives pressure thrust
To mix the cold bypass air into the hot stream before it reaches the turbine, cooling the blades
samples.explanation: Gas leaves the last turbine stage with some residual swirl and around the hub of the turbine disc. The exhaust cone gives a smooth, gradually widening annulus that avoids turbulence behind the disc, and the struts remove the swirl so the gas leaves axially. Both reduce losses and so improve thrust.
whyWrong: The cone and struts are static; they cannot brake the turbine.
Choking happens at the propelling nozzle, not at the exhaust cone.
Mixing occurs downstream of the turbine, in the exhaust mixer if one is fitted; it is not the cone's purpose.
samples.examTip: 'Straighten the flow' is the exhaust; 'accelerate and turn' is the turbine nozzle.

samples.prompt: The convergent propelling nozzle of a turbojet becomes choked at high power. What does this mean, and how does it affect thrust?
options: The gas reaches the speed of sound and then keeps accelerating to supersonic speed in the convergent section
The exit pressure falls below ambient, so the nozzle produces a thrust loss
Mach 1 is reached at the exit, the exit pressure rises above ambient, and pressure thrust is added
The gas stops flowing because the nozzle is blocked, so thrust falls to zero
samples.explanation: When the nozzle pressure ratio is high enough, the gas reaches Mach 1 at the exit and cannot accelerate further in a convergent nozzle. The exit pressure then stays above ambient, and the pressure difference across the exit area adds pressure thrust: Fn = ṁ (Vj − V) + A (pe − p0).
whyWrong: In a convergent nozzle the gas cannot exceed Mach 1; supersonic acceleration needs a divergent section.
A choked convergent nozzle has an exit pressure above, not below, ambient.
'Choked' means the flow has reached Mach 1 at the throat; flow continues at its maximum rate.
samples.examTip: Pressure thrust exists only when the exit pressure is above ambient, that is when the nozzle is choked.

samples.prompt: Jet mixing noise rises very steeply with the jet's velocity. Which design change reduces it most on a civil engine?
options: A higher turbine entry temperature, giving a faster but smaller jet
Removing the acoustic lining from the bypass duct
Changing to a convergent-divergent nozzle to accelerate the jet further
A higher bypass ratio, giving a larger, slower jet for the same thrust
samples.explanation: Jet mixing noise rises roughly with the eighth power of jet velocity, so even a modest reduction in jet speed gives a large noise reduction. High-bypass engines produce their thrust with a large, slow jet, and are much quieter. Lobed mixers and chevron nozzles help further by speeding up mixing, and acoustic linings absorb fan noise.
whyWrong: A faster jet is noisier: mixing noise rises roughly with the eighth power of jet velocity.
Acoustic linings absorb fan and compressor noise; removing them makes the engine louder.
A higher jet velocity increases noise, not reduces it.
samples.examTip: Any change that slows the jet for the same thrust reduces noise.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Lubrication
topics: The Pressure Relief Valve Lubrication System

samples.prompt: In a gas turbine engine, the primary reason for using synthetic oil instead of mineral oil is:
options: Synthetic oil is cheaper to produce
Synthetic oil has a lower viscosity at all temperatures
Mineral oil burns, scums, and oxidizes under high temperatures and speeds
Mineral oil cannot be filtered effectively
samples.explanation: Under the high temperatures and speeds of a gas turbine, mineral oils burn, form scum and oxidise. Synthetic oils were developed to resist this; they are more expensive, not cheaper.

samples.prompt: What is the purpose of a magnetic chip detector in a gas turbine oil system?
options: To collect ferrous particles from the oil and give early warning of bearing or gear wear
To remove water from the oil before it reaches the bearings
To measure the oil pressure in the bearing chambers
To detect fuel leaking into the oil
samples.explanation: Chip detectors are magnetic plugs in the scavenge lines. Steel particles shed by a failing bearing or gear collect on them. Inspecting the plug, or a cockpit warning from an electrical detector, lets a failure be found before it becomes serious.
whyWrong: Water is not attracted by a magnet; the detector catches steel particles.
Oil pressure is measured by a transmitter in the pressure line, not by the chip detector.
A fuel leak into the oil shows as rising oil quantity, not on the chip detector.
samples.examTip: Scavenge lines carry oil from the bearings, so that is where chip detectors are fitted.

samples.prompt: Which description of gas turbine lubrication is correct for most engines?
options: The bearing chambers are sealed by flooding them completely with oil, so no air can enter them at all
A total-loss system, in which the oil is burnt with the fuel
A self-contained recirculatory system with synthetic oil and scavenge pumps for each bearing chamber
A system using mineral oil, which withstands higher temperatures than synthetic oil
samples.explanation: A typical gas turbine uses a recirculatory dry-sump system: a pressure pump feeds the bearings and gears, several scavenge pumps return the oil from each bearing chamber to the tank through filters and coolers. Synthetic oil copes with the high temperatures, and the chambers are sealed by pressurised air through labyrinth seals.
whyWrong: Bearing chambers are sealed by air-pressurised labyrinth or carbon seals; flooding would overheat and churn the oil.
Total-loss lubrication is used only on a few short-life engines, such as some missile engines.
Synthetic oils are used precisely because they work at the higher temperatures found in gas turbines.
samples.examTip: Gas turbines use far less oil than piston engines because no oil is burnt in the cylinders.

samples.prompt: In many turbofans the engine oil is cooled by the fuel in a fuel-cooled oil cooler. What is the second benefit of this arrangement?
options: The oil is thinned by mixing with fuel, which helps cold starts
The fuel is warmed, which helps prevent ice crystals blocking the fuel filter
The heat is removed from the fuel tanks, preventing vapour formation
The fuel is cooled, which raises its density and the engine's thrust
samples.explanation: The fuel-cooled oil cooler is a heat exchanger: hot oil gives up its heat to the cold fuel on its way to the burners. The oil is cooled, and the fuel is warmed above the temperature at which ice crystals from dissolved water could block the filter. Some engines add an air-cooled oil cooler as well.
whyWrong: Fuel and oil never mix in a serviceable cooler; they are separated by the heat exchanger walls.
The heat goes into the fuel heading for the engine, not back into the tanks (unless a return system is fitted).
The fuel gains heat from the oil; it is warmed, not cooled.
samples.examTip: One heat exchanger, two benefits: cool oil, warm fuel.

samples.prompt: During cruise, a pilot notices the engine oil quantity indication slowly rising while all other oil indications are normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Fuel leaking into the oil in the fuel-cooled oil cooler, where fuel pressure is higher
Oil returning from the bearing chambers faster than the pressure pump delivers it
Normal thermal expansion of the oil as the engine warms up during the first hours of cruise
A blocked oil filter causing oil to collect in the tank
samples.explanation: Inside the fuel-cooled oil cooler the fuel is at a higher pressure than the oil, so a leak sends fuel into the oil, not the reverse. The oil quantity rises and the oil is diluted, which reduces its lubricating ability and can be a fire risk. The abnormal checklist must be followed.
whyWrong: The scavenge pumps already return more volume than the pressure pump delivers; that does not create extra oil.
The oil reaches a stable temperature soon after start; a continuing rise in cruise is not expansion.
A blocked filter opens its bypass and gives a warning; it does not increase the quantity.
samples.examTip: Fuel side is higher pressure: a leaking FCOC adds fuel to the oil.

samples.prompt: In a gas turbine engine, thrust is produced primarily in accordance with:
options: Newton's first law of motion
Newton's second law of motion
Newton's third law of motion
Bernoulli's principle
samples.explanation: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The engine accelerates air backwards, and the reaction force pushes the aircraft forward. Newton's first law deals with inertia, second law with F=ma, and Bernoulli's principle relates to pressure and velocity in fluids.

samples.prompt: A turbojet flies at 200 m/s TAS with an air mass flow of 80 kg/s and a jet velocity of 600 m/s. Assuming an unchoked nozzle and ignoring fuel flow, what is the net thrust?
samples.explanation: Net thrust = ṁ (Vj − V) = 80 kg/s × (600 − 200) m/s = 80 × 400 = 32,000 N = 32.0 kN. Gross thrust is 80 × 600 = 48,000 N, and the ram drag 80 × 200 = 16,000 N is the momentum the engine must give the air just to bring it up to flight speed.
whyWrong: Gave the gross thrust, mass flow × jet velocity, and left out the ram drag.
Added the ram drag (80 × 200) instead of subtracting it.
Gave the ram drag alone, mass flow × flight speed.
samples.examTip: On the ground (V = 0) gross and net thrust are equal; in flight always subtract ṁV.

samples.prompt: A turbojet in level flight at 250 m/s TAS has an air mass flow of 83 kg/s and a jet velocity of 650 m/s. The nozzle is unchoked and the fuel mass flow can be ignored. What is the net thrust?
samples.explanation: Formula: Fn = ṁ (Vj − V) for each stream (net thrust = gross thrust − ram drag); 1 kt = 0.5144 m/s. Net thrust = gross thrust − ram drag = ṁ × Vj − ṁ × V = ṁ (Vj − V). Fn = 83 kg/s × (650 − 250) m/s = 83 × 400 = 33,200 N ≈ 33.2 kN. The ram drag (83 × 250 = 20,750 N) is the momentum the engine must give the intake air just to bring it up to flight speed.
whyWrong: Ignored the ram drag and gave the gross thrust, mass flow × jet velocity: gives 54.0 kN.
Added the ram drag instead of subtracting it; the intake momentum opposes the jet momentum: gives 74.7 kN.
Gave the ram drag alone, mass flow × flight speed, instead of the net thrust: gives 20.8 kN.
samples.examTip: Convert any speed in knots to m/s before subtracting, and apply ram drag to every stream that enters the intake.

samples.prompt: A turbojet in level flight at 80 m/s TAS has an air mass flow of 45 kg/s and a jet velocity of 640 m/s. The nozzle is unchoked and the fuel mass flow can be ignored. What is the net thrust?
options: 3.6 kN
samples.explanation: Formula: Fn = ṁ (Vj − V) for each stream (net thrust = gross thrust − ram drag); 1 kt = 0.5144 m/s. Net thrust = gross thrust − ram drag = ṁ × Vj − ṁ × V = ṁ (Vj − V). Fn = 45 kg/s × (640 − 80) m/s = 45 × 560 = 25,200 N ≈ 25.2 kN. The ram drag (45 × 80 = 3,600 N) is the momentum the engine must give the intake air just to bring it up to flight speed.
whyWrong: Ignored the ram drag and gave the gross thrust, mass flow × jet velocity: gives 28.8 kN.
Gave the ram drag alone, mass flow × flight speed, instead of the net thrust: gives 3.6 kN.
Added the ram drag instead of subtracting it; the intake momentum opposes the jet momentum: gives 32.4 kN.
samples.examTip: Convert any speed in knots to m/s before subtracting, and apply ram drag to every stream that enters the intake.

samples.prompt: How does the net thrust of a turbojet at a fixed rpm change as airspeed increases from zero at constant altitude?
options: It falls at first as ram drag grows, then partly recovers as ram compression raises mass flow
It falls steadily to zero at the speed of sound, where the intake can pass no more air
It stays constant, because thrust depends only on rpm
It rises steadily, because the intake rams more air into the engine
samples.explanation: Net thrust = ṁ (Vj − V). As V rises, the velocity change (Vj − V) falls, so thrust falls. At higher speeds the ram pressure rise in the intake increases the air density and mass flow, which partly offsets the loss. The result is a dip followed by a partial recovery.
whyWrong: Ram recovery offsets part of the loss; thrust does not fall steadily to zero at Mach 1.
Thrust depends on mass flow and velocity change, both of which change with airspeed.
The ram drag effect dominates at first, so net thrust initially falls.
samples.examTip: Separate the two effects: ram drag (speed) and ram recovery (more mass flow).

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Reverse Thrust
topics: Ground Manoeuvring — Reverse Thrust is Not Normally Used

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic types of thrust reversal systems?
options: Clamshell Doors
Bucket Doors (External Doors)
Variable Inlet Guide Vanes
Blocker Doors
samples.explanation: The three basic types are Clamshell Doors, Bucket Doors, and Blocker Doors. Variable Inlet Guide Vanes are not a reverse thrust system; they are used for compressor airflow control.

samples.prompt: Just after lift-off, a reverse thrust lever is accidentally raised. Which design feature should stop the reverser from deploying?
options: The fuel control unit, which shuts off fuel if reverse is selected
The fan speed governor, which prevents any reverse selection while N1 is above idle
An air/ground interlock that allows deployment only with weight on the wheels
A thermal switch that prevents deployment when the EGT is high
samples.explanation: Reversers on most airliners are prevented from deploying unless the aircraft is on the ground: sensing comes from weight-on-wheels switches, radio altimeter or wheel spin-up logic. A mechanical interlock also stops the reverse levers being raised unless the forward thrust levers are at idle.
whyWrong: Shutting down an engine on reverse selection would be unsafe; the reverser simply does not deploy.
Reverse thrust levers can normally only be raised with the forward levers at idle, but the in-flight protection is the air/ground logic.
EGT plays no part in reverser deployment logic.
samples.examTip: 'Weight on wheels' answers most in-flight reverser questions.

samples.prompt: On a high-bypass turbofan, how is reverse thrust normally produced?
options: Clamshell doors close behind the hot jet nozzle, reversing only the core flow
Blocker doors close the bypass duct and divert the fan air outwards and forwards through cascade vanes
The fan blades change pitch to a negative angle
The engine is rotated on its pylon to point the exhaust forwards
samples.explanation: Most of a high-bypass engine's thrust comes from the fan stream, so the reverser works there. A translating sleeve moves aft, blocker doors close the bypass duct, and the fan air leaves through cascade vanes that turn it outwards and forwards. The hot core flow usually continues rearwards.
whyWrong: Clamshell or bucket reversers on the hot stream are typical of low-bypass engines; on a high-bypass engine most thrust is in the fan stream.
Variable-pitch fans have been studied but are not used on current airliners.
Engines are fixed to the pylon; nothing rotates the whole engine.
samples.examTip: Cascade = cold stream; clamshell/bucket = hot stream.

samples.prompt: Why is reverse thrust normally reduced to idle reverse or cancelled below a speed specified in the flight manual during the landing roll?
options: To prevent the reversed exhaust and debris being re-ingested, which can cause compressor stall and damage
To save fuel during the taxi to the gate
Because reverse thrust becomes more effective at low speed and could make the aircraft roll backwards
Because the cascade vanes overheat at low speed
samples.explanation: At low speed, the forward-directed efflux is no longer swept back by the airflow and can reach the intake. Hot gas and runway debris ingested into the engine can cause compressor stall, overheating and foreign object damage. The flight manual therefore sets a speed below which reverse is reduced to idle and then stowed.
whyWrong: Fuel saving is not the reason; the risk to the engine is.
Reverse thrust is most effective at high speed, which is why it is selected early in the landing roll.
The vanes are not overheated at low speed; the danger is re-ingestion.
samples.examTip: Reverse is most effective, and safest, at high speed early in the landing roll.

samples.prompt: Why does a reverser produce less reverse thrust than the engine's forward thrust at the same rpm?
options: Reverse thrust only uses the hot stream, which gives little thrust
The engine's fuel control limits rpm to idle whenever the reverser is deployed
The air passes through the engine in the opposite direction when the reverser is deployed
The efflux is turned only partly forwards, so only part of its momentum acts rearwards
samples.explanation: The reverser deflects the jet outwards and forwards at an angle (often around 45°) to keep it clear of the aircraft and intake. Only the forward component of the deflected flow produces retarding force, so reverse thrust is a fraction of forward thrust. On high-bypass engines the hot core stream may still give a little forward thrust.
whyWrong: High-bypass reversers deflect the fan stream, not just the hot stream.
Reverse rpm is limited to less than take-off rpm, but even at equal rpm the reverse thrust is smaller.
Air always flows through the engine from front to back; only the exit flow is deflected.
samples.examTip: Reverse is a deceleration aid; braking calculations normally assume a certain contribution or none at all.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Gearboxes and Accessory Drives
topics: Allowing for Expansion of the Compressor Shaft

samples.prompt: The drive for the accessory unit is usually taken from which shaft?
options: Low pressure compressor shaft
High pressure compressor shaft
Low pressure turbine shaft
High pressure turbine shaft
samples.explanation: The accessory drive is usually taken from the high pressure compressor shaft, via an internal gearbox and radial driveshaft, to the external gearbox.

samples.prompt: In a stub shaft drive system, how is the stub shaft held in correct position?
options: By the compressor shaft itself
By the location bearing
By the bevel gear
By the idler gear
samples.explanation: In a stub shaft drive, the compressor shaft is free to move axially, while the stub shaft carrying the bevel gear is held in the correct position by the location bearing.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT normally mounted on or driven by a turbofan's accessory gearbox?
options: The fan
The generator (or integrated drive generator)
The engine-driven hydraulic pump
The fuel pump
samples.explanation: The accessory gearbox drives the engine's own systems (fuel pumps, oil pumps, the starter) and the aircraft's systems (hydraulic pumps, generators). The fan is driven directly by the low-pressure turbine through the LP shaft, or through a power gearbox on a geared turbofan, not by the accessory gearbox.
whyWrong: The generator or IDG is mounted on the gearbox.
The engine-driven hydraulic pump is mounted on the gearbox.
The HP fuel pump is a typical gearbox accessory.
samples.examTip: Anything that makes thrust is on a main shaft; accessories are on the gearbox.

samples.prompt: Why is an AC generator driven through a constant-speed drive (or built into an integrated drive generator) on a turbofan?
options: To increase the generator's output voltage in step with engine speed as the engine accelerates
To hold the generator at constant speed as engine rpm varies, keeping the AC frequency constant
To allow the generator to be used as a starter motor
To disconnect the generator automatically when the engine is at idle
samples.explanation: The frequency of an AC generator depends on its rotational speed, but the HP spool speed varies widely between idle and take-off. A constant-speed drive (hydromechanical) between the gearbox and generator outputs a constant speed, so the generator produces a fixed frequency, typically 400 Hz.
whyWrong: Voltage is controlled by the generator control unit; the drive governs speed and so frequency.
Starting is done by a separate air turbine starter on most turbofans.
The generator is meant to supply power at all engine speeds from idle upwards.
samples.examTip: Speed governs frequency; excitation governs voltage.

samples.prompt: On a two-spool turbofan, from which spool is the external accessory gearbox normally driven, and why?
options: The LP spool, because it turns more slowly and needs no reduction gearing
The LP spool, because it turns the fan, which has the most power available
Neither: the gearbox is driven by its own small air turbine
The HP spool, because it is the spool rotated by the starter, so the fuel and oil pumps work during the start
samples.explanation: A radial (tower) drive shaft and bevel gears take power from the HP spool to the accessory gearbox. The starter is mounted on the same gearbox and turns the HP spool during the start, so the fuel pump, oil pump and other accessories are already running as the engine lights up and accelerates.
whyWrong: Speed reduction is easily done with gears; the important point is which spool the starter turns.
The LP spool is not turned by the starter, so accessories on it would be idle during the start.
The air turbine starter drives the gearbox to start the engine; in running, the HP spool drives the gearbox.
samples.examTip: Starter, fuel pump and oil pump all sit on the HP-driven gearbox.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Ignition Systems
topics: The High Energy Ignition Unit (HEIU) — Detailed Circuit Analysis

samples.prompt: The high energy ignition unit (HEIU) operates on the principle of:
options: Charging a small capacitor and discharging it across an igniter plug
Charging a very large capacitor and discharging it across an igniter plug
Using a magneto to generate high voltage directly
Using a battery to directly power the igniter plug
samples.explanation: A high energy ignition unit charges a large storage capacitor and then discharges it across the igniter plug face as a very high energy spark; no magneto is used.

samples.prompt: The output of a high energy ignition system is approximately:
options: 6 joules
3 joules
12 joules
25 joules
samples.explanation: High energy ignition units have an output of up to about 12 joules per spark, compared with about 3-6 joules for low energy (continuous) ignition.

samples.prompt: Why does a gas turbine need its ignition system only for starting (and as a precaution in some conditions), whereas a piston engine needs it continuously?
options: The gas turbine burns kerosene, which ignites itself at room temperature
The gas turbine's igniters are too weak to be used for more than a few seconds
The gas turbine's compressor delivery air is hot enough to ignite the fuel at all times, including during the start
Once lit, gas turbine combustion is continuous and self-sustaining; each piston power stroke needs a fresh spark
samples.explanation: Once the flame is established in the primary zone, it is held there continuously and lights the incoming mixture. Ignition is needed to light the engine on start or relight, and continuous ignition is selected as a precaution when the flame might be blown out, such as in heavy rain, icing or severe turbulence, and on take-off and landing on some types.
whyWrong: Kerosene does not ignite spontaneously at room temperature; it needs a strong spark to light.
Igniters can be run continuously at low energy; the limit is life, not a few seconds.
During the start the compressor air is far too cool to ignite the fuel; that is why igniters are needed.
samples.examTip: Continuous ignition protects against flame-out in heavy precipitation, icing and turbulence.

samples.prompt: A maintenance engineer is about to remove an igniter plug from a gas turbine that has just been shut down. Why must they first wait the time stated in the maintenance manual after the ignition is switched off?
options: The fuel in the combustion chamber may still be burning
The high-energy ignition unit stores a charge in its capacitor that can be lethal
The igniter tip is too hot to touch for several hours
The magneto may still be live
samples.explanation: High-energy ignition units charge a capacitor to a high voltage and discharge it through the plug. The stored energy can kill. The unit is designed to bleed this charge away after switching off, but the manual's waiting time and precautions must be observed before disconnecting any lead.
whyWrong: Combustion stops when the fuel is shut off; the danger is electrical.
The tip may be hot, but the specific waiting time is to let the capacitor discharge.
Gas turbines use capacitor discharge units, not magnetos.
samples.examTip: 'Capacitor' and 'lethal' are the key words in turbine ignition safety.

samples.prompt: Why do many turbine ignition units offer both a high-energy and a low-energy output?
options: Low energy is used for starting because the fuel ignites more easily on the ground
High energy for reliable starts and relights; low energy for continuous use, which extends igniter life
High energy is needed only for the APU; low energy is used for the main engines
High energy is used in cruise to improve fuel efficiency; low energy is used for take-off and landing
samples.explanation: A cold start or a relight in thin, cold air needs a powerful spark from a capacitor discharge unit. When ignition is left on continuously as a precaution, a lower energy output is enough to relight a disturbed flame and wears the igniter plugs and exciter much less.
whyWrong: Starting needs the strong spark, especially for a cold start or a relight at altitude.
Both outputs are features of the main engine ignition, not of the APU.
Ignition has no effect on cruise efficiency once the flame is lit.
samples.examTip: Continuous ignition is a precaution, not a combustion aid; it uses the low output.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Auxiliary Power Units and Engine Starting
topics: The Requirements of a Starting System

samples.prompt: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of an Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) on an aircraft?
options: To provide emergency thrust during engine failure
To operate aircraft systems on the ground without running the main engines
To replace the main engines during cruise flight
To provide backup power only during in-flight emergencies
samples.explanation: The APU provides electrical power and bleed air to run the aircraft systems (and start the engines) on the ground without operating the main engines. It produces no useful thrust.

samples.prompt: What is the normal sequence of events during the automatic start of a turbofan with an air turbine starter?
options: Fuel introduced, ignition on, starter engaged, starter cuts out at light-up
Ignition on, starter engaged, fuel introduced at idle N2, light-up, starter remains engaged throughout
Rotate HP spool, ignition on, fuel at the set N2, light-up, starter cut-out, accelerate to idle
Starter rotates the LP spool, fuel and ignition at the same time, starter cuts out when N1 reaches idle
samples.explanation: The starter accelerates the HP spool to give airflow through the engine. Ignition is switched on and fuel is introduced at the scheduled N2. Light-up shows as an EGT rise. The starter keeps assisting until the engine passes self-sustaining speed, then cuts out, and the engine accelerates to idle on its own.
whyWrong: Fuel before rotation would pool in the combustion chamber and give a wet or hot start.
The starter must disengage well before idle to avoid overspeeding it; it does not stay engaged.
The starter drives the HP spool, not the LP spool, and cuts out on N2.
samples.examTip: Fuel always comes after enough airflow; anything else risks a hot or wet start.

samples.prompt: During a start, the EGT rises rapidly towards its limit soon after light-up. What is the likely cause and the correct immediate action?
options: Too little fuel for the airflow; increase the fuel flow to accelerate the engine through the hot band
A hot start (too much fuel for the airflow); shut off the fuel and keep motoring to cool the engine
A failed igniter; switch on continuous ignition and continue
A normal start; the EGT always peaks at its limit during light-up
samples.explanation: A hot start comes from an over-rich condition: too much fuel or too little air, for example a weak starter, low bleed pressure or a tailwind. Shutting off the fuel stops the heat input, and continuing to motor the engine passes cool air through the turbine and removes residual fuel.
whyWrong: Increasing fuel would raise the temperature further.
A failed igniter gives no light-up at all, not a rapid EGT rise.
A normal start peaks below the start limit; approaching the limit is not normal.
samples.examTip: In every start abort, fuel off first; motoring clears fuel and heat.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the auxiliary power unit (APU) of a typical airliner is correct?
options: A turbine started by main-engine bleed air that cannot be run on the ground because of noise rules
A thrust unit used for taxiing when the main engines are shut down
A small gas turbine supplying bleed air and electrical power, normally battery-started
A piston engine that drives a hydraulic pump for the brakes
samples.explanation: The APU is a small gas turbine, normally in the tail, driving a generator and supplying compressed air through a load compressor or bleed. It is started by an electric starter from the aircraft battery and gives independence from ground power: bleed air for air conditioning and main engine starting, and AC power. Many APUs can also be used in flight within limits.
whyWrong: The APU is normally started electrically and is used mostly on the ground.
The APU exhaust produces negligible thrust; it is not a propulsion unit.
Airliner APUs are gas turbines, and their main outputs are bleed air and electrical power.
samples.examTip: APU bleed is the usual air source for main engine starts away from ground carts.

samples.prompt: During a start, the engine lights up normally but the N2 stops increasing below idle and the EGT starts to rise slowly. What type of start is this?
options: A hung start
A normal start that needs more time
A hot start
A wet start
samples.explanation: In a hung (stagnated) start the engine lights but does not accelerate to idle, usually because of insufficient starter power or bleed pressure, or a fuel scheduling fault. The engine is too slow to compress enough air, so EGT tends to rise. The start must be abandoned per the checklist before limits are exceeded.
whyWrong: The engine has failed to accelerate; waiting will only increase the EGT.
A hot start is a rapid rise of EGT towards or above its limit; here the defining feature is the stagnant rpm.
A wet start is a failure to light, with no EGT rise.
samples.examTip: Hung = rpm problem; hot = EGT problem; wet = no light-up.

samples.prompt: The two main types of gas turbine fuel in common use in civilian aircraft are:
options: JET A1 and JET B
JET A and JET B
JET A1 and JET A
AVTAG and AVGAS
samples.explanation: The two main civil turbine fuels are JET A1 (AVTUR) and JET A, both kerosene types. Wide-cut JET B (AVTAG) is rarely used in civil aviation because of its higher fire risk, and AVGAS is a piston engine fuel.

samples.prompt: What is the maximum freezing point specified for Jet A-1, and how does it compare with Jet A?
options: −47 °C; Jet A has a lower maximum freezing point of −60 °C
−40 °C; Jet A has a lower maximum freezing point of −47 °C
−47 °C; Jet A has a higher maximum freezing point of −40 °C
−58 °C; Jet A has the same freezing point
samples.explanation: Jet A-1, the international kerosene grade, has a maximum freezing point of −47 °C. Jet A, used mainly within the USA, has a maximum of −40 °C. On long cold flights the fuel temperature must be kept above the freezing point of the fuel on board, with the margin the manufacturer specifies.
whyWrong: Jet A freezes at a higher temperature than Jet A-1, not a lower one.
Swaps the two grades: Jet A-1 is the lower-freezing international grade.
−58 °C is not the specification value for either grade.
samples.examTip: Know both numbers; options often swap them.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is loaded with 12,000 litres of Jet A-1 with a specific gravity of 0.80. What is the mass of fuel loaded?
samples.explanation: Mass (kg) = volume (L) × specific gravity = 12,000 × 0.80 = 9,600 kg. In pounds that is about 21,160 lb. Errors in this conversion have caused aircraft to run out of fuel, so the fuel slip and the gauges should always be cross-checked.
whyWrong: Divided by the specific gravity instead of multiplying.
Assumed a specific gravity of 1.0, as for water.
Multiplied the kilograms by 2.2 as if converting to pounds, then kept the kilogram label.
samples.examTip: Fuel is lighter than water, so the kg figure must be smaller than the litre figure.

samples.prompt: Why is a fuel system icing inhibitor (FSII) added to some turbine fuels?
options: To raise the flash point of the fuel and reduce fire risk
To prevent static electricity building up during refuelling
To lower the freezing point of the kerosene itself below −60 °C for polar and long-haul routes
