To stop water in the fuel freezing into ice crystals that could block the filters
samples.explanation: Kerosene always holds some dissolved water, which comes out of solution as the fuel cools and can freeze into ice crystals. FSII mixes with that water and lowers its freezing point, so it stays liquid. It also has a biocidal effect against microbial growth. Aircraft without fuel heaters often need it.
whyWrong: Flash point is a property of the base fuel; FSII does not raise it.
Static dissipator additive does that job, not FSII.
FSII acts on the water in the fuel, not on the freezing point of the kerosene.
samples.examTip: FSII = water ice; antistatic additive = static; anti-oxidant = storage.

samples.prompt: Compared with a kerosene fuel such as Jet A-1, a wide-cut fuel such as Jet B:
options: Is a high-octane gasoline that can be used in piston engines as a direct alternative to AVGAS 100LL
Has a lower flash point and higher volatility: more fire risk, but easier starting in severe cold
Is identical in properties but cheaper
Has a higher flash point and lower volatility, so it is safer to handle
samples.explanation: Jet B is a blend of kerosene and lighter gasoline fractions. It evaporates more readily, has a much lower flash point and a lower freezing point, which helps in very cold climates, but it is more hazardous to handle and more prone to vapour loss at altitude. Jet A-1 has a minimum flash point of 38 °C.
whyWrong: Wide-cut fuel is a blend of kerosene and gasoline fractions for turbines; it is not an avgas.
Wide-cut fuel has quite different volatility and flash point from kerosene.
Reversed: the gasoline fraction in wide-cut fuel lowers its flash point and raises its volatility.
samples.examTip: Jet A-1 flash point 38 °C minimum; wide-cut fuels are far lower.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Fuel Systems
topics: Booster Pumps and Pylon Shut Off Valve
Fuel Control Unit (FCU) or Fuel Flow Regulator (FFR)
HP Fuel Cock (HP Fuel Shut Off Valve)

samples.prompt: The booster pumps in the fuel system are located in:
options: The engine fuel system
The airframe fuel tanks
The fuel control unit
The high pressure pump casing
samples.explanation: The tank booster pumps belong to the airframe fuel system: they deliver fuel from the tanks to the engine's LP pump. The engine fuel system starts at the LP pump.

samples.prompt: In a typical turbine engine fuel system, why is the fuel heater (or fuel-cooled oil cooler) placed upstream of the low-pressure fuel filter?
options: To vaporise the fuel before it reaches the burners
To raise the fuel pressure before it reaches the HP pump
To lower the fuel viscosity so the HP pump needs less power
To melt or prevent ice crystals that would otherwise block the filter
samples.explanation: Water in the fuel can form ice crystals when the fuel is very cold. These would collect on the fine LP filter and block it. Heating the fuel before the filter, using engine oil (FCOC) or bleed air, keeps it above the icing temperature. A filter bypass and warning protect against blockage if it occurs.
whyWrong: Fuel is atomised at the burners, not vaporised in the supply line; vapour in the line would cause vapour lock.
Heating does not raise pressure; that is the job of the pumps.
Viscosity changes are a minor side effect; the purpose is ice protection.
samples.examTip: Sequence: LP pump, heater/FCOC, LP filter, HP pump, FCU, flowmeter, burners.

samples.prompt: Which statement about a FADEC (full authority digital engine control) is correct?
options: It acts only as a backup to a conventional hydromechanical fuel control
It only advises the pilot, who then sets the fuel flow manually through a mechanical link to the FCU
It has a single channel, so any fault leads to an engine shutdown
It controls fuel flow and engine geometry through two independent channels, with no manual reversion
samples.explanation: A FADEC has full authority over fuel flow, variable stator vanes, bleed valves and other engine systems, with no manual or hydromechanical backup. Redundancy comes from two independent channels, each able to control the engine. It also protects against overspeed and overtemperature and reduces pilot workload.
whyWrong: That describes a supervisory control; full authority means there is no hydromechanical backup.
Full authority means the FADEC itself controls the engine, not the pilot.
FADECs have two channels; if one fails, the other takes over.
samples.examTip: 'Full authority' = no backup; 'dual channel' = redundancy.

samples.prompt: What does the fuel control unit (FCU) of a gas turbine do during a rapid acceleration?
options: Limits the rate of fuel increase so the engine accelerates without surge or overtemperature
Shuts off fuel briefly to allow the compressor to recover
Delivers the full fuel flow immediately, so the engine reaches take-off thrust as fast as possible
Diverts fuel to the afterburner to give extra thrust
samples.explanation: The FCU meters fuel according to thrust lever position, engine speed, compressor delivery pressure and inlet temperature. During acceleration it follows a schedule that keeps the fuel/air ratio within limits, so the compressor does not surge and the turbine is not overheated. A similar schedule on deceleration prevents a weak flame-out.
whyWrong: Cutting fuel during acceleration would risk a flame-out.
Instant full fuel flow would over-fuel the engine, causing surge or a temperature exceedance.
Civil turbofans have no afterburner.
samples.examTip: Turbofans take several seconds to accelerate from idle; this is the acceleration schedule at work.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the fuel shut-off valves of a turbofan is correct?
options: Neither valve can be operated by the crew; both close automatically when the engine stops
Start lever: HP valve at the engine (normal shutdown). Fire handle: LP valve, isolating the engine from the tanks
Both valves are worked only by the fire handle
The LP shut-off valve, worked by the start lever, stops fuel at the burners; the HP valve isolates the engine from the tanks
samples.explanation: Normal engine shutdown is done with the fuel (start) lever, which closes the HP shut-off valve at the engine and leaves the fuel system upstream full. In a fire, the fire handle closes the LP valve, usually at the wing spar, so no fuel reaches the engine area.
whyWrong: Both valves are crew-controlled: the start lever for normal shutdown, the fire handle in an emergency.
The start lever normally works the HP valve for normal shutdown; the fire handle closes the LP valve.
Reversed: the HP valve (start lever) is at the engine, and the LP valve (fire handle) is at the tank end.
samples.examTip: The LP valve is upstream, near the tanks: that is why it is the fire isolation valve.

chapters.title: Gas Turbines - Bleed Air
topics: Disposal of Cooling and Sealing Air

samples.prompt: Air bled from the engine compressor for external use is typically taken from:
options: LP compressor outlet only
HP compressor outlet only
LP compressor outlet supplemented by HP compressor outlet when required
Combustion chamber cooling ports
samples.explanation: External bleed air normally comes from a continuous low pressure bleed at the LP compressor outlet, supplemented by a high pressure bleed from the HP compressor when the LP pressure is insufficient.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of engine bleed air on a turbofan airliner?
options: Starting the other engines through a cross-bleed
Air conditioning and pressurisation
Cooling the engine's lubricating oil in the oil tank
Wing and engine intake anti-icing
samples.explanation: Bleed air is used for air conditioning and pressurisation, wing and nacelle anti-icing, engine starting, pressurising hydraulic reservoirs and water tanks, and other pneumatic services. The oil is cooled by heat exchangers using fuel or fan air, not by bleed air in the tank.
whyWrong: Bleed from a running engine (or the APU) can be routed to start another engine.
Air conditioning and pressurisation are the largest users of bleed air.
Hot bleed air is used for thermal anti-icing of wing leading edges and engine intakes.
samples.examTip: If the option is about oil cooling, think FCOC or air-cooled oil cooler.

samples.prompt: What happens when a large amount of bleed air is taken from an engine at a fixed thrust setting, for example with engine and wing anti-ice on?
options: EGT and fuel flow rise and the maximum available thrust falls
EGT falls because cool air is removed from the combustion chamber
The engine produces more thrust because less air is wasted
There is no effect, because bleed air is taken from the fan only
samples.explanation: The compressor has done work on the bleed air, but that air leaves before the turbine and does not return energy. To hold the same thrust, more fuel must be burnt per kilogram of remaining core air, so EGT and fuel flow rise. Performance data apply corrections for bleed configuration, and maximum thrust may be reduced.
whyWrong: Removing air from the core increases the temperature needed for the same output, so EGT rises.
Bleed air has already been compressed with energy from the turbine, so taking it costs thrust.
Core bleeds are taken from the compressor stages, not only from the fan.
samples.examTip: Check the performance tables for 'anti-ice on' or 'packs off' corrections.

samples.prompt: Why does bleed air usually pass through a precooler before entering the aircraft's pneumatic manifold?
options: To reduce its pressure so the packs can use it
To heat it with exhaust gas so it is hot enough for anti-icing
To cool it, using fan air, to a temperature the ducts and users can safely accept
To remove water from the air so the air-conditioning packs and their turbines do not ice up
samples.explanation: Air from the HP stages can be several hundred degrees Celsius. The precooler, an air-to-air heat exchanger in the pylon, uses cool fan air to bring the bleed temperature down to a level that the ducts, valves and users can tolerate safely.
whyWrong: Pressure is regulated by valves; the precooler changes temperature.
Bleed air is already very hot; the precooler cools it.
Water removal is done inside the air-conditioning packs.
samples.examTip: Precooler = temperature; pressure regulating valve = pressure.

samples.prompt: Many turbofans take bleed air from an intermediate compressor stage, switching to a high-pressure stage at low power. Why?
options: The HP stage is used at low power because its air is cooler
The switch protects the APU and its load compressor from back-pressure surges during a high-speed descent
The intermediate stage wastes less energy but lacks pressure at low power, when the HP port is opened
The intermediate stage is used at low power to prevent compressor surge
samples.explanation: Taking air from the lowest stage that gives enough pressure wastes the least compressor work. At high power the intermediate stage is sufficient. At idle (for example in descent) its pressure is too low, so an HP valve opens automatically to maintain the supply to the pneumatic system.
whyWrong: HP air is hotter, not cooler; it is used because its pressure is high enough.
The APU is not involved in engine bleed port selection.
Bleed port selection is for system pressure, not stall protection (handling bleed valves do that job).
samples.examTip: HP bleed is the low-power source; intermediate bleed is the high-power source.

samples.prompt: A pilot raises the nose in level flight. Which angle changes, and which stays fixed by the design of the aeroplane?
options: Both change, because incidence is measured from the relative airflow
The angle of incidence changes; the angle of attack stays fixed
The angle of attack changes; the angle of incidence stays fixed
Neither changes until the elevator trim is moved to a new setting
samples.explanation: The angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow (the free-stream direction), so it changes whenever the pilot changes attitude relative to the flight path. The angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the wing root chord and the longitudinal axis, chosen so that the fuselage is roughly level in the cruise.
whyWrong: Incidence is measured from the longitudinal axis, not the relative airflow; only the angle of attack uses the relative airflow.
Reverses the two: incidence is the rigging angle between the wing chord and the aeroplane's longitudinal axis, set at manufacture.
The angle of attack changes as soon as the attitude changes relative to the flight path; trim only changes the control force.
samples.examTip: If an option says 'the pilot changes the angle of incidence', it is wrong for a conventional fixed wing.

samples.prompt: A wing has a span of 11.0 m and a wing area of 16.2 m². What is its aspect ratio?
samples.explanation: Aspect ratio = span² ÷ area = 11.0² ÷ 16.2 = 121 ÷ 16.2 = 7.47, about 7.5. The same answer comes from span ÷ mean chord: the mean chord is 16.2 ÷ 11.0 = 1.47 m and 11.0 ÷ 1.47 = 7.5.
whyWrong: Divided span by area; the aspect ratio is span² ÷ area (or span ÷ mean chord).
Used the semi-span (5.5 m) in place of the full span.
Gives the mean chord (area ÷ span = 1.47 m), which is a length, not the aspect ratio.
samples.examTip: A light aeroplane's aspect ratio is usually about 6 to 9; a glider's is 20 or more. Use that to sense-check.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the mean camber line of an aerofoil is INCORRECT?
options: On a symmetrical aerofoil it lies above the chord line along its whole length
It meets the chord line at the leading edge and the trailing edge
It is the line drawn halfway between the upper and lower surfaces
The maximum distance between it and the chord line is the camber
samples.explanation: The mean camber line joins the leading and trailing edges and runs midway between the upper and lower surfaces. Its greatest distance from the chord line is the camber. On a symmetrical aerofoil the upper and lower surfaces are mirror images, so the mean camber line lies ON the chord line and the camber is zero.
whyWrong: This is correct: both lines are drawn between the same leading-edge and trailing-edge points.
This is a correct definition: the mean camber line runs midway between the surfaces.
This is correct: camber is the maximum separation of the mean camber line from the chord line, usually given as a percentage of chord.
samples.examTip: Read INCORRECT questions twice: three options will be textbook definitions.

samples.prompt: A light aeroplane has a mass of 1,100 kg and a wing area of 16.0 m². What is its wing loading in SI units? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
options: 7.0 N/m²
674 N/m²
samples.explanation: Wing loading = weight ÷ wing area. Weight = mg = 1,100 × 9.81 = 10,791 N. Wing loading = 10,791 ÷ 16.0 = 674 N/m². A higher wing loading raises the stall speed and reduces the gust response.
whyWrong: Used the area of one wing (8.0 m²) instead of the total wing area.
Divided the mass by the area and then by g instead of multiplying by g.
Divided the mass in kg by the area: that is kg/m², not a force per area in newtons.
samples.examTip: In SI questions 'weight' always means newtons; multiply kilograms by g.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements: 1. The relative airflow is parallel to, and opposite in direction to, the flight path. 2. Lift acts at right angles to the relative airflow. 3. Drag acts parallel to the chord line. 4. Total reaction is the resultant of lift and drag. Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
samples.explanation: Lift and drag are defined relative to the airflow, not to the aerofoil: lift is the component of the total reaction perpendicular to the relative airflow and drag is the component parallel to it. The relative airflow is the free stream seen from the aeroplane, parallel and opposite to the flight path. Statement 3 confuses the reference: the chord line is used only to measure the angle of attack.
whyWrong: Includes 3 (drag is parallel to the relative airflow, not the chord) and leaves out 2, the basic definition of lift.
Includes 3: drag is defined parallel to the relative airflow, not the chord line.
Leaves out 1 and 4 and includes 3, which is wrong.
samples.examTip: Any option tying lift or drag to the chord line is a trap.

chapters.title: The Atmosphere
topics: Measuring Dynamic Pressure — The Airspeed Indicator
Speed of Sound and Mach Number

samples.prompt: Which set gives the ISA mean sea level values used for aerodynamic calculations?
samples.explanation: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere at mean sea level has pressure 1013.25 hPa, temperature +15 °C (288.15 K) and density 1.225 kg/m³. Temperature falls at 6.5 °C per km (about 1.98 °C per 1,000 ft) up to the tropopause at 11 km (36,090 ft), where it is −56.5 °C.
whyWrong: Laboratory 'room conditions'; ISA sea level is +15 °C.
0.0765 is the sea-level density in pounds per cubic foot, not kg/m³.
These are the 'standard temperature and pressure' figures used in chemistry, not the ISA.
samples.examTip: Density questions in SI expect 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane climbs at a constant indicated airspeed through the ISA troposphere. Which statement describes what happens to its TAS and why?
options: TAS stays the same, because the indicated airspeed is held constant
TAS decreases, because the falling temperature reduces the local speed of sound
TAS increases, because density falls with height and the same dynamic pressure needs a higher true speed
TAS increases, because the falling pressure makes the airspeed indicator over-read
samples.explanation: The ASI responds to dynamic pressure q = ½ρV². Holding IAS constant holds q (and EAS) roughly constant. As ρ falls with height, V must rise to keep ½ρV² the same: TAS = EAS ÷ √σ. At 10,000 ft σ is about 0.74, so TAS is about 16% above EAS.
whyWrong: IAS measures dynamic pressure ½ρV², so at lower density the same IAS means a higher TAS.
The local speed of sound governs Mach number, not the IAS–TAS relationship.
The ASI does not over-read with height; it correctly shows dynamic pressure, and TAS really is higher.
samples.examTip: Rule of thumb: TAS ≈ IAS + 2% per 1,000 ft.

samples.prompt: What is the ISA temperature at 40,000 ft (FL400)?
samples.explanation: ISA: 15°C at mean sea level, falling 1.98°C per 1 000 ft to −56.5°C at the tropopause (36 090 ft), then constant. FL400 is above the tropopause, so the ISA temperature is −56.5°C.
whyWrong: Used 6.5°C per 1 000 ft (that figure is per kilometre)
Used the DALR (3°C per 1 000 ft) instead of the ISA lapse rate
Reversed the sign of the result
samples.examTip: Common trap: used 6.5°C per 1 000 ft (that figure is per kilometre).

samples.prompt: On a hot, humid afternoon at a sea-level aerodrome the QNH is 1013 hPa. Compared with a cool, dry morning at the same QNH, the air density is:
options: Higher, because water vapour adds mass to every cubic metre of air
Lower, because both the higher temperature and the water vapour reduce density
Unchanged, because the pressure is the same on both occasions
Lower because of the temperature, though the humidity raises it slightly
samples.explanation: From ρ = P ÷ (RT), at constant pressure a higher temperature lowers density. Water vapour molecules are lighter than nitrogen and oxygen, so replacing dry air with vapour lowers the density further. Both effects reduce lift, thrust and propeller efficiency, so take-off and climb performance suffer.
whyWrong: Water vapour (molecular mass about 18) is lighter than the dry air (about 29) it displaces, so humid air is LESS dense.
Density depends on temperature and composition as well as pressure: ρ = P ÷ (RT).
Gets the temperature right but the humidity wrong: moist air is lighter than dry air at the same pressure and temperature.
samples.examTip: High, hot and humid are the three enemies of take-off performance.

samples.prompt: At a certain level the static pressure is 700 hPa and the temperature is −5 °C. What is the relative density σ = ρ/ρ₀? (ISA MSL: 1013.25 hPa, 288.15 K)
whyWrong: Inverted the whole expression (ρ₀/ρ instead of ρ/ρ₀).
Multiplied by the temperature ratio instead of dividing by it: colder air makes the density HIGHER for the same pressure.
Used the pressure ratio alone and ignored the temperature ratio.
samples.examTip: Always convert to kelvin; a ratio of Celsius values is meaningless.

samples.prompt: According to the principle of continuity, if the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow is reduced, which of the following occurs?
options: The mass flow increases and velocity remains constant
The mass flow decreases and velocity increases
The mass flow remains constant and velocity increases
The mass flow remains constant and static pressure increases
samples.explanation: Continuity: mass flow ρAV is constant. At low subsonic speed ρ is constant, so A × V = constant and a reduced area means increased velocity (and, by Bernoulli, decreased static pressure).

samples.prompt: Air flows steadily through a venturi. Compared with the wide inlet, which statement describes the flow at the throat (incompressible, frictionless flow)?
options: Speed higher, static pressure lower, total pressure unchanged
Speed higher, static pressure higher, total pressure higher
Speed lower, static pressure lower, total pressure unchanged
Speed higher, static pressure lower, total pressure lower
samples.explanation: Continuity: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so a smaller area means a higher speed. Bernoulli: static pressure + dynamic pressure (½ρV²) = total pressure, constant along a streamline. As the dynamic pressure rises at the throat, the static pressure must fall by the same amount.
whyWrong: Static pressure falls where speed rises; total pressure is constant along a streamline.
Continuity (AV = constant) makes the flow FASTER in the narrower throat.
In frictionless flow total pressure is conserved; only the split between static and dynamic pressure changes.
samples.examTip: 'Total pressure lower' is wrong unless the question mentions friction or a shock.

samples.prompt: Two aeroplanes fly at different altitudes but with exactly the same dynamic pressure. Which speed is the same for both?
options: True airspeed (TAS)
Groundspeed over the surface
Equivalent airspeed (EAS)
Local Mach number
samples.explanation: EAS is defined as the speed at sea-level density that gives the same dynamic pressure: ½ρ₀EAS² = ½ρTAS². So equal dynamic pressure means equal EAS. Lift and drag at a given angle of attack depend on dynamic pressure, which is why EAS (and IAS) is the speed that matters for aerodynamics.
whyWrong: TAS for a given dynamic pressure is higher in the thinner air at the higher altitude.
Groundspeed depends on TAS and wind, and neither is fixed by dynamic pressure.
Mach number depends on TAS and on temperature, not on dynamic pressure alone.
samples.examTip: Aerodynamic limits (stall, VA, flap limits) are fixed in IAS/EAS, not TAS.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies at a TAS of 110 kt where the air density is 0.653 kg/m³. What is the dynamic pressure, to the nearest 10 Pa? (1 kt = 0.5144 m/s)
samples.explanation: Formula: q = ½ρV² (V in m/s, q in Pa); at constant density q ∝ V². q = ½ρV². Convert the speed: 110 kt × 0.5144 = 56.59 m/s. q = 0.5 × 0.653 kg/m³ × 56.59² m²/s² = 1,046 Pa (N/m²), about 1.05 kPa.
whyWrong: Used the sea-level density of 1.225 kg/m³ instead of the density given: gives 1,960 Pa.
Left out the ½ in q = ½ρV², which doubles the answer: gives 2,090 Pa.
Put the speed in knots straight into the formula instead of converting to m/s first: gives 3,950 Pa.
samples.examTip: Convert knots to m/s (× 0.5144) before squaring.

samples.prompt: A pitot tube senses 101,925 Pa and the static vent 99,500 Pa. Taking the air density as 1.225 kg/m³, what is the airspeed? (1 m/s = 1.944 kt)
options: 63 kt
122 kt
135 kt
86 kt
samples.explanation: Dynamic pressure q = pitot − static = 101,925 − 99,500 = 2,425 Pa. From q = ½ρV²: V = √(2q/ρ) = √(2 × 2,425 ÷ 1.225) = √3,959 = 62.9 m/s. 62.9 × 1.944 = 122 kt. Using sea-level density gives the equivalent airspeed.
whyWrong: Gave the speed in m/s (62.9) and did not convert to knots.
Used a density of 1.0 kg/m³ instead of 1.225 kg/m³.
Left out the factor 2: V = √(2q/ρ), not √(q/ρ).
samples.examTip: With ρ₀ = 1.225 the result is EAS; with the local density it is TAS.

samples.prompt: With reference to aerofoil terminology, which of the following correctly defines the chord line?
options: A line joining the leading edge to the trailing edge, equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces
A straight line joining the centres of curvature of the leading and trailing edges of an aerofoil
The maximum distance between the upper and lower surfaces of an aerofoil
A line joining the leading edge to the trailing edge along the upper surface
samples.explanation: The chord line is defined as a straight line joining the centres of curvature of the leading and trailing edges. Option A describes the mean camber line. Option C describes maximum thickness. Option D is incorrect as the chord line is not along the upper surface.

samples.prompt: As the angle of attack of a cambered aerofoil increases from small values towards the stalling angle, the centre of pressure:
options: Moves rearward
Moves forward, then rearward, then forward again
Moves forward
Stays at the quarter-chord point
samples.explanation: On a cambered aerofoil the suction peak near the leading edge grows as the angle of attack increases, so the point where the total reaction acts (the centre of pressure) moves forward. At the stall the upper-surface flow separates, the suction peak collapses and the CP moves rapidly rearward, giving a nose-down pitch.
whyWrong: The CP moves rearward only after the stall, or as the angle of attack is reduced.
There is one forward movement up to the stall, then a rearward jump at the stall; no third reversal.
That describes the aerodynamic centre, about which the pitching moment is constant; the CP itself moves.
samples.examTip: Do not confuse CP (moves) with AC (fixed, about 25% chord in subsonic flow).

samples.prompt: Air flows at 68 m/s through a duct of cross-section 6 m², which narrows to 2.4 m². What is the speed in the narrow section (incompressible flow)?
samples.explanation: For incompressible flow A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so V₂ = 68 × 6 ÷ 2.4 = 170.0 m/s.
whyWrong: Squared the area ratio
Took the square root of the area ratio
Inverted the area ratio (speed falls in a narrower duct)
samples.examTip: Common trap: squared the area ratio.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the aerodynamic centre of an aerofoil in subsonic flow is correct?
options: It is the point about which the pitching moment coefficient stays constant as the angle of attack changes, at about 25% chord
It is the point about which the pitching moment is always zero, whatever the camber of the aerofoil
It is the point at about 50% chord where the lift on the upper and lower surfaces is equal
It is the point through which the total reaction acts, and it moves forward as the angle of attack increases
samples.explanation: Lift changes with angle of attack can be treated as acting at the aerodynamic centre, so the pitching moment about the AC does not change with angle of attack. In subsonic flow it lies at about 25% of the chord. For a cambered aerofoil the moment about it is a constant nose-down value; for a symmetrical aerofoil it is zero.
whyWrong: Only for a symmetrical aerofoil is the moment about the AC zero; a cambered aerofoil has a constant nose-down moment there.
About 50% chord is where the aerodynamic centre moves in supersonic flow.
That describes the centre of pressure, which moves with the angle of attack.
samples.examTip: Stability analysis uses the AC because it stays put; the CP does not.

samples.prompt: As the angle of attack of an aerofoil is increased below the stall, the stagnation point at the leading edge:
options: Moves down and back on the lower surface
Moves up and back on the upper surface
Moves forward of the leading edge into the free stream
Stays exactly at the leading edge
samples.explanation: The stagnation point is where the flow divides and comes to rest. At a higher angle of attack the lower surface faces the oncoming air more directly, so the dividing point moves down and aft under the leading edge. More air then flows around the leading edge onto the upper surface, strengthening the suction peak there.
whyWrong: The stagnation point moves to the lower surface, because the aerofoil meets the airflow more nose-up.
The stagnation point is a point on the surface; it cannot lie ahead of the aerofoil.
It stays at the leading edge only at one particular angle of attack, close to zero lift.
samples.examTip: Stall-warning vanes on the leading edge work because of this movement.

chapters.title: Lift
topics: Effect of Aircraft Weight on Minimum Flight Speed

samples.prompt: An aeroplane in level flight slows down while the pilot keeps the altitude constant. To keep lift equal to weight the pilot must:
options: Increase the angle of attack, raising CL to make up for the lower dynamic pressure
Decrease the angle of attack, because lift rises as the speed falls
Keep the angle of attack constant, because lift depends only on weight
Increase the angle of attack only below the minimum drag speed
samples.explanation: L = ½ρV²S·CL. With ρ and S fixed, a lower V means less dynamic pressure, so CL (angle of attack) must increase to hold L = W. Each speed in level flight has its own angle of attack; the slowest speed is reached at CLmax, the stall.
whyWrong: Lift falls with V² at constant angle of attack, so the angle must go up, not down.
Lift equals weight in level flight, but the angle of attack needed depends on the speed.
The angle of attack must rise at every speed reduction, above or below Vmd.
samples.examTip: 'Lift is constant in level flight' is true; 'angle of attack is constant' is not.

samples.prompt: A wing of area 20 m² operates at a lift coefficient of 0.50 in air of density 1.225 kg/m³ at 60 m/s. How much lift does it produce?
samples.explanation: L = ½ρV²S·CL = 0.5 × 1.225 × 60² × 20 × 0.50 = 0.5 × 1.225 × 3,600 × 10 = 22,050 N, about 22 kN (enough to support about 2,250 kg in level flight).
whyWrong: Applied the ½ twice, halving the correct answer.
Used V instead of V² (½ × 1.225 × 60 × 20 × 0.5).
Left out the ½ in L = ½ρV²S·CL.
samples.examTip: Write the formula out with units before substituting; most slips are a missing ½ or a missing square.

samples.prompt: Two wings have the same aerofoil section and area. Wing X has a high aspect ratio and wing Y a low aspect ratio. Compared with Y, wing X has:
options: A steeper lift curve, so it reaches a given CL at a lower angle of attack
A steeper lift curve and a much higher CLmax for the same section
The same lift curve slope, because the aerofoil section is the same
A shallower lift curve and a higher stalling angle of attack
samples.explanation: A finite wing loses some effective angle of attack to downwash from its tip vortices. On a high aspect ratio wing the tips are a smaller part of the span, so the downwash and induced angle are smaller and the lift curve is steeper: a given CL needs less angle of attack. Low aspect ratio wings have a shallower curve and stall at a higher angle of attack.
whyWrong: Aspect ratio changes the slope much more than CLmax, which is set mainly by the section.
The section sets the two-dimensional slope, but the finite wing's slope falls as the aspect ratio falls.
Describes the LOW aspect ratio wing: strong tip vortices reduce the effective angle of attack and flatten the curve.
samples.examTip: Sweepback flattens the lift curve in the same way.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flying at 185 kt TAS changes speed to 148 kt TAS at the same altitude, holding the angle of attack constant. What happens to the lift?
options: Lift decreases by 49%
Lift decreases by 36%
Lift decreases by 40%
Lift decreases by 20%
samples.explanation: Formula: L = ½ρV²S·CL; at constant CL and ρ, L ∝ V² and V ∝ √W. L = ½ρV²S·CL. With density and angle of attack (CL) unchanged, L ∝ V². L₂/L₁ = (148/185)² = 0.6400, a change of -36.0%.
whyWrong: Cubed the speed ratio, which is how parasite power varies, not lift: gives Lift decreases by 49%.
Used the small-change approximation (twice the percentage speed change), which is poor for a change this large: gives Lift decreases by 40%.
Made lift proportional to speed rather than speed squared: gives Lift decreases by 20%.
samples.examTip: Speed ratio first, then square it.

samples.prompt: An aircraft of mass 6,900 kg flies level at 140 kt TAS at a certain angle of attack. Its mass changes to 7,600 kg. At what TAS must it fly to stay level at the same angle of attack and altitude?
options: 170 kt
133 kt
154 kt
147 kt
samples.explanation: Formula: L = ½ρV²S·CL; at constant CL and ρ, L ∝ V² and V ∝ √W. In level flight L = W = ½ρV²S·CL. At constant angle of attack (CL) and density, V ∝ √W. V₂ = 140 × √(7,600/6,900) = 140 × 1.0495 = 146.9 kt.
whyWrong: Squared the mass ratio instead of taking its square root: gives 170 kt.
Inverted the mass ratio, so the speed moves the wrong way: gives 133 kt.
Scaled the speed in direct proportion to mass, forgetting the square root: gives 154 kt.
samples.examTip: Speed ratio first, then square it.

chapters.title: Drag
topics: Effect of Lift on Parasite Drag
The Effect of Aircraft Gross Weight on Total Drag
The Effect of Altitude on Total Drag
The Effect of Configuration on Total Drag

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a component of parasite drag?
options: Skin-friction drag
Form (pressure) drag
Interference drag
Induced drag
samples.explanation: Total drag = parasite drag + induced drag. Parasite (zero-lift) drag is made up of skin friction, form drag and interference drag and varies with V². Induced drag is the by-product of producing lift: the tip vortices tilt the lift vector rearward. It varies with 1/V² at constant weight.
whyWrong: Skin friction comes from the boundary layer's viscous shear: it is parasite drag.
Form drag comes from flow separation and the pressure difference between front and back: it is parasite drag.
Interference drag arises where components meet, such as the wing root: it is parasite drag.
samples.examTip: If it depends on lift, it is induced; if it exists at zero lift, it is parasite.

samples.prompt: In level flight at 170 kt, an aircraft's induced drag is 1,600 N. What is it at 85 kt (same weight and altitude)?
samples.explanation: Induced drag ∝ 1/V² (in level flight at constant weight): 1,600 × (85/170)^−2 = 6,400 N.
whyWrong: Assumed drag is proportional to 1/V
Assumed drag is proportional to V
Confused the parasite and induced drag laws
samples.examTip: Common trap: assumed drag is proportional to 1/V.

samples.prompt: In level flight at constant mass, an aeroplane's induced drag is 6.0 kN at 120 kt TAS. What is the induced drag at 180 kt TAS at the same altitude?
options: 9.0 kN
4.0 kN
2.7 kN
samples.explanation: At constant weight, CL ∝ 1/V² and induced drag Di = ½ρV²S·CDi with CDi ∝ CL², so Di ∝ 1/V². Di = 6.0 × (120/180)² = 6.0 × 0.444 = 2.67 kN, about 2.7 kN.
whyWrong: Made induced drag proportional to speed.
Made induced drag inversely proportional to V instead of V².
Applied the parasite drag law (∝ V²) to induced drag.
samples.examTip: Faster flight means less induced drag but more parasite drag.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane's mass increases (more fuel and payload). Assuming the same configuration, which statement describes its minimum drag speed and its minimum drag?
options: Vmd decreases because the induced drag rises; the minimum drag increases
Vmd increases and the minimum drag increases; the best L/D ratio is reduced
Vmd increases and the minimum drag increases; the best L/D ratio is unchanged
Vmd is unchanged because it is a fixed angle of attack; the minimum drag increases
samples.explanation: Best L/D occurs at one angle of attack, so it is unchanged. Holding that angle at a higher weight needs a higher speed: Vmd ∝ √W. Minimum drag = W ÷ (L/D)max, so it rises in proportion to weight. On the drag curve the whole U moves up and to the right.
whyWrong: Higher induced drag at every speed moves the crossing with parasite drag to a HIGHER speed.
The best L/D is a property of the aerodynamic shape at one angle of attack; mass does not change it.
The angle of attack for best L/D is fixed, but a heavier aeroplane flies that angle at a higher speed (∝ √W).
samples.examTip: 'Same angle of attack, higher speed' is the pattern for every mass change.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane flies level and trimmed at a speed below its minimum drag speed. A gust reduces its speed slightly with the throttle left alone. What follows?
options: Drag increases, so the speed keeps decreasing: the aeroplane is speed unstable
Drag decreases, so the speed recovers on its own: the aeroplane is speed stable
Drag increases, but the extra lift at the lower speed restores it
Drag is unchanged, so the aeroplane stays at the new lower speed
samples.explanation: Below Vmd, on the 'back of the drag curve', drag rises as speed falls. A small loss of speed therefore increases drag, which slows the aeroplane further: speed instability. Above Vmd a speed loss reduces drag, so the speed recovers. This is why approaches below Vmd need active thrust management or an autothrottle.
whyWrong: Below Vmd the drag curve slopes the other way: slowing down INCREASES drag.
In level flight lift must equal weight; slowing down does not create extra lift to help.
On the back of the drag curve drag changes with speed; it does not stay constant.
samples.examTip: On a slow, flapped approach, think 'power for speed': the speed will not look after itself.

chapters.title: Stalling
topics: Aircraft Behaviour Close to the Stall
Use of Flight Controls Close to the Stall

samples.prompt: A typical stalling angle of attack for a wing without sweepback is:
samples.explanation: A typical unswept wing stalls at a critical angle of attack of about 16°. Lower values (around 4°) are near the best L/D angle, and 30-45° is far beyond the stall of a conventional aerofoil.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane stalls at 50 kt IAS in straight and level flight. At what IAS will it stall in a level, coordinated turn at 60° of bank?
options: 100 kt
71 kt
25 kt
35 kt
samples.explanation: Load factor n = 1/cos 60° = 2. Stall speed varies with √n: Vs = 50 × √2 = 50 × 1.414 = 70.7, about 71 kt. The stalling angle of attack is unchanged; the wing simply has to produce twice the lift.
whyWrong: Multiplied by the load factor (2) instead of its square root.
Multiplied by cos 60° (0.5) instead of dividing by its square root.
Divided by √2: a turn raises the stall speed, it never lowers it.

samples.prompt: Which statement about the stalling angle of attack of a given wing, in a given configuration and at low Mach number, is correct?
options: It stays the same whatever the mass, bank angle or load factor
It is higher at altitude, because the TAS is higher
It decreases in a turn, because the load factor is higher
It increases as the mass increases, because more lift is needed
samples.explanation: The stall happens when the airflow separates at the critical angle of attack, which depends on the aerofoil, its configuration (flap, slats), contamination and, at high speed, Mach number. Mass, bank and load factor change the speed at which that angle is reached, not the angle itself. That is why a stall can happen at any speed and any attitude.
whyWrong: TAS does not change the critical angle; at low Mach the stall is a matter of angle of attack.
A turn raises the stall speed (√n), but the wing still stalls at the same angle of attack.
More mass raises the stall SPEED, not the stalling angle of attack.
samples.examTip: Stall warning systems that sense angle of attack work at any weight for this reason.

samples.prompt: Why do designers give a straight wing washout (a lower angle of incidence at the tip than at the root)?
options: To move the centre of pressure towards the tips and so reduce the bending moment
So the root stalls first, keeping the ailerons effective and reducing the tendency to drop a wing
To increase the CLmax of the whole wing by loading the tips more heavily
So the tip stalls first, giving the pilot an early warning through aileron buffet
samples.explanation: With washout the tip meets the air at a smaller angle of attack than the root, so the root reaches the critical angle first. The ailerons, in the still-attached tip flow, remain effective, and the separated root wake can strike the tailplane and give buffet as a natural warning. Stall strips on the inboard leading edge do the same job.
whyWrong: Washout shifts load inboard, not outboard, which REDUCES root bending.
Washout unloads the tips; it lowers the whole wing's CLmax slightly in exchange for safer stall behaviour.
Tip-first stalling is exactly what washout prevents: it costs aileron control and causes wing drop.
samples.examTip: Swept wings tend to stall at the tips, the opposite: hence pitch-up.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane with a T-tail is taken well past the stall with a high nose attitude. Why might normal recovery with the elevator fail?
options: The tailplane stalls first in every T-tail design, so the nose pitches up violently at any stall
The engines on the rear fuselage produce so much thrust that the nose cannot be lowered
The tailplane may sit in the separated wake of the wing, so the elevator loses effectiveness (a deep stall)
The wing's centre of pressure moves forward at the stall, giving a strong nose-up moment
samples.explanation: At very high angles of attack the turbulent wake from the stalled wing rises and can envelop a high-mounted tailplane. The elevator then has little or no authority to lower the nose, and the aeroplane may stay stalled: a deep or super stall. Designs at risk use stick pushers to prevent the angle of attack ever reaching that region.
whyWrong: In normal design the wing stalls before the tailplane; the problem is the wake at very high angles of attack.
Rear-mounted engines may flame out in the wake, but thrust does not prevent nose-down pitch.
At the stall the CP of a straight wing moves REARWARD, which pitches the nose down.
samples.examTip: Stick shaker warns; stick pusher acts.

samples.prompt: When flaps are lowered the stalling angle of attack of the wing:
options: remains the same, but CLMAX increases
increases and CLMAX increases
decreases, but CLMAX increases
decreases, but CLMAX remains the same
samples.explanation: Lowering flaps increases the effective angle of attack, so the basic wing section reaches its critical angle at a lower geometric angle. CLMAX increases due to increased camber. Option A is incorrect because stalling angle changes. Option B is incorrect because stalling angle decreases, not increases. Option D is incorrect because CLMAX increases.

samples.prompt: Which trailing-edge flap type increases both the wing area and the camber, and generally gives the largest increase in CLmax?
options: Split flap
Fowler flap
Plain flap
Krueger flap
samples.explanation: A Fowler flap runs aft on tracks before deflecting, so it increases the chord (area) and the camber, and its slot(s) re-energise the boundary layer over it. That gives the largest CLmax increase of the trailing-edge flaps for a moderate drag increase at small settings, which is why airliners use it.
whyWrong: A split flap hinges down from the lower surface: high drag, camber change, no area increase.
A plain flap only increases camber; it does not extend aft, so the area is unchanged.
A Krueger flap is a leading-edge device, hinged from the lower surface of the leading edge.
samples.examTip: 'Increases wing area' points to Fowler.

samples.prompt: Which statement about extending trailing-edge flap at a constant IAS is INCORRECT?
options: The stall speed decreases because CLmax increases
The stalling angle of attack increases
The drag increases, more so at large flap angles
The nose attitude for level flight at that speed is lower
samples.explanation: Trailing-edge flap increases camber, so CLmax rises and stall speed falls, and the required lift is produced at a lower angle of attack (lower nose attitude). But the camber makes the upper-surface flow separate earlier, so the stalling angle of attack DECREASES. Drag rises with flap angle, which is useful for a steep approach.
whyWrong: Correct: Vs ∝ 1/√CLmax, and flap raises CLmax.
Correct: flap adds both profile drag and induced drag; large settings are mainly 'drag flap' for landing.
Correct: the cambered wing needs a smaller angle of attack for the same lift, so the nose is lower and the view is better.
samples.examTip: Only leading-edge devices increase the stalling angle of attack.

samples.prompt: A wing's CLmax rises from 1.5 clean to 2.1 with landing flap. If the clean stall speed is 60 kt IAS at a given mass, what is the stall speed with landing flap at the same mass?
options: 51 kt
43 kt
71 kt
84 kt
samples.explanation: At the stall W = ½ρVs²S·CLmax, so Vs ∝ 1/√CLmax. Vs(flap) = 60 × √(1.5 ÷ 2.1) = 60 × √0.714 = 60 × 0.845 = 50.7, about 51 kt.
whyWrong: Scaled the speed by the CL ratio itself (60 × 1.5/2.1) instead of its square root.
Inverted the ratio under the square root (60 × √(2.1/1.5)), giving a higher speed instead of a lower one.
Inverted the ratio and left out the square root (60 × 2.1/1.5): more CLmax must LOWER the stall speed.
samples.examTip: Check the direction: more lift capability means a lower stall speed.

samples.prompt: Shortly after take-off the pilot retracts the flaps fully while the aeroplane is still close to the flap-extended stall speed. What is the main danger?
options: The aeroplane balloons upwards, because the drag falls suddenly and the speed rises
The engine overspeeds, because the reduced drag unloads the propeller suddenly
The ailerons become ineffective, because flap retraction stops the airflow over them
The aeroplane sinks and may stall, because CLmax falls and the clean stall speed is higher than the current speed
samples.explanation: Retracting the flaps removes camber and area: CLmax falls and the stall speed rises to the clean value. If the current speed is below that, the wing cannot carry the weight, so the aeroplane sinks and may stall at low height. Flaps are therefore retracted in stages, each above its minimum manoeuvring speed.
whyWrong: Ballooning comes from flap EXTENSION; retraction loses lift.
Drag reduction does not unload a propeller enough to overspeed it; the risk is aerodynamic.
Ailerons remain in the airflow; the issue is the loss of lift, not aileron airflow.
samples.examTip: Retraction = lift loss and sink; extension = ballooning and pitch change.

chapters.title: Airframe Contamination
topics: Effect of Frost and Ice on the Aircraft

samples.prompt: Frost on an aircraft surface consists of:
options: A thick layer of clear ice
A thin coating of crystalline ice
A layer of rain ice
A white opaque formation with flow back
samples.explanation: Frost is a fairly thin coating of crystalline ice that forms when water vapour deposits directly as ice on a surface below 0°C. A thick transparent layer is clear ice, ice from supercooled rain is rain ice, and a white opaque deposit is rime ice (which has no flow back).

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an effect of ice accretion on a wing's leading edge?
options: A reduction in CLmax
A reduction in the stall speed
A reduction in the stalling angle of attack
An increase in drag
samples.explanation: Leading-edge ice changes the shape and roughness of the aerofoil. Drag rises, CLmax falls and the flow separates at a lower angle of attack. With a lower CLmax the stall speed INCREASES, so an iced aeroplane must be flown faster on the approach. The extra mass of the ice adds a little more to the stall speed.
whyWrong: Ice disrupts the leading-edge flow, so separation happens at a lower CL.
Separation occurs earlier, so the critical angle falls.
Ice roughness and shape changes add both form drag and skin-friction drag.
samples.examTip: Anything that 'improves' a stall in an icing option is wrong.

samples.prompt: A thin layer of hoar frost covers the upper surface of a wing before take-off. Compared with a clean wing, what is its effect?
options: CLmax falls and the wing stalls at a lower angle of attack and a higher speed, possibly before the stall warning
CLmax rises because the rough surface makes the boundary layer turbulent, as vortex generators do
Only the drag increases; the stall speed and stalling angle are unchanged
The stall speed falls because the extra mass of the frost is negligible but the camber increases
samples.explanation: Even frost as rough as medium sandpaper can cut CLmax substantially and lower the stalling angle of attack. The wing may then stall at a speed above the normal rotation speed and before an angle-of-attack stall warning, which is set for a clean wing, activates. That is why the clean-aircraft concept requires the critical surfaces to be free of frost, ice and snow at take-off, unless the aeroplane's manual allows a specified amount.
whyWrong: Roughness spread over the whole surface thickens and weakens the boundary layer; it does not help like a vortex generator.
Frost reduces lift as well as adding drag; the stall comes earlier.
The frost does not add useful camber; it disrupts the airflow and raises the stall speed.
samples.examTip: Polishing or 'it's only frost' is the classic fatal trap; de-ice.

samples.prompt: Why does ice usually build up first and fastest on the tailplane leading edge, probes and aerials rather than on the thick inboard wing?
options: Thin, small-radius parts deflect the airflow less, so more supercooled droplets strike them
The tailplane is in the propeller slipstream, which is colder than the free stream
The pressure there is lowest, so the droplets freeze at a higher temperature
These parts are made of metal, which conducts the cold better than composite wing skins
samples.explanation: A large, blunt leading edge pushes the air aside well ahead of itself, and many small droplets follow the deflected air round it. A thin edge disturbs the flow only very close to itself, so droplets, with their inertia, cannot turn in time and hit it: its collection efficiency is higher. That is why the tailplane often ices before the wing, and why ice is often first seen on wipers and probes.
whyWrong: Slipstream air is not colder; the effect is about how droplets follow the airflow.
Small pressure differences do not change the freezing point of supercooled droplets in a useful way.
Collection depends on the shape and size of the part, not on its material.
samples.examTip: Watch the wiper arm or OAT probe for the first sign of ice.

samples.prompt: On an approach in icing conditions the pilot selects full flap. The nose suddenly pitches down and the control column goes light. A tailplane stall is suspected. What is the recommended initial action?
options: Push the control column forward and add full power, as for a wing stall
Extend the remaining flap to increase lift, and push forward
Lower the landing gear to increase drag and trim fully nose-down
Return the flaps to the previous setting and pull back on the control column
samples.explanation: The tailplane normally pushes down. Its small leading-edge radius collects ice efficiently, and extending flap increases the downwash, raising its negative angle of attack. An iced tailplane can then stall, so it stops pushing the tail down and the nose drops. Recovery is the opposite of a wing stall: reduce the flap to the previous setting and pull back to reduce the tail's negative angle of attack. Power changes should follow the aircraft manual, because extra power can make things worse on some types.
whyWrong: Pushing forward increases the tailplane's negative angle of attack and deepens a tailplane stall.
More flap increases the downwash on the tail, which caused the tail stall in the first place.
Gear and nose-down trim do nothing to reduce the tail's angle of attack.
samples.examTip: Nose-down pitch plus light controls after flap selection in icing = think tailplane stall.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane is disturbed in pitch and its nose initially moves back towards the trimmed attitude, but it then oscillates with growing amplitude. It is:
options: Statically and dynamically stable
Statically stable but dynamically unstable
Statically unstable but dynamically stable
Neutrally stable both statically and dynamically
samples.explanation: Static stability describes the initial tendency after a disturbance: here the aeroplane starts back towards trim, so it is statically stable. Dynamic stability describes what happens over time: growing oscillations mean dynamic instability. Static stability is necessary for dynamic stability but does not guarantee it.
whyWrong: Growing oscillations mean the dynamic response is unstable.
The INITIAL tendency to return is static stability, so it is statically stable.
Neutral static stability would show no initial tendency to return at all.
samples.examTip: 'Initially returns' = statically stable; then read what the motion does next.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about the effect of moving the centre of gravity forward, within the limits: 1. Static longitudinal stability increases. 2. Stick force per g increases. 3. The stall speed decreases. 4. More elevator is needed to flare for landing. Which are correct?
options: 1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
samples.explanation: A forward CG increases the distance between the CG and the neutral point (static margin), so the aeroplane is more stable and needs larger stick forces to manoeuvre. It also needs more tail down-load to trim, so the wing must lift weight plus tail load: the stall speed and trim drag rise. In the flare the elevator may run out of authority, which is why the forward CG limit exists.
whyWrong: Leaves out 2 and 4 and includes 3, which is wrong.
Includes 3: a forward CG needs more tail down-force, so the wing carries more and the stall speed RISES.
Leaves out 1, the main effect of a forward CG, and includes 3.
samples.examTip: Aft CG gives the opposite and sets the aft limit (minimum stability).

samples.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the two longitudinal dynamic modes of a conventional aeroplane?
options: Both modes are rapid oscillations in angle of attack, damped mainly by the fin
The phugoid is a yawing and rolling motion; the short period is a pitching motion
Phugoid: a slow exchange of speed and height at almost constant angle of attack; short period: a quick, well-damped pitch oscillation
Phugoid: a rapid pitching oscillation at almost constant speed; short period: a slow and lightly damped exchange of speed and height
samples.explanation: The phugoid has a period of tens of seconds: the aeroplane climbs and slows, then dives and speeds up, at nearly constant angle of attack. It is lightly damped but slow, so a pilot corrects it easily. The short-period mode is a quick oscillation in angle of attack and pitch, lasting a few seconds and normally heavily damped by the tailplane.
whyWrong: The phugoid is slow (tens of seconds or more), and pitch damping comes from the tailplane, not the fin.
Yawing and rolling describe the lateral modes (Dutch roll, spiral), not the phugoid.
Reverses the two modes.
samples.examTip: 'Constant angle of attack, varying speed' = phugoid.

samples.prompt: Which of the following does NOT increase the lateral stability (dihedral effect) of an aeroplane?
options: Dihedral
A high-mounted wing
Sweepback
Anhedral
samples.explanation: In a sideslip the dihedral effect produces a rolling moment that lifts the lower wing. Dihedral, sweepback and a high wing position all add to it. Anhedral reduces it, which is why high-wing swept transports often use anhedral: they would otherwise have too much lateral stability and a strong Dutch-roll tendency.
whyWrong: Dihedral is the classic way to give lateral stability: the lower wing meets the sideslip at a greater angle of attack.
A high wing gains a stabilising rolling moment from the cross-flow around the fuselage in a sideslip.
Sweepback gives the into-sideslip wing a larger effective speed and lift, so it adds dihedral effect.
samples.examTip: Anhedral on a high-wing jet is a deliberate correction, not a defect.

samples.prompt: A swept-wing jet has strong lateral stability (dihedral effect) but relatively weak directional stability. After a yaw disturbance it is most likely to show:
options: Dutch roll, a combined yawing and rolling oscillation
Directional divergence, a steady increase in sideslip
A phugoid, a slow exchange of speed and height
Spiral instability, a slowly tightening spiral dive
samples.explanation: Strong dihedral effect makes the aeroplane roll firmly away from any sideslip, while weak directional stability lets the yaw overshoot. The result is an oscillation in which yaw and roll alternate: Dutch roll. Swept wings add a strong dihedral effect, so jets use yaw dampers. With strong directional and weak lateral stability the aeroplane instead tends to enter a slowly tightening spiral.
whyWrong: Directional divergence comes from negative directional stability, not merely weak directional stability.
The phugoid is a longitudinal mode, not a response to yaw.
Spiral instability is the result of the opposite balance: strong directional and weak lateral stability.
samples.examTip: Yaw damper fixes Dutch roll; it is the first thing to check when the motion appears.

samples.prompt: Yawing is a rotation around:
options: the normal axis controlled by elevator
the lateral axis controlled by rudder
the longitudinal axis controlled by ailerons
the normal axis controlled by rudder
samples.explanation: Yaw is rotation about the normal axis and is controlled by the rudder. Option A incorrectly pairs normal axis with elevator, B pairs lateral axis with rudder, and C pairs longitudinal axis with ailerons.

samples.prompt: A pilot rolls an aeroplane to the right using ailerons alone. In which direction does the nose initially yaw, and why?
options: Right, because the up-going aileron on the right wing increases that wing's drag
Right, because the rolling wing tilts the lift vector into the turn and pulls the nose round
Left, because the down-going aileron on the left wing increases that wing's lift and induced drag
Left, because the up-going aileron on the left wing reduces that wing's drag
samples.explanation: To roll right the left aileron goes down and the right aileron goes up. The down aileron increases the left wing's lift and therefore its induced drag; the up aileron reduces the right wing's lift and drag. The extra drag on the left wing yaws the nose left, away from the intended turn: adverse aileron yaw. The pilot corrects it with right rudder.
whyWrong: The right aileron goes UP and reduces that wing's lift and induced drag, so the right wing does not drag the nose round.
Tilting the lift vector produces the turn later; the initial yaw from the ailerons is opposite (adverse).
In a right roll the LEFT aileron goes down, not up, so this describes the wrong surface.
samples.examTip: Raising an aileron DECREASES that wing's lift.

samples.prompt: Which design features are used to reduce adverse aileron yaw?
options: Differential ailerons and Frise ailerons
Anti-balance tabs and servo tabs on the ailerons
Mass balance weights and horn balances
Washout and stall strips
samples.explanation: Differential ailerons move the up aileron through a larger angle than the down aileron, adding profile drag to the down-going wing. Frise ailerons have an offset hinge, so the nose of the up-going aileron projects below the wing into the airflow and adds drag on that side. Both reduce the drag imbalance. Coupling the ailerons to rudder or using roll spoilers are other methods.
whyWrong: Tabs alter control forces; they do not change the drag balance between the wings.
Mass balance prevents flutter and horn balance reduces stick forces; neither corrects adverse yaw.
Washout and stall strips shape the stall pattern, not the yaw from aileron deflection.
samples.examTip: 'Up aileron moves further' = differential.

samples.prompt: To trim an aeroplane for a nose-up attitude using an elevator trim tab, the tab moves:
options: Down, so the airflow on it holds the elevator up
Up, in the same direction as the elevator
Down, together with the elevator
Up, so the airflow on it pushes the tailplane down
samples.explanation: Nose-up trim needs the elevator held up. The trim tab is deflected down: the air striking it pushes the trailing edge of the elevator up and holds it there, so the pilot no longer needs to pull. Trim tabs always move opposite to the control surface they hold.
whyWrong: A trim tab moves OPPOSITE to the surface it holds; moving with it would increase the force.
The elevator must go up for nose-up trim, so it cannot move down with the tab.
The tab deflects the elevator, not the whole tailplane, and it moves down for nose-up trim.
samples.examTip: Anti-balance tabs are the exception: they move WITH the surface to increase feel.

samples.prompt: Why do many swept-wing jets lock out their outboard ailerons at high speed and roll with inboard ailerons and spoilers instead?
options: At high dynamic pressure outboard ailerons can twist the flexible wing tip enough to reduce or reverse the rolling moment
Outboard ailerons cause too much adverse yaw at high speed, which the yaw damper cannot correct
Outboard ailerons stall at high speed because the local Mach number there is lowest
Outboard ailerons are needed only with flap extended, because they cannot move with flap retracted
samples.explanation: A down-going aileron near the flexible tip pushes the trailing edge up, twisting the tip nose-down and reducing its angle of attack. At high dynamic pressure that twist can cancel the aileron's lift change, or even reverse it: aileron reversal. Inboard ailerons and roll spoilers act on the stiffer inner wing, so they remain effective. The outboard ailerons are unlocked when the flaps are extended at low speed.
whyWrong: Adverse yaw is greatest at LOW speed and high CL, not at high speed.
Ailerons do not stall at high speed; and the tip Mach number is not the lowest on the wing.
They are locked out when the flaps are retracted (high speed), but that is a design choice to avoid twisting, not a mechanical limit.
samples.examTip: Outboard ailerons lock out when the flaps are RETRACTED.

chapters.title: Flight Mechanics
topics: Effect of Weight, Altitude and Temperature
Rate of Descent in the Glide

samples.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes Vx and Vy?
options: Vx gives the greatest height gain per distance, and it is always higher than Vy
Vx gives the greatest height gain per time (maximum excess power); Vy gives the greatest height per distance (maximum excess thrust)
Vx and Vy are the same speed, but Vx is quoted as IAS and Vy as TAS
Vx gives the greatest height gain per distance (maximum excess thrust); Vy gives the greatest height gain per time (maximum excess power)
samples.explanation: The climb angle depends on excess thrust ÷ weight, so Vx is the speed of maximum (T − D): best angle, used to clear obstacles. The rate of climb depends on excess power ÷ weight, (T − D) × V / W, so Vy is the speed of maximum excess power: best rate, used to reach altitude quickly. Vy is faster than Vx; the two meet at the absolute ceiling.
whyWrong: Vx is LOWER than Vy below the absolute ceiling.
Reverses the two definitions.
They are different speeds in different units of performance, not one speed in two unit systems.
samples.examTip: 'Obstacle' in the question means Vx.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane flies a level turn at constant bank angle. If the TAS is doubled at the same bank angle, the turn radius:
options: Becomes four times as large
Doubles
Stays the same, because the bank angle sets the radius
Halves
samples.explanation: r = V² ÷ (g tan φ). At the same bank angle, g tan φ is unchanged, so r ∝ V²: doubling the TAS gives four times the radius. The rate of turn, ω = g tan φ / V, halves.
whyWrong: Radius depends on V², not V: r = V²/(g tan φ).
Bank sets the load factor, not the radius; the radius also depends on speed.
More speed at the same bank gives a LARGER radius.
samples.examTip: Faster = wider and slower-rate turn at the same bank.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies a level, coordinated turn at 85 kt TAS and 35° of bank. What is the radius of the turn, to the nearest 10 m? (g = 9.81 m/s², 1 kt = 0.5144 m/s)
samples.explanation: Formula: n = 1/cos φ; r = V²/(g tan φ); ω = g tan φ / V (V in m/s). r = V² ÷ (g tan φ). V = 85 kt × 0.5144 = 43.73 m/s. r = 43.73² ÷ (9.81 × tan 35°) = 1,912 ÷ 6.867 = 278 m (0.15 nm).
whyWrong: Used the speed in knots without converting it to m/s: gives 1,050 m.
Gave the diameter of the turn instead of its radius: gives 560 m.
Used sin φ instead of tan φ in r = V²/(g tan φ): gives 340 m.
samples.examTip: Convert knots to m/s first; tan for radius and rate, cos for load factor.

samples.prompt: What bank angle gives a rate-one turn (3°/s) at 180 kt TAS? (g = 9.81 m/s², 1 kt = 0.5144 m/s)
samples.explanation: tan φ = Vω ÷ g. V = 180 × 0.5144 = 92.6 m/s; ω = 3°/s = 0.05236 rad/s. tan φ = 92.6 × 0.05236 ÷ 9.81 = 0.494, so φ = 26.3°, about 26°. The rule of thumb (TAS ÷ 10) + 7 gives 25°, close enough for flying.
whyWrong: Used only TAS ÷ 10 and forgot to add 7 in the rule of thumb (and the rule is only approximate).
Used sin φ instead of tan φ: tan φ = Vω/g.
Used the speed in knots without converting to m/s.
samples.examTip: The rule of thumb works well between about 100 and 250 kt.

samples.prompt: A pilot rolls from 30° to 60° of bank in a level turn at constant IAS. Which statement is correct?
options: The load factor rises from 1.15 to 2, and the stall speed is unchanged because the IAS is constant
The load factor rises from about 1.15 to 2, and the stall speed rises by about 31%
The load factor doubles from 1 to 2, and the stall speed doubles
The load factor rises from 1.5 to 3, and the stall speed rises by about 41%
samples.explanation: n = 1/cos φ: 1/cos 30° = 1.155 and 1/cos 60° = 2.0. Stall speed ∝ √n, so it changes by √(2.0 ÷ 1.155) = √1.732 = 1.316, an increase of about 31%. Steep turns eat into the stall margin quickly.
whyWrong: The stall speed depends on the load factor, not the IAS being flown.
At 30° the load factor is already 1.15, and stall speed goes with √n, not n.
Uses wrong load factors: 1/cos 30° = 1.155 and 1/cos 60° = 2.
samples.examTip: Compare the two turns directly: ratio of the square roots of the load factors.

chapters.title: High Speed Flight
topics: Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS
Variation of TAS with Altitude at a Constant Mach Number
Influence of Temperature on Mach Number at a Constant Flight Level and IAS
Pressure Distribution at Transonic Mach Numbers

samples.prompt: At 15°C, the speed of sound is approximately:
options: 340 knots
661 knots
340 metres per second
661 metres per second
samples.explanation: At 15°C, the speed of sound is 340 metres per second, which is approximately 661 knots. Option B gives the value in knots, not metres per second.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane accelerates at constant altitude. At M0.72 the airflow over its wing first reaches Mach 1.0 at one point on the upper surface. For this aeroplane, M0.72 is its:
options: Maximum operating Mach number (MMO)
Drag-divergence Mach number
Critical Mach number (Mcrit)
Mach number for bow-wave detachment
samples.explanation: Air accelerates over the wing, so the local Mach number there is higher than the free-stream Mach. Mcrit is the free-stream Mach number at which the fastest local flow just reaches Mach 1. Above it a supersonic pocket forms, ending in a shock wave, and drag (wave drag) begins to rise; the steep rise (drag divergence) comes a little later.
whyWrong: MMO is a certified limit (the barber's pole) set above Mcrit with a margin; it is not defined by the first sonic point.
Drag divergence comes a little above Mcrit, once the shocks have strengthened and the drag rises steeply.
A bow wave forms only in supersonic flight, ahead of the aeroplane, at a free-stream Mach number above 1.
samples.examTip: Thin sections and sweepback raise Mcrit.

samples.prompt: What is the local speed of sound where the outside air temperature is −40 °C? (LSS kt = 38.94 √T, T in kelvin)
options: 246 kt
661 kt
573 kt
595 kt
samples.explanation: T = −40 + 273.15 = 233.15 K. LSS = 38.94 × √233.15 = 38.94 × 15.27 = 594.6 kt, about 595 kt. The speed of sound depends only on temperature: colder air, slower sound.
whyWrong: Used the Celsius temperature magnitude (38.94 × √40) instead of kelvin.
661 kt is the ISA sea-level value at +15 °C.
573 kt is the value at −56.5 °C, the ISA tropopause temperature.
samples.examTip: Altitude affects LSS only through temperature.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane climbs at a constant TAS through the ISA troposphere. What happens to its Mach number?
options: It increases, because the temperature and so the local speed of sound fall
It stays the same, because Mach number follows the TAS
It decreases, because the density falls and the airspeed indicator under-reads
It increases, because the dynamic pressure rises with the TAS held constant
samples.explanation: M = TAS ÷ LSS, and LSS = 38.94√T falls as the temperature falls with height in the troposphere. At constant TAS the Mach number therefore rises. Above the tropopause in ISA the temperature is constant, so constant TAS then means constant Mach.
whyWrong: Constant TAS gives constant Mach only where the temperature (LSS) is constant, as in the lower stratosphere.
Mach number does not depend on density; it is TAS ÷ LSS.
At constant TAS the dynamic pressure FALLS with height.
samples.examTip: Climbing at constant IAS increases Mach even faster (TAS rises and LSS falls).

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about the flow through a normal shock wave: 1. The flow behind the shock is subsonic. 2. Static pressure, temperature and density all increase. 3. Total (stagnation) pressure increases. 4. The flow direction changes. Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
samples.explanation: Across a normal shock the flow decelerates suddenly from supersonic to subsonic, and static pressure, temperature and density rise. The process is irreversible, so some energy is lost and total pressure decreases; that loss shows up as wave drag. A normal shock lies at right angles to the flow and does not change its direction; an oblique shock turns the flow and leaves it still supersonic if weak.
whyWrong: Includes 3: a shock is an irreversible compression, so total pressure FALLS.
Leaves out 1 and includes 3 and 4, both wrong.
Includes 4: a NORMAL shock does not turn the flow; an oblique shock does.
samples.examTip: 'Total pressure increases' in any shock option is wrong.

chapters.title: High Speed Flight II: Buffet, Sweep and Supersonic Flow
topics: The Aerodynamic Ceiling and Coffin Corner

samples.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between Mach number, TAS, and local speed of sound?
options: M = TAS × a
M = a / TAS
M = TAS / a
M = IAS / a
samples.explanation: Mach number is defined as the ratio of True Airspeed (TAS) to the local speed of sound (a). Option A is incorrect as it multiplies rather than divides. Option B inverts the ratio. Option D uses IAS instead of TAS, which is incorrect as Mach number uses TAS.

samples.prompt: An aircraft stalls at 125 kt in level flight. What is its stall speed in a level 50° banked turn?
options: 100 kt
156 kt
143 kt
194 kt
samples.explanation: Load factor n = 1/cos 50° = 1.556. Stall speed rises with √n: 125 × √1.556 = 156 kt.
whyWrong: Divided by √n instead of multiplying
Used sin of the bank angle instead of cos
Multiplied by the load factor instead of √n
samples.examTip: Common trap: divided by √n instead of multiplying.

samples.prompt: A wing swept back 30° flies at Mach 0.80. Using the simple cosine rule, what Mach number does the airflow normal to the leading edge see?
samples.explanation: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the leading edge accelerates over the section. M(normal) = M × cos Λ = 0.80 × cos 30° = 0.80 × 0.866 = 0.69. In practice the benefit is less than the simple rule suggests, but sweepback clearly raises Mcrit.
whyWrong: Multiplied by sin 30° instead of cos 30°.
Ignores the sweep; only the component normal to the leading edge drives the pressure distribution.
Divided by cos 30° instead of multiplying.

samples.prompt: Why does a swept-back wing tend to pitch up at the stall?
options: The roots stall first, so the separated wake hits the tailplane and forces it down
The tips stall first, so lift is lost ahead of the CG and the centre of pressure moves rearward
The tips stall first, so lift is lost behind the CG and the centre of pressure moves forward
The leading-edge slats retract automatically at high angle of attack
samples.explanation: On a swept wing spanwise flow thickens the boundary layer towards the tips, which are also more highly loaded, so the tips tend to stall first. The tips are behind the root on a swept wing, so losing their lift moves the centre of pressure forward and pitches the nose up, deepening the stall. Fences, vortilons, saw-tooth leading edges and washout are used to limit it.
whyWrong: Root-first stalling is the benign pattern of a straight wing with washout; it pitches the nose down.
On a swept wing the tips lie BEHIND the root, so losing tip lift moves the CP forward, not rearward.
Slats do not retract on their own; this is not the mechanism.
samples.examTip: Swept-wing pitch-up and straight-wing nose drop are a favourite contrast.

samples.prompt: A heavy jet cruises close to its maximum altitude. The crew notice that the margin between the low-speed buffet and the high-speed buffet is very small. What is this situation called, and what makes it worse?
options: Coffin corner; reducing mass, because the stall speed falls below the low-speed buffet
Dutch roll; turning, because the yaw damper becomes ineffective at altitude
Mach tuck; reducing speed, because the centre of pressure moves forward
Coffin corner; a turn or turbulence, because the higher load factor brings the two buffet limits even closer
samples.explanation: As altitude rises, the IAS for the stall (and low-speed buffet) corresponds to an ever higher Mach number, while the high-speed buffet Mach stays roughly fixed. Near the aeroplane's ceiling the two meet: the 'coffin corner'. A higher load factor, from a turn or turbulence, raises the low-speed buffet speed and lowers the high-speed buffet Mach, so the margin shrinks further. Buffet-onset charts give the altitude that preserves a chosen margin.
whyWrong: Burning fuel (less mass) WIDENS the margin; it is high mass and high load factor that narrow it.
Dutch roll is a lateral-directional oscillation and is unrelated to buffet margins.
Mach tuck is a nose-down pitch at high Mach; it is not about buffet margins.
samples.examTip: Check the buffet margin with the planned bank angle before accepting a higher cruise level.

chapters.title: Limitations
topics: Effect of Aircraft Weight on VA

samples.prompt: On a light aeroplane's airspeed indicator, what does the top of the green arc mark?
options: VFE, the maximum flap-extended speed
VA, the design manoeuvring speed at maximum mass
VNE, the never-exceed speed
VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed
samples.explanation: The green arc is the normal operating range, from VS1 (stall, clean) to VNO. The yellow (caution) arc runs from VNO to VNE, to be used only in smooth air. The white arc is the flap operating range, from VS0 to VFE, and the red line is VNE.
whyWrong: VFE is the top of the white arc.
VA is not normally marked on the ASI; it is placarded or in the manual.
VNE is the red radial line at the top of the yellow arc.
samples.examTip: Bottom of the white arc = VS0 (landing configuration); bottom of the green = VS1.

samples.prompt: For an aeroplane certificated in the Normal category under CS-23 / FAR 23, the limit manoeuvring load factors are:
samples.explanation: Normal category light aeroplanes are designed for limit load factors of +3.8 g and −1.52 g (the negative limit is 0.4 × the positive). Utility is +4.4 / −1.76 and Aerobatic +6.0 / −3.0. A structure must carry the limit load without permanent deformation and 1.5 × limit (the ultimate load) without failure.
whyWrong: +2.5 / −1.0 are typical large transport (CS-25) limits in the clean configuration.
+6.0 / −3.0 are the Aerobatic category limits.
+4.4 / −1.76 are the Utility category limits.
samples.examTip: Negative limit = 0.4 × positive for Normal and Utility; −3 for Aerobatic.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 60 kt IAS at maximum mass and a positive limit load factor of 3.8. What is its design manoeuvring speed VA at that mass?
options: 117 kt
228 kt
91 kt
126 kt
samples.explanation: VA is the speed at which the aeroplane stalls exactly at the limit load factor: VA = Vs × √n = 60 × √3.8 = 60 × 1.949 = 117 kt. Below VA a full, abrupt control input stalls the wing before the limit load is reached; above it the structure can be overstressed.
whyWrong: Multiplied by the load factor instead of its square root.
Used √(3.8 − 1.5) or a similar subtraction; VA = Vs√n.
Used the Utility category factor of 4.4 instead of 3.8 (60 × √4.4).

samples.prompt: A pilot flying a light aeroplane well below maximum mass meets severe turbulence. The manual gives VA only at maximum mass. What should the pilot consider?
options: The safe manoeuvring speed is lower at the lower mass, because the stall speed falls with √mass
The manoeuvring speed only matters above maximum mass
VA does not depend on mass, so the published figure applies
The safe manoeuvring speed is higher at the lower mass, because the aeroplane is lighter
samples.explanation: VA = Vs√n, and Vs ∝ √(mass). At a lower mass the stall speed falls, so the speed at which a full control input or a gust produces the limit load factor also falls: VA ∝ √(mass). Flying at the maximum-mass VA when light could allow the limit load to be exceeded before the stall offers protection.
whyWrong: VA is a structural protection at all masses; the concern is lower masses, not higher.
VA = Vs√n and Vs ∝ √W, so VA ∝ √W: it does depend on mass.
A lighter aeroplane reaches the limit load factor at a LOWER speed, so its VA is lower.
samples.examTip: Rough-air speed questions usually test this √mass rule.

samples.prompt: Two aeroplanes fly through the same vertical gust at the same EAS. Aeroplane P has a much higher wing loading than aeroplane Q. Which statement is correct?
options: P experiences the smaller load factor increment, because the same change in lift is shared by more weight per unit area
Both experience the same increment, because the gust and EAS are the same
P experiences the larger load factor increment, because it is heavier
Q experiences the smaller increment, because its lower stall speed protects it
samples.explanation: A vertical gust changes the angle of attack by about U/V, changing lift by ½ρV²S × a × U/V. The load factor change Δn = ΔL/W ∝ ρ V a U ÷ (2 W/S). A higher wing loading (W/S) therefore gives a smaller Δn, a smoother ride. A higher speed or a steeper lift curve gives a larger Δn.
whyWrong: The increment depends on wing loading and the lift-curve slope as well as gust and speed.
