The lift change from the gust is the same per square metre; dividing by a larger weight per square metre gives a SMALLER Δn.
The lower stall speed does not reduce the gust response; a lightly loaded wing feels gusts more.
samples.examTip: Swept wings (shallow lift curve) and high wing loading both soften gust response.

chapters.title: Windshear
topics: Effects of Windshear — Energy Gain and Energy Loss

samples.prompt: Microbursts are associated with which type of cloud?
options: Stratus clouds
Cumulonimbus clouds
Cirrus clouds
Altocumulus clouds
samples.explanation: Microbursts are intense, localised downdraughts produced by thunderstorms (cumulonimbus clouds), and sometimes by heavy showers or virga below convective cloud.

samples.prompt: On a stabilised approach at 140 kt IAS into a 30 kt headwind, the wind suddenly drops to calm. Ignoring any pilot input, what is the immediate IAS?
options: 125 kt
140 kt
170 kt
110 kt
samples.explanation: Inertia keeps the groundspeed at 140 − 30 = 110 kt for a moment. With the wind now calm, airspeed = groundspeed = 110 kt: a 30 kt loss of IAS. The aeroplane also tends to sink below the glide path until thrust and attitude restore the speed.
whyWrong: Halved the change; the whole 30 kt change appears in the airspeed at first.
Assumed the aeroplane instantly adapts; its inertia holds the groundspeed, not the airspeed.
Added the lost headwind; losing a headwind REDUCES airspeed.
samples.examTip: Headwind decreasing (or tailwind increasing) = performance-decreasing shear.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a performance-decreasing windshear for an aeroplane on final approach?
options: A sudden increase in tailwind
Entry into a strong downdraft
A sudden decrease in headwind
A sudden increase in headwind
samples.explanation: A shear is performance-increasing if it raises the airspeed or lifts the aeroplane, and performance-decreasing if it lowers the airspeed or pushes it down. An increasing headwind raises the IAS, so the aeroplane goes above the glide path: performance increasing. It is often followed by the opposite shear, so it still demands attention.
whyWrong: Gaining tailwind lowers the airspeed: performance decreasing.
A downdraft pushes the aeroplane below the glide path: performance decreasing.
Losing headwind lowers the airspeed: performance decreasing.
samples.examTip: Think airspeed first: up is increasing, down is decreasing.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane flies an approach through a microburst. What sequence of effects should the crew expect?
options: A tailwind first, then a downdraft, then an increasing headwind that brings the aeroplane back up
An increasing headwind (airspeed up, above the glide path), then a downdraft, then a tailwind (airspeed down, sinking)
An updraft in the centre with an increasing headwind on the far side
A steady downdraft only, with no change in the horizontal wind
samples.explanation: A microburst is a concentrated downdraft that spreads out on hitting the ground. An approaching aeroplane first meets the outflow as an increasing headwind: airspeed rises and it balloons above the path, which tempts the pilot to reduce thrust. It then flies through the downdraft and finally into the tailwind outflow, losing airspeed and sinking just when it is low and slow.
whyWrong: Reverses the order: the outflow ahead of the core meets the approaching aeroplane as a headwind.
The core of a microburst is a downdraft, not an updraft.
The downdraft spreads out at the ground, so strong horizontal outflow winds are part of the hazard.
samples.examTip: The early airspeed gain is the trap: do not take the thrust off.

samples.prompt: During take-off the crew get a windshear warning just after lift-off. Which recovery technique is generally recommended (subject to the aircraft manual)?
options: Reduce thrust to avoid an overspeed in the gust, and climb at the normal speed
Maximum thrust, wings level, pitch to the recommended attitude, and no configuration change until clear
Raise the landing gear and flaps at once to clean up the aeroplane, then follow the normal climb profile and speeds
Lower the nose to gain speed, retract the flaps to reduce drag, and accept a shallow descent until the airspeed recovers
samples.explanation: Windshear recovery uses all available energy: maximum (go-around or take-off) thrust, wings level, and pitch to the recommended attitude or flight-director guidance, accepting stick-shaker limits if necessary. Gear and flap are left alone until the aeroplane is clear of the shear, because changing configuration costs lift. Speed is sacrificed to protect height.
whyWrong: Reducing thrust is the wrong response; maximum thrust is needed.
Changing configuration during the encounter can reduce lift and add a transient sink; it is left until clear.
Trading height for speed close to the ground is exactly what causes windshear accidents.
samples.examTip: 'Retract flap' or 'reduce thrust' in a windshear option is wrong.

chapters.title: Propellers
topics: Moments and Forces Generated by a Propeller

samples.prompt: A propeller blade element's chord line makes 25° with the plane of rotation and 7° with the relative airflow. Which set names the three angles correctly?
options: Angle of attack 25°, blade angle 7°, helix angle 32°
Helix angle 25°, angle of attack 7°, blade angle 32°
Blade angle 25°, angle of attack 7°, helix angle 18°
Blade angle 25°, helix angle 7°, angle of attack 18°
samples.explanation: Blade (pitch) angle: chord line to the plane of rotation, here 25°. Angle of attack: chord line to the relative airflow, here 7°. Helix angle: the element's resultant path through the air (from rotation plus forward speed) to the plane of rotation, so helix = blade angle − angle of attack = 25° − 7° = 18°.
whyWrong: The angle of attack is measured from the airflow and the blade angle from the plane of rotation; this reverses them.
Calls the chord's angle to the plane of rotation the helix angle; the helix angle is the AIRFLOW's angle to that plane.
Swaps the helix angle and the angle of attack: the angle between the chord and the airflow is the angle of attack.
samples.examTip: Learn the three angles as a set; questions swap their definitions.

samples.prompt: Why is a propeller blade twisted, with the blade angle decreasing from root to tip?
options: The tip moves more slowly than the root, so it needs a larger blade angle to produce the same thrust as the inner part of the blade
Rotational speed rises with radius, so the helix angle falls towards the tip; less blade angle there keeps the AoA roughly constant
Twist moves the centre of thrust to the tip, which increases propeller efficiency
Twist prevents the blade from bending forward under the thrust load
samples.explanation: Every blade element moves forward at the same TAS, but its rotational speed is 2πr × rpm, which grows with radius. The helix angle is therefore large near the root and small near the tip. To give each element a similar, efficient angle of attack, the blade angle must also fall from root to tip: the blade is twisted.
whyWrong: The tip moves FASTER than the root; this reverses the reason.
Twist spreads the loading evenly; it is not intended to concentrate thrust at the tip.
Blade bending is handled by the structure; twist is an aerodynamic feature.
samples.examTip: Root: large helix and blade angles; tip: small ones.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane with a fixed-pitch propeller accelerates in level flight at a constant rpm. What happens to the propeller blade's angle of attack?
options: It decreases, because the higher forward speed increases the helix angle
It decreases, because the blade angle reduces as the rpm rises
It stays the same, because the blade angle is fixed
It increases, because the higher forward speed reduces the helix angle
samples.explanation: AoA = blade angle − helix angle. On a fixed-pitch propeller the blade angle cannot change. Higher TAS at the same rotational speed increases the helix angle, so the angle of attack falls and the propeller absorbs less power. A fixed-pitch propeller is efficient at only one combination of TAS and rpm, which is why 'climb' and 'cruise' propellers exist.
whyWrong: A fixed-pitch blade angle cannot change; the rpm is constant in this question anyway.
With a fixed blade angle, any change in helix angle changes the angle of attack.
More forward speed INCREASES the helix angle.
samples.examTip: Low speed with a coarse fixed-pitch propeller: very high AoA, risk of blade stall on take-off.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane with a constant-speed propeller enters a shallow dive with the throttle and rpm lever untouched. What does the constant-speed unit do?
options: Increases the blade angle (coarsens) to hold the rpm as the TAS rises
Reduces the manifold pressure to prevent an overspeed
Holds the blade angle constant and lets the rpm rise
Decreases the blade angle (fines) to hold the rpm as the TAS rises
samples.explanation: In the dive the TAS rises, the helix angle increases and the blade's angle of attack and torque fall, so the propeller tries to speed up. The governor senses the overspeed and increases the blade angle (coarser pitch), restoring the angle of attack and the load, so the rpm stays at the selected value.
whyWrong: The CSU controls blade angle, not manifold pressure; that is set by the throttle.
Holding the blade angle constant is fixed-pitch behaviour; the governor exists to change it.
Fining the blade at higher TAS would reduce the load further and let the rpm run away.
samples.examTip: 'Constant speed' means constant rpm, not constant airspeed.

samples.prompt: A propeller turns at 2,400 rpm. At a radius of 1.0 m the blade angle is 20°, and the aeroplane flies at 120 kt TAS. What is the angle of attack of that blade element (ignore induced flow)?
whyWrong: Used 2,400 as revolutions per second instead of per minute, so the helix angle came out almost zero.
Gave the helix angle, not the angle of attack.
Added the helix angle to the blade angle.
samples.examTip: Rotational speed uses 2πr; the tip uses the full radius, i.e. π × diameter.

samples.prompt: A new control zone is being designed around an aerodrome. According to ICAO Annex 11, which vertical limits define a control zone (CTR)?
options: From 1,000 ft above aerodrome elevation up to the base of the TMA
From the surface of the earth up to a specified upper limit
From the surface up to FL 245 in every case
From a specified height above the surface (not less than 700 ft) up to a specified upper limit
samples.explanation: A control zone is controlled airspace extending upwards from the surface of the earth to a specified upper limit. It protects IFR flights arriving at and departing from the aerodrome right down to the ground. A control area, by contrast, starts at a specified limit above the earth, which Annex 11 sets at not less than 200 m (700 ft) above ground or water.
whyWrong: Invents a lower limit: the whole point of a CTR is that it starts at the surface to protect departures and arrivals.
No fixed upper limit is laid down; the CTR's upper limit is set to suit the procedures it protects.
That is a control area (CTA), whose lower limit is above the surface.
samples.examTip: If the lower limit is 'the surface', the answer is a CTR.

samples.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a terminal control area (TMA)?
options: A control area where ATS routes converge near one or more major aerodromes
A control zone extending from the surface around a single aerodrome
Uncontrolled airspace in which only flight information service is given to terminal traffic
Airspace above an aerodrome reserved for aerodrome traffic within the circuit
samples.explanation: A TMA is a type of control area, so it starts above the surface. It is placed where many ATS routes converge near one or more busy aerodromes so that arriving and departing IFR traffic can be sequenced under an approach control service. The CTRs of the aerodromes normally sit underneath it.
whyWrong: Confuses a TMA (an elevated control area) with a CTR, which starts at the surface.
A TMA is controlled airspace; FIS-only airspace is Class G.
That describes an aerodrome traffic zone, which protects circuit traffic and is much smaller.
samples.examTip: TMA and CTA both start above the ground; only the CTR starts at the surface.

samples.prompt: Within a flight information region (FIR), which services are provided as a minimum?
options: Air traffic control service and alerting service
Air traffic control service, flight information service and alerting service
Air traffic advisory service only
Flight information service and alerting service
samples.explanation: An FIR is airspace of defined dimensions within which flight information service and alerting service are provided. ATC service exists only within the controlled airspace (CTRs, CTAs, TMAs, airways) inside it. India is divided into four FIRs: Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai.
whyWrong: ATC is given only in controlled airspace, which is a subset of the FIR.
Adds ATC, which is not provided throughout an FIR.
Advisory service is only given in advisory airspace or on advisory routes.
samples.examTip: FIR is about information and alerting, never ATC by itself.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane is pushed back at 0905, starts its take-off roll at 0921, lands at 1047 and stops on stand at 1056. Using the ICAO definition of flight time for aeroplanes, what is the flight time?
options: 1 h 51 min
1 h 42 min
1 h 35 min
1 h 26 min
samples.explanation: Flight time for aeroplanes is the total time from the moment the aeroplane first moves for the purpose of taking off until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight (block time). Here 0905 to 1056 = 1 h 51 min.
whyWrong: Starts at off-blocks but ends at touchdown, omitting the taxi-in.
Starts at take-off and ends on stand, mixing the two definitions.
Measures from the start of the take-off roll to touchdown: that is airborne time, not flight time.
samples.examTip: Flight time includes taxiing; airborne time does not.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Annex 11, the lateral limits of a control zone shall extend from the centre of the aerodrome, in the directions from which approaches may be made, to at least:
options: 9.3 km (5 NM)
46 km (25 NM)
samples.explanation: Annex 11 requires the lateral limits of a CTR to encompass at least the airspace not covered by control areas that contains the paths of IFR flights arriving and departing, and to extend at least 9.3 km (5 NM) from the centre of the aerodrome in the directions from which approaches may be made. In practice many CTRs are larger.
whyWrong: Halves the figure; 2.5 NM would not contain an instrument approach.
25 NM is the radius of a minimum sector altitude, not a CTR.
Doubles the figure; 10 NM is not the Annex 11 minimum for a CTR.
samples.examTip: 25 NM belongs to MSA; 5 NM belongs to the CTR.

samples.prompt: Article 1 of the Chicago Convention establishes that every State has:
options: Complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory
The right to overfly any other contracting State without landing
Exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory up to FL 660
Sovereignty over the airspace above the high seas adjacent to its coast
samples.explanation: Article 1 says the contracting States recognise that every State has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory. Article 2 defines territory as the land areas and the territorial waters adjacent to them under the sovereignty of that State. Over the high seas, Article 12 requires the rules established under the Convention (Annex 2) to apply.
whyWrong: Overflight is a freedom of the air granted by separate agreements, not a right under Article 1.
No altitude limit is stated; sovereignty is over the airspace above the territory.
The high seas belong to no State; Article 12 applies the ICAO rules of the air there.
samples.examTip: Sovereignty covers land plus territorial waters, not the high seas.

samples.prompt: A contracting State finds it cannot comply with an ICAO Standard. What does Article 38 of the Chicago Convention require it to do?
options: Comply anyway, because Standards are binding without exception
Apply to the ICAO Council for a temporary exemption before the Standard takes effect
Notify ICAO immediately of the difference between its national practice and the Standard
Do nothing, because only Recommended Practices need to be notified
samples.explanation: Article 38: a State that finds it impracticable to comply with an international Standard, or that adopts different regulations, shall give immediate notification to ICAO of the differences. ICAO then notifies all other States. The differences are also published in the State's AIP, section GEN 1.7.
whyWrong: States may depart from Standards, but must say so.
There is no exemption procedure; the Convention requires notification of the difference.
Reverses the rule: notifying differences from Standards is the obligation; for Recommended Practices it is only invited.
samples.examTip: 'Must' goes with Standards, 'invited/should' with Recommended Practices.

samples.prompt: An Indian airline wants to carry passengers between Delhi and Mumbai on a foreign-registered aircraft it has leased. Which concept in the Chicago Convention lets India reserve such domestic traffic for its own carriers?
options: Article 5 non-scheduled flight rights
Article 17 nationality of aircraft
The fifth freedom of the air
Cabotage (Article 7)
samples.explanation: Article 7 lets each State refuse permission to the aircraft of other contracting States to take on passengers, mail and cargo for carriage for remuneration to another point within its territory. This carriage within one State is called cabotage, and most States reserve it for their own carriers.
whyWrong: Article 5 lets non-scheduled flights of other States fly into or across a State; it does not cover domestic carriage.
Article 17 says aircraft take the nationality of their State of registry; it does not deal with domestic traffic rights.
The fifth freedom concerns traffic between two foreign States, not traffic within one State.
samples.examTip: 'Within the same country' = cabotage, never a freedom of the air number.

samples.prompt: An airline of State A flies from its home base to State B, picks up passengers in B and carries them on to State C. Which freedom of the air is it exercising on the B–C sector?
options: Fourth freedom
Fifth freedom
Third freedom
Second freedom
samples.explanation: 1st: overfly a foreign State. 2nd: land in it for non-traffic purposes (fuel, maintenance). 3rd: carry traffic from the home State to a foreign State. 4th: carry traffic from a foreign State to the home State. 5th: carry traffic between two foreign States on a service that starts or ends in the home State. The B–C sector is fifth freedom.
whyWrong: The fourth freedom is carrying traffic from another State back to the home State.
The third freedom is carrying traffic from the home State to another State.
The second freedom is a technical stop without traffic rights.
samples.examTip: Freedoms 1 and 2 are the 'transit' freedoms; 3 to 5 are traffic freedoms.

samples.prompt: Under the Tokyo Convention, an aircraft is considered to be 'in flight' for the purpose of the commander's powers:
options: From the moment the aircraft first moves under its own power until it comes to rest at the end of the flight
From the time the flight plan is activated until it is closed
From the moment all external doors are closed after embarkation until any such door is opened for disembarkation
From the start of the take-off run until the end of the landing run
samples.explanation: For the commander's powers, the Tokyo Convention treats the aircraft as in flight from the moment all its external doors are closed after embarkation until any such door is opened for disembarkation. This covers taxiing with passengers on board. A forced landing continues the period until the authorities take over.
whyWrong: That is the ICAO flight time definition, which has nothing to do with the doors.
Flight plan activation is an ATS matter, not the trigger for the commander's powers.
That is a much shorter, purely airborne window and would leave taxiing and boarding gaps uncovered.
samples.examTip: Doors, not wheels, define the commander's authority period.

chapters.title: Aircraft Nationality
topics: Certificate of Registration — Contents and Validity
Display of State Marks and Advertisements

samples.prompt: Which of these is correctly written as the nationality and registration mark of an Indian aircraft?
options: IN-KGW
KGW-VT
VTKGW
VT-KGW
samples.explanation: India's nationality mark is VT, followed by a hyphen and a registration mark of three letters, for example VT-KGW. ICAO Annex 7 requires a hyphen between the nationality mark and the registration mark when the nationality mark is made of letters.
whyWrong: IN is not India's nationality mark; India uses VT.
The nationality mark always comes first, followed by the registration mark.
Runs the marks together; Annex 7 requires a hyphen between them when both are letters.
samples.examTip: The hyphen is part of the legal mark.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Annex 7, the marks on the lower surface of the wings of a heavier-than-air aircraft shall be at least how high?
options: 30 cm
50 cm
15 cm
75 cm
samples.explanation: Annex 7: marks on the wings of heavier-than-air aircraft shall be at least 50 cm high; marks on the fuselage (or equivalent) and on the vertical tail surfaces shall be at least 30 cm high. The letters are capital Roman characters without ornamentation, and numbers are Arabic numerals.
whyWrong: 30 cm is the Annex 7 minimum for the fuselage and vertical tail marks.
Far too small to be seen from the ground.
Larger than the minimum; Annex 7 sets 50 cm.
samples.examTip: Two numbers to remember: 50 (wings) and 30 (fuselage/tail).

samples.prompt: Under ICAO Annex 7, which of the following registration marks would NOT be allowed because it could be confused with an urgent or distress signal?
options: VT-TTA
VT-SON
VT-PAR
VT-PAN
samples.explanation: Annex 7 forbids letter combinations that could be confused with the five-letter combinations of the International Code of Signals, three-letter combinations beginning with Q used in the Q code, the distress signal SOS, or other urgent signals such as XXX, PAN and TTT. PAN is the urgency signal, so VT-PAN is not allowed.
whyWrong: TTA is not TTT and is acceptable.
SON is not SOS and is acceptable.
PAR is not a signal; it is an acceptable combination.
samples.examTip: Look for SOS, PAN, XXX, TTT or a leading Q.

samples.prompt: An aircraft's identification plate required by ICAO Annex 7 must be:
options: Carried loose in the journey log book so that it can be shown to inspectors
Made of any durable plastic, showing the owner's name, and fixed inside the flight deck
Painted on the vertical tail, showing the manufacturer's serial number only
Fireproof, bearing the nationality and registration mark, fixed near the main entrance
samples.explanation: Annex 7 requires an identification plate inscribed with at least the nationality or common mark and registration mark. It must be made of fireproof metal or other fireproof material of suitable physical properties, and secured in a prominent position near the main entrance (or, for unmanned free balloons, as the Annex describes). It survives a fire and identifies the wreckage.
whyWrong: The plate must be secured to the aircraft so that it survives an accident.
Plastic is not fireproof, and the owner's name is not the required inscription.
Confuses the plate with the painted marks; the plate is a separate fireproof item.
samples.examTip: 'Fireproof' and 'near the main entrance' are the two key words.

samples.prompt: During a flight, a bird strike causes structural damage to an Indian-registered aircraft at a foreign aerodrome. According to ICAO Annex 8, who decides whether the damage makes the aircraft unairworthy?
options: The State in which the damage occurred
The State of the operator's main base only
The State of registry
The aircraft manufacturer
samples.explanation: Annex 8 makes the State of registry the judge of whether damage is such that the aircraft is no longer airworthy. If damage is sustained in another State, that State may prevent the aircraft from resuming its flight while informing the State of registry. The State of registry may then allow a flight under prescribed limitations to an aerodrome where it can be restored to an airworthy condition.
whyWrong: The local State may prevent it from flying while it is there, but the airworthiness judgement belongs to the State of registry.
The State of registry, not merely the operator's base, holds the airworthiness responsibility.
The manufacturer gives technical support, but the regulatory decision is the State's.
samples.examTip: Registry State = owner of the CofA = decides airworthiness.

chapters.title: Section 4
topics: Table of Cruising Levels — CVSM and RVSM
Air Traffic Services — Classification and Designation

samples.prompt: Two power-driven aeroplanes are converging at about the same level. Aeroplane X sees aeroplane Y on its right. Which aircraft must give way?
options: X, the aircraft that has the other on its right
Both must turn right
The aircraft at the higher speed
Y, the aircraft that has the other on its left
samples.explanation: Annex 2: when two aircraft are converging at approximately the same level, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way. The aircraft with the right of way maintains its heading and speed. Giving way normally means avoiding passing over, under or in front of the other aircraft unless well clear.
whyWrong: Both turning right is the rule for head-on approaches, not converging.
Speed does not decide right of way.
Y has right of way because it is on X's right; it maintains heading and speed.
samples.examTip: 'Has the other on its right' gives way; 'is on the right' has priority.

samples.prompt: An aeroplane is approaching a glider at about the same level on converging courses. A balloon is also nearby. Which is the correct order of right of way, from the aircraft that gives way to all others to the one that has priority over all others?
options: Balloon, glider, airship, power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft
Airship, power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft, balloon, glider
Glider, balloon, airship, power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft
Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft, airship, glider, balloon
samples.explanation: Annex 2: power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, gliders and balloons; airships give way to gliders and balloons; gliders give way to balloons. The less manoeuvrable the aircraft, the greater its priority. Power-driven aircraft also give way to aircraft seen towing other aircraft or objects.
whyWrong: Reverses the order: the balloon is the least manoeuvrable and has priority over all.
Airships have priority over power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft, not the other way round.
A glider must give way to a balloon, but it has priority over power-driven aircraft and airships.
samples.examTip: The more manoeuvrable, the more it gives way.

samples.prompt: An aircraft in the circuit without radio receives a series of green flashes from the control tower. What does it mean?
options: Cleared to land
Return for landing
Land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
samples.explanation: Annex 2 light signals to aircraft in flight: steady green = cleared to land; steady red = give way to other aircraft and continue circling; series of green flashes = return for landing (a clearance to land and taxi will follow in due course); series of red flashes = aerodrome unsafe, do not land; series of white flashes = land at this aerodrome and proceed to apron. A red pyrotechnic means: notwithstanding any previous instructions, do not land for the time being.
whyWrong: A steady green, not flashes, is the clearance to land.
That is a series of white flashes.
That is a series of red flashes.
samples.examTip: Steady signals are the stronger instructions; flashes are the 'stand by / prepare' versions.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is overtaking another from behind. Under ICAO Annex 2, which statement is correct?
options: The overtaking aircraft alters heading to the left, whether climbing, descending or level
Both aircraft alter heading to the right
The aircraft ahead has right of way; the overtaking aircraft alters heading to the right
The overtaking aircraft has the right of way because it is faster
samples.explanation: An overtaking aircraft is one approaching another from the rear on a line forming an angle of less than 70° with the plane of symmetry of the latter (so its navigation lights would be the white tail light). The overtaken aircraft has right of way, and the overtaking aircraft, whether climbing, descending or in level flight, keeps out of the way by altering heading to the right. This remains so until it is entirely past and clear.
whyWrong: The alteration is to the right, not the left.
Both turning right is the head-on rule; the overtaken aircraft maintains heading and speed.
Speed gives no priority; the aircraft ahead has right of way.
samples.examTip: '70° from the rear' ties in with the 140° white tail light sector.

samples.prompt: At night, in level cruise, a pilot sees another aircraft's steady red navigation light (no green light visible) at the same level, ahead and to the right, at a constant relative bearing. What is happening and what should the pilot do?
options: The other aircraft is being overtaken; the pilot must pass it on the left
It is converging from the right; the pilot gives way, passing behind it
The other aircraft is approaching head-on; both must turn right
The other aircraft is converging from the right but must give way, because the pilot sees its red light
samples.explanation: Navigation lights: red on the left wingtip and green on the right, each showing through 110° from dead ahead, with white at the tail through 140° (70° each side). Seeing only the red light on your right means you are looking at the left side of an aircraft crossing from your right. A constant relative bearing means a collision course. You have it on your right, so you give way, passing behind it rather than in front.
whyWrong: An aircraft seen from behind shows its white tail light, not its red light.
A head-on aircraft shows both red and green lights at once.
Reverses the rule: the aircraft that has the other on its right gives way, and here that is the observing pilot.
samples.examTip: Constant relative bearing means collision course.

chapters.title: Section 5
topics: ATS Routes in India — Specific Rules

samples.prompt: An ATIS broadcast has just been updated from information 'Echo'. What will the new broadcast be called?
options: Information Echo Two
Information Alpha
Information Echo, with a new time
Information Foxtrot
samples.explanation: Each ATIS message is identified by a letter of the ICAO spelling alphabet, assigned in consecutive alphabetical order. A new message with the next letter is issued as soon as a significant change occurs. On first contact with approach or tower the pilot confirms receipt by quoting the letter.
whyWrong: ATIS messages use single consecutive letters of the spelling alphabet, not numbers.
The sequence continues; it does not restart after each change.
A new message must have a new letter so that pilots can tell which one they have.
samples.examTip: Quote the ATIS letter on first contact: 'with information Foxtrot'.

samples.prompt: Which of these situations would cause the distress phase (DETRESFA) to be declared?
options: A routine position report is 30 minutes overdue
The fuel on board is considered exhausted, and nothing has been heard from the aircraft
The pilot reports a failed alternator but expects to reach the destination normally
The aircraft is known to be the subject of unlawful interference
samples.explanation: Annex 11: the distress phase exists when, after the alert phase, further unsuccessful attempts and widespread inquiries point to the probability that the aircraft is in distress; when the fuel on board is considered exhausted or insufficient to reach safety; when information indicates that operating efficiency is impaired so much that a forced landing is likely; or when information is received that the aircraft is about to make or has made a forced landing.
whyWrong: An overdue report starts the uncertainty phase, not distress.
Impaired efficiency that does not make a forced landing likely is at most an alert-phase case.
Unlawful interference triggers the alert phase.
samples.examTip: Rank the triggers by how bad the news is.

samples.prompt: An IFR flight should have made a position report at 1015. Nothing has been heard, and no attempt to call it has yet been made. At what time at the latest does the uncertainty phase (INCERFA) begin?
samples.explanation: Annex 11: the uncertainty phase exists when no communication has been received within 30 minutes after the time a communication should have been received, or from the time an unsuccessful attempt to establish communication was first made, whichever is earlier. With no earlier unsuccessful call, INCERFA begins at 1015 + 30 min = 1045.
whyWrong: 15 minutes is not the ICAO trigger.
One hour is the flight plan delay rule for an uncontrolled flight, not the uncertainty phase.
5 minutes is the alert-phase trigger for an aircraft cleared to land that does not land.
samples.examTip: The 30-minute clock starts at the earlier of 'report was due' and 'first failed call'.

samples.prompt: An aircraft has been cleared to land. Five minutes after its estimated time of landing it has not landed and radio contact has not been re-established. Which phase is declared?
options: Distress phase (DETRESFA)
No phase until 30 minutes have elapsed
Uncertainty phase (INCERFA)
Alert phase (ALERFA)
samples.explanation: Annex 11: the alert phase exists when an aircraft cleared to land fails to land within five minutes of the estimated time of landing and communication has not been re-established. Other ALERFA triggers: inquiries after INCERFA fail to give news; information that the aircraft's operating efficiency is impaired but not so far that a forced landing is likely; or the aircraft is known or believed to be the subject of unlawful interference.
whyWrong: Distress needs reasonable certainty of grave danger, such as fuel exhaustion or a forced landing.
The 30-minute rule is for INCERFA; this specific case has its own 5-minute trigger.
INCERFA is skipped here; Annex 11 makes this case an alert phase directly.
samples.examTip: Unlawful interference also goes straight to ALERFA.

samples.prompt: To which flights is the alerting service provided, according to ICAO Annex 11?
options: Only aircraft provided with ATC service
ATC-served flights, other known flights where practicable, and hijack cases
Only aircraft that request it on the frequency of the FIC
Only aircraft that have filed an IFR flight plan
samples.explanation: Alerting service is provided to all aircraft provided with ATC service, in so far as practicable to all other aircraft having filed a flight plan or otherwise known to the ATS, and to any aircraft known or believed to be the subject of unlawful interference. The flight information centre or area control centre is the central point that collects information and alerts the rescue coordination centre.
whyWrong: Too narrow: it extends to other known flights as far as practicable.
Alerting is not on request; ATS starts it when a phase is triggered.
VFR flights with a flight plan also receive alerting service.
samples.examTip: A VFR flight plan buys you alerting service.

chapters.title: Area Control Service
topics: General Provisions for Separation of Controlled Traffic
Separation Minima Based on ATS Surveillance Systems

samples.prompt: Vertical or horizontal separation shall be provided between all flights in which airspace classes?
options: Class A, B and C airspaces
Class A and B airspaces
Class B, C and D airspaces
Class A, B, C and D airspaces
samples.explanation: As per PANS ATM Doc 4444, vertical or horizontal separation shall be provided between all flights in Class A and B airspaces. Option A is incorrect because Class C requires separation only between IFR flights and between IFR and VFR flights, not between all flights. Option C is incorrect as Class D and E have different separation requirements. Option D is incorrect as it includes airspaces where separation is not provided between all flights.

samples.prompt: According to Doc 4444, what is the vertical separation minimum between two IFR flights in RVSM airspace between FL 290 and FL 410 inclusive?
samples.explanation: The vertical separation minimum is 1,000 ft below FL 290 and 2,000 ft at or above FL 290, except that within designated RVSM airspace between FL 290 and FL 410 inclusive it is 1,000 ft between RVSM-approved aircraft. Above FL 410 it returns to 2,000 ft.
whyWrong: 2,000 ft is the minimum above FL 290 outside RVSM, or for a non-RVSM aircraft in RVSM airspace.
Not a standard vertical minimum: ICAO uses 1,000 ft or 2,000 ft.
500 ft is the VFR offset from IFR levels, not a separation minimum.
samples.examTip: FL 410 is the top RVSM level, so FL 410 to FL 430 needs 2,000 ft.

samples.prompt: Which equipment is required for an aircraft to be approved for RVSM operations?
options: ACAS II and a GNSS receiver only
An autopilot and a single air data computer
Two independent altimetry systems, altitude alerter, altitude hold and Mode C/S
One altimeter, a radar altimeter and an SSR transponder without altitude reporting
samples.explanation: RVSM approval needs, as a minimum: two independent altitude measurement systems, one altitude alerting system, one automatic altitude control system, and an SSR transponder with an altitude reporting system that can be connected to the measurement system in use. Height-keeping performance is then monitored.
whyWrong: ACAS and GNSS are useful but are not the RVSM equipment set.
One air data source is not enough; two independent systems are required.
A single altimeter cannot be cross-checked, and a radio altimeter measures height above the surface, not pressure altitude.
samples.examTip: 'Two independent' is the key phrase.

samples.prompt: Two aircraft at the same cruising level follow the same track without ATS surveillance. Navigation aids allow frequent determination of position and speed. What is the longitudinal separation minimum based on time?
options: 5 minutes
15 minutes
10 minutes
3 minutes
samples.explanation: Doc 4444 time-based longitudinal separation, same cruising level and same track: 15 minutes basic; 10 minutes if navigation aids permit frequent determination of position and speed; 5 minutes if the preceding aircraft has a TAS 20 kt or more faster and both departed from the same aerodrome, passed the same reporting point or were otherwise positively spaced; 3 minutes if it is 40 kt or more faster.
whyWrong: 5 minutes needs the preceding aircraft to be at least 20 kt faster after departing the same aerodrome or passing the same reporting point.
15 minutes is the basic minimum without such navigation aids.
3 minutes needs the preceding aircraft to be at least 40 kt faster under the same conditions.
samples.examTip: The faster aircraft must be AHEAD; a faster follower closes the gap.

samples.prompt: An aircraft has reported leaving FL 180 in a descent through moderate weather with light turbulence. When may ATC assign FL 180 to another aircraft on the same route?
options: Only after 5 minutes have passed since the first aircraft vacated it
Only after the first aircraft reports reaching its cleared level
Once the first aircraft reports vacating it, as there is no severe turbulence
As soon as the first aircraft is cleared to descend, before it starts to descend
samples.explanation: Doc 4444: an aircraft may be assigned a level previously occupied by another aircraft after the latter has reported vacating it. Where severe turbulence is known to exist, the aircraft is in a cruise climb, or there is a significant difference in climb/descent performance, ATC withholds the level until the other aircraft has reported at or passing another level that gives the required minimum separation.
whyWrong: There is no time-based rule for releasing a vacated level.
That stricter rule is used only in severe turbulence, cruise climb or large performance differences.
Clearing the first aircraft to descend does not free the level; it must have vacated it.
samples.examTip: Severe turbulence turns 'vacated' into 'reached'.

chapters.title: Approach Control
topics: Separation in the Vicinity of Aerodromes

samples.prompt: What does an expected approach time (EAT) mean?
options: The time a delayed arrival is expected to leave the holding fix for its approach
The time at which the aircraft is expected to touch down
The time at which the aircraft is expected to reach the final approach fix
The time at which the aircraft is expected to enter the terminal area
samples.explanation: An EAT is the time at which ATC expects that an arriving aircraft, following a delay, will leave the holding fix to complete its approach for a landing. The actual time of leaving the holding fix depends on the approach clearance. Doc 4444 requires an EAT to be passed when the delay is expected to be 10 minutes or more.
whyWrong: Touchdown is later; the EAT is at the holding fix.
The final approach fix is reached after leaving the hold, not at the EAT.
Terminal area entry has its own estimate and is not the EAT.
samples.examTip: EAT refers to the holding fix, never the runway.

samples.prompt: An IFR flight is cleared for a visual approach. Which statement is correct?
options: The pilot becomes responsible for terrain clearance only below 500 ft
The flight becomes VFR and must cancel its IFR flight plan
The flight remains IFR, and ATC continues to provide separation from other arriving and departing traffic
ATC no longer provides any service until the aircraft has landed
samples.explanation: A visual approach is an approach by an IFR flight when either part or all of an instrument approach procedure is not completed and the approach is executed with visual reference to terrain. The flight stays IFR, and ATC continues to provide separation from other arriving and departing aircraft. Where it is told to follow a preceding aircraft, the pilot is responsible for avoiding that aircraft's wake.
whyWrong: The pilot keeps visual reference to terrain throughout; there is no 500 ft threshold.
A visual approach is flown by an IFR flight; the flight plan is not cancelled.
ATC still separates the aircraft from other arriving and departing aircraft.
samples.examTip: A visual approach is NOT a change to VFR.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Doc 4444, an aircraft with a maximum certificated take-off mass of 136,000 kg belongs to which wake turbulence category?
options: Light (L)
Super (J)
Heavy (H)
Medium (M)
samples.explanation: ICAO wake turbulence categories by MTOM: Heavy (H) 136,000 kg or more; Medium (M) less than 136,000 kg and more than 7,000 kg; Light (L) 7,000 kg or less. Super (J) is assigned to specified types, currently the A380-800. The letter goes in Item 9 of the flight plan.
whyWrong: Light is 7,000 kg or less.
Super is a specific listed type (the A380), not a mass band.
Medium is less than 136,000 kg but more than 7,000 kg; 136,000 kg itself is Heavy.
samples.examTip: 136,000 exactly is Heavy ('or more').

samples.prompt: On final approach under radar control, a Light aircraft follows a Heavy aircraft. What is the minimum wake turbulence radar separation?
options: 4 NM
6 NM
3 NM
5 NM
samples.explanation: Doc 4444 wake turbulence distance minima (radar, approach and departure): Heavy behind Heavy 4 NM; Medium behind Heavy 5 NM; Light behind Heavy 6 NM; Light behind Medium 5 NM. Behind a Super: Heavy 6 NM, Medium 7 NM, Light 8 NM.
whyWrong: 4 NM is Heavy behind Heavy.
3 NM is the reduced radar minimum, not a wake minimum.
5 NM is Medium behind Heavy, or Light behind Medium.
samples.examTip: The smaller the follower, the bigger the gap.

samples.prompt: Under Doc 4444, ATC may clear an IFR flight for a visual approach provided that the pilot can maintain visual reference to the terrain and:
options: The aircraft is within 5 NM of the threshold
The ceiling is at or above the initial approach level, or the pilot reports it can be done
The reported visibility is at least 10 km and there is no cloud below 5,000 ft
The flight plan was originally filed as VFR
samples.explanation: Doc 4444: an IFR flight may be cleared for a visual approach provided the pilot can maintain visual reference to the terrain and the reported ceiling is at or above the level of the beginning of the initial approach segment for the aircraft so cleared, or the pilot reports at the initial approach level, or at any time during the instrument approach, that the meteorological conditions are such that with reasonable assurance a visual approach and landing can be completed.
whyWrong: Distance from the threshold is not a condition for a visual approach clearance.
No fixed 10 km/5,000 ft weather condition is laid down.
The flight is IFR; its original flight rules are not the test.
samples.examTip: The ceiling is compared with the initial approach level, not the MDA.

chapters.title: Use Of Air Traffic
topics: ATS Surveillance System — Definition and Scope

samples.prompt: A crew loses all two-way radio communication in controlled airspace. Which SSR code should they select?
samples.explanation: Special SSR Mode A codes: 7500 unlawful interference, 7600 radio communication failure, 7700 emergency. Doc 8168: code 2000 when an aircraft has received no instructions from ATC to operate the transponder, for example on entering an area where SSR is used.
whyWrong: 7500 is for unlawful interference.
2000 is used when entering SSR airspace without ATC instructions.
7700 is the general emergency code.
samples.examTip: The special codes go in order of the problem's scale: someone on board, the radio, the whole aircraft.

samples.prompt: What is the basic horizontal separation minimum based on ATS surveillance systems in Doc 4444?
options: 3 NM, reducible to 2.5 NM in every case
5 NM, reducible to 3 NM where the system's capabilities permit
20 NM, reducible to 10 NM with DME
10 NM, reducible to 5 NM with SSR
samples.explanation: Doc 4444: the horizontal separation minimum based on radar and/or ADS-B and/or MLAT is 5 NM. It may be reduced to 3 NM, where prescribed, when the capabilities of the system permit. Separation is measured between the centres of the position symbols, and the position indications must never touch or overlap unless vertical separation exists.
whyWrong: 3 NM is the reduced figure, not the basic one; 2.5 NM applies only on final approach under specific conditions.
20/10 NM is the procedural DME longitudinal minimum.
10 NM is not the basic surveillance minimum.
samples.examTip: Procedural DME 20/10; surveillance 5/3.

samples.prompt: Mode C (or Mode S altitude) level information displayed on the controller's screen is based on:
options: GNSS geometric altitude
Pressure altitude (1013.25 hPa), whatever the pilot's subscale
The altitude on the pilot's altimeter with QNH set
The radio altimeter height above the surface
samples.explanation: The altitude encoder sends pressure altitude referenced to the standard 1013.25 hPa, in 100 ft increments, regardless of the setting on the pilot's subscale. Below the transition level the ATC system corrects the display to altitude using the local QNH. This is why a wrong subscale setting shows up as a difference between the reported and displayed levels.
whyWrong: SSR level information is barometric, not geometric.
The transponder reports independent of the subscale; the ground system converts to altitude using QNH.
A radio altimeter gives height above ground, which is not used for ATC level information.
samples.examTip: Changing your subscale does not change your Mode C readout.

samples.prompt: Which method can be used to identify an aircraft with primary surveillance radar only?
options: Asking the pilot to squawk ident
Reading the aircraft identification in the SSR label
Observing a heading change of 30° or more that the controller instructed
Instructing a change of SSR code and observing it
samples.explanation: Doc 4444 PSR identification methods: relating a particular position indication to an aircraft reporting its position over a point shown on the display, or its range and bearing from such a point; relating the position indication of a departing aircraft observed within 1 NM (2 km) of the end of the runway; and observing a position indication that executes an instructed heading change of 30° or more. The other methods all need SSR.
whyWrong: Ident works only with SSR.
SSR labels need a transponder.
Code changes also need SSR.
samples.examTip: 'Squawk', 'code' and 'label' all mean SSR.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is assigned FL 240 in RVSM airspace. Its Mode C readout shows FL 244. According to Doc 4444, what should the controller do?
options: Nothing, because the readout is within the 300 ft tolerance
Ask the pilot to check the pressure setting and confirm the level
Treat the aircraft as having left FL 240 and reassign the level to another aircraft
Ask the pilot to switch off Mode C
samples.explanation: Doc 4444: the tolerance for verifying displayed level information is ±60 m (±200 ft) in RVSM airspace and ±90 m (±300 ft) in other airspace. If the displayed level differs from the assigned level by more than the tolerance, the pilot is advised and asked to check the pressure setting and confirm the level. If the discrepancy persists, the controller may ask the pilot to stop Mode C transmission.
whyWrong: In RVSM airspace the tolerance is ±200 ft; ±300 ft is the value elsewhere.
A display discrepancy is checked with the pilot first; it does not by itself free the level.
Switching off the readout is only done if it remains outside tolerance after the checks.
samples.examTip: RVSM halves the room for error: 200 instead of 300.

chapters.title: Aeronautical
topics: AIRAC — Aeronautical Information Regulation and Control

samples.prompt: A pilot planning a flight to an Indian aerodrome needs its runway data and aerodrome charts. In which part of AIP India will they be found?
options: ENR (En-route)
AIC (Aeronautical Information Circular)
GEN (General)
AD (Aerodromes)
samples.explanation: The AIP is in three parts: GEN (general: regulations, differences from ICAO in GEN 1.7, abbreviations, services), ENR (en route: rules, airspace, ATS routes, navigation aids, cruising levels) and AD (aerodromes and heliports: AD 2 entries with runway data, lighting and charts). In India, the AIS, including the AIP, is provided by the Airports Authority of India.
whyWrong: ENR holds en-route rules, airspace, ATS routes and navigation aids.
An AIC is a separate publication, not a part of the AIP.
GEN holds national regulations, differences, charges, units and services.
samples.examTip: Charts of a particular aerodrome are always in AD 2.

samples.prompt: A replacement NOTAM is issued to supersede an earlier one. Which NOTAM type is it?
options: NOTAMC
NOTAMN
NOTAMS
NOTAMR
samples.explanation: NOTAM types: NOTAMN (new information), NOTAMR (replaces a previous NOTAM, quoting its number) and NOTAMC (cancels a previous NOTAM). A checklist of valid NOTAM is issued at intervals of not more than one month.
whyWrong: NOTAMC cancels an earlier NOTAM.
NOTAMN contains new information.
There is no 'NOTAMS' type.
samples.examTip: A NOTAMR always quotes the number of the NOTAM it replaces.

samples.prompt: Which information should be published in an Aeronautical Information Circular (AIC) rather than in a NOTAM or the AIP?
options: A runway closure tomorrow morning
A permanent new frequency for an aerodrome tower
The activation of a danger area for the next six hours
Advance notice of a planned major change in national legislation affecting flight operations
samples.explanation: An AIC carries information that qualifies neither for a NOTAM nor for inclusion in the AIP but relates to flight safety, air navigation, technical, administrative or legislative matters: long-term forecasts of major changes in legislation, regulations or procedures, explanatory or advisory material, and similar notices.
whyWrong: A short-notice closure is a NOTAM item.
A permanent operational change goes in the AIP by amendment.
Short-term activation of an airspace restriction is a NOTAM item.
samples.examTip: If it is neither urgent nor permanent operational data, think AIC.

samples.prompt: A runway will be closed for resurfacing for four months, and the AIS must publish extensive text and charts about the temporary arrangements. In which publication should this appear?
options: An AIP Supplement
An AIC
An AIP Amendment
A NOTAM only
samples.explanation: Annex 15: temporary changes of long duration (three months or longer), and information of short duration that contains extensive text and/or graphics, are published as AIP Supplements. Supplements are printed on coloured (yellow) paper so they stand out, and a checklist of valid Supplements is issued regularly. Permanent changes are made by AIP Amendments.
whyWrong: An AIC is for explanatory or advisory material, not operational arrangements.
AIP Amendments are for permanent changes.
A NOTAM is for short or urgent items; a temporary change lasting three months or longer, with extensive graphics, goes in an AIP Supplement (a NOTAM may point to it).
samples.examTip: Permanent → Amendment; temporary and long or bulky → Supplement; temporary and short → NOTAM.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about AIP publications: 1. Permanent changes to the AIP are published as AIP Amendments. 2. AIP Supplements are printed on yellow paper. 3. Differences from ICAO Standards are listed in GEN 1.7. 4. AIC is the part of the AIP that contains aerodrome charts. Which are correct?
options: 1 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
samples.explanation: (1) True: AIP Amendments carry permanent changes. (2) True: Supplements are on yellow paper. (3) True: GEN 1.7 lists the State's significant differences from ICAO SARPs and procedures. (4) False: an AIC (Aeronautical Information Circular) is separate from the AIP and is used for advisory, explanatory or administrative information.
whyWrong: Includes 4: an AIC is a separate circular, and aerodrome charts are in AD.
Keeps the false statement 4 and drops the true statements 2 and 3.
Leaves out statement 1, the basic rule for permanent changes.
samples.examTip: AIC is never part of the AIP.

chapters.title: Section 10
topics: Operating Procedures — Pilot at Scene of Accident
Ground-Air Visual Signal Code — Rescue Units

samples.prompt: Who is designated as the Chairman of the National Aeronautical Search & Rescue Coordination Committee (NASARCC)?
options: Director General, Indian Coast Guard
Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation
Director General, Civil Aviation
Chairman, Airports Authority of India
samples.explanation: Per AIP India (GEN 3.6), the National Aeronautical Search and Rescue Coordination Committee (NASARCC) has the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation as its chairman. The Director General, Indian Coast Guard chairs the National Maritime SAR Board (NMSARB), not NASARCC.

samples.prompt: A runway threshold has been permanently displaced. How is the section of runway before the displaced threshold marked?
options: With white crosses showing that it is closed
With white arrows along the centre line pointing towards the displaced threshold
With a single yellow line along the centre
With yellow chevrons pointing towards the threshold
samples.explanation: When a threshold is permanently displaced, arrows are placed on the portion of the runway before it, and a transverse white bar marks the displaced threshold. That portion is available for taxiing, take-off and the landing roll-out of aircraft landing from the opposite direction, but not for touchdown in the direction of the arrows. Yellow chevrons are reserved for pre-threshold areas unsuitable for normal use.
whyWrong: Crosses mean the area is unusable; the displaced section can still be used for take-off and roll-out.
Yellow is for taxiway markings, not runway markings.
Yellow chevrons mark a pre-threshold area that is unfit for normal use by aircraft (for example a blast pad).
samples.examTip: White arrows: usable for take-off; yellow chevrons: do not use.

samples.prompt: Two parallel runways have a magnetic bearing of 263° when viewed from the direction of approach. The left runway is designated 26L. What is the designation of the same strip of concrete seen from the opposite end?
samples.explanation: Annex 14: the runway designation number is the whole number nearest one-tenth of the magnetic bearing of the centre line seen from the direction of approach: 263° → 26. The reciprocal is 083° → 08. Viewed from the other end, the left runway becomes the right one, so 26L is 08R.
whyWrong: Forgets that left and right swap when the runway is viewed from the other end.
263° − 180° = 083°, which rounds to 08, not 09.
Gives the other runway of the pair, seen from the same end.
samples.examTip: Reciprocal designations always differ by 18, and L ↔ R.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Annex 14, how many longitudinal stripes make up the threshold marking of a 45 m wide runway?
samples.explanation: Annex 14 threshold marking: the number of stripes depends on runway width: 18 m → 4, 23 m → 6, 30 m → 8, 45 m → 12, 60 m → 16. The stripes are white and start 6 m from the threshold.
whyWrong: 8 stripes are used on a 30 m runway.
6 stripes are used on a 23 m runway.
16 stripes are used on a 60 m runway.
samples.examTip: Count the stripes in a photo to estimate the runway width.

samples.prompt: A non-radio pilot sees two digits, '27', displayed vertically on the control tower. What do they mean?
options: The runway in use for landing, in tens of degrees true
The QNH: 1027 hPa
The surface wind direction, 270° true
The direction for take-off, in tens of degrees magnetic: take off towards 270°M
samples.explanation: Annex 2: two or more digits displayed vertically on or near the control tower indicate to aircraft on the manoeuvring area the direction for take-off, expressed in units of 10° to the nearest 10° of the magnetic compass. A landing T or a horizontal signal shows the landing direction.
whyWrong: The signal gives take-off direction in degrees magnetic, not true.
Pressure settings are not shown by this ground signal.
Wind is shown by the wind sleeve or indicator, not by digits on the tower.
samples.examTip: Magnetic, like runway designations.

samples.prompt: On a 3° approach a pilot sees three red lights and one white light on the PAPI. What does this show?
options: The aircraft is well below the approach slope
The aircraft is slightly above the approach slope
The aircraft is on the approach slope
The aircraft is slightly below the approach slope
samples.explanation: PAPI has four units in a wing bar, normally on the left of the runway. The units are set at slightly different angles, so the number of red lights increases as the aircraft goes lower: 4 white = too high; 3 white 1 red = slightly high; 2 white 2 red = on slope; 1 white 3 red = slightly low; 4 red = too low.
whyWrong: Well below shows four red.
Slightly high shows three white and one red.
On slope shows two white and two red.
samples.examTip: Count the reds: 0 high, 1 slightly high, 2 on, 3 slightly low, 4 low.

samples.prompt: Which statement about runway threshold and runway end lights is correct?
options: Threshold lights are red and runway end lights are green
Threshold lights show green to the approach; end lights show red along the runway
Threshold lights are flashing yellow; runway end lights are steady white
Both are white omnidirectional lights
samples.explanation: Threshold lights are fixed unidirectional lights showing green in the direction of approach. Runway end lights are fixed unidirectional lights showing red in the direction of the runway. Often the same fitting shows green one way and red the other. Wing bar lights at a displaced threshold are also green.
whyWrong: Reverses the colours.
Flashing yellow belongs to runway guard lights.
They are coloured and unidirectional, so each is seen only from the relevant direction.
samples.examTip: Seeing green at the near end and red at the far end is correct.

samples.prompt: A runway has a TORA of 2,800 m, a stopway of 150 m and a clearway of 300 m. What is the ASDA?
samples.explanation: Declared distances: TORA = length of runway available for the take-off run; TODA = TORA + clearway; ASDA = TORA + stopway; LDA = runway length available for the landing run. ASDA = 2,800 + 150 = 2,950 m (TODA would be 2,800 + 300 = 3,100 m).
whyWrong: Added both the stopway and the clearway.
Ignored the stopway, which is part of ASDA.
Added the clearway: that gives TODA, not ASDA.
samples.examTip: Clearway is for climbing over, stopway is for stopping on.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Annex 14, a precision approach category I lighting system consists of a row of lights on the extended centre line extending, wherever possible, over a distance of:
options: 420 m from the threshold, with a crossbar at 300 m
300 m from the threshold, with no crossbar
900 m from the threshold, with a crossbar 30 m long at 300 m from the threshold
1,500 m from the threshold, with crossbars every 150 m
samples.explanation: Annex 14: a precision approach CAT I lighting system consists of a row of lights on the extended centre line extending, wherever possible, over 900 m from the threshold, with a crossbar 30 m long at 300 m from the threshold. A simple approach lighting system needs at least 420 m with a crossbar (18 m or 30 m long) at 300 m. CAT II/III systems add red side-row barrettes in the inner 270 m.
whyWrong: 420 m is the simple approach lighting system.
Far too short for a precision approach system.
Invents a longer system with several crossbars.
samples.examTip: The crossbar is always 300 m from the threshold.

samples.prompt: Approaching a runway with a CAT II/III approach lighting system, a pilot sees red side-row barrettes on each side of the centre line. Where are they?
options: In the inner 270 m of the approach lighting, nearest the threshold
In the outer 300 m of the system
Across the end of the runway
Along the edges of the runway in the last 600 m
samples.explanation: In a precision approach CAT II and III lighting system, the inner 300 m has the centre line barrettes plus two side rows of red barrettes extending 270 m from the threshold. They give strong roll and position guidance in low visibility and tell the pilot that the threshold is close.
whyWrong: The outer part of the system has only the centre line and crossbars.
Runway end lights are red but are part of the runway lighting, not the approach system.
Runway edge lights may turn yellow in the last 600 m, but they are not side-row barrettes.
samples.examTip: Red in the approach lights means 'very close to the threshold': do not go below them.

chapters.title: (doc 8168, Vol 1-flight Procedures)
topics: Fixes as an Aid in Obstacle Avoidance

samples.prompt: Doc 8168 divides an instrument approach procedure into up to five segments. Which list is in the correct order?
options: Arrival, initial, final, intermediate, missed approach
Arrival, intermediate, initial, final, missed approach
Initial, arrival, intermediate, final, missed approach
Arrival, initial, intermediate, final, missed approach
samples.explanation: An instrument approach may have arrival, initial, intermediate, final and missed approach segments. The arrival route leads from the en-route structure to the IAF; the initial segment runs from the IAF to the IF; the intermediate segment from the IF to the FAF/FAP, where the aircraft is configured; the final segment to the MAPt or DA; and the missed approach from there to a holding or en-route point.
whyWrong: The intermediate segment links the initial and final segments.
The initial segment starts at the IAF, before the intermediate segment.
The arrival route comes before the initial approach fix.
samples.examTip: Learn the fixes with the segments: IAF, IF, FAF, MAPt.

samples.prompt: Unless otherwise published, Doc 8168 instrument departures are designed for a procedure design gradient (PDG) of:
options: 2.5 %, which includes an allowance of 0.8 % for obstacle clearance
3.3 %, made up of a 2.0 % obstacle surface plus 1.3 % for obstacle clearance
5.0 %, to allow for engine failure
3.3 %, made up of a 2.5 % obstacle identification surface plus 0.8 % for increasing obstacle clearance
samples.explanation: The obstacle identification surface (OIS) rises at 2.5 % from 5 m (16 ft) above the departure end of the runway (DER). The PDG of 3.3 % gives a minimum obstacle clearance of zero at the DER that grows by 0.8 % of the horizontal distance flown. If obstacles penetrate the OIS, a higher PDG is published.
whyWrong: 2.5 % is the obstacle identification surface alone; the PDG adds 0.8 %.
The split is 2.5 % plus 0.8 %, not 2.0 % plus 1.3 %.
5 % is not the standard PDG and engine failure is an operator performance matter.
samples.examTip: 3.3 − 2.5 = 0.8: know all three numbers.

samples.prompt: What minimum obstacle clearance does Doc 8168 provide in the primary area of the initial approach segment?
samples.explanation: Doc 8168 MOC in the primary area: initial approach segment 300 m (984 ft); intermediate segment 150 m (492 ft); final segment of a non-precision approach with a FAF typically 75 m (246 ft); missed approach intermediate phase 30 m (98 ft) and final phase 50 m (164 ft). In the secondary areas the MOC reduces linearly to zero at the outer edge.
whyWrong: 30 m is the intermediate phase of the missed approach.
150 m is the intermediate segment.
75 m is a typical final segment value for a non-precision approach with a FAF.
samples.examTip: The MOC halves from initial to intermediate to final.

samples.prompt: A minimum sector altitude (MSA) published on an approach chart provides at least what obstacle clearance, and within what radius?
options: 150 m (500 ft) within 25 NM
300 m (1,000 ft) within 25 NM (46 km) of the navigation aid or reference point
300 m (1,000 ft) within 10 NM
600 m (2,000 ft) within 30 NM
samples.explanation: An MSA is the lowest altitude that can be used which will provide a minimum clearance of 300 m (1,000 ft) above all objects within a sector of a circle of 25 NM (46 km) radius centred on a significant point, the aerodrome reference point or the heliport reference point. Sectors are bounded by bearings to the point, with a 5 NM buffer beyond each sector boundary.
whyWrong: Too little clearance: 150 m is the intermediate approach MOC.
The MSA radius is 25 NM, not 10 NM.
2,000 ft over mountainous terrain is an en-route consideration, not the MSA standard.
samples.examTip: The MSA is for emergencies and orientation, not for descent on the procedure.

samples.prompt: Under ICAO Doc 8168, what is the maximum holding speed for a Category C aircraft at FL 180 in normal (non-turbulent) conditions?
options: 265 kt
280 kt
230 kt
240 kt
samples.explanation: ICAO holding speeds (IAS): up to and including 14,000 ft, 230 kt (170 kt for Category A and B); above 14,000 ft to 20,000 ft, 240 kt; above 20,000 ft to 34,000 ft, 265 kt; above 34,000 ft, M 0.83. In turbulence, 280 kt or M 0.8, whichever is less, may be used up to 34,000 ft (170 kt for A/B), after informing ATC.
whyWrong: 265 kt applies above 20,000 ft up to 34,000 ft.
280 kt is the turbulence speed, used only in turbulent conditions and after notifying ATC.
230 kt applies up to and including 14,000 ft.
samples.examTip: FL 180 sits in the 14,000–20,000 ft band.

chapters.title: Precision Approach
topics: Final Approach Point (FAP) vs. Final Approach Fix (FAF)
Determination of Decision Altitude (DA) or Decision Height (DH)
ICAO Classification of Instrument Approach Operations
Simultaneous ILS Operations on Parallel Runways
RNAV Approach Procedures Based on VOR/DME

samples.prompt: For a 3° glide path, interception occurs between what distances from the threshold?
options: 3 NM and 10 NM
5 NM and 15 NM
2 NM and 8 NM
4 NM and 12 NM
samples.explanation: In PANS-OPS, for a 3 degree glide path, interception occurs between 6 km (3 NM) and 19 km (10 NM) from the threshold, which matches 300 m to 900 m in height.

samples.prompt: What is the difference between a decision altitude/height (DA/H) and a minimum descent altitude/height (MDA/H)?
options: DA/H is used for non-precision approaches and MDA/H for precision approaches
A DA/H is a decision point for going around; an MDA/H is a floor that may be flown level to the MAPt
DA/H is always higher than MDA/H on the same runway
There is no practical difference; both terms mean the same in Doc 8168
samples.explanation: DA/H: a specified altitude or height in a 3D (precision or APV) approach at which a missed approach must be initiated if the required visual reference to continue has not been established. MDA/H: a specified altitude or height in a 2D (non-precision) or circling approach below which descent must not be made without the required visual reference; the aircraft may level at the MDA and continue to the MAPt.
whyWrong: Reverses the use: DA/H for precision and APV (3D) approaches, MDA/H for non-precision and circling.
Precision approach minima are normally lower than non-precision minima.
The two are used differently: one is a decision point, the other a floor.
samples.examTip: DA/H goes with a glide path; MDA/H goes with level flight.

samples.prompt: According to ICAO Annex 6, a Category I precision approach operation has a decision height not lower than:
options: 30 m (100 ft), with an RVR of at least 300 m
60 m (200 ft), with a visibility of at least 800 m or an RVR of at least 550 m
60 m (200 ft), with an RVR of at least 300 m
75 m (250 ft), with a visibility of at least 1,500 m
samples.explanation: CAT I: DH not lower than 60 m (200 ft) and either a visibility not less than 800 m or an RVR not less than 550 m. CAT II: DH lower than 60 m (200 ft) but not lower than 30 m (100 ft), RVR not less than 300 m. CAT IIIA: DH lower than 30 m (100 ft) or no DH, RVR not less than 175 m. CAT IIIB: DH lower than 15 m (50 ft) or no DH, RVR less than 175 m but not less than 50 m. CAT IIIC: no DH and no RVR limitations.
whyWrong: Those are the Category II limits.
Correct DH but mixes in the Category II RVR.
75 m (250 ft) is the boundary between Type A and Type B approaches, not the CAT I DH.
samples.examTip: CAT I is the only one with a visibility (800 m) alternative to RVR.

samples.prompt: Annex 6 classifies an approach with vertical guidance whose DH is 60 m (200 ft) as which type?
options: Type C
Type 2D
Type B
Type A
samples.explanation: Annex 6 classifies instrument approach operations by their lowest minima: Type A has an MDH or DH at or above 75 m (250 ft); Type B has a DH below 75 m (250 ft). Type B is further divided into CAT I, II and III. They can be flown as 2D (lateral guidance only) or 3D (lateral and vertical guidance) operations.
whyWrong: There is no Type C in Annex 6.
'2D' describes an approach without vertical guidance, not a type based on height.
Type A has a minimum descent height or DH at or above 75 m (250 ft).
samples.examTip: 200 ft is below 250 ft, so CAT I is always Type B.

samples.prompt: On a non-precision approach, the MDH is normally referenced to aerodrome elevation. When is it referenced to the threshold elevation instead?
options: When the threshold elevation is more than 2 m (7 ft) above the aerodrome elevation
When the threshold elevation is more than 2 m (7 ft) below the aerodrome elevation
Only for circling approaches
Always on runways longer than 2,400 m
samples.explanation: Doc 8168: OCH for a non-precision approach is referenced to the aerodrome elevation, or to the threshold elevation if the threshold is more than 2 m (7 ft) below the aerodrome elevation. Precision approach OCH is always referenced to the threshold, and circling OCH to the aerodrome elevation.
whyWrong: A threshold higher than the aerodrome elevation cannot exist, since aerodrome elevation is the highest point of the landing area.
Circling MDH is referenced to the aerodrome elevation.
Runway length is irrelevant to the reference datum.
samples.examTip: Precision → threshold; circling → aerodrome; NPA → aerodrome unless the threshold is 7 ft lower.

samples.prompt: Which statement correctly defines the transition level?
options: The lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude
The highest flight level at which QNH may still be used
The altitude at or below which the vertical position of an aircraft is controlled by reference to altitudes
The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition layer
samples.explanation: Transition altitude: the altitude at or below which the vertical position of an aircraft is controlled by reference to altitudes. Transition level: the lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude. Transition layer: the airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level. The transition level changes with QNH so that the layer stays adequate.
whyWrong: QNH is not used at flight levels at all; above the transition level, 1013.2 hPa is set.
That is the transition altitude.
The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level is the transition layer.
samples.examTip: TA is fixed and published; TL is given by ATC/ATIS and moves with the QNH.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is on the ground at an aerodrome. With QFE set, what should the altimeter read? With QNH set, what should it read?
options: QFE: zero; QNH: the pressure altitude
QFE: the aerodrome elevation; QNH: zero
QFE: the pressure altitude; QNH: the aerodrome elevation
QFE: zero (approximately); QNH: the aerodrome elevation
samples.explanation: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at aerodrome elevation (or at the runway threshold), so with it set the altimeter reads height above that datum: zero on the ground. QNH is the altimeter subscale setting that makes the altimeter read the aerodrome elevation on the ground, and altitude above MSL in flight.
whyWrong: Pressure altitude needs the standard setting, not QNH.
Reverses the two settings.
Pressure altitude needs 1013.2 hPa set, not QFE.
samples.examTip: A pre-flight altimeter check with QNH set compares the reading with the known elevation.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is climbing out from an aerodrome with QNH set, cleared to FL 90. When should the pilot change the altimeter setting to 1013.2 hPa?
options: On reaching FL 90
On leaving the aerodrome traffic zone
On passing the transition altitude
On reaching the transition level
samples.explanation: Doc 8168: in the climb, the altimeter setting is changed from QNH to 1013.2 hPa on passing the transition altitude, and vertical position is then expressed as flight levels. In the descent, the change from 1013.2 hPa to QNH is made on passing the transition level, once cleared to an altitude.
whyWrong: Waiting until the cleared level means flying through the layer on the wrong setting.
The aerodrome traffic zone has nothing to do with altimeter settings.
Waiting until the transition level in the climb leaves the aircraft on QNH while it is already in the flight level structure.
samples.examTip: The change happens at the boundary of the layer that you cross first.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is at FL 50 and the regional QNH is 1003 hPa. Assuming 30 ft per hPa, what is the aircraft's altitude?
samples.explanation: Pressure difference = 1013 − 1003 = 10 hPa; 10 × 30 = 300 ft. With QNH lower than standard, the MSL pressure surface lies below the 1013 hPa surface, so the altitude is less than the pressure altitude: 5,000 − 300 = 4,700 ft.
whyWrong: Used 27 ft per hPa although the question specifies 30 ft per hPa.
Ignored the difference between QNH and the standard setting.
Applied the correction the wrong way: with QNH below 1013, the aircraft is LOWER than the flight level suggests.
samples.examTip: QNH below 1013 → altitude below the FL figure.

samples.prompt: Within the transition layer, how is an aircraft's vertical position expressed?
options: In flight levels when climbing, and in altitudes when descending
Always in altitudes
In altitudes when climbing, and in flight levels when descending
Always in flight levels
samples.explanation: Because the climbing aircraft changes to 1013.2 hPa at the transition altitude and the descending one changes to QNH at the transition level, within the layer a climbing aircraft reports flight levels and a descending aircraft reports altitudes. Level flight within the transition layer is normally avoided.
whyWrong: A climbing aircraft has already changed to 1013.2 hPa at the transition altitude.
Reverses the rule.
A descending aircraft has already changed to QNH at the transition level.
samples.examTip: Work out which setting the aircraft must have after crossing the first boundary.

chapters.title: Section 15
topics: Dropping of Articles and Parachute Descents
Carriage of Persons in Unauthorised Parts
Maximum Age Limit for Professional Pilots (Rule 28A)

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT permitted under the Indian rules on the carriage of persons?
options: Carrying a sick passenger who has been certified fit to travel and is accompanied as required
Carrying a passenger in an approved seat with a safety belt fastened for take-off and landing
Carrying a person in a part not designed for people, such as on the wing or in the undercarriage bay
Carrying an infant on an adult's lap with a supplementary belt where the operator's manual allows it
samples.explanation: The Aircraft Rules 1937 forbid carrying any person in any part of an aircraft that is not designed for the accommodation of persons, and on the wings or undercarriage. People must be carried in approved accommodation, normally a seat with a belt. The other three options describe normal, regulated carriage.
whyWrong: A sick passenger may travel with the right medical clearance.
Normal carriage in an approved seat is the standard case.
Lap-held infants are allowed by many operators under approved procedures.
samples.examTip: With 'NOT permitted', pick the unsafe one; the other three are routine.

samples.prompt: A crew member's licence has been left at home and the flight is an international commercial flight from Delhi. Why is this a problem even though the pilot is properly qualified?
options: It is a problem only for the commander; the licences of co-pilots and cabin crew need not be carried
It is a problem only if the destination State asks for it on arrival; there is no requirement before departure
The licence of each crew member must be carried on board, so the flight does not meet the documentation requirement
It is not a problem: a photocopy of the pilot's log book page showing the licence number is an accepted substitute on board
samples.explanation: Article 29 of the Chicago Convention and the national rules made under it require the appropriate licence for each crew member to be carried on board. Being qualified is not enough: the document is the evidence another State relies on under Article 33 to recognise that qualification. Without it the flight is not properly documented.
