samples.examTip: Choose an NDB whose bearing line crosses the coast at right angles.

samples.prompt: Which of the following ADF errors is NOT caused by the propagation of the signal between the NDB and the aircraft?
options: Night effect
Mountain effect
Coastal refraction
Quadrantal error
samples.explanation: Night effect, coastal refraction and mountain effect all happen along the path of the wave. Quadrantal error happens at the aircraft: the metal airframe re-radiates the signal and distorts the field around the loop, which is why it can be measured and compensated for in the installation.
whyWrong: Night effect is a propagation error: sky waves from the ionosphere.
Mountain effect is a propagation error: reflection and diffraction by high ground.
Coastal refraction is a propagation error: bending of the surface wave at a coastline.
samples.examTip: Ask where the error happens: along the path, or at the aircraft.

chapters.title: VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)
topics: The Cone of Ambiguity (Cone of Confusion)

samples.prompt: VOR operates within which frequency range?
samples.explanation: VOR uses 108–117.95 MHz: 108–112 MHz shared with ILS localisers (even tenths), and 112–117.95 MHz VOR only. 118–136 MHz is VHF communications and 960–1215 MHz is DME.

samples.prompt: How does an aircraft's VOR receiver determine which radial it is on?
options: It measures the time between a pulse and its reply
It finds the null of a rotating loop aerial
It compares the depths of the 90 Hz and 150 Hz modulation in the received signal
It compares the phase of a variable 30 Hz signal with a reference 30 Hz signal
samples.explanation: A conventional VOR radiates a reference 30 Hz signal, the same in every direction, and a variable 30 Hz signal whose phase changes with bearing. They are in phase on magnetic north at the station. The receiver measures the phase difference, which equals the radial: 90° of phase lag means the 090° radial.
whyWrong: Pulse timing is the DME principle.
A loop null is the ADF principle.
Comparing 90 Hz and 150 Hz is the ILS principle.
samples.examTip: Match the principle: phase = VOR, timing = DME, modulation depth = ILS, null = ADF.

samples.prompt: An aircraft passes directly over a VOR at high level. Why do the CDI and TO/FROM flag fluctuate briefly?
options: The DME paired with the VOR interferes with it overhead
It is in the cone of confusion above the station, where there is no usable bearing
The VOR's identification interrupts the bearing signal every 30 seconds
The aircraft is too high to receive the VOR properly, because VOR is limited to line of sight
samples.explanation: The VOR aerials radiate poorly straight upwards, so in a cone above the station the bearing information is unusable. Passing through it, the CDI swings and the flag flickers, then the flag settles on FROM. The cone gets wider in distance terms with height, so the effect lasts longer at high level.
whyWrong: DME is on UHF, a different band; it does not interfere with the VHF VOR.
The Morse ident is a separate audio tone and does not disturb the bearing.
Overhead is the closest point to the station; line-of-sight range is not a problem there.
samples.examTip: Station passage on a VOR is the flag changing from TO to FROM.

samples.prompt: What is the main advantage of a Doppler VOR (DVOR) over a conventional VOR?
options: It works on UHF, so it has more channels
It can be received well beyond line of sight, even at low level
Much smaller site errors from nearby buildings and terrain
It does not need a paired DME
samples.explanation: A DVOR uses a large circle of aerials switched in sequence so that the variable signal is produced by the Doppler effect. Its wide aperture makes it much less sensitive to reflections from nearby obstacles (site errors), so it is used where a conventional VOR would be unreliable. To the aircraft receiver it looks the same.
whyWrong: DVOR uses the same 108–117.95 MHz VHF band as a conventional VOR.
DVOR is still VHF and limited to line of sight.
A DVOR can have a DME paired with it exactly as a conventional VOR does.
samples.examTip: Same frequencies and receiver: the advantage is accuracy at difficult sites.

samples.prompt: A VOR is sited where the variation is 2°W, and an aircraft 100 nm east of it is where the variation is 6°W. The aircraft is on the 090° radial. What is its true bearing from the VOR (QTE)?
samples.explanation: VOR radials are measured against magnetic north at the VOR, so use the station's variation. True = magnetic − west variation: 090° − 2° = 088°(T). (An ADF bearing, measured at the aircraft, would use the aircraft's variation instead.)
whyWrong: Used the variation at the aircraft; VOR radials are referenced to magnetic north at the station.
Added the aircraft's variation, two mistakes at once.
Added westerly variation instead of subtracting it.
samples.examTip: Ask where the bearing is measured; use the variation at that place.

samples.prompt: The localizer transmitter is located approximately how far from the up-wind end of the runway?
samples.explanation: The localizer (LLZ) transmits in the VHF band and is located about 300 m from the up-wind end of the runway. Option A (200 m) is the approximate distance of the glide path from the runway edge. Options C and D are incorrect standard distances.

samples.prompt: How are ILS localiser frequencies arranged within the 108–112 MHz band, which they share with VORs?
options: Localisers use odd tenths of a megahertz (108.10, 108.15, 108.30 ...); VORs use the even tenths
Localisers use even tenths; VORs use the odd tenths
Localisers and VORs both use any frequency in the band, separated geographically
Localisers use 108.0–112.0 MHz and their glide paths 112.0–117.95 MHz
samples.explanation: Between 108 and 112 MHz, localisers take the odd first decimal (108.1, 108.3 ... 111.9, plus the .x5 channels such as 108.15) and VORs take the even first decimal. Each localiser is paired with a UHF glide-path frequency, so tuning the localiser also selects the glide path and any paired DME.
whyWrong: Reversed: in 108–112 MHz the odd-tenth frequencies are the localisers.
The band is split by frequency, odd and even tenths, not just by geography.
Glide paths are UHF, about 329–335 MHz; 112–118 MHz is VOR only.
samples.examTip: 110.3 = ILS; 110.4 = VOR; anything above 112.0 = VOR.

samples.prompt: An ILS has a 3° glide path and a threshold crossing height of 50 ft. How high above the threshold should the aircraft be at 5 nm from the threshold?
samples.explanation: Height = distance × tan(angle) + TCH = 5 × 6,076 ft × tan 3° + 50 = 30,380 × 0.0524 + 50 = 1,592 + 50 = 1,642 ft, about 1,640 ft. The 1 in 60 rule (300 ft per nm) is a good cross-check but reads about 5% low.
whyWrong: Used the 1 in 60 approximation (300 ft per nm), which is about 5% low for a 3° path.
Left out the 50 ft threshold crossing height.
Used the 1 in 60 approximation (300 ft per nm) and forgot the threshold crossing height.
samples.examTip: Check whether the distance is from the threshold or from the DME: they are rarely the same point.

samples.prompt: On final approach along an ILS, which modulation predominates on each side of the localiser course and above the glide path?
options: 90 Hz on the right of the localiser course and below the glide path; 150 Hz on the left and above
90 Hz on both sides; the difference is in the phase, as in a VOR
90 Hz on the left of the localiser course and above the glide path; 150 Hz on the right and below
150 Hz on the left of the localiser course and above the glide path; 90 Hz on the right and below
samples.explanation: The localiser radiates two lobes modulated at 90 Hz and 150 Hz. Seen from an aircraft on the approach, 90 Hz predominates on the left and 150 Hz on the right; on the centreline the depths are equal (zero DDM). The glide path works the same way vertically: 90 Hz above, 150 Hz below.
whyWrong: Mixed up both: 90 Hz is on the left and above.
The ILS compares modulation depths (DDM), not phases.
Reversed: 150 Hz is on the right (the 'blue' sector) and below the glide path.
samples.examTip: The receiver compares modulation depth, not phase.

samples.prompt: An aircraft intercepts an ILS glide path from above, descending steeply towards the runway. What is the particular hazard?
options: It may capture a false glide path, which can look like a normal indication
The glide-path signal is only radiated above 6°, so no indication is received
The localiser signal is lost above the glide path
The marker beacons are not received above the glide path
samples.explanation: The glide-path aerial pattern produces false glide paths at multiples of the nominal angle (for a 3° path, near 6° and 9°), and on some of them the sensing is reversed. Intercepting from below, at or above the published altitude, ensures the correct path is captured. Cross-check height against DME or the outer marker.
whyWrong: The usable glide-path coverage starts well below the nominal path; there is no '6° minimum'.
Localiser coverage extends well above the glide path.
Marker beacons radiate an upward fan; they are not limited to the glide-path height.
samples.examTip: Cross-check the glide path with a height/distance check at the FAF.

chapters.title: Microwave Landing System (MLS)
topics: ILS Disadvantages — Why MLS Was Needed

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of ILS mentioned in the chapter?
options: Only 40 channels available worldwide
Fixed and narrow azimuth and glide slope beams
Cannot be sited in hilly areas
Requires complex computer programming for each approach
samples.explanation: ILS's drawbacks include only 40 channels, fixed narrow beams, no special procedures for slower aircraft, siting problems in hilly terrain and multipath interference. Complex programming is an MLS characteristic, not an ILS one.

samples.prompt: The MLS azimuth coverage is ±40° of the runway on-course line. What is the total angular coverage in degrees?
samples.explanation: Total coverage = +40° + (-40°) = 80° total angular coverage. Option A (40°) is only one side. Option B (60°) is incorrect. Option D (120°) is incorrect.

samples.prompt: In what frequency band does the microwave landing system (MLS) operate?
options: SHF, about 9.3–9.4 GHz
UHF, 329–335 MHz
SHF, about 5.0–5.1 GHz
VHF, 108–112 MHz
samples.explanation: MLS operates in the 5,031–5,090.7 MHz band (C band, about 6 cm wavelength), with 200 channels. The short wavelength allows narrow scanning beams from small aerials and makes MLS far less sensitive to reflections from buildings than ILS.
whyWrong: 9.3–9.4 GHz is used by airborne weather radar.
329–335 MHz is the ILS glide-path band.
108–112 MHz is the ILS localiser band.
samples.examTip: MLS around 5 GHz; weather radar around 9.4 GHz; do not confuse them.

samples.prompt: How does an aircraft's MLS receiver work out its azimuth angle from the runway centreline?
options: It measures the phase difference between two 30 Hz signals
It measures the Doppler shift of the signal from a rotating aerial
It times the interval between the TO and FRO sweeps of a narrow scanning beam
It compares the depths of 90 Hz and 150 Hz modulation
samples.explanation: MLS uses a Time Reference Scanning Beam: a narrow fan sweeps TO and then FRO across the coverage. The aircraft receives two pulses, and the time between them is directly proportional to its angle from the centreline. The elevation station does the same vertically.
whyWrong: That is how a conventional VOR works.
Doppler is used by DVOR; MLS uses time reference scanning.
That is how an ILS localiser works.
samples.examTip: Time between sweeps = angle.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of MLS over ILS?
options: Its wide coverage allows curved and segmented approaches
It is much less affected by reflections from buildings and taxiing aircraft
The approach path angle can be selected by the pilot
It needs no special receiver in the aircraft
samples.explanation: MLS offers wide azimuth and elevation coverage, selectable approach paths, many channels and good resistance to multipath. Its drawback is that it needs a dedicated MLS receiver (and precision DME), which most aircraft do not carry; that, and the arrival of GNSS-based approaches, is why MLS saw little use.
whyWrong: This is an advantage: azimuth coverage of at least ±40° supports curved and segmented approaches.
This is an advantage: narrow scanning beams at 5 GHz suffer far less multipath than ILS.
This is an advantage: any glide path within the elevation coverage can be flown.
samples.examTip: Ask which option is a benefit for the airport and which a cost for the aircraft.

samples.prompt: In a secondary radar system, the transponder can be located:
options: Only on the ground
Only in the aircraft
In the aircraft or on the ground
Only at the airport
samples.explanation: In a secondary radar system, the interrogator and transponder can be either way round: the transponder is in the aircraft for SSR, and on the ground for DME.

samples.prompt: An ATC radar must detect aircraft at a greater range without range ambiguity. Which change is needed?
options: Shorten the pulse width
Reduce the aerial rotation rate
Reduce the pulse repetition frequency
Increase the pulse repetition frequency
samples.explanation: Each echo must return before the next pulse is sent, otherwise it is displayed at the wrong range. Maximum unambiguous range = c ÷ (2 × PRF), so a longer range needs a lower PRF (and enough power).
whyWrong: Pulse width affects minimum range and range resolution, not maximum range.
Rotation rate affects how often each target is updated (and hits per scan), not unambiguous range.
A higher PRF gives less time between pulses, so the maximum unambiguous range falls.
samples.examTip: Long-range radars have low PRFs; short-range radars can use high PRFs.

samples.prompt: A radar echo returns 1,270 µs after the pulse was transmitted. What is the range of the target?
samples.explanation: Formula: Range = c × t ÷ 2; max range = c ÷ (2 × PRF); min range = c × τ ÷ 2. Range = c × t ÷ 2 = 3 × 10⁸ m/s × 1,270 × 10⁻⁶ s ÷ 2 = 190.5 km = 102.9 nm. Shortcut: each nautical mile of range takes 2 × 1,852 ÷ 3 × 10⁸ = 12.35 µs, so 1,270 ÷ 12.35 = 102.9 nm.
whyWrong: Halved the time twice: gives 51.4 nm.
Gave kilometres instead of nautical miles: gives 190.5 nm.
Forgot to halve the time, although the echo time covers the journey out and back: gives 205.7 nm.
samples.examTip: Echo time: about 12.36 µs per nautical mile of range.

samples.prompt: A primary radar's maximum detection range is to be doubled with no other change. By what factor must its transmitted power be increased?
samples.explanation: For a primary radar the energy is spread out on the way to the target and again on the way back, so the echo strength falls with the fourth power of range. Maximum range is therefore proportional to the fourth root of power: doubling the range needs 2⁴ = 16 times the power. For SSR, where each leg is one-way, range is proportional to the square root of power.
whyWrong: Range proportional to the square root of power applies to one-way systems such as SSR, not to a primary echo.
Assumes range is proportional to power.
No standard relation gives 8; it is a guess between 4 and 16.
samples.examTip: 16 for primary, 4 for secondary.

samples.prompt: Two aircraft at the same range from a surveillance radar are 1° apart in bearing and appear as a single echo. Which change would most help the radar show them separately?
options: A higher transmitter power
A lower pulse repetition frequency
A narrower horizontal beam width
A shorter pulse width
samples.explanation: Targets at the same range merge if they are both inside the beam at the same time, so bearing (azimuth) resolution depends on the horizontal beam width. A larger aerial or a shorter wavelength narrows the beam. Range resolution, for targets on the same bearing, depends instead on pulse width (c × τ ÷ 2).
whyWrong: More power increases detection range but does not separate targets within one beam width.
PRF sets maximum unambiguous range.
Pulse width sets range resolution, the separation of targets on the same bearing.
samples.examTip: Same range, different bearing = beam width. Same bearing, different range = pulse width.

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a primary radar system used by Air Traffic Control?
options: Area Surveillance Radar
Secondary Surveillance Radar
Precision Approach Radar
Airport Surface Movement Radar
samples.explanation: SSR is a secondary radar: it needs a transponder in the aircraft to reply. Area surveillance, precision approach and surface movement radars are all primary radars, relying on reflected echoes.

samples.prompt: What does a precision approach radar (PAR) give the controller that an airport surveillance radar does not?
options: The aircraft's identity and pressure altitude
Positions of aircraft and vehicles on the taxiways
Azimuth and elevation relative to the final approach path, for a talk-down
Coverage of all traffic within about 200 nm of the radar head, at all levels
samples.explanation: A PAR has two aerials scanning the final approach: one in azimuth and one in elevation. The controller sees the aircraft against the centreline and the glide path and passes corrections ('slightly left of centreline, on glide path') down to the decision height. It covers only the final approach, typically about the last 10 nm.
whyWrong: Identity and pressure altitude come from SSR, not from any primary radar.
That is surface movement radar (SMR).
That is long-range en-route surveillance radar coverage.
samples.examTip: PAR is a precision approach without any special aircraft equipment.

samples.prompt: Why does a surface movement radar (SMR) use a very short wavelength and a very short pulse?
options: To obtain a long range so that arriving aircraft can be seen at 50 nm
To resolve individual aircraft and vehicles only a few metres apart
To penetrate heavy rain with little attenuation
To allow the use of a very low PRF
samples.explanation: On an airport surface the radar must separate targets only a few metres apart. A short pulse gives good range resolution (c × τ ÷ 2) and a short wavelength gives a narrow beam from a reasonable aerial, which gives good bearing resolution. The cost is short range and some loss in heavy rain.
whyWrong: SMR only needs a few nautical miles of range; long range needs lower frequencies and lower PRFs.
Short wavelengths are attenuated MORE by rain; this is a weakness of SMR.
A short-range radar can use a high PRF; there is no need for a low one.
samples.examTip: Resolution needs short pulses and narrow beams; range needs power and low PRF.

samples.prompt: On a primary surveillance radar display, a moving target indicator (MTI) is switched on. What effect does it have?
options: It shows each aircraft's identity code in a label beside its echo
It shows the aircraft's pressure altitude
It suppresses echoes from fixed objects, leaving moving targets
It increases the maximum range of the radar
samples.explanation: MTI compares successive echoes from the same place. Echoes that do not change between pulses (ground clutter) are cancelled, while echoes from moving aircraft, whose phase changes because of the Doppler effect, remain. A drawback is that a target moving tangentially to the radar, with no radial speed, can be suppressed (a 'blind speed' or tangential fade).
whyWrong: Identity codes come from SSR Mode A.
Pressure altitude comes from SSR Mode C or Mode S.
MTI is a clutter filter; it does not increase the range.
samples.examTip: MTI can lose an aircraft flying a circle round the radar head.

samples.prompt: An en-route surveillance radar must cover traffic out to about 200 nm. Compared with an airport surveillance radar, it is likely to use:
options: A shorter wavelength and a higher PRF
A longer wavelength and a higher PRF
A longer wavelength and a lower PRF
A shorter wavelength and a lower PRF
samples.explanation: Long range needs a low PRF so that echoes return before the next pulse, plus high power and a longer wavelength (for example 23 cm rather than 10 cm), which suffers less atmospheric and rain attenuation. The airport radar, needing only about 60 nm, can use a shorter wavelength, a higher PRF and faster rotation for quicker updates.
whyWrong: Both changes reduce range: higher PRF limits unambiguous range and shorter wavelengths suffer more attenuation.
The longer wavelength is right, but a high PRF limits the unambiguous range.
The low PRF is right, but shorter wavelengths are attenuated more by rain and the atmosphere.
samples.examTip: Range and resolution pull in opposite directions; long-range radars give up resolution.

samples.prompt: Airborne Weather Radar is an example of:
options: Primary radar operating on a frequency of 8800 MHz in the SHF band
Secondary radar operating on a frequency of 9.375 MHz in the UHF band
Secondary radar operating on a frequency of 9375 MHz in the SHF band
Primary radar operating on a frequency of 9375 MHz in the SHF band
samples.explanation: AWR is a primary radar that uses the echo principle. It operates at 9375 MHz which falls in the SHF (Super High Frequency) band. Options B and C are incorrect because AWR is not secondary radar. Option A has the wrong frequency.

samples.prompt: Why do most airborne weather radars operate in the X band, at about 9.4 GHz (3.2 cm)?
options: It allows the radar to see through cumulonimbus to the clear air beyond, with no shadow
It is the only band that detects clear-air turbulence
This band is not attenuated at all by heavy rain
Rain reflects it well, and a narrow beam fits a small nose aerial
samples.explanation: Echo strength from rain rises steeply as wavelength falls, so about 3 cm gives strong returns from precipitation, and the short wavelength allows a narrow pencil beam from an aerial that fits in a nose radome. The trade-off is attenuation: in very heavy rain the beam is absorbed and storms beyond can be hidden.
whyWrong: Heavy rain attenuates X band and can cast a radar shadow behind it.
No weather radar detects clear-air turbulence; it needs precipitation to give an echo.
X band IS attenuated by heavy rain, which can hide weather behind a storm.
samples.examTip: Weather radar sees water, not turbulence or clear air.

samples.prompt: Which of the following gives the WEAKEST return on an airborne weather radar?
options: Dry snow
Wet snow
Wet hail
Heavy rain
samples.explanation: Radar reflectivity depends on the size of the particles and whether they are liquid. Large wet particles (wet hail, heavy rain, wet snow) return strongly; dry snow and dry hail return weakly despite their size, and cloud droplets and clear-air turbulence hardly at all.
whyWrong: Wet snow reflects well because of its liquid coating.
Wet hail is the strongest reflector of all.
Heavy rain gives a strong return.
samples.examTip: Weak echo is not the same as safe weather.

samples.prompt: A colour weather radar shows an area of red with a patch of magenta in the centre, and the colours change from green to red over a very short distance on one side. What does this indicate?
options: Ground returns from a mountain range, because the antenna tilt has been set too far down
A radar shadow caused by attenuation
Light rain near the edge of the radar's range, safe to penetrate
Very heavy rain with a steep gradient, a sign of severe turbulence: avoid it widely
samples.explanation: Colours rise in intensity from green through yellow and red to magenta. Magenta shows the heaviest rainfall, and a tight colour gradient (green to red in a short distance) shows rapidly changing rainfall rate, which goes with strong updraughts and turbulence. Such cells should be avoided by a wide margin and never penetrated.
whyWrong: Ground returns do not show a gradient in a storm-like pattern; changing the tilt would confirm them.
A shadow shows as an absence of returns (black) behind heavy rain, not as magenta.
Red and magenta are the highest intensities, not light rain.
samples.examTip: Hooks, fingers, scalloped edges and steep gradients all indicate severe weather.

samples.prompt: A pilot flying at FL 300 sees a storm echo at 40 nm, but as the tilt is raised by 2° the echo disappears. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The beam is now passing above the top of the reflective part of the storm
The radar has switched automatically into mapping mode
Raising the tilt always removes all weather returns at that range
The storm has dissipated
samples.explanation: Raising the tilt lifts the beam. At 40 nm, 2° of tilt raises the beam centre by about 40 × 200 = 8,000 ft (1 in 60). If the echo disappears, the beam is above the top of the strongly reflective part of the storm, which can still have a dry, turbulent top above it, so do not assume the storm is low enough to overfly.
whyWrong: Mapping mode is selected by the pilot and uses a fan-shaped beam; it does not remove weather echoes.
Only echoes below the beam are lost; a storm extending higher would still show.
A storm does not dissipate in the few seconds of a tilt change; the geometry has changed.
samples.examTip: Echo lost on raising tilt = beam above the wet part of the cell, not above the storm.

samples.prompt: On which frequencies does SSR interrogate and reply?
options: Interrogation 1,030 MHz; reply 1,093 MHz, offset by 63 MHz as in DME
Both on 1,030 MHz, separated in time
Interrogation 1,030 MHz from the ground; reply 1,090 MHz from the aircraft
Interrogation 1,090 MHz from the ground; reply 1,030 MHz from the aircraft
samples.explanation: SSR ground stations interrogate on 1,030 MHz and transponders reply on 1,090 MHz. Mode S and ACAS use the same pair. Because the reply is transmitted by the aircraft, SSR needs far less power than a primary radar and has no clutter.
whyWrong: The 63 MHz offset is a DME feature; SSR replies are 60 MHz above, on 1,090 MHz.
Using one frequency for both would let replies trigger other transponders.
Reversed: the ground interrogates on 1,030 MHz.
samples.examTip: Ground 1030, aircraft 1090: the aircraft's number is higher.

samples.prompt: Consider these SSR codes: 1. 7500: unlawful interference 2. 7600: radio communication failure 3. 7700: emergency 4. 7000: entering SSR airspace without an assigned code Which pairings are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
samples.explanation: The special-purpose codes are 7500 (unlawful interference), 7600 (radio failure) and 7700 (emergency). A pilot entering an area where SSR is in use, with no code assigned, squawks 2000. 7000 is a VFR conspicuity code in some regions.
whyWrong: Leaves out 7500, the unlawful interference code.
Leaves out 7600, the radio failure code.
7000 is used in some regions as a VFR conspicuity code; the code for entering SSR airspace with no assigned code is 2000.
samples.examTip: Code 2000 is the 'no assigned code' code, not 7000.

samples.prompt: What is the main advantage of Mode S over Modes A and C?
options: It works in a different frequency band, so its replies can never interfere with Mode A and C replies
A unique 24-bit address allows selective interrogation, which avoids garbling and allows data link
It gives altitude to the nearest foot
It needs no transponder in the aircraft
samples.explanation: A Mode S transponder has a unique 24-bit aircraft address (about 16.7 million combinations). Ground stations can call each aircraft individually, so replies from aircraft close together no longer overlap (garble), and the link can carry data such as selected altitude and heading. ACAS also relies on Mode S.
whyWrong: Mode S uses the same 1,030/1,090 MHz pair as Modes A and C.
Mode S reports pressure altitude in 25 ft or 100 ft steps, not to the nearest foot.
Mode S is a transponder mode; the aircraft must carry a Mode S transponder.
samples.examTip: 'Selective' is the key word: the S stands for Select.

samples.prompt: The pilot sets QNH 1003 hPa on the altimeter and climbs to 5,000 ft altitude. What level does the transponder report in Mode C?
options: About 4,700 ft pressure altitude, from the 1013.25 hPa datum
About 5,300 ft pressure altitude, from the 1013.25 hPa datum
5,000 ft, because Mode C uses the subscale setting
Mode C reports height above the ground from the radio altimeter
samples.explanation: Mode C encodes pressure altitude, referenced to 1013.25 hPa, in 100 ft steps, independent of the subscale. With QNH 1003 the 1013.25 hPa level is about 10 × 30 = 300 ft below sea level, so pressure altitude ≈ 5,000 + 300 = 5,300 ft. ATC's system converts it back to altitude using the QNH.
whyWrong: Applied the 10 hPa difference the wrong way: with QNH below 1013 the pressure altitude is higher than the altitude.
Mode C is always referenced to 1013.25 hPa, whatever the pilot sets.
Mode C uses the pressure (encoding) altimeter, not the radio altimeter.
samples.examTip: Low QNH: pressure altitude above altitude (about 30 ft per hPa).

samples.prompt: A controller sees false SSR replies scattered on the display, caused by the aircraft's transponder replying to interrogations from a different ground station. What is this called?
options: FRUIT
Garbling
Side-lobe interrogation
Ducting
samples.explanation: FRUIT (False Replies Unsynchronised In Time) are replies triggered by other interrogators. They arrive at random times, so they appear as scattered false returns; a defruiter rejects replies that do not repeat from one interrogation to the next. Garbling, in contrast, is overlap between two genuine replies.
whyWrong: Garbling is the overlap of replies from two aircraft close together in range and bearing.
Side-lobe interrogation is a nearby aircraft replying to the aerial's side lobes; it is suppressed by the P2 pulse.
Ducting is an abnormal propagation effect, not a reply problem.
samples.examTip: Random scattered replies = FRUIT; two close aircraft = garble.

samples.prompt: A VOR/DME share the same first two letters of their respective identifiers; the last identifying letter of the DME is a Z. This means that:
options: They are co-located
They are more than 600 m apart but serve the same location
They are widely separated and do not serve the same location
They are a maximum distance of 30 m apart
samples.explanation: When VOR and DME are not associated but serve the same location, the first two letters of the call sign are the same, and the last letter for DME is 'Z'. Option A describes associated facilities with identical call signs. Option C describes widely separated facilities with totally different identifications. Option D describes the maximum separation for associated facilities in TMAs.

samples.prompt: Distance Measuring Equipment is an example of _______ radar operating on a frequency of _______ in the _______ band.
options: Primary, 8800 MHz, SHF
Secondary, 1030 MHz, UHF
Secondary, 962 MHz, UHF
Primary, 9375 MHz, SHF
samples.explanation: DME is a secondary radar system operating between 960 and 1215 MHz in the UHF band. The emission code is P0N. Option A is incorrect as DME is not primary radar and does not operate at 8800 MHz. Option B is incorrect because 1030 MHz is the secondary surveillance radar frequency, not DME. Option D is incorrect as DME is secondary radar, not primary.

samples.prompt: What delay does a DME ground beacon add before it replies, and why?
options: A random delay, so each aircraft can identify its own replies
A fixed 50 µs, so that even very short ranges can be measured
A fixed 12.36 µs, the time for one radar nautical mile
No delay; the reply is instantaneous
samples.explanation: The ground transponder waits a fixed 50 µs (X channels) after receiving an interrogation before replying. The airborne set subtracts it when computing range: range = (elapsed time − 50 µs) ÷ 12.36 µs per nm. The delay ensures that even overhead the reply arrives after the airborne set has stopped transmitting.
whyWrong: The random element is the aircraft's interrogation timing (jitter); the beacon's delay is fixed.
12.36 µs is the round-trip time per nautical mile, not the beacon delay.
There is a fixed delay; without it the airborne set would still be transmitting when close replies arrived.
samples.examTip: Random = aircraft jitter; fixed 50 µs = beacon delay.

samples.prompt: How does an airborne DME recognise the replies to its own interrogations among the replies the beacon sends to other aircraft?
options: Each aircraft interrogates on its own unique frequency within the band, so replies cannot be mixed up
The beacon adds the aircraft's address to each reply
It accepts only the strongest reply received
It varies its interrogation interval at random and locks on to replies that keep a constant delay
samples.explanation: Each airborne set varies the interval between its interrogations at random. Replies to its own interrogations always follow them by the same delay (set by the range), while replies to other aircraft arrive at random times. The set locks on to the replies that stay synchronised (stroboscopic search).
whyWrong: All aircraft using a beacon interrogate on its paired frequency; they are not separated in frequency.
Addressing is a Mode S feature; DME replies carry no address.
Signal strength does not identify a reply; a nearby aircraft's reply could be stronger.
samples.examTip: 'Jitter' and 'stroboscopic' both point to how DME finds its own replies.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies past a DME station, 10 nm abeam it, and the DME-derived groundspeed falls almost to zero. Why?
options: Groundspeed is the rate of change of range, which is near zero abeam the station
The aircraft has entered the DME's cone of silence
The aircraft has flown out of line-of-sight range
The beacon has become saturated by too many aircraft and has stopped replying to this one
samples.explanation: DME groundspeed is the rate at which the slant range changes. It equals true groundspeed only when the aircraft flies directly towards or away from the station. Abeam the station the range hardly changes, so the indicated groundspeed (and time to station) is meaningless.
whyWrong: Being 10 nm abeam is not overhead; a cone-of-confusion effect applies only near the vertical.
Line-of-sight range at normal heights is much more than 10 nm.
Saturation reduces replies to weaker aircraft, but would not make a 'zero groundspeed'.
samples.examTip: Off the radial, DME groundspeed reads low.

chapters.title: Area Navigation Systems (RNAV)
topics: Operation of a Simple 2D RNAV System
Principle of Operation of a Simple 2D RNAV System
Limitations and Accuracy of Simple RNAV Systems

samples.prompt: In a simple 2D RNAV system, waypoints are known as phantom stations because:
options: They transmit their own navigation signals
The equipment computes QDM and distance as if the waypoint itself is a VOR/DME station
They are imaginary points that cannot be used for navigation
They only exist in the pilot's flight plan
samples.explanation: A 2D RNAV computer calculates the QDM and distance to each waypoint and presents them as if the waypoint were a VOR/DME, hence 'phantom station'.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is approved for RNP 1 on a departure. What does the '1' mean?
options: The lateral navigation error must stay within 1 nm for at least 95% of the flight time
The procedure must be flown within 1° of the published track
The aircraft must be within 1 nm of track at all times, without exception
One GNSS receiver is enough for the procedure
samples.explanation: The number in an RNAV or RNP designation is the lateral total system error, in nautical miles, that must not be exceeded for at least 95% of the total flight time. RNP 1 therefore means within 1 nm of the defined path 95% of the time, with monitoring and alerting if this cannot be met.
whyWrong: PBN accuracies are distances in nautical miles, not angles.
The value is a 95% accuracy figure, not an absolute limit (integrity requirements cover the rare larger errors).
The number says nothing about how many receivers are needed.
samples.examTip: Designation number = nm, 95% of flight time.

samples.prompt: Under PBN, what is the difference between an RNAV specification and an RNP specification?
options: RNP requires on-board performance monitoring and alerting; RNAV does not
RNP specifications apply en route only; RNAV specifications apply on approach only
An RNAV specification defines accuracy in nautical miles; an RNP specification in metres
An RNP specification is only for GNSS; an RNAV specification is only for VOR/DME
samples.explanation: In ICAO PBN (Doc 9613), both types state a lateral accuracy in nautical miles that must be met 95% of the flight time. An RNP specification adds a requirement for on-board performance monitoring and alerting: the system must warn the crew when it cannot meet the required performance. RNAV 5 and RNAV 1 do not include it; RNP 1 and RNP APCH do.
whyWrong: Both exist in several phases of flight (for example RNAV 1 terminal, RNP APCH approach).
Both use the same accuracy convention: the number is nautical miles, 95% of the flight time.
Both kinds can be met by different sensors; PBN describes performance, not specific sensors.
samples.examTip: 'Monitoring and alerting' is the key phrase that turns RNAV into RNP.

samples.prompt: What is the difference between a fly-by and a fly-over waypoint?
options: At a fly-by waypoint the aircraft must cross the point exactly; a fly-over waypoint may be cut short
Fly-by: the turn starts before the waypoint; fly-over: the turn starts only after passing it
Fly-over waypoints are used only en route; fly-by waypoints only on approach
A fly-by waypoint is defined by a VOR; a fly-over waypoint by GNSS
samples.explanation: For a fly-by waypoint the RNAV system anticipates the turn and starts it before the waypoint, so the aircraft rolls out on the next leg without overshooting. A fly-over waypoint must be overflown before the turn starts, so the aircraft overshoots and then rejoins; it is used where the point itself matters, such as a missed approach point.
whyWrong: Reversed: it is the fly-over waypoint that must be crossed.
Both types are used in all phases; for example a missed approach point is a fly-over waypoint.
Waypoints are defined by coordinates; the type describes how the turn is flown, not the sensor.
samples.examTip: On charts, a fly-over waypoint symbol is circled.

samples.prompt: RNAV equipment uses a VOR/DME to define a waypoint 25 nm from the station on its 060° radial. The aircraft is 25 nm from the station on the 120° radial. How far is it from the waypoint?
options: 50 nm
25 nm
35 nm
0 nm
samples.explanation: The station and the two points form a triangle with two sides of 25 nm and a 60° angle between them at the station. An isosceles triangle with a 60° apex angle is equilateral, so the third side is also 25 nm. In general d = √(d₁² + d₂² − 2 d₁ d₂ cos θ).
whyWrong: Added the two distances, as if the radials were opposite.
Used Pythagoras as if the radials were 90° apart (√(25² + 25²) = 35 nm).
Same DME distance does not mean the same place; the radials differ by 60°.
samples.examTip: Spot the 60° equilateral case before reaching for the cosine rule.

samples.prompt: In the expanded ILS mode, the glide slope indications are suppressed when:
options: The aircraft is below the glide slope
The aircraft track is more than 90 degrees removed from the ILS localizer course
The localizer is not captured
The aircraft is above the glide slope
samples.explanation: In expanded ILS mode, the glide slope pointer is suppressed when the aircraft's track is more than 90° from the localiser course, for example on a back course.

samples.prompt: A pilot wants to step through the FMS route waypoint by waypoint on the navigation display, with the display oriented to north. Which ND mode is used?
options: MAP (ARC)
PLAN
VOR rose
ILS (APP) rose
samples.explanation: PLAN mode shows the route oriented to true north, centred on a selected waypoint rather than on the aircraft. Stepping through it lets the crew check the flight plan entered in the FMS. Weather radar is not shown in PLAN mode, because the picture is not tied to the aircraft's heading.
whyWrong: MAP shows the route ahead in track-up or heading-up, centred on the aircraft.
VOR rose shows a compass rose with a course deviation display for the tuned VOR.
The ILS/APP rose shows localiser and glide-path deviation for the tuned ILS.
samples.examTip: Weather radar and TCAS overlays need MAP/ARC, not PLAN.

samples.prompt: On the PFD speed tape, the speed trend arrow extends from 240 kt up to 252 kt. What does it show?
options: The maximum speed for the present configuration
The speed the aircraft would reach at the top of descent
The speed that the autothrottle or autopilot has been commanded to fly
The speed expected in about 10 seconds at the present acceleration
samples.explanation: The trend vector projects the current rate of change of airspeed forward: its tip shows the speed expected in about 10 seconds. Here the aircraft is accelerating at about 1.2 kt per second and will reach about 252 kt.
whyWrong: The maximum speed is shown by a separate barber's pole or red band.
The trend arrow is a short-term prediction, not a flight-plan prediction.
The selected speed is shown by a separate speed bug.
samples.examTip: A long trend arrow towards a limit is an early warning of an overspeed or low speed.

samples.prompt: Which statement about EFIS is NOT correct?
options: The ND MAP mode always shows the display oriented to true north
Red is used for warnings that need immediate crew action, and amber for cautions
Weather radar returns can be overlaid on the ND in MAP or ARC mode
The symbol generators take data from the aircraft's sensors and draw the display images
samples.explanation: In MAP or ARC mode the ND is oriented to the aircraft's track or heading, so the picture ahead matches the view from the cockpit. It is PLAN mode that is north-up. Symbol generators turn sensor data into images, and warning colours follow the red-for-warning, amber-for-caution convention.
whyWrong: This is correct: red for warnings and amber for cautions is standard practice.
This is correct: weather and terrain overlays are shown in MAP/ARC.
This is correct: symbol generators (display computers) produce the images from sensor data.
samples.examTip: North-up belongs to PLAN only.

samples.prompt: During an ILS approach the left symbol generator fails and its displays blank. What is the normal crew action?
options: Switch the ND to PLAN mode, which uses a separate computer
Abandon the approach at once, because a symbol generator failure removes all ILS guidance
Select the other symbol generator for the affected displays and continue cross-checking
Reset the IRS, because the symbol generator takes its power from it
samples.explanation: EFIS is designed with redundant symbol generators (display computers). If one fails, source selection switches the affected screens to another generator, and the standby instruments remain. The approach can continue if the remaining displays and guidance meet the requirements, with careful cross-checking.
whyWrong: PLAN mode is a display format on the same symbol generator, not a separate computer.
The ILS receivers are unaffected; only the display path has failed, and other displays are still available.
The IRS is a sensor; resetting it would remove attitude and heading data and make things worse.
samples.examTip: Distinguish a sensor failure (wrong data) from a display failure (no picture).

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS)?
options: WAAS
GLONASS
GAGAN
EGNOS
samples.explanation: GLONASS is a core global navigation constellation, like GPS, Galileo and BeiDou. WAAS (USA), EGNOS (Europe), MSAS (Japan) and GAGAN (India) are SBAS: they broadcast corrections and integrity information from geostationary satellites to improve GPS.
whyWrong: WAAS is the US SBAS.
GAGAN is the Indian SBAS.
EGNOS is the European SBAS.
samples.examTip: An SBAS does not give position on its own; it improves a core constellation.

samples.prompt: A satellite signal takes 69.1 ms to reach the receiver. What range does that represent?
samples.explanation: The GNSS signal travels one way, so range = c × t = 299 792 km/s × 69.1 ms = 20,716 km.
whyWrong: Converted the range to nautical miles but labelled it km
Multiplied by 1.852 as if the result were in nm
Halved the time as if it were a radar round trip
samples.examTip: Common trap: converted the range to nautical miles but labelled it km.

samples.prompt: Why does a GNSS receiver need signals from at least four satellites for a three-dimensional position?
options: Each satellite gives only one coordinate, and a fourth is needed for velocity
Four satellites are needed to remove ionospheric delay
There are four unknowns: latitude, longitude, altitude and the receiver's clock error
Three satellites give position; the fourth is always needed for RAIM
samples.explanation: The receiver's quartz clock is not accurate enough, so every measured range has the same unknown clock bias (hence 'pseudorange'). Solving for three position coordinates plus the clock bias needs four equations: four satellites. A fifth allows RAIM to detect a faulty satellite and a sixth to exclude it.
whyWrong: Each satellite gives a range, not a coordinate; velocity comes from the Doppler shift or position changes.
Ionospheric delay is corrected by a model, by dual frequencies or by augmentation, not by a fourth satellite.
RAIM fault detection needs a fifth satellite, beyond the four used for position.
samples.examTip: Baro-aiding can replace one satellite for RAIM.

samples.prompt: Which source of error usually contributes most to the position error of a single-frequency GPS receiver without augmentation?
options: Ionospheric delay
Receiver noise
Satellite clock error
Tropospheric delay
samples.explanation: Signals are slowed by free electrons in the ionosphere, by an amount that changes with time of day, season and solar activity. A single-frequency receiver can only apply a broadcast model, which leaves a significant residual error. Dual-frequency receivers measure it, and SBAS such as GAGAN broadcasts corrections for it; this matters particularly near the geomagnetic equator, which lies close to southern India.
whyWrong: Receiver noise is small with modern receivers.
Satellite clocks are atomic and corrected by the control segment; their residual error is smaller.
Tropospheric delay is smaller than ionospheric delay and is well modelled.
samples.examTip: Dual frequency and SBAS both attack ionospheric error.

samples.prompt: Before an RNP approach, the GNSS receiver predicts that RAIM will not be available at the destination for the estimated time of arrival. What does this mean?
options: The receiver's accuracy will be improved by SBAS during that period
Its position integrity cannot be checked then, so the approach cannot be relied on
The approach can be flown normally but only in daylight
The receiver will have no position at all during that period, whatever the satellite geometry
samples.explanation: RAIM uses redundant satellites to check that the position is trustworthy. A prediction of no RAIM means there will not be enough satellites with suitable geometry to detect a faulty one, so the crew would not be warned of a bad position. An RNP approach that depends on it should not be planned for that time; use another approach or another time.
whyWrong: RAIM unavailability says nothing about SBAS; if anything it means fewer satellites in view.
RAIM availability depends on satellite geometry, not on daylight.
Position may still be available from four satellites; it is the integrity check that is missing.
samples.examTip: No RAIM = no integrity, not necessarily no position.

chapters.title: Introduction to Radio Transmission in Aviation

samples.prompt: Air-to-Ground Communication primarily involves:
options: Pilots communicating with nearby aircraft
Pilots communicating with Air Traffic Control (ATC)
Ground staff communicating with each other
Passengers making phone calls
samples.explanation: Air-to-ground communication is the exchange between pilots and Air Traffic Control (ATC) for clearances, instructions and flight updates. Pilot-to-pilot exchange (A) is air-to-air communication; ground staff talking among themselves and passenger phone calls are not aeronautical air-ground communication.

samples.prompt: A pilot at Delhi talks to Delhi Ground on VHF. Which ICAO telecommunication service does this air-ground exchange belong to?
options: The aeronautical mobile service
The aeronautical broadcasting service
The aeronautical fixed service
The aeronautical radionavigation service
samples.explanation: ICAO Annex 10 divides aeronautical telecommunications into the fixed, mobile, radionavigation and broadcasting services. The aeronautical mobile service is between aeronautical stations on the ground and aircraft stations, or between aircraft stations, so every pilot–controller RT exchange is part of it.
whyWrong: Broadcasting is one-way transmission to all aircraft, such as ATIS or VOLMET, not a two-way exchange.
The fixed service links specified fixed points on the ground, such as the AFTN between ATS units.
Radionavigation is for position and guidance (VOR, DME, ILS), not for communication.
samples.examTip: If the exchange involves an aircraft in two-way contact, the answer is 'mobile'.

samples.prompt: A trainee wants the ICAO manual that explains standard RT phraseology with complete example exchanges for each phase of flight. Which document is it?
options: Doc 7030, Regional Supplementary Procedures
Doc 8168, Aircraft Operations (PANS-OPS)
Annex 2, Rules of the Air
Doc 9432, Manual of Radiotelephony
samples.explanation: ICAO Doc 9432, the Manual of Radiotelephony, explains RT technique and standard phraseology with worked examples. The binding phraseologies themselves are in PANS-ATM (Doc 4444) chapter 12, and the communication procedures in Annex 10 Volume II.
whyWrong: Doc 7030 lists regional differences and additions to the PANS, not RT examples.
PANS-OPS covers instrument procedure design and flight procedures, not RT technique.
Annex 2 contains the rules of the air, including the interception and light signals, but not an RT manual.
samples.examTip: Know the three RT references: Annex 10 Vol II (procedures), Doc 4444 (phraseology), Doc 9432 (manual).

samples.prompt: A pilot is assessed at ICAO language proficiency Level 4 (Operational). Within what interval should the pilot be formally re-evaluated?
options: At least once every three years
At least once every six years
Never: Level 4 is valid for life
At least once every year, with the medical
samples.explanation: ICAO Annex 1 requires at least Level 4 for pilots and controllers who use RT, and recommends formal re-evaluation at least every three years for Level 4 and every six years for Level 5. Level 6 holders need no further evaluation.
whyWrong: Six years is the interval for Level 5 (Extended).
Only Level 6 (Expert) is exempt from re-evaluation.
Language proficiency is not tied to the medical certificate.
samples.examTip: The trap is mixing the Level 5 interval with Level 4.

samples.prompt: In which language must air-ground radiotelephony be conducted at an aeronautical station serving an international aerodrome?
options: Any language the pilot and controller agree on, provided both hold Level 4 in it
English only, at every aeronautical station worldwide, whatever routes or aerodromes it serves
The language of the aircraft's State of Registry, with English as a fallback
The station's normal language or English, with English available on request
samples.explanation: Annex 10 Volume II requires air-ground RT to be conducted in the language normally used by the station on the ground or in English. At stations serving designated international aerodromes and routes, English must be available on request from any aircraft station.
whyWrong: Communication is not negotiated case by case; it is the ground station's language or English.
ICAO allows the language normally used by the ground station; English must be available, not exclusive.
The State of Registry has no bearing on the language of the ground station.
samples.examTip: 'English only' sounds safe but is not the ICAO rule; look for 'or English, available on request'.

chapters.title: Radio Frequency Bands and Their Uses

samples.prompt: Which frequency band is allocated to aeronautical VHF voice communication with ATC?
samples.explanation: Civil VHF RT uses 117.975–137.000 MHz, just above the VOR/ILS band. Channels are 25 kHz apart, and 8.33 kHz in some congested regions. VHF propagates by line of sight, so it gives clear, static-free speech at short to medium range.
whyWrong: That is the HF aeronautical mobile band used for long-range communication.
108–117.975 MHz is the VHF navigation band used by VOR and ILS localisers.
225–400 MHz is the military UHF band.
samples.examTip: If an option starts at 108 MHz it is the navigation band, not communications.

samples.prompt: A civil aircraft in an emergency cannot raise ATC on the frequency in use. Which frequency is the international VHF aeronautical emergency frequency?
samples.explanation: 121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency frequency on VHF. It is monitored by ATS units, many aircraft and SAR services. A distress or urgency call is first made on the frequency in use; 121.5 MHz is used when contact there is not possible.
whyWrong: 243.0 MHz is the military UHF emergency frequency, twice 121.5 MHz.
406 MHz is used by emergency locator transmitters to reach the satellite search-and-rescue system, not for voice.
123.45 MHz is the air-to-air channel for exchanging information in remote and oceanic areas.
samples.examTip: Use the frequency in use first; switch to 121.5 MHz only if that fails.

samples.prompt: Why is HF used for voice communication on oceanic routes such as those over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea?
options: HF is free of static and fading, which makes it clearer than VHF at all ranges
HF sky waves are refracted by the ionosphere, so they reach well beyond line of sight
HF propagates only by line of sight, which at cruising level covers the ocean
HF ground waves follow the sea surface for several thousand nautical miles by day and night
samples.explanation: HF (3–30 MHz) sky waves are refracted back to Earth by the ionosphere, so a single hop can cover more than a thousand nautical miles. The price is variable quality: ionospheric changes, static and fading mean that HF needs careful frequency selection and often SELCAL.
whyWrong: HF suffers from static and fading; its advantage is range, not quality.
Line of sight is the VHF limitation; it cannot cover an ocean crossing.
Ground waves at HF are attenuated within a few hundred nautical miles; long range comes from sky waves.
samples.examTip: Range beyond the horizon = sky wave = HF.

samples.prompt: With 25 kHz channel spacing, how many VHF communication channels are there between 118.000 MHz and 119.000 MHz (count 118.000 but not 119.000)?
samples.explanation: Number of channels = bandwidth ÷ spacing = 1,000 kHz ÷ 25 kHz = 40 (118.000, 118.025, 118.050 ... 118.975). Reducing the spacing to 8.33 kHz gives three times as many channels, which is why it is used in congested airspace.
whyWrong: 20 channels would need 50 kHz spacing.
100 channels would need 10 kHz spacing, which is not used for aeronautical voice.
120 channels per MHz comes from 8.33 kHz spacing.
samples.examTip: 1 MHz = 1,000 kHz: convert before dividing.

samples.prompt: What is the wavelength of a VHF communication signal on 120.0 MHz?
samples.explanation: λ = c ÷ f = 300,000,000 m/s ÷ 120,000,000 Hz = 2.5 m. A quick form is λ (m) = 300 ÷ f (MHz) = 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 m. VHF signals are 'metric' waves (1–10 m).
whyWrong: A wavelength of 250 m belongs to a 1.2 MHz medium-frequency signal.
Ten times too short: 0.25 m corresponds to 1,200 MHz.
Ten times too long: 25 m is the wavelength of a 12 MHz HF signal.
samples.examTip: Check the band: 30–300 MHz must give 1–10 m.

chapters.title: Advantages and Limitations of Radio Communication

samples.prompt: What happens to the effective range of VHF signals when an aircraft increases its altitude?
options: The range decreases due to thinner air
The range increases because line-of-sight distance increases
The range remains unchanged
The range decreases due to increased interference
samples.explanation: VHF range is line of sight, so climbing raises the radio horizon and increases the range (about 1.23 x sqrt(height in ft) NM). Thinner air does not reduce VHF range, and the range does not stay the same or fall because of interference.

samples.prompt: On a busy Delhi Approach frequency, two pilots press their transmit switches at the same moment. What is the result?
options: The ground receiver stores the second call and replays it once the first one has finished
ATC hears both calls on separate channels, because aeronautical VHF RT works as a duplex system
The calls block or garble each other, and neither pilot hears the other while transmitting
The stronger signal always gets through cleanly, so only the weaker pilot needs to call again
samples.explanation: On a simplex channel only one station can usefully transmit at a time. If two transmit together, listeners hear a squeal or a garbled mix, and each transmitting station cannot hear the other, so neither knows the call failed. Listening before keying, keeping calls short and expecting an acknowledgement prevent missed clearances.
whyWrong: Nothing is stored or replayed: a blocked transmission is simply lost.
Aeronautical VHF RT is simplex, on one channel; there is no separate return path.
Neither call can be relied on: overlapping transmissions often produce a squeal or nothing readable.
samples.examTip: If a call or readback is not acknowledged, assume it was blocked and call again.

samples.prompt: An aircraft flies at 10,000 ft. The ground station's VHF antenna is 400 ft above the surrounding sea-level terrain. What is the approximate maximum VHF range between them?
options: 123 nm
125 nm
148 nm
120 nm
samples.explanation: VHF range (nm) ≈ 1.23 × (√h aircraft + √h station), with heights in feet. = 1.23 × (√10,000 + √400) = 1.23 × (100 + 20) = 1.23 × 120 = 148 nm. Terrain, power and receiver sensitivity can make the real range shorter.
whyWrong: Ignored the ground antenna height; the two horizons add.
Added the heights before taking the square root: 1.23 × √10,400; each height has its own root.
Left out the 1.23 factor: √10,000 + √400 = 120.
samples.examTip: Take each square root separately, then add.

samples.prompt: An HF operator wants the best signal on an oceanic route. Which general rule for choosing an HF frequency applies?
options: Use a lower frequency by day and a higher frequency by night
Use the highest available frequency at all times for the longest range
Use the same frequency throughout, because the ionosphere is stable
Use a higher frequency by day and a lower frequency by night
samples.explanation: By day the ionosphere is more strongly ionised, so it refracts higher frequencies, and lower frequencies are absorbed. At night ionisation falls, so higher frequencies pass straight through and a lower frequency must be used. The usual rule is 'high by day, low by night'.
whyWrong: Reverses the rule: daytime ionisation is stronger, so higher frequencies are refracted by day.
Above the maximum usable frequency the signal passes through the ionosphere and is lost.
The ionosphere changes markedly between day and night, especially around sunrise and sunset.
samples.examTip: Expect changes around sunrise and sunset, when the ionosphere changes fastest.

samples.prompt: On Mumbai Approach frequency a pilot hears a continuous carrier with background engine noise and no replies from ATC. What is the most likely cause, and what should the pilot check first?
options: Severe ionospheric fading: wait for the signal to return without changing any settings or the frequency
An ATC equipment failure: change to 121.5 MHz at once and declare an emergency
A stuck transmitter, possibly their own: check that their own PTT switch is not jammed
Normal frequency congestion: transmit over the noise until ATC answers
samples.explanation: A continuous open carrier with engine or cockpit noise means a transmitter is keyed. It may be in the pilot's own aircraft (a jammed PTT or a stuck microphone), so the first check is one's own transmit switch and audio panel. If it is another aircraft, ATC will try to alert it, and other frequencies or the next sector can be used.
whyWrong: VHF is not affected by ionospheric fading; that is an HF phenomenon.
A carrier with cockpit noise usually comes from an aircraft, not from ATC; the first step is to check one's own equipment.
Transmitting over a carrier only adds to the blocking; nobody will hear the call.
samples.examTip: If ATC seems to have gone silent, always rule out your own stuck transmit switch.

chapters.title: Radio Operations and Equipment
topics: Automatic Volume Control (AVC) / Automatic Gain Control (AGC)

samples.prompt: What does the squelch control on a VHF communication receiver do?
options: It mutes the background noise when no strong enough signal is received
It filters out the controller's voice so that only aircraft are heard
It selects which radio the microphone transmits on
It increases the receiver gain so that weak stations at long range can be heard more clearly
samples.explanation: Without signals, a receiver produces a constant hiss. The squelch circuit cuts the audio until a signal above a threshold arrives, so the pilot hears only real transmissions. Setting the squelch too tightly can cut out weak but wanted stations.
whyWrong: Squelch acts on signal strength, not on who is speaking.
The transmit selection is made on the audio panel, not by the squelch.
Increasing gain for weak signals is the job of the gain or volume control; squelch suppresses noise.
samples.examTip: If a distant station is hard to hear, open (reduce) the squelch, then restore it.

samples.prompt: A pilot of VT-KAX asks Delhi Ground for a radio check. Ground replies "VT-KAX, DELHI GROUND, READ YOU THREE". What does this mean?
options: Readable now and then
Perfectly readable
Readable, but with difficulty
Readable, with no difficulty at all
samples.explanation: The ICAO readability scale is: 1 unreadable; 2 readable now and then; 3 readable but with difficulty; 4 readable; 5 perfectly readable. A reply of THREE means the message can be understood only with effort, so the pilot should check the equipment or try another frequency before relying on it.
whyWrong: 'Readable now and then' is readability 2.
'Perfectly readable' is readability 5.
'Readable' is readability 4.
samples.examTip: The scale is one to FIVE, pronounced FIFE.

samples.prompt: Which transmitting technique is recommended for clear RT?
options: Speak faster than in normal conversation, to keep the frequency free for other users
Raise the voice for the important parts of the message, such as levels
Release the transmit switch briefly between phrases, so ATC can interrupt
Speak evenly, at no more than about 100 words per minute, at constant volume
samples.explanation: Annex 10 recommends: listen before transmitting; key the transmitter before speaking and do not release it until the message is complete; speak each word clearly at an even rate not exceeding about 100 words per minute; keep the volume constant; and hold the microphone at a constant distance from the mouth. Slow down when the message will be written down.
whyWrong: Fast speech causes requests to 'say again', which uses more airtime, not less.
Changes of volume distort the signal; a constant level is clearer.
Releasing between phrases lets another station key in and split the message.
samples.examTip: Press, pause, speak, finish, release: never clip the first or last word.

samples.prompt: How long should a radio test transmission (radio check) normally last?
options: Not more than about 30 seconds
At least one full minute
Not more than about 10 seconds
As long as needed for the ground station to tune in
samples.explanation: Test transmissions are kept short so that they do not block the channel; Annex 10 limits them to about 10 seconds. A radio check consists of the station called, the station calling, the words RADIO CHECK and the frequency used.
whyWrong: 30 seconds is the recommended maximum length of an ATIS broadcast, not of a test transmission.
A one-minute test would block the frequency for everyone else.
Test transmissions are deliberately short; the ground station is already on the frequency.
samples.examTip: Keep test calls short and never on the emergency frequency unless unavoidable.

samples.prompt: What does SELCAL allow the crew of an aircraft on an HF oceanic frequency to do?
options: Talk to another aircraft on the same frequency without the ground station hearing
Send position reports by data link instead of by voice
Stop a continuous listening watch: a ground-sent tone code alerts them
Select the best HF frequency automatically as the ionosphere changes
samples.explanation: Selective calling (SELCAL) gives each aircraft a four-letter tone code. When the ground station sends that code, a chime and light alert the crew, who then answer by voice. It removes the need to listen to noisy HF for hours, but the crew must still check SELCAL on first contact with each station.
whyWrong: SELCAL is a calling system, not a private channel.
Position reports by data link use CPDLC or ADS-C, not SELCAL.
Frequency selection is done by the crew from the published family of frequencies; SELCAL does not choose it.
samples.examTip: SELCAL calls; it does not carry the message itself.

samples.prompt: What does the RT word WILCO mean?
options: I have received all of your last transmission
Yes
Wait, and I will call you back as soon as I am able
I understand your message and will comply with it
samples.explanation: WILCO, from 'will comply', means 'I understand your message and will comply with it'. ROGER means only that the last transmission has been received. Neither replaces a required readback of a clearance or instruction.
whyWrong: That is the meaning of ROGER, which does not promise compliance.
Yes is AFFIRM.
That is STANDBY.
samples.examTip: ROGER WILCO is redundant: WILCO already includes receipt.

samples.prompt: How is the altimeter setting QNH 1009 transmitted?
options: QNH ONE ZERO ZERO NINE HECTOPASCALS
QNH TEN ZERO NINE
QNH ONE ZERO ZERO NINER
QNH ONE THOUSAND AND NINE
samples.explanation: Altimeter settings are transmitted digit by digit using RT pronunciation: 1009 becomes ONE ZERO ZERO NINER. The unit is added only when needed to avoid confusion, for example 'QNH NINER NINER FIFE HECTOPASCALS'.
whyWrong: Nine is pronounced NINER on RT; 'hectopascals' is said only when a setting could be confused, such as below 1000.
Pressure settings are spoken digit by digit, not as groups of numbers.
Pressure settings are never spoken as whole numbers.
samples.examTip: NINER avoids confusion with the German 'nein'; FIFE avoids confusion with 'fire'.

samples.prompt: Mumbai Approach transmits: "SPICEJET 271, DESCEND TO ALTITUDE 5000 FEET, QNH 1006". The pilot replies "ROGER, SPICEJET 271". Why is this reply unacceptable?
options: Level instructions and QNH must be read back; ROGER is not a readback
ROGER may only be used by ATC, never by pilots
The call sign should come before ROGER in every reply
The pilot should have said AFFIRM, because the instruction is a question
samples.explanation: PANS-ATM lists the items that must be read back, including level instructions, altimeter settings, SSR codes, heading and speed instructions, runway-in-use and new frequencies. A correct reply is "DESCEND ALTITUDE 5000 FEET, QNH 1006, SPICEJET 271". ROGER only says the message was received, so ATC cannot detect a misheard level or QNH.
whyWrong: Both pilots and controllers may say ROGER; it simply cannot replace a readback.
In replies the call sign normally comes at the end; the order is not the problem.
AFFIRM means yes and answers a question; this is an instruction that must be read back.
samples.examTip: Ask: could a mishearing of this item cause an accident? If yes, read it back.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is cleared to climb to an altitude of 12,500 ft. How should the controller say the altitude?
options: FLIGHT LEVEL ONE TWO FIFE
ONE TWO FIFE ZERO ZERO
ONE TWO TOUSAND FIFE HUNDRED
TWELVE THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED
samples.explanation: For whole hundreds and thousands, each digit of the thousands is spoken, followed by TOUSAND, then the hundreds digit and HUNDRED: 12,500 = ONE TWO TOUSAND FIFE HUNDRED. Flight levels are spoken digit by digit after FLIGHT LEVEL (for example FLIGHT LEVEL ONE TWO ZERO).
whyWrong: An altitude on QNH is not a flight level; mixing them causes level busts.
Whole hundreds and thousands are spoken with HUNDRED and TOUSAND, not as five separate digits.
Numbers on RT are not spoken as ordinary words such as 'twelve'.
samples.examTip: 'Altitude' means QNH; 'flight level' means 1013.2 hPa. Never mix them in one readback.

samples.prompt: Consider these statements about standard RT words: 1. AFFIRM means 'yes'. 2. NEGATIVE can mean 'permission not granted'. 3. ROGER is a correct answer to a question that needs a yes or no. 4. I SAY AGAIN is used to repeat for clarity or emphasis. Which are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
samples.explanation: AFFIRM means yes. NEGATIVE means no, permission not granted, that is not correct, or not capable. I SAY AGAIN repeats for clarity or emphasis. ROGER means 'I have received all of your last transmission' and must never be used to answer a question requiring a direct yes or no, or in place of a readback.
whyWrong: Accepts the false statement 3 and leaves out the true statements 1 and 4.
Statement 3 is false: ROGER only confirms receipt; a question needing yes or no is answered AFFIRM or NEGATIVE.
Leaves out statement 2: NEGATIVE means no, permission not granted, that is not correct, or not capable.
samples.examTip: AFFIRM, not AFFIRMATIVE: the short form avoids confusion with NEGATIVE when the start is clipped.

chapters.title: Distress and Urgency Communication Procedures
topics: Distress Message Format — The C-I-P Mnemonic

samples.prompt: What is the difference between a distress and an urgency condition?
options: Distress: grave, imminent danger needing immediate help. Urgency: a safety concern without that need
Distress: any technical failure of the aircraft. Urgency: any illness of a passenger or crew member on board
Distress: a condition that has already caused an accident. Urgency: a condition that might cause one later
Distress: declared only by ATC on the pilot's behalf. Urgency: declared only by the pilot
samples.explanation: Distress (MAYDAY) is a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance. Urgency (PAN PAN) concerns the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of a person on board or in sight, but does not require immediate assistance. Each signal is preferably spoken three times.
whyWrong: The category depends on how grave and immediate the danger is, not on whether it is technical or medical.
Distress exists before any accident; it is the grave and imminent danger that matters.
Either condition is normally declared by the pilot; ATC may act on it but does not choose it.
samples.examTip: The deciding words are 'imminent' and 'immediate assistance'.

samples.prompt: After "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY" and the name of the station addressed, which order of content does ICAO give for the distress message?
options: Position, level and heading; aircraft identification; nature of the distress; intention of the commander
Aircraft identification; position, level and heading; fuel endurance; nature of the distress
Aircraft identification; nature of the distress; intention of the commander; position, level and heading
Nature of the distress; aircraft identification; persons on board; intention of the commander
samples.explanation: Annex 10 Volume II lists the distress message content, as far as possible in this order: the name of the station addressed (when time and circumstances permit); the identification of the aircraft; the nature of the distress condition; the intention of the person in command; and the present position, level and heading. Other useful information, such as persons on board and endurance, may follow.
whyWrong: Position comes last: first the station must know who is calling and what is wrong.
Fuel endurance is optional extra information, and the intention of the commander is missing.
The identification comes before the nature of the distress; persons on board is useful extra information, not a core item.
samples.examTip: Whatever else is wrong, the call sign comes straight after the station addressed.

samples.prompt: An aircraft in distress is being disturbed by other stations on the frequency. Which phrase may the aircraft in distress, or the station controlling the distress traffic, use to impose silence?
options: SEELONCE MAYDAY, ALL STATIONS
PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS STANDBY
BREAK BREAK, RADIO SILENCE, ALL STATIONS
ALL STATIONS, STOP TRANSMITTING, MAYDAY
samples.explanation: Annex 10 allows the station in distress, or the station in control of distress traffic, to impose silence on all stations or on a particular station with STOP TRANSMITTING followed by the distress signal MAYDAY. Other stations must then keep off the frequency until DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED is announced.
whyWrong: SEELONCE is maritime phraseology, not ICAO aeronautical RT.
PAN PAN is the urgency signal and STANDBY asks a station to wait for a call; neither imposes distress silence.
BREAK BREAK separates messages to different aircraft on a busy frequency; it does not impose silence.
samples.examTip: Marine phrases (SEELONCE, MAYDAY RELAY on VHF marine) are not the ICAO aviation answer.

samples.prompt: The station controlling a distress situation is satisfied that the emergency is over. How does it tell the other stations that normal working may resume?
options: It transmits MAYDAY CANCELLED, OUT
It transmits DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED
It transmits SILENCE FINISHED
It transmits RESUME NORMAL OPERATIONS, OVER
samples.explanation: When distress traffic has ceased, the station that controlled it transmits a message on the frequency used, addressed to all stations, including the words DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED. The aircraft itself, once no longer in distress, transmits a message cancelling the distress condition.
whyWrong: Cancelling a distress is done by the aircraft that declared it; the station ending distress traffic uses DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED.
SILENCE FINISHED is maritime wording.
This is not standard phraseology, and OVER would invite a reply from every station.
samples.examTip: Silence is lifted only by DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED; until then keep off the frequency unless assisting.

samples.prompt: A passenger on an Air India A321 has a suspected heart attack and the crew want priority to land at Nagpur, but the aircraft is not in danger. Which signal is correct?
options: PAN PAN MEDICAL, spoken three times
PAN PAN, spoken three times
MAYDAY, spoken three times
SECURITE, spoken three times
samples.explanation: A seriously ill person on board is an urgency condition: the safety of a person on board is affected, but the aircraft does not need immediate assistance. The signal is PAN PAN (preferably three times). PAN PAN MEDICAL (pronounced MAY-DEE-CAL) identifies a protected medical transport, such as a military medical evacuation aircraft, under the 1949 Geneva Conventions.
whyWrong: The MEDICAL signal is reserved for medical transports protected under the Geneva Conventions, not for an ill passenger on a scheduled flight.
The aircraft is not in grave and imminent danger, so this is urgency, not distress.
SECURITE is a maritime safety signal, not used in ICAO aviation RT.
samples.examTip: The word 'medical' in the situation does not mean the MEDICAL signal; ask whether the aircraft is a protected medical transport.

chapters.title: Aeronautical Information Services and Regulations
topics: Message Categories and Priorities in Radiotelephony

samples.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a category of message within the AFTN system?
options: Distress Messages
Urgency Messages
Meteorological Messages
Passenger Manifest Messages
samples.explanation: AFTN message categories (Annex 10 Vol II) are distress, urgency, flight safety, meteorological, flight regularity, aeronautical information services, aeronautical administrative and service messages. Passenger manifests are not an AFTN category.

samples.prompt: A pilot at Mumbai copies ATIS information KILO before calling for clearance. How should the pilot show that the current ATIS has been received?
options: By saying 'INFORMATION KILO' on first contact with the ATC unit
By saying 'ATIS RECEIVED' without naming the letter
By reading the whole ATIS back to Clearance Delivery word for word
By saying nothing: ATC assumes that every aircraft has the latest ATIS
samples.explanation: Each new ATIS message is identified by the next letter of the ICAO alphabet. Pilots acknowledge receipt by quoting the letter on initial contact with approach, tower or ground (for example 'INFORMATION KILO'). If the letter is out of date, ATC passes the changes.
whyWrong: Without the letter ATC cannot tell whether the pilot has the current or an older broadcast.
The ATIS is not read back; naming its letter is enough.
ATC cannot assume it: the letter on first contact is how ATC knows the information is current.
samples.examTip: If ATC says 'INFORMATION LIMA NOW CURRENT', listen to the new broadcast or note the changes given.

samples.prompt: Which item is NOT normally included in a departure ATIS broadcast?
options: Each flight's SSR code
The runway in use
The current transition level
The surface wind and QNH
samples.explanation: ATIS broadcasts information common to all departing or arriving aircraft: aerodrome, letter, time, runway in use, approach or departure procedures, surface wind, visibility, weather, cloud, temperature and dew point, QNH, transition level and significant information. SSR codes are allocated individually in each aircraft's clearance.
whyWrong: The runway in use is a core ATIS item.
The transition level is included in ATIS broadcasts, and must be read back if given.
Surface wind and QNH are always broadcast.
samples.examTip: If an item is different for each aircraft, it cannot be on ATIS.

samples.prompt: What does a VOLMET broadcast provide?
options: Continuous ATC clearances for aircraft that have lost two-way communication
Weather reports and forecasts for a group of aerodromes, for aircraft in flight
A summary of NOTAMs for the flight information region, updated every AIRAC cycle
Departure and arrival information for one aerodrome, including the runway in use and approach type
samples.explanation: VOLMET is a continuous broadcast of meteorological information for aircraft in flight: current reports (METAR/SPECI), aerodrome forecasts (TAF) and SIGMET for a group of aerodromes, on HF or VHF. It lets a crew check the weather at destination and alternates without calling a ground station.
whyWrong: Aircraft with communication failure follow the published failure procedures; no clearances are broadcast for them.
NOTAM summaries are not broadcast by VOLMET; AIRAC concerns planned changes to published information.
