That describes ATIS, which is specific to one aerodrome's arrivals and departures.
samples.examTip: ATIS is one aerodrome's operating information; VOLMET is weather for many aerodromes.

samples.prompt: Which of the following has the HIGHEST priority on the aeronautical mobile service?
options: Flight safety messages
Flight regularity messages
Direction-finding communications
Meteorological messages
samples.explanation: Annex 10 Volume II orders messages as: 1 distress calls, messages and traffic; 2 urgency messages, including medical transports; 3 communications relating to direction finding; 4 flight safety messages; 5 meteorological messages; 6 flight regularity messages. Without distress or urgency in the options, direction finding is highest.
whyWrong: Flight safety messages come after direction-finding communications in the ICAO order.
Flight regularity messages have the lowest priority of the four.
Meteorological messages rank below flight safety messages.
samples.examTip: Direction finding sits just below urgency because it is often used to locate an aircraft in difficulty.

chapters.title: Basic Call Structure and Pre-Flight Checks

samples.prompt: What is the correct order of elements in an initial call (basic call structure)?
options: Who you are, Whom you are calling, Where you are, What is your message
Whom you are calling, Who you are, Where you are, What is your message
Where you are, Whom you are calling, Who you are, What is your message
What is your message, Whom you are calling, Who you are, Where you are
samples.explanation: Doc 9432 sets the initial call order as: station being called, then own call sign, then position, then the message (whom, who, where, what). A reverses the first two elements, while C and D start with position or the message.

samples.prompt: Which call-sign suffix identifies an area control centre?
options: CONTROL
RADIO
INFORMATION
APPROACH
samples.explanation: Ground station call signs combine the location and a suffix for the type of unit: CONTROL (area control centre), APPROACH, ARRIVAL, DEPARTURE, TOWER, GROUND (surface movement control), DELIVERY (clearance delivery), APRON, INFORMATION (FIS), RADIO (aeronautical station). For example, 'DELHI CONTROL' is the area control centre.
whyWrong: RADIO is an aeronautical station, such as an HF station, that is not an ATC unit.
INFORMATION is a flight information service unit.
APPROACH is the approach control unit.
samples.examTip: RADIO is not an ATC unit: it relays messages and provides information, it does not issue its own clearances.

samples.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the ICAO types of aircraft radiotelephony call sign?
options: The operator's telephony designator followed by the last four characters of the registration
The departure aerodrome followed by the flight number
The characters of the aircraft's registration, such as VT-KAX
The operator's telephony designator followed by the flight identification
samples.explanation: Annex 10 Volume II recognises three types of aircraft call sign: (a) the characters of the registration marking; (b) the operator's telephony designator followed by the last four characters of the registration; and (c) the operator's telephony designator followed by the flight identification. A departure aerodrome name is never part of a call sign.
whyWrong: This is the type (b) call sign, used by some operators.
The registration marking is the basic type (a) call sign.
This is the type (c) call sign, for example AIR INDIA 101.
samples.examTip: Location names belong to ground stations, not to aircraft.

samples.prompt: When may a pilot of VT-KAX start using an abbreviated form of the call sign?
options: Only on the ground, never in flight
Whenever the frequency is busy, to save time
Only after the ATC unit has used the abbreviated form first
As soon as the ground station has answered the pilot's first call
samples.explanation: Abbreviated call signs may be used only after satisfactory communication has been established and when no confusion is likely. An aircraft station uses its abbreviated call sign only after it has been addressed that way by the aeronautical station. If there is a similar call sign on the frequency, ATC will keep using the full form.
whyWrong: Abbreviation is permitted in flight and on the ground once ATC has introduced it.
A busy frequency is exactly when confusion is most likely; it does not permit abbreviation.
An answer to the first call is not enough: the ground station must abbreviate first.
samples.examTip: Similar call signs on frequency = full call signs every time.

samples.prompt: IFLY 4521 and IFLY 4512 are both on Mumbai Approach. The pilot of IFLY 4512 hears "IFLY 45.., DESCEND FLIGHT LEVEL 120" with the end of the call sign clipped. What should the pilot do?
options: Ignore the call; ATC will repeat it if it was meant for IFLY 4512
Begin the descent, since the call sign heard was close enough to its own
Read back the descent without a call sign, so that ATC can correct it if wrong
Ask ATC to confirm which aircraft the descent was for before acting on it
samples.explanation: When similar call signs are on the frequency, or a call sign is not fully heard, the pilot must not act on the instruction. The correct action is to ask ATC to confirm, using the full call sign, for example 'MUMBAI APPROACH, IFLY 4512, CONFIRM DESCENT FLIGHT LEVEL 120 WAS FOR IFLY 4512'. ATC may also change one call sign to remove the risk.
whyWrong: Ignoring a possible instruction leaves ATC thinking it has been received; the doubt must be resolved.
Acting on a call sign that may belong to the other aircraft is a classic cause of level busts.
A readback without a call sign leaves ATC unable to tell who is replying, and may be read as acceptance.
samples.examTip: Similar call signs are a known hazard: listen for the full call sign every time.

chapters.title: Ground Operations Pushback, Start-Up, and Taxi
topics: Pushback Request — The First Radio Call
Start-Up Request — The Second Radio Call
Taxi Request — The Third Radio Call

samples.prompt: What information is included in the standard pushback request call?
options: Stand, SCC, POB, Request Push Back, ATIS Info or Wx obtained
Stand, Fuel, Destination, Request Push Back
Stand, Flight Level, Request Push Back
Stand, SCC, Destination, Request Push Back
samples.explanation: The pushback request contains: stand, SCC (security check carried out), POB (persons on board), 'request push back' and the ATIS information letter (or 'Wx obtained'). B, C and D omit POB or the ATIS/weather item.

samples.prompt: Air India 865 is at stand 32 at Delhi with ATIS information FOXTROT. Which start-up request is in the standard form?
options: DELHI GROUND, AIR INDIA 865, STAND 32, REQUEST TAKE-OFF, INFORMATION FOXTROT
DELHI GROUND, AIR INDIA 865, READY TO START ENGINES AT STAND 32
AIR INDIA 865, DELHI GROUND, STAND 32, REQUEST START UP, INFORMATION FOXTROT
DELHI GROUND, AIR INDIA 865, STAND 32, REQUEST START UP, INFORMATION FOXTROT
samples.explanation: A start-up request names the station called, then the aircraft call sign, its location, REQUEST START UP and the ATIS information letter. ATC replies START UP APPROVED, START UP AT (time), or EXPECT START UP AT (time).
whyWrong: TAKE-OFF is used only in a take-off clearance or its cancellation, and start-up is what is wanted.
Not standard: it omits the ATIS letter and uses non-standard wording instead of REQUEST START UP.
The order is reversed: an initial call begins with the station called, then the calling station.
samples.examTip: Check the order first: the station you are calling always comes first in an initial call.

samples.prompt: A Cessna 172, VT-KAX, is told to BACKTRACK runway 09 after entering it at an aerodrome with no parallel taxiway. What does the instruction mean?
options: Leave the runway by the nearest taxiway and wait for instructions
Taxi along the runway in the direction opposite to that of take-off
Hold position on the runway until the traffic behind has landed
Return to the stand, because the take-off clearance has been withdrawn
samples.explanation: BACKTRACK means taxi on the runway in the opposite direction to that in which it will be used, typically on runways without a full-length parallel taxiway, to reach the threshold for take-off. It is a runway instruction, so it must be read back.
whyWrong: Leaving the runway is VACATE, not BACKTRACK.
Holding on the runway is LINE UP AND WAIT or HOLD POSITION, not a backtrack.
A withdrawn clearance is given as an instruction to return or hold, not as BACKTRACK.
samples.examTip: Backtrack is a runway movement: it is always read back.

samples.prompt: Delhi Ground transmits: "SPICEJET 123, TAXI TO HOLDING POINT G1 RUNWAY 27 VIA TAXIWAY E, HOLD SHORT OF RUNWAY 29". Which reply is correct?
options: ROGER, TAXIING TO G1, SPICEJET 123
TAXI HOLDING POINT G1 RUNWAY 27 VIA E, SPICEJET 123
TAXI HOLDING POINT G1 RUNWAY 27 VIA E, HOLDING SHORT RUNWAY 29, SPICEJET 123
WILCO, SPICEJET 123
samples.explanation: Taxi instructions that include a clearance limit and an instruction to hold short of a runway must be read back. PANS-ATM requires readback of instructions to hold short of, enter, cross or backtrack on any runway; the pilot says HOLDING SHORT with the runway designator. Missing hold-short readbacks are a known runway incursion cause.
whyWrong: ROGER does not read back the runway or the hold-short instruction, both of which are mandatory readback items.
Leaves out the hold-short instruction, which is the most safety-critical part of the clearance.
WILCO acknowledges but does not read back; ATC cannot check the clearance limit or the hold short.
samples.examTip: In a long taxi clearance, find the runway items first and make sure they are in the readback.

samples.prompt: After crossing runway 27 as instructed, an aircraft is told to report when clear. What should the pilot report once the whole aircraft is past the runway-holding position on the far side?
options: OFF THE RUNWAY NOW
RUNWAY VACATED
CLEAR OF THE ACTIVE
CROSSING COMPLETE
samples.explanation: The PANS-ATM phraseology is CROSS RUNWAY (number) [REPORT VACATED], and the pilot reports RUNWAY VACATED when the aircraft is entirely clear of the runway, beyond the relevant runway-holding position. Non-standard variations increase the risk of misunderstanding during runway operations.
whyWrong: Not standard, and 'now' adds nothing.
'Active' is not a standard ICAO term and does not name the runway.
Not standard phraseology; ATC listens for the standard words.
samples.examTip: Standard words only near runways: VACATED, HOLDING SHORT, LINING UP.

samples.prompt: A pilot has lined up on the runway and is ready for departure. What is the correct phraseology to inform ATC?
options: "DELHI TOWER AIRINDIA 430, READY FOR TAKEOFF"
"DELHI TOWER AIRINDIA 430, LINED UP RWY 27, READY FOR DEPARTURE"
"DELHI TOWER AIRINDIA 430, REQUEST TAKEOFF CLEARANCE"
"DELHI TOWER AIRINDIA 430, LINED UP, REQUEST IMMEDIATE DEPARTURE"
samples.explanation: A lined-up aircraft reports: 'DELHI TOWER AIRINDIA 430, LINED UP RWY 27, READY FOR DEPARTURE'. A and C misuse the word TAKE-OFF, and D 'immediate departure' is only for asking to expedite, not a routine ready call.

samples.prompt: An aircraft reaches holding point G1 for runway 28 at Delhi and is ready to go. How should the pilot tell Delhi Tower?
options: DELHI TOWER, AIR INDIA 865, REQUEST TAKE-OFF CLEARANCE
DELHI TOWER, AIR INDIA 865, READY FOR TAKE-OFF
DELHI TOWER, AIR INDIA 865, READY TO ROLL RUNWAY 28
DELHI TOWER, AIR INDIA 865, READY FOR DEPARTURE
samples.explanation: To avoid any confusion with a take-off clearance, the word TAKE-OFF is used only when the take-off is cleared or cancelled. At all other times the word DEPARTURE (or AIRBORNE) is used, so a pilot reports READY FOR DEPARTURE.
whyWrong: The pilot does not use the word TAKE-OFF in a request; it is reserved for the clearance itself.
TAKE-OFF is reserved for the take-off clearance and its cancellation, so 'ready for take-off' could be mistaken for one.
'Ready to roll' is not standard phraseology.
samples.examTip: If a pilot's call contains 'take-off', it is wrong phraseology.

samples.prompt: An aircraft has already started its take-off roll when the controller sees a vehicle entering the runway. Which instruction should the controller use?
options: HOLD POSITION, CANCEL TAKE-OFF, I SAY AGAIN, CANCEL TAKE-OFF
ABORT, ABORT, ABORT
STOP IMMEDIATELY, with the call sign repeated
GO AROUND, I SAY AGAIN, GO AROUND
samples.explanation: PANS-ATM gives two cases. Before the take-off roll has begun: HOLD POSITION, CANCEL TAKE-OFF, I SAY AGAIN CANCEL TAKE-OFF, and the pilot replies HOLDING. Once the roll has started: (call sign) STOP IMMEDIATELY, (repeat call sign) STOP IMMEDIATELY, and the pilot replies STOPPING.
whyWrong: HOLD POSITION, CANCEL TAKE-OFF is used before the aircraft has started to roll.
ABORT is not ICAO phraseology for a rejected take-off.
GO AROUND is for an aircraft on approach, not one on the take-off roll.
samples.examTip: The pilot answers HOLDING to a cancellation and STOPPING to STOP IMMEDIATELY.

samples.prompt: Tower transmits: "IFLY 2135, BEHIND THE LANDING A320 ON SHORT FINAL, LINE UP AND WAIT RUNWAY 27, BEHIND". Which readback is correct?
options: WILCO, IFLY 2135
BEHIND THE LANDING A320, LINE UP AND WAIT RUNWAY 27, BEHIND, IFLY 2135
LINE UP AND WAIT RUNWAY 27, IFLY 2135
LINING UP RUNWAY 27 BEHIND, IFLY 2135
samples.explanation: A conditional clearance has the call sign, the condition, the identification of the traffic or vehicle it refers to, the clearance, and a brief repetition of the condition. The pilot reads it all back, including the condition and the traffic, so that both agree which aircraft must pass first.
whyWrong: WILCO does not read back the runway or the condition.
Leaves out the condition; a conditional clearance must be read back with its condition.
Omits the identification of the traffic the condition refers to, so ATC cannot tell the right aircraft has been seen.
samples.examTip: Say the condition first in the readback, just as ATC did.

samples.prompt: When may ATC issue a conditional clearance affecting the active runway?
options: Only when surface movement radar is in operation and shows the traffic concerned
At any time, provided the pilot reads back the condition correctly
Only when both the controller and the pilot can see the traffic in the condition
Only at night, when the other traffic can be identified clearly by its navigation lights
samples.explanation: PANS-ATM permits conditional phrases such as 'behind landing aircraft' for movements affecting the active runway only when the aircraft or vehicles concerned are seen by the appropriate controller and pilot. If either cannot see the traffic, misidentification could lead to a runway incursion.
whyWrong: Surface radar does not replace visual identification of the traffic by both parties.
A correct readback is needed, but it does not remove the need for both to see the traffic.
Conditional clearances are not limited to night; the requirement is that the traffic is seen.
samples.examTip: If you cannot see the traffic named in the condition, say so; do not accept the clearance.

chapters.title: In-Flight Emergencies and Abnormal Situations
topics: 9.2.3 Termination of Distress and Silence — The "All Clear"

samples.prompt: After a rapid decompression, the crew of a jet start an emergency descent. Which SSR code may they select to indicate an emergency, if no other code has been assigned for it?
samples.explanation: Mode A code 7700 indicates an emergency. 7600 indicates radio failure and 7500 unlawful interference. If ATC has already assigned a code and is working the aircraft, the crew may keep it, but 7700 makes the emergency visible to every radar unit.
whyWrong: 7500 indicates unlawful interference.
7600 indicates a radio communication failure.
2000 is used when no code has been assigned, for example entering SSR airspace from areas without it.
samples.examTip: Dial carefully: passing through 7500 or 7600 while setting 7700 can give a false alert.

samples.prompt: An A320 inbound to Mumbai is committed to land there. Any change to its clearance could make it land with less than the planned final reserve fuel, but no emergency yet exists. What should the crew tell ATC?
options: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL
MINIMUM FUEL
REQUEST PRIORITY, LOW FUEL
PAN PAN, FUEL SHORTAGE
samples.explanation: Annex 6 requires the pilot to advise MINIMUM FUEL when committed to land at a specific aerodrome and any change to the existing clearance may result in landing with less than the planned final reserve fuel. It is not an emergency and does not give priority; it warns ATC that a fuel emergency is possible if there are further delays.
whyWrong: MAYDAY FUEL is for the point where the fuel expected on landing is below the planned final reserve.
Non-standard phrasing: it does not give ATC the defined meaning of MINIMUM FUEL.
PAN PAN is not the ICAO phrase for this fuel state; MINIMUM FUEL is defined for exactly this case.
samples.examTip: MINIMUM FUEL is a warning; MAYDAY FUEL is the emergency.

samples.prompt: During a climb, an Air India A321 receives a TCAS resolution advisory (RA). What should the pilot transmit as soon as workload permits?
options: MAYDAY, TCAS RA, CLIMBING
TCAS RA
REQUEST DEVIATION FOR TRAFFIC
PAN PAN, TRAFFIC ALERT
samples.explanation: PANS-ATM phraseology: the pilot reports '(call sign) TCAS RA' as soon as possible after starting the manoeuvre. ATC then stops issuing instructions to that aircraft until the pilot reports 'CLEAR OF CONFLICT, RETURNING TO (assigned clearance)' or '(assigned clearance) RESUMED'.
whyWrong: An RA is not a distress situation; MAYDAY is not used.
The pilot follows the RA at once; there is no request, only a report.
PAN PAN is not used, and 'traffic alert' describes a TA, not an RA.
samples.examTip: Fly the RA first, then report; never manoeuvre against an RA.

samples.prompt: Holding at Delhi, the crew calculate that the usable fuel on landing at the nearest suitable aerodrome will be less than the planned final reserve fuel. What must the crew do?
options: Declare a fuel emergency by broadcasting MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL
Squawk 7600 and divert without a clearance
Request priority without declaring an emergency
Advise MINIMUM FUEL and continue holding until ATC gives an onward clearance
samples.explanation: Annex 6 requires the pilot-in-command to declare a situation of fuel emergency by broadcasting MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL when the calculated usable fuel predicted to be available on landing at the nearest aerodrome where a safe landing can be made is less than the planned final reserve fuel.
whyWrong: 7600 is the communication failure code; the crew's radio still works and must be used.
When the final reserve is predicted to be used, the rule requires a MAYDAY, not an informal request.
MINIMUM FUEL is for the earlier stage, before the final reserve is predicted to be used.
samples.examTip: Final reserve is the dividing line: protecting it is MINIMUM FUEL, using it is MAYDAY FUEL.

samples.prompt: An aircraft is following a TCAS 'climb' RA when ATC, unaware of it, instructs a descent. What should the pilot reply?
options: WILCO, DESCENDING
UNABLE, TCAS RA
STANDBY, TCAS
NEGATIVE, CLIMBING FOR TRAFFIC
samples.explanation: When an ATC instruction conflicts with an RA, the pilot follows the RA and tells ATC 'UNABLE, TCAS RA'. Once clear, the pilot reports CLEAR OF CONFLICT and returns to the assigned clearance.
whyWrong: Complying with an ATC instruction opposite to the RA could cause a collision; the RA takes precedence.
STANDBY leaves ATC thinking the descent may follow; the pilot must say clearly that it cannot.
Not the standard reply; UNABLE, TCAS RA is the defined phrase.
samples.examTip: RA beats ATC every time during the encounter.

samples.prompt: When an aircraft station fails to establish contact with the aeronautical station on the designated frequency, what is the FIRST action it shall take?
options: Transmit the message twice on the designated frequency preceded by "TRANSMITTING BLIND"
Attempt to establish contact on another frequency appropriate to the route
Select SSR code 7600 immediately
Proceed to the nearest suitable aerodrome
samples.explanation: If an aircraft cannot make contact on the designated frequency, it first tries another frequency appropriate to the route, or other aircraft or aeronautical stations (Annex 10 Vol II). Blind transmission comes only after these attempts fail, 7600 is for airborne radio equipment failure, and diverting to the nearest aerodrome is the VFR RCF procedure.

samples.prompt: A VFR aircraft in the Bhubaneswar circuit has lost its radio. Tower shows it a steady red light. What does this mean?
options: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
Return for landing; clearance to land will follow
Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
samples.explanation: Annex 2 light signals to aircraft in flight: steady green, cleared to land; steady red, give way to other aircraft and continue circling; series of green flashes, return for landing; series of red flashes, aerodrome unsafe, do not land; series of white flashes, land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron; red pyrotechnic, notwithstanding any previous instructions, do not land for the time being.
whyWrong: 'Land and proceed to the apron' is a series of white flashes.
'Return for landing' is a series of green flashes.
'Aerodrome unsafe, do not land' is a series of red flashes.
samples.examTip: Steady red in flight never means 'divert'; that is the flashing red.

samples.prompt: An aircraft's VHF receiver has failed, but the crew believe the transmitter still works. How should they make their reports?
options: Make no transmissions at all, because ATC cannot reply and the calls would only block the frequency
Prefix TRANSMITTING BLIND DUE TO RECEIVER FAILURE, send each message twice, give the next call time
Send each message once, preceded by RADIO CHECK, and wait for a reply
Transmit only on 121.5 MHz with the words MAYDAY, RADIO FAILURE
samples.explanation: Annex 10 Volume II: when an aircraft station is unable to establish communication because of receiver failure, it transmits reports at the scheduled times or positions on the channel in use, preceded by TRANSMITTING BLIND DUE TO RECEIVER FAILURE. It transmits the message, follows it with a complete repetition, and also gives the time of its next intended transmission.
whyWrong: The transmitter may work, so reports should still be made blind; ATC and other aircraft can then act on them.
No reply can be heard with a failed receiver; the message is repeated in full instead.
A receiver failure alone is not distress; messages are transmitted blind on the channel in use.
samples.examTip: Set 7600 as well, so radar units know about the failure.

samples.prompt: An aircraft on the ground at Jaipur, with radio failure, receives a series of green flashes from the tower. What does this mean, and how does the pilot acknowledge by day?
options: Cleared to taxi; acknowledge by moving the ailerons or the rudder
Return to the starting point; acknowledge by rocking the wings
Stop; acknowledge by switching the navigation lights on and off twice
Cleared for take-off; acknowledge by flashing the landing lights twice
samples.explanation: Light signals to aircraft on the ground: series of green flashes, cleared to taxi; steady green, cleared for take-off; steady red, stop; series of red flashes, taxi clear of the landing area in use; series of white flashes, return to the starting point. By day, an aircraft on the ground acknowledges by moving its ailerons or rudder; by night, by flashing its landing lights or navigation lights twice.
whyWrong: Return to the starting point is a series of white flashes, and rocking the wings is an in-flight acknowledgement.
Stop is a steady red; switching navigation lights is a night acknowledgement.
Cleared for take-off is a steady green to an aircraft on the ground; flashing lights is a night acknowledgement.
samples.examTip: Ground acknowledgements use the controls by day and the lights by night.

samples.prompt: An IFR flight with radio failure is in IMC in airspace where an ATS surveillance system is in use. Unless a regional procedure says otherwise, what should it do with its level and speed?
options: Keep the last assigned speed and level (or minimum flight altitude if higher) for 7 min, then flight plan
Descend to the minimum flight altitude and land at the nearest aerodrome
Keep the last assigned speed and level (or minimum flight altitude if higher) for 20 min, then flight plan
Climb at once to the flight-planned level and continue along the route at the planned cruising speed
samples.explanation: ICAO procedures for IFR communication failure in IMC: maintain the last assigned speed and level, or the minimum flight altitude if higher, for 20 minutes after failing to report at a compulsory reporting point where procedural separation is applied, or for 7 minutes where an ATS surveillance system is used. The 7 minutes run from the latest of reaching the last assigned level or minimum flight altitude, setting 7600, or failing to report at a compulsory point. The aircraft then adjusts level and speed in accordance with the filed flight plan.
whyWrong: Leaving the route and descending would be unpredictable for ATC; in IMC the aircraft continues to its destination.
20 minutes applies where procedural separation is used, not where an ATS surveillance system is used.
Changing level at once could take the aircraft into the path of traffic that ATC has not yet moved.
samples.examTip: Surveillance = 7 min; procedural = 20 min. Squawk 7600 throughout.
